options: It loses many customers because comparable alternatives limit its pricing discretion.
It keeps most customers because many sellers guarantee each store a loyal share.
It raises the market price because one seller’s posted price defines equilibrium.
It forces rival prices down because customers cannot compare standardized products.
q.commonError: Assuming a small firm can raise price without losing demand.
q.feedback: Independent rivals, a standardized good and easy comparison make close alternatives available. An individual store has little ability to sustain an above-market price.

key: It loses many customers because comparable alternatives limit its pricing discretion.

q.q: An economist points to a wheat farmer selling at the going market price. Why is the farmer a price taker?
options: The farmer's individual output is too small to control the market price
The farmer legally sets the national wheat price
The farmer faces no competitors
The farmer can ignore supply and demand
q.feedback: A price taker accepts the market price because no single seller has enough influence to set it.

key: The farmer's individual output is too small to control the market price

q.q: A market has many buyers but only one seller, and that seller has control over price. Is this a competitive market?
options: No, because one seller has market power
Yes, because many buyers are enough
Yes, because all markets are competitive
No, because buyers never matter
q.feedback: A competitive market requires many buyers and sellers, with no single participant controlling price.

key: No, because one seller has market power

q.q: Which seller is most clearly a price taker?
options: A patented-drug producer.
A small grain farmer selling a standardized crop at a market quotation.
A sole local utility.
A platform with locked-in users.
q.commonError: Misidentifying the conditions that limit market power.
q.feedback: A small grain farmer supplies a tiny share of a standardized market. Buyers can turn to other farmers, so this farmer generally accepts the quoted market price.

key: A small grain farmer selling a standardized crop at a market quotation.

q.q: What makes sustained economic profit difficult in a competitive market?
options: A single seller restricts output.
Buyers face high switching costs.
Entry by new firms expands supply.
Products become more unique.
q.commonError: Misidentifying the conditions that limit market power.
q.feedback: Entry adds market supply when existing firms earn economic profit. The resulting competitive pressure makes that profit harder to sustain.

key: Entry by new firms expands supply.

q.q: A market has many buyers and sellers and standardized products. What does this imply about an individual seller’s ability to set price?
options: Each seller controls market demand.
Each seller can raise price without losing sales.
Buyers cannot compare offers.
An individual seller faces strong pressure to accept the market price.
q.commonError: Misidentifying the conditions that limit market power.
q.feedback: With many sellers offering standardized products, buyers can switch to competing offers. An individual seller therefore has little scope to charge above the market price.

key: An individual seller faces strong pressure to accept the market price.

q.q: An online marketplace makes prices easy to compare and lets buyers switch with one click. This tends to:
options: Create a monopoly automatically.
Make demand for every seller inelastic.
Reduce each seller’s ability to charge above rivals.
Eliminate all production costs.
q.commonError: Failing to apply competition logic to digital markets.
q.feedback: Transparent prices and low switching costs constrain seller pricing power.

key: Reduce each seller’s ability to charge above rivals.

q.q: A price-taking seller is one that:
options: Sets any price without losing customers.
Controls the total market supply.
Cannot noticeably affect the market price by changing its own output.
Faces no competitors.
q.feedback: A price taker is too small relative to the market to influence the market price.

key: Cannot noticeably affect the market price by changing its own output.

q.q: Which feature most supports a competitive market?
options: One dominant seller.
Legal barriers blocking entry.
A unique product with no substitutes.
Many buyers and sellers with no single participant controlling price.
q.commonError: Using the everyday meaning of rivalry instead of the market structure.
q.feedback: Competitive markets disperse market power among many participants.

key: Many buyers and sellers with no single participant controlling price.

q.q: Which observation most strongly contradicts the strict competitive-market model?
options: A firm can raise price persistently without losing many customers.
A firm earns accounting profit in one month.
Market demand changes over time.
Some firms have different bookkeeping methods.
q.commonError: Using temporary profit as conclusive evidence of market power.
q.feedback: Persistent price discretion indicates a downward-sloping firm demand curve rather than price taking.

key: A firm can raise price persistently without losing many customers.

q.q: A market has free entry but strong network effects favor the largest platform. What is the best conclusion?
options: Legal freedom to enter makes the incumbent face perfectly elastic demand despite its user network.
Formal entry may be easy while effective competition remains weak.
Network effects remove the incumbent’s advantage because every entrant can start with an equally valuable user network.
The incumbent’s user advantage implies formal entry is restricted, so the premise of free entry cannot hold.
q.commonError: Equating legal permission to enter with practical competitive viability.
q.feedback: Permission to enter does not ensure that a new platform can attract enough users to compete effectively. When a platform becomes more valuable as its user base grows, the incumbent’s network can be an entry obstacle even without legal restrictions. That advantage does not establish perfectly elastic demand or equal starting networks.

key: Formal entry may be easy while effective competition remains weak.

q.q: A restaurant market has many sellers, but each offers a differentiated experience. Which statement is best?
options: The market may be competitive in a broad sense without meeting the strict price-taking benchmark.
The large number of restaurants makes each a price taker despite customers’ preferences for particular experiences.
Differentiation gives each restaurant the pricing freedom of a sole supplier because other dining experiences are distinct.
Competition should be assessed only through price differences, since differences in service quality do not affect buyer choice.
q.commonError: Treating market structures as all-or-nothing labels.
q.feedback: Many restaurants can compete for customers even when differentiated experiences give individual sellers some price discretion. Differentiation means the strict identical-product price-taking benchmark need not hold, but competing restaurants can still constrain each other’s prices.

key: The market may be competitive in a broad sense without meeting the strict price-taking benchmark.

q.q: A firm in a competitive market raises price above the market price while rivals do not. The likely result is:
options: Higher sales because price signals quality.
A sharp loss of customers to close substitutes.
No change because buyers cannot switch.
Automatic market-wide inflation.
q.commonError: Assuming a small firm can raise price without losing demand.
q.feedback: Buyers can switch to other sellers offering the same or similar product.

key: A sharp loss of customers to close substitutes.

q.q: A licensing rule sharply limits new sellers. What is the most direct competitive effect?
options: The rule guarantees lower prices.
The rule creates perfect information.
Reduced entry can increase the market power of existing sellers.
The rule makes every firm a price taker.
q.commonError: Ignoring how entry barriers protect incumbents.
q.feedback: Barriers can weaken competitive pressure and preserve market power.

key: Reduced entry can increase the market power of existing sellers.

q.q: A market has many sellers, but buyers face high search costs and cannot compare prices. Why might price-taking be weakened?
options: Many sellers always eliminate market power.
High search costs strengthen competition by making buyers compare prices more carefully.
Price comparison is unrelated to competition.
Information frictions can give individual sellers some pricing discretion.
q.commonError: Assuming seller count alone determines competitiveness.
q.feedback: Competition also depends on buyer information and ability to switch.

key: Information frictions can give individual sellers some pricing discretion.

q.q: Two exchanges each list hundreds of sellers of standardized grain. On X, buyers can immediately compare prices and switch suppliers. On Y, contracts impose large switching charges. Which claim best separates seller count from effective competition?
options: An individual seller likely has less pricing discretion on Y because switching charges protect buyer choice.
The same seller count ensures equal pricing discretion even when switching costs differ.
An individual seller likely has less pricing discretion on X because buyers can readily use competing offers.
Standardization gives each seller a unique product, preventing price taking on either exchange.
q.commonError: Listing many traders without explaining why individual price control is limited.
q.feedback: Many sellers support competition when buyers can substitute among their offers. Price transparency and low switching costs on X make an individual price increase harder to sustain. Seller count alone does not establish equal competitive pressure.

key: An individual seller likely has less pricing discretion on X because buyers can readily use competing offers.

q.q: A market appears fragmented by seller count, but four firms own most capacity through subsidiaries. What should an analyst examine?
options: Only the number of storefronts.
Whether prices are written in dollars.
Whether consumers enjoy variety.
Control of effective output rather than the number of brand names.
q.commonError: Counting labels instead of economic control.
q.feedback: Competitive pressure depends on independent control of capacity and decisions.

key: Control of effective output rather than the number of brand names.

q.q: A new technology lowers switching costs to nearly zero. Holding other factors constant, what competitive effect is most likely?
options: Sellers face more elastic demand and less pricing discretion.
Sellers gain more market power.
Entry becomes legally impossible.
Market demand becomes perfectly inelastic.
q.commonError: Reversing the effect of easier switching.
q.feedback: When customers can switch easily, a price increase causes a larger loss of buyers.

key: Sellers face more elastic demand and less pricing discretion.

q.q: A wheat farmer sells at the posted market price because charging more would cause buyers to switch. This illustrates:
options: Price-taking behavior.
Monopoly pricing.
A binding price floor.
Perfect price discrimination.
q.commonError: Treating any chosen price as market power.
q.feedback: The farmer accepts the market price because close substitutes are readily available.

key: Price-taking behavior.

q.q: If one small seller exits a highly competitive market, the market price usually changes little because:
options: Demand becomes perfectly vertical.
The seller represents a tiny share of total market supply.
The seller owns a patent.
All remaining sellers coordinate prices.
q.commonError: Overstating the influence of one small firm.
q.feedback: A small participant has little effect on total market supply.

key: The seller represents a tiny share of total market supply.

q.q: Which change would make a market less competitive?
options: More firms entering.
Lower switching costs for buyers.
A merger that leaves one firm with substantial control over output.
Better price information.
q.feedback: Concentration can give firms greater ability to influence price.

key: A merger that leaves one firm with substantial control over output.

q.q: Why does easy entry matter in a competitive market?
options: Economic profits attract new sellers, reducing market supply as existing firms divide sales among more rivals.
Economic profits attract new sellers, lowering each entrant’s costs until all firms share the same cost curve.
Economic profits attract new sellers, raising market demand as buyers redistribute purchases among rivals.
Economic profits attract new sellers, increasing competition and making those profits harder to sustain.
q.commonError: Ignoring how entry responds to profit opportunities.
q.feedback: Profit opportunities attract entrants when entry is easy. Their additional supply puts downward pressure on price and economic profits. Redistributing sales does not itself increase market demand, and entry does not make firms’ production costs identical.

key: Economic profits attract new sellers, increasing competition and making those profits harder to sustain.

q.q: A price taker is a seller that:
options: Accepts the market price because its own output is too small to move it.
Sets the market price for all firms.
Has no production costs.
Faces no buyers.
q.feedback: Price takers choose output but cannot materially influence the market price.

key: Accepts the market price because its own output is too small to move it.

q.q: A market becomes more competitive when:
options: One seller acquires rivals.
Entry and switching become easier.
Products lose all substitutes.
Buyers receive less price information.
q.commonError: Reversing the effects of entry and switching costs.
q.feedback: Easier entry and switching strengthen competitive pressure.

key: Entry and switching become easier.

q.q: Which event shifts demand?
options: Consumer income changes
The good's own price changes
Quantity supplied changes
There is movement along the demand curve.
q.feedback: Income is a demand shifter. The good's own price causes movement along demand.

key: Consumer income changes

q.q: If consumer income rises and tablets are a normal good, what happens?
options: Demand for tablets increases
Quantity demanded falls
Supply of tablets increases
Demand for tablets decreases
q.feedback: For a normal good, higher income increases demand.

key: Demand for tablets increases

q.q: Consumers expect the price of laptops to rise next month, so they buy more laptops today. What happens today?
options: Current demand increases
Current quantity demanded falls
Supply decreases
Demand stays fixed because only current price matters
q.feedback: Expectations about future prices can shift current demand.

key: Current demand increases

q.q: A recession lowers consumer income. If restaurant meals are a normal good, what happens to demand for restaurant meals?
options: Demand decreases
Demand increases
Quantity demanded increases because price changed
Supply increases
q.feedback: For a normal good, lower income decreases demand.

key: Demand decreases

q.q: The law of demand says that, other things equal:
options: As price falls, quantity demanded rises
As price falls, demand always shifts left
As price rises, supply shifts left
As price rises, quantity demanded rises
q.feedback: The law of demand says price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions.

key: As price falls, quantity demanded rises

q.q: When the price of a good falls, what happens to quantity demanded?
options: Quantity demanded increases
Demand decreases
Supply increases
The demand curve shifts left
q.feedback: A change in the good's own price causes movement along the demand curve.

key: Quantity demanded increases

q.q: A change in which factor would shift the demand curve?
options: Consumer income
The good's own price
Movement along the curve
Quantity supplied
q.feedback: Income is a demand shifter. The good's own price changes quantity demanded.

key: Consumer income

q.q: If income rises and tablets are a normal good, what happens to demand for tablets?
options: Demand increases
Demand decreases
Quantity demanded decreases because price changed
Supply decreases
q.feedback: For a normal good, higher income increases demand.

key: Demand increases

q.q: Two goods are substitutes when:
options: One good can be used in place of the other
The goods are typically consumed together
The goods use the same raw material in production
A price change for one good leaves demand for the other unrelated
q.feedback: Substitutes are goods that can replace one another.

key: One good can be used in place of the other

q.q: Two goods are complements when:
options: They are commonly used together
One good can be used in place of the other
The goods are produced using the same inputs
A price change for one good leaves demand for the other unchanged.
q.feedback: Complements are goods used together.

key: They are commonly used together

q.q: If the price of a substitute for iPhones falls, what happens to demand for iPhones?
options: Demand for iPhones decreases
Demand for iPhones increases
Supply of iPhones increases
Quantity demanded of iPhones increases because iPhone price fell
q.feedback: If a substitute gets cheaper, buyers shift away from the original good.

key: Demand for iPhones decreases

q.q: If the price of printer ink rises, what likely happens to demand for printers?
options: Demand for printers decreases
Demand for printers increases
Supply of printers increases
Quantity supplied of printers increases
q.feedback: Printers and ink are complements, so higher ink prices reduce demand for printers.

key: Demand for printers decreases

q.q: A product gets cheaper because supply increases. Students say demand increased because quantity sold rose. What is the error?
options: They confused an increase in quantity demanded with an increase in demand
They correctly identified a demand shift
They confused a price floor with a price ceiling
They ignored that supply can never change price
q.feedback: If price falls because supply increases, buyers move along the demand curve. Quantity demanded rises, but demand itself does not shift.

key: They confused an increase in quantity demanded with an increase in demand

q.q: A product becomes cheaper and sales rise. A follow-up survey finds that buyers now want more at EVERY unchanged price after a favorable health report. A student attributes all extra purchases to movement along the old demand curve. Which correction uses the survey evidence?
options: Demand is unchanged; every increase in sales is a movement along demand.
Demand shifts left; lower prices mean buyers want less at each fixed price.
Supply must shift left; buyer surveys establish producers’ costs.
Demand shifts right; the price change alone cannot explain greater planned purchases at a fixed price.
q.feedback: Unlike a supply-driven price fall alone, the survey reports greater demand at fixed prices after new health information. That identifies a demand shift, although the survey alone does not determine the separate supply change or how much of observed sales growth each cause explains.

key: Demand shifts right; the price change alone cannot explain greater planned purchases at a fixed price.

q.q: The price of headphones falls from $80 to $60, and consumers buy more headphones. What is the most precise statement?
options: Quantity demanded increases
Demand increases
Supply increases
Demand shifts right
q.feedback: A change in the good's own price causes movement along demand, so quantity demanded changes.

key: Quantity demanded increases

q.q: A consumer's income rises, and meal delivery is a normal good. At every price, consumers now want more meal delivery. What happened?
options: Demand increased
Quantity demanded increased because price fell
Supply increased
Demand decreased
q.feedback: Income is a demand shifter. For a normal good, higher income increases demand.

key: Demand increased

q.q: The price of peanut butter rises. If jelly is a complement, what happens in the jelly market?
options: Demand for jelly decreases
Demand for jelly increases
Supply of jelly decreases
Quantity demanded of jelly increases
q.feedback: Peanut butter and jelly are complements. If peanut butter gets more expensive, demand for jelly falls.

key: Demand for jelly decreases

q.q: The price of bus rides rises. If subway rides are substitutes, what happens in the subway market?
options: Demand for subway rides increases
Demand for subway rides decreases
Supply of subway rides decreases
Quantity supplied of bus rides increases
q.feedback: When the price of a substitute rises, demand for the other good increases.

key: Demand for subway rides increases

q.q: Consumers expect the price of coffee to fall next month. What happens to current demand for coffee, other things equal?
options: Current demand decreases
Current demand increases
Current quantity supplied increases
Supply shifts left
q.feedback: If buyers expect a lower future price, they delay purchases, reducing current demand.

key: Current demand decreases

q.q: Refer to the graph. The price of a substitute rises, shifting demand from D1 to D2 while supply remains S1. Which chain of graph evidence explains the resulting equilibrium change?
options: Demand shifts right; equilibrium moves from P2, Q1 to P3, Q2, so both price and quantity rise
Demand shifts left; equilibrium moves from P3, Q2 to P2, Q1, so both price and quantity fall
Supply shifts right; equilibrium moves from P2, Q1 to P1, Q2, so price falls as quantity rises
Supply shifts left; equilibrium moves from P2, Q3 to P3, Q2, so price rises as quantity falls
q.feedback: The higher substitute price increases demand. With supply fixed at S1, the graph moves from the D1/S1 intersection at P2, Q1 to the D2/S1 intersection at P3, Q2.

key: Demand shifts right; equilibrium moves from P2, Q1 to P3, Q2, so both price and quantity rise

q.q: Refer to the graph. A close substitute becomes cheaper, reducing demand from D2 to D1 while supply remains S2. Which explanation correctly traces the change in equilibrium?
options: Demand shifts left; equilibrium moves from P2, Q3 to P1, Q2, reducing both price and quantity
Demand shifts right; equilibrium moves from P1, Q2 to P2, Q3, increasing both price and quantity
Supply shifts left; equilibrium moves from P2, Q3 to P3, Q2, increasing price and reducing quantity
Supply shifts right; equilibrium moves from P3, Q2 to P2, Q3, reducing price and increasing quantity
q.feedback: A cheaper substitute reduces demand for this good. With S2 unchanged, the equilibrium moves from D2/S2 at P2, Q3 to D1/S2 at P1, Q2.

key: Demand shifts left; equilibrium moves from P2, Q3 to P1, Q2, reducing both price and quantity

q.q: Refer to the supply and demand graph with D1, D2, S1, and S2. Which comparison best captures the difference between moving from D1 to D2 and moving along D1?
options: D1 to D2 is a demand shift; movement along D1 is a quantity demanded change
D1 to D2 is a quantity demanded change; movement along D1 is a demand shift
D1 to D2 is a supply shift; movement along D1 is a supply decrease
D1 to D2 is a price ceiling; movement along D1 is a price floor
q.feedback: A non-price determinant shifts demand; a price change causes movement along a demand curve.

key: D1 to D2 is a demand shift; movement along D1 is a quantity demanded change

q.q: The price of tablets falls, and consumers buy more tablets. No non-price determinant changed. What happened?
options: Quantity demanded increased along the existing demand curve.
Demand increased and the curve shifted right
Supply increased and the curve shifted right
Demand decreased because price fell
q.feedback: A change in the good's own price causes movement along demand, not a demand shift.

key: Quantity demanded increased along the existing demand curve.

q.q: The price of a substitute for coffee rises. What happens in the coffee market, holding other factors constant?
options: Demand for coffee increases, raising equilibrium price and quantity
Quantity demanded of coffee decreases along the same curve
Supply of coffee increases because coffee is now profitable
Demand for coffee decreases because substitutes are now expensive
q.feedback: When a substitute becomes more expensive, demand for the original good rises.

key: Demand for coffee increases, raising equilibrium price and quantity

q.q: The price of peanut butter falls. What happens to the demand for jelly, assuming they are complements?
options: Demand for jelly increases
Quantity demanded of jelly falls along the same curve
Supply of jelly decreases
Demand for jelly decreases because peanut butter is cheaper
q.feedback: A lower price for a complement increases demand for the related good.

key: Demand for jelly increases

q.q: A student says, 'Demand increased because the price rose.' What is the correct response?
options: A demand increase can raise price; a price rise alone moves along demand.
That is correct because demand always means the current price
That describes a supply increase
That proves the good is inferior
q.feedback: A price rise can be caused by a demand increase, but the price rise itself does not shift demand.

key: A demand increase can raise price; a price rise alone moves along demand.

q.q: Streaming subscriptions are normal goods. Incomes rise, a rival streaming service lowers its price, and broadband needed for both services becomes more expensive. A manager credits income alone for rising subscriptions. Which inference is defensible?
options: Income and the rival-price cut push demand right; broadband cost changes supply, so observed growth isolates the two demand effects.
Income pushes demand right; rival-price and broadband-cost changes push left, so observed growth need not measure the income effect alone.
Income pushes demand left; the rival-price cut and broadband cost push right, so observed growth rules out normal-good status.
All three changes push demand right; an unchanged subscription price would show that subscriptions rose along the old demand curve.
q.feedback: Income raises normal-good demand. A cheaper substitute and a dearer complement reduce it. Observed growth is the net result and cannot identify the isolated income effect; a fixed own price does not prevent a demand shift.

key: Income pushes demand right; rival-price and broadband-cost changes push left, so observed growth need not measure the income effect alone.

q.q: Tea and coffee are substitutes. Coffee prices rise while consumer income falls, and tea is a normal good. What can be concluded about tea demand without knowing effect sizes?
options: Tea demand rises because the substitute-price effect is larger than the income effect
Tea demand falls because the income effect is larger than the substitute-price effect
The direction of the tea-demand shift is ambiguous
Tea demand is unchanged because tea's own price did not change
q.commonError: Assuming one of two opposing demand shifters must dominate.
q.feedback: The higher coffee price raises demand for tea, while lower income reduces demand for tea because it is normal. Without relative effect sizes, the net shift cannot be determined.

key: The direction of the tea-demand shift is ambiguous

q.q: A market survey shows that at every possible price consumers now plan to buy more electric bikes than before. Which event cannot explain the change?
options: A subsidy to buyers
A rise in gasoline prices
A fall in the price of electric bikes itself
Stronger preferences for low-emission travel
q.feedback: A change in the good’s own price causes movement along demand, not a shift of the entire demand curve.

key: A fall in the price of electric bikes itself

q.q: The price of streaming subscriptions rises, and consumers buy fewer subscriptions. What happened?
options: Quantity demanded decreased
Demand decreased
Supply increased
Demand shifted right
q.feedback: A change in the good's own price changes quantity demanded, not demand.

key: Quantity demanded decreased

q.q: Consumers expect laptop prices to rise next month, so more laptops are purchased today. What happens to current demand for laptops?
options: Demand increases
Quantity demanded decreases
Supply decreases
Demand stays fixed because only current price matters
q.feedback: Expectations about higher future prices can increase demand today.

key: Demand increases

q.q: A popular celebrity endorsement makes more buyers want a product at every price. What happens?
options: Demand shifts right
Quantity demanded falls
Supply shifts left
The product's own price changed
q.feedback: A change in tastes shifts demand; more buyers wanting the product shifts demand right.

key: Demand shifts right

q.q: The price of tablets rises. What happens in the market for tablet cases, a complement?
options: Demand for tablet cases decreases
Demand for tablet cases increases
Supply of tablet cases increases
Quantity supplied of tablets decreases
q.feedback: If tablets become more expensive, fewer tablets are bought, reducing demand for tablet cases.

key: Demand for tablet cases decreases

q.q: The price of tea rises. If coffee is a substitute for tea, what happens to demand for coffee?
options: Demand for coffee increases
Demand for coffee decreases
Quantity demanded of coffee decreases because coffee price changed
Supply of coffee decreases
q.feedback: When a substitute becomes more expensive, demand for the other good rises.

key: Demand for coffee increases

q.q: A new health report says blueberries are especially beneficial. What likely happens in the blueberry market?
options: Demand increases, price rises, and quantity rises
Supply decreases, price rises, and quantity falls
Demand decreases, price falls, and quantity falls
Quantity supplied falls because demand rose
q.feedback: A favorable taste or information change increases demand, raising price and quantity.

key: Demand increases, price rises, and quantity rises

q.q: Refer to the supply and demand graph. If demand shifts from D1 to D2 while supply remains at S2, what happens to equilibrium price and quantity?
options: Price rises and quantity rises
Price falls and quantity falls
Price rises and quantity falls
Price falls and quantity rises
q.feedback: Moving from D1 with S2 to D2 with S2 raises equilibrium price from P1 to P2 and raises equilibrium quantity from Q2 to Q3.

key: Price rises and quantity rises

q.q: Refer to the graph. Consumer income rises for a normal good while production conditions remain unchanged. Which equilibrium movement provides evidence of the resulting demand change?
options: From P1, Q2 to P2, Q3 along S2, showing demand shifts right from D1 to D2
From P2, Q1 to P1, Q2 along D1, showing supply shifts right from S1 to S2
From P3, Q2 to P2, Q3 along D2, showing supply shifts right from S1 to S2
From P2, Q3 to P1, Q2 along S2, showing demand shifts left from D2 to D1
q.feedback: Higher income raises demand for a normal good. With supply fixed at S2, the equilibrium moves along S2 from D1/S2 at P1, Q2 to D2/S2 at P2, Q3.

key: From P1, Q2 to P2, Q3 along S2, showing demand shifts right from D1 to D2

q.q: A shop cuts a product’s price and sells more. A separate survey finds the quantity buyers want at every fixed price is unchanged. Which account fits both observations?
options: Movement down the same curve; unchanged fixed-price plans provide no evidence of a demand shift.
A rightward demand shift; rising purchases provide evidence of stronger demand despite unchanged fixed-price plans.
Movement up the same curve; a lower price reduces the quantity buyers desire at that price.
A leftward demand shift; unchanged fixed-price plans provide evidence that consumers now want fewer units.
q.feedback: A price cut raises quantity demanded along the same curve. An unchanged fixed-price schedule rules out attributing the increase to a demand shift.

key: Movement down the same curve; unchanged fixed-price plans provide no evidence of a demand shift.

q.q: Coffee buyers remain on the same downward-sloping demand curve. Their quantity demanded falls from 80 to 60 cups per day. With non-price determinants unchanged, which price change is consistent with this movement?
options: A rise in coffee’s own price.
A fall in coffee’s own price.
An unchanged coffee price.
A change in coffee’s production cost with its price unchanged.
q.feedback: Moving to a smaller quantity on the same downward-sloping demand curve requires a higher own price. A demand shift would change the curve rather than move along it.

key: A rise in coffee’s own price.

q.q: A household’s income rises. With tablet prices, tastes and all other demand determinants unchanged, it plans to buy fewer tablets. How should tablets be classified for this household over this income range?
options: Normal, because any income change shifts demand.
Inferior, because higher income reduces its demand.
Normal, because the tablet price has not changed.
Inferior, because the tablet price must have risen.
q.feedback: An inferior good has lower demand when income rises, other things equal. This is an income-driven demand shift; the unchanged tablet price rules out an own-price movement.

key: Inferior, because higher income reduces its demand.

q.q: When only the price of a good changes, what happens on the demand curve?
options: There is movement along the demand curve
The demand curve shifts right
The demand curve shifts left
Supply shifts right
q.feedback: A good's own price changes quantity demanded, not demand.

key: There is movement along the demand curve

q.q: The price of coffee falls. What is the most precise result?
options: Quantity demanded of coffee increases
Demand for coffee increases
Supply of coffee decreases
Demand for coffee decreases
q.feedback: Because coffee's own price changed, buyers move along the demand curve.

key: Quantity demanded of coffee increases

q.q: The price of streaming subscriptions rises, and fewer subscriptions are purchased. What is the most precise explanation?
options: Quantity demanded decreased because the good's own price changed
Demand decreased because the curve shifted left
Supply increased because sellers charged more
Demand increased because price rose
q.feedback: The good's own price changed, so this is a movement along demand and a change in quantity demanded.

key: Quantity demanded decreased because the good's own price changed

q.q: Bus fares fall, while a campus adds students who use the bus. Considering each change separately, how does it affect demand for bus rides?
options: Lower fares shift demand right; more students move buyers along demand.
Lower fares move buyers along demand; more students shift demand left.
Both changes move buyers along the same demand curve.
Lower fares move buyers along demand; more students shift demand right.
q.feedback: The fare is the ride's own price, so its fall increases quantity demanded along a curve. More potential riders are a non-price determinant: at each fare, the campus buys more rides, shifting demand right.

key: Lower fares move buyers along demand; more students shift demand right.

q.q: The price of peanut butter rises. If jelly is a complement, what happens to demand for jelly?
options: Demand for jelly decreases
Demand for jelly increases
Supply of jelly decreases
Quantity supplied of jelly increases
q.feedback: Complements are used together. If peanut butter becomes more expensive, demand for jelly falls.

key: Demand for jelly decreases

q.q: The price of bus rides rises. If subway rides are substitutes, what happens to demand for subway rides?
options: Demand for subway rides increases
Demand for subway rides decreases
Supply of subway rides increases
Quantity demanded of bus rides increases
q.feedback: When the price of a substitute rises, demand for the other good increases.

key: Demand for subway rides increases

q.q: The good’s own price declines while every non-price determinant stays fixed. Which demand-side change occurs?
options: Demand increases through a rightward shift of the curve.
Demand decreases through a leftward shift of the curve.
Quantity demanded stays fixed because the curve did not shift.
Quantity demanded increases through a movement along the existing curve.
q.commonError: Using demand and quantity demanded as interchangeable terms.
q.feedback: A change in the good’s own price causes movement along the demand curve and changes quantity demanded.

key: Quantity demanded increases through a movement along the existing curve.

q.q: Which event shifts demand for bus rides to the right?
options: The price of subway rides, a substitute, increases.
The price of bus rides decreases while all non-price determinants remain fixed.
Bus companies add routes and lower their operating costs.
The cost of diesel fuel decreases for bus operators.
q.commonError: Selecting an own-price movement or a supply shifter as a demand shifter.
q.feedback: A higher price for a substitute makes bus rides more attractive at every bus fare and shifts demand right.

key: The price of subway rides, a substitute, increases.

q.q: Income falls and purchases of instant noodles rise. What does this evidence suggest?
options: Instant noodles are a normal good for these consumers
Instant noodles are an inferior good for these consumers
A lower noodle price caused movement along the demand curve
A supply decrease raised purchases despite the income change
q.commonError: Treating all goods as normal or confusing demand evidence with supply.
q.feedback: Demand for an inferior good rises when income falls, holding other determinants constant.

key: Instant noodles are an inferior good for these consumers

q.q: Electric scooters are normal goods. Household incomes rise, but a close substitute becomes cheaper. At an unchanged scooter price, can we predict the direction of scooter purchases without knowing the strength of each effect?
options: Yes, purchases rise; higher income and the cheaper substitute both push demand right.
Yes, purchases fall; higher income and the cheaper substitute both push demand left.
No; higher income pushes demand right while the cheaper substitute pushes it left.
No change occurs; an unchanged scooter price prevents any change in quantity purchased.
q.commonError: Explaining a full demand-schedule change as movement along one curve.
q.feedback: Income growth increases normal-good demand, while a cheaper substitute reduces scooter demand. Their unknown relative strengths make the net fixed-price quantity effect ambiguous.

key: No; higher income pushes demand right while the cheaper substitute pushes it left.

q.q: Movie tickets are a normal good. Income rises, but the price of streaming subscriptions, a substitute, falls. What is the strongest conclusion about movie-ticket demand?
options: Demand rises because higher income and a cheaper substitute both increase demand for movie tickets.
Demand falls because the cheaper substitute lowers ticket demand while income does not shift demand for a normal good.
Quantity demanded changes along one curve because both events change the ticket price
The net shift is uncertain because the two effects oppose each other
q.commonError: Claiming certainty when opposing demand shifters act simultaneously.
q.feedback: Higher income increases demand for a normal good, while a cheaper substitute reduces demand for movie tickets. The effects oppose each other and their relative sizes are not supplied, so the net shift cannot be determined. These are demand shifters, not changes caused by the ticket’s own price.

key: The net shift is uncertain because the two effects oppose each other

q.q: Concert attendance falls after ticket prices rise. A fan claims demand decreased. Surveys show fans’ planned purchases at each fixed price are unchanged, but later a popular performer joins the tour. Which sequence is supported?
options: The first decline is movement along demand; the later performer change can shift demand right.
The first decline is a leftward demand shift; the later performer change is movement down that curve.
Both events are movements along demand because each changes the number of tickets sold.
Both events shift demand left because ticket price and performer popularity are market conditions.
q.commonError: Calling an own-price movement a change in demand.
q.feedback: Unchanged fixed-price plans imply the first attendance decline is due to movement along demand. Greater performer appeal changes a nonprice determinant and can shift the demand schedule right.

key: The first decline is movement along demand; the later performer change can shift demand right.

q.q: Income rises for a normal good while the price of a close substitute falls. What can be concluded about demand for the normal good?
options: The net demand shift is uncertain because the two effects oppose each other.
Demand must rise because income rises for a normal good.
Demand must fall because the substitute becomes cheaper.
Demand stays fixed; both changes are movements along the original curve.
q.commonError: Assuming one of two opposing demand shifters must dominate.
q.feedback: Higher income raises demand for the normal good; a cheaper substitute lowers it. Either effect can dominate, or they can offset. Own-price movements do not describe these determinants.

key: The net demand shift is uncertain because the two effects oppose each other.

q.q: A survey shows buyers want more electric scooters at every listed price than they did last month. Which statement is most precise?
options: Quantity demanded increased because the scooter price fell.
Demand increased, so the entire demand schedule shifted right.
Demand increased only at the market price.
The law of demand stopped applying to electric scooters.
q.commonError: Calling an across-the-board schedule change a movement along demand.
q.feedback: Wanting more at every price is a rightward shift of demand, not a change in quantity demanded caused by the good’s own price.

key: Demand increased, so the entire demand schedule shifted right.

q.q: Coffee is a normal good. Consumer income rises, buyers expect coffee prices to fall next month, and the current price of tea, a substitute, rises. What can be concluded about current coffee demand?
options: Demand must rise: two favorable determinants outweigh one unfavorable determinant regardless of their sizes.
Demand must fall: an expected future price decline outweighs current income and substitute-price effects.
Demand is indeterminate: income and the substitute price raise it, while waiting for a lower future price reduces it.
Demand is unchanged: income, expectations, and related-good prices affect only movement along the curve.
q.commonError: Adding demand shifters mechanically without recognizing opposing effects.
q.feedback: The two positive demand effects need not outweigh the negative expectations effect. Counting determinants cannot replace comparing their magnitudes.

key: Demand is indeterminate: income and the substitute price raise it, while waiting for a lower future price reduces it.

q.q: On the displayed gourmet-donut demand curve, what price and quantity are shown at point A?
options: $10 and 100 thousand donuts
$5 and 225 thousand donuts
$10 and 225 thousand donuts
$14 and 100 thousand donuts
q.feedback: At point A, the demand curve pairs a price of $10 with a quantity demanded of 100 thousand donuts.

key: $10 and 100 thousand donuts

q.q: In the displayed coffee market, the move from D0 to D1 represents:
options: A decrease in demand
An increase in quantity demanded caused only by a lower price
An increase in demand
A decrease in supply
q.feedback: D1 lies to the right of D0, showing that consumers demand more coffee at each common price.

key: An increase in demand

q.q: How should the change in the tea demand curve from D0 to D1 be classified?
options: A decrease in demand
An increase in demand
A decrease in quantity demanded caused only by a higher price
An increase in supply
q.feedback: D1 lies to the left of D0, showing that consumers demand less tea at each common price.

key: A decrease in demand

q.q: Suppose the only change in the gourmet-donut market is that the good's own price falls from $10 to $5. The displayed graph shows the market moving from A to B. Which conclusion is correct?
options: Quantity demanded rises 125 thousand; demand is unchanged.
Demand rises 125 thousand; D shifts right.
Quantity demanded falls 125 thousand; demand is unchanged.
Demand falls 125 thousand; D shifts left.
q.feedback: A change in the good's own price causes a movement along a fixed demand curve. Quantity demanded rises from 100 thousand to 225 thousand, but demand does not shift.

key: Quantity demanded rises 125 thousand; demand is unchanged.

q.q: Refer to the graph. A buyer group starts on D0 at $6. After demand changes to D1, price is $10. Which statement reconciles the demand change with the final quantity?
options: Demand decreased, causing final quantity to be 25 thousand below the starting quantity.
Demand increased, so final quantity must be 75 thousand above the starting quantity.
Demand increased, yet final quantity is 25 thousand below the starting quantity.
Demand was unchanged, and the price increase reduced quantity by 100 thousand.
q.feedback: The initial quantity is 150 thousand and the final quantity is 125 thousand. D1 is right of D0, but movement up the new demand curve offsets more than the 75-thousand rightward shift.

key: Demand increased, yet final quantity is 25 thousand below the starting quantity.

q.q: Refer to the graph. Compare the initial point on D0 at $6 with the final point on D1 at $4. Which explanation correctly separates the demand shift from the subsequent price movement?
options: The shift to D1 lowers quantity at each price; moving down D1 then raises quantity to 100 thousand, only partly offsetting the shift
The shift to D1 raises quantity at each price; moving down D1 then lowers quantity to 100 thousand
Demand stays on D0 because the price fall accounts for the entire move to 100 thousand
Supply shifts left first, and movement along D1 restores quantity to 150 thousand
q.feedback: At $6, shifting from D0 to D1 reduces quantity demanded. The later price decline produces movement down D1 to 100 thousand, but that movement does not fully undo the demand decrease.

key: The shift to D1 lowers quantity at each price; moving down D1 then raises quantity to 100 thousand, only partly offsetting the shift

q.q: Refer to the graph. Calculate the quantity response per $1 price decrease from A to B, then infer which demand relationship that calculation illustrates.
options: Quantity demanded rises 25 thousand per $1 decrease, illustrating movement along a downward-sloping demand curve
Demand rises 25 thousand per $1 decrease, illustrating a rightward shift of the demand curve
Quantity demanded falls 25 thousand per $1 decrease, illustrating movement up the demand curve
Demand falls 125 thousand per $1 decrease, illustrating a leftward shift of the demand curve
q.feedback: From A to B, price falls $5 and quantity demanded rises 125 thousand, or 25 thousand per dollar. Because the good's own price changes, this is movement along the demand curve, not a curve shift.

key: Quantity demanded rises 25 thousand per $1 decrease, illustrating movement along a downward-sloping demand curve

q.q: Refer to the graph. At $6, compare D0 with D1. If this is a normal good, which change could explain the difference, and how large is it?
options: A fall in the good’s own price; 75 thousand more units demanded at that price.
Higher consumer income; 75 thousand more units demanded at that price.
Higher consumer income; 100 thousand more units demanded at that price.
A cheaper substitute; 75 thousand more units demanded at that price.
q.feedback: At $6, D0 shows 150 thousand and D1 shows 225 thousand: a 75-thousand increase at the same price. Higher income shifts demand right for a normal good; an own-price fall moves along a curve, and a cheaper substitute shifts demand left.

key: Higher consumer income; 75 thousand more units demanded at that price.

q.q: Refer to the tea graph. Compare D0 with D1 at both $4 and $6. Which inference is supported by the repeated horizontal gap?
options: Demand decreases by 100 thousand units at each shown price, indicating a leftward curve shift
Quantity demanded decreases by 100 thousand solely because tea's own price rises
Demand increases by 100 thousand units at each shown price, indicating a rightward curve shift
Supply decreases by 100 thousand units, causing movement from D0 to D1
q.feedback: At both $4 and $6, D1 lies 100 thousand units left of D0. A repeated horizontal difference at fixed prices identifies a decrease in demand rather than movement along one curve.

key: Demand decreases by 100 thousand units at each shown price, indicating a leftward curve shift

q.q: Refer to the graph. A report attributes the entire A-to-B change to stronger tastes for donuts. A second survey finds the quantity desired at every fixed price is unchanged. Which diagnosis fits both pieces of evidence?
options: The report is supported; quantity rises 125 thousand because demand shifted right.
The report confuses movement with a shift; quantity rises 125 thousand because price is lower.
The report confuses movement with a shift; quantity falls 125 thousand because price is lower.
The report is supported; demand shifted right even though the fixed-price schedule is unchanged.
q.feedback: A and B are on the same demand curve, at 100 and 225 thousand. The unchanged fixed-price schedule rules out a taste-driven demand shift. The graph shows an increase in quantity demanded caused by a lower price.

key: The report confuses movement with a shift; quantity rises 125 thousand because price is lower.

q.q: Refer to the graph. First compare D0 with D1 at a price of $10. Then follow D1 as price falls from $10 to $6. Which option correctly decomposes the two quantity changes into a demand shift and a movement along D1?
options: 50→125 from the price fall; 125→225 from a supply shift.
50→150 from the demand shift; 150→225 from the price fall.
50→25 from the demand shift; 25→225 from the price fall.
50→125 from the demand shift; 125→225 from the price fall.
q.feedback: At $10 the shift from D0 to D1 raises quantity demanded from 50 to 125 thousand. Moving down D1 from $10 to $6 raises it again from 125 to 225 thousand, for a total increase of 175 thousand.

key: 50→125 from the demand shift; 125→225 from the price fall.

q.q: The market begins on D0 at $6 and 150 thousand units. Demand shifts to D1 while price is still $6, and then price falls to $4. Which decomposition matches the graph?
options: 150→250 from the demand shift; 250→100 from the price fall.
150→50 from the demand shift; 50→100 from the price fall.
150→50 from the price fall; 50→100 from the demand shift.
150→100 from the demand shift; 100→50 from the price fall.
q.feedback: At $6, D0 shows 150 thousand and D1 shows 50 thousand. Moving down D1 to $4 raises quantity demanded to 100 thousand. Final quantity remains 50 thousand below the starting level.

key: 150→50 from the demand shift; 50→100 from the price fall.

q.q: The market moves from point A to point B on the displayed demand curve. What is the most precise description?
options: Demand increases, shifting D to the right.
Price falls, causing an increase in quantity demanded along D.
Price falls, causing quantity demanded to decrease along D.
Supply increases, shifting S to the right.
q.feedback: A and B lie on the same demand curve. The lower price is associated with a larger quantity demanded, so this is a movement along demand, not a shift.

key: Price falls, causing an increase in quantity demanded along D.

q.q: Moving from point A to point B on the displayed demand curve changes quantity demanded by:
options: A decrease of 125 thousand donuts
An increase of 5 thousand donuts
An increase of 125 thousand donuts
An increase of 225 thousand donuts
q.feedback: Quantity demanded rises from 100 thousand at A to 225 thousand at B, an increase of 125 thousand.

key: An increase of 125 thousand donuts

q.q: At a price of $10 on the displayed coffee graph, how does quantity demanded change when demand shifts from D0 to D1?
options: It decreases from 125 thousand to 50 thousand
It increases from 100 thousand to 175 thousand
It stays at 125 thousand
It increases from 50 thousand to 125 thousand
q.feedback: At $10, D0 shows 50 thousand units and D1 shows 125 thousand, so quantity demanded at that price rises by 75 thousand.

key: It increases from 50 thousand to 125 thousand

q.q: If coffee is a normal good, which event is consistent with the shift from D0 to D1 shown in the graph?
options: Consumer income rises
The price of coffee falls while all demand shifters stay unchanged
Coffee producers adopt cheaper technology
The price of coffee rises and buyers move up D0
q.feedback: For a normal good, higher income increases demand, shifting the entire demand curve to the right.

key: Consumer income rises

q.q: Refer to the graph. At a price of $4, how does quantity demanded change as demand shifts from D0 to D1?
options: It increases from 100 thousand to 200 thousand
It decreases from 200 thousand to 100 thousand
It decreases from 300 thousand to 200 thousand
It stays at 100 thousand
q.feedback: At $4, D0 shows 200 thousand units while D1 shows 100 thousand, a decrease of 100 thousand at the same price.

key: It decreases from 200 thousand to 100 thousand

q.q: For a normal good such as tea, which change in a demand shifter could generate the illustrated curve movement?
options: The price of tea rises while all demand shifters stay unchanged
Tea producers receive a subsidy
Consumer income falls
The price of tea falls and buyers move down D0
q.feedback: For a normal good, lower income decreases demand and shifts the entire demand curve left.

key: Consumer income falls

q.q: How does equilibrium change as demand moves from D0 to D1?
options: Demand decreases, lowering price and quantity
Demand increases, raising price and quantity
Supply decreases, raising price and reducing quantity
Supply increases, lowering price and raising quantity
q.imageAlt: The movie-ticket market has price in dollars on the vertical axis and quantity in thousands on the horizontal axis. S0 is an upward-sloping supply curve. D0 and D1 are downward-sloping demand curves, with D1 lying to the right of D0 at each displayed price. Point A is the D0-S0 intersection at quantity 200 and price $10. Point B is the D1-S0 intersection at quantity 250 and price $12.
q.feedback: Demand shifts right; price rises from 10 to 12 and quantity rises from 200 to 250 thousand.
q.graphDescription: The movie-ticket market has price in dollars on the vertical axis and quantity in thousands on the horizontal axis. S0 is an upward-sloping supply curve. D0 and D1 are downward-sloping demand curves, with D1 lying to the right of D0 at each displayed price. Point A is the D0-S0 intersection at quantity 200 and price $10. Point B is the D1-S0 intersection at quantity 250 and price $12.

key: Demand increases, raising price and quantity

q.q: A policy forecast is testable, but the economist also recommends adoption. How should the forecast and recommendation be distinguished?
options: Both are positive claims because the recommendation follows evidence
Positive analysis informs a separate normative choice
Both are normative because the topic is public policy
The forecast itself determines whether the policy should be adopted.
q.commonError: Giving economists authority to choose society’s values.
q.feedback: Economists can estimate consequences; recommendations also require value judgments.

key: Positive analysis informs a separate normative choice

q.q: A model works only under one assumption. What should advice report?
options: Report only the baseline result
Drop the assumption from the analysis
How the conclusion changes when the assumption changes
Delay all advice until the assumption can be proven true.
q.commonError: Presenting an estimate as a guarantee.
q.feedback: Responsible advice reports assumptions, uncertainty, and plausible unintended consequences.

key: How the conclusion changes when the assumption changes

q.q: A subsidy changes behavior beyond its intended target. Which economic idea helps explain these additional responses?
options: Only the directly targeted behavior should be included in the analysis
Responses outside the target are irrelevant to the policy’s effects
Unintended responses occur only when enforcement fails.
Incentives can create unintended consequences
q.feedback: A subsidy changes the payoff from an action. People may adjust related choices as well as the behavior the policy targets, creating effects the designer did not intend. Those responses belong in the policy’s benefit-and-cost analysis even when the subsidy is enforced as designed.

key: Incentives can create unintended consequences

q.q: An economist estimates how a bus fee changes ridership. What role is primary?
options: Scientist analyzing a testable consequence
Adviser making a value judgment about whether the fee is fair
Policymaker deciding whether the fee should be adopted
Administrator responsible for enforcing the fee.
q.commonError: Giving economists authority to choose society’s values.
q.feedback: Economists can estimate consequences; recommendations also require value judgments.

key: Scientist analyzing a testable consequence

q.q: An adviser compares costs borne by commuters and taxpayers. What should the adviser make explicit?
options: The combined cost alone, without showing how it is divided between the two groups.
The costs each group bears and the tradeoffs between the policy alternatives.
The adviser’s preferred outcome alone, without showing the costs of other choices.
The taxpayers’ costs alone, without including the costs borne by commuters.
q.commonError: Treating efficiency as the only criterion of social desirability.
q.feedback: An informative comparison identifies which costs fall on commuters and which fall on taxpayers, and how those costs change across policy alternatives. A single total can conceal the distribution of costs and the tradeoffs facing the decision maker.

key: The costs each group bears and the tradeoffs between the policy alternatives.

q.q: Why can economics inform but not dictate a school policy?
options: Economics cannot measure the effects of school policies
School policies have no economic tradeoffs
The final choice also depends on social values
Evidence cannot help identify the likely consequences of alternative policies.
q.commonError: Giving economists authority to choose society’s values.
q.feedback: Economists can estimate consequences; recommendations also require value judgments.

key: The final choice also depends on social values

q.q: A forecast gives a range rather than one number. Why?
options: The range identifies which policy society should prefer
A range means the evidence is too weak to be useful
Every value inside the range is equally likely.
Policy effects are uncertain, not guaranteed
q.commonError: Presenting an estimate as a guarantee.
q.feedback: Responsible advice reports assumptions, uncertainty, and plausible unintended consequences.

key: Policy effects are uncertain, not guaranteed

q.q: What can an economist contribute without choosing society’s values?
options: Evidence about likely consequences
Choose society’s moral priorities
Decide which policy lawmakers must adopt
Guarantee that the chosen policy will succeed.
q.commonError: Giving economists authority to choose society’s values.
q.feedback: Economists can estimate consequences; recommendations also require value judgments.

key: Evidence about likely consequences

q.q: A projection includes a confidence range. What does it acknowledge?
options: The true effect is guaranteed to lie inside the range
Uncertainty in the predicted effect
The range identifies the policy society should prefer
Every value in the range is equally likely.
q.commonError: Presenting an estimate as a guarantee.
q.feedback: Responsible advice reports assumptions, uncertainty, and plausible unintended consequences.

key: Uncertainty in the predicted effect

q.q: A policy creates winners and losers. What should analysis show?
options: Only the total effect on surplus
Only which groups lose
The distribution as well as the total effect
Ignore distribution whenever the aggregate effect is positive.
q.commonError: Treating efficiency as the only criterion of social desirability.
q.feedback: Economic analysis clarifies tradeoffs but does not uniquely rank every social goal.

key: The distribution as well as the total effect

q.q: Volunteers in a training pilot earn more later. A second study assigns training by lottery and finds little effect. Before recommending expansion, what should the adviser resolve?
options: Whether volunteer enthusiasm proves the training caused their earnings
Whether the lottery result makes all participant preferences irrelevant
Whether selection explains the first result and whether the lottery setting fits expansion
Whether the larger positive estimate is easier to communicate
q.commonError: Treating all empirical designs as equally informative.
q.feedback: Volunteers can differ before training. The lottery helps separate selection from treatment, while its population and implementation still need to fit the expansion setting.

key: Whether selection explains the first result and whether the lottery setting fits expansion

q.q: Policy A creates $40 million of gains for high-income households and $10 million of losses for low-income households. Policy B creates $22 million of gains for low-income households and costs high-income households $5 million. With no other effects, which advice distinguishes efficiency from distribution?
options: A has the larger unweighted net gain, while B favors low-income households; the ranking depends on the stated social criterion.
B has the larger unweighted net gain, while A favors low-income households; efficiency alone therefore selects B.
A has the larger unweighted net gain, so it necessarily satisfies a goal of improving low-income households’ welfare.
B favors low-income households, so A cannot have a positive unweighted net gain even if its benefits exceed losses.
q.commonError: Treating efficiency as the only criterion of social desirability.
q.feedback: Unweighted net gains are 40-10=30 for A and 22-5=17 for B. Efficiency totals and incidence differ. Choosing between them requires stating how distribution enters the social ranking.

key: A has the larger unweighted net gain, while B favors low-income households; the ranking depends on the stated social criterion.

q.q: A subsidy model estimated that firms would add 100 jobs when credit was available at 5%. Credit is now rationed and borrowing costs 12%; the model still predicts 100 jobs because it treats financing as fixed. What is the best next analysis?
options: Keep the 100-job forecast because the subsidy is unchanged; treat financing as an unrelated macroeconomic detail.
Reestimate firms’ financing responses and compare predictions under feasible credit conditions before transferring the old forecast.
Replace 100 jobs with the latest observed hiring total; that difference directly measures the subsidy’s causal effect.
Reject all subsidy models because one institutional change means simplified forecasts cannot provide policy evidence.
q.commonError: Presenting an estimate as a guarantee.
q.feedback: Credit conditions affect the mechanism through which firms finance expansion. The old forecast is conditional on assumptions that changed; observed hiring alone does not identify a counterfactual subsidy effect.

key: Reestimate firms’ financing responses and compare predictions under feasible credit conditions before transferring the old forecast.

q.q: Two advisers agree that a flood barrier yields $60 million in avoided damage, costs $35 million and relocates 200 households. One favors it; the other rejects involuntary relocation. Which further step would clarify rather than merely repeat their disagreement?
options: Collect a more precise construction-cost estimate until both advisers must adopt the same view of relocation.
Add the number of relocated households directly to the dollar cost and select the policy with the smallest sum.
State the relocation criterion, examine feasible less-displacing alternatives and show how each changes net benefits and affected households.
Treat the shared positive net benefit as evidence that objections to relocation are errors in economic forecasting.
q.commonError: Giving economists authority to choose society’s values.
q.feedback: The advisers share the main predictions but differ over a social criterion. Examining feasible alternatives and explicit tradeoffs informs the choice; greater forecast precision cannot itself settle the value judgment.

key: State the relocation criterion, examine feasible less-displacing alternatives and show how each changes net benefits and affected households.

q.q: A pilot worked elsewhere but institutions differ locally. What is the key warning?
options: A successful pilot automatically generalizes to other settings
Institutional differences matter only for normative judgments
A large effect elsewhere guarantees a large local effect.
Evidence may not transfer to the new setting
q.commonError: Presenting an estimate as a guarantee.
q.feedback: Responsible advice reports assumptions, uncertainty, and plausible unintended consequences.

key: Evidence may not transfer to the new setting

q.q: A model omits enforcement costs. What should the policy estimate do?
options: Include feasible implementation and administration costs
Ignore enforcement costs if the policy objective is worthwhile
Count only the direct statutory cost of the program
Assume administration uses no scarce resources.
q.commonError: Confusing statutory design with actual implementation.
q.feedback: Enforcement and administration use scarce staff time, equipment and other resources. A feasible policy estimate must include those implementation costs when comparing benefits with costs. Omitting them can overstate net benefits even if the policy’s stated goal is desirable.

key: Include feasible implementation and administration costs

q.q: An efficient proposal conflicts with a legal-rights goal. What follows?
options: The efficient proposal must be adopted
Efficiency evidence does not uniquely decide social desirability
The legal-rights goal is irrelevant to policy evaluation
The conflict proves the proposal is economically inefficient.
q.commonError: Treating efficiency as the only criterion of social desirability.
q.feedback: Economic analysis clarifies tradeoffs but does not uniquely rank every social goal.

key: Efficiency evidence does not uniquely decide social desirability

q.q: A recommendation changes under plausible assumptions. What should the economist do?
options: Report only the baseline estimate
Use the assumption that produces the most favorable result
Report sensitivity rather than one certain answer
Delay all advice until uncertainty is eliminated.
q.commonError: Presenting an estimate as a guarantee.
q.feedback: Responsible advice reports assumptions, uncertainty, and plausible unintended consequences.

key: Report sensitivity rather than one certain answer

q.q: Two advisers accept the same estimate: consolidating offices saves staff time but lengthens rural travel. One favors consolidation and the other opposes it. Which information best explains their different recommendations?
options: Which adviser used more decimal places in the shared estimate
Whether the two advisers agree that travel is measurable
Whether consolidation is being proposed by a public institution
How each weighs staff savings against rural access
q.commonError: Assuming all economist disagreement is partisan or all is empirical.
q.feedback: Agreement about effects leaves room for different weights on efficiency and access. Those priorities can explain the recommendations without inventing a forecast disagreement.

key: How each weighs staff savings against rural access

q.q: Two access plans have the same total measured benefit. One imposes concentrated losses on residents with few alternatives; the other spreads smaller losses. What additional step supports a defensible recommendation?
options: Choose either plan because equal totals establish identical welfare for every resident
Increase numerical precision until one value criterion becomes unnecessary
Count only beneficiaries because costs are already reflected in the total
State how concentrated hardship is weighed, and show each plan's distribution
q.commonError: Treating efficiency as the only criterion of social desirability.
q.feedback: Equal totals conceal different distributions. A recommendation needs an explicit evaluation of concentrated hardship and evidence about who gains and loses.

key: State how concentrated hardship is weighed, and show each plan's distribution

q.q: A permit reform saves time for compliant firms but increases inspections. It has positive net benefit at high compliance and negative net benefit at low compliance. Local compliance is unmeasured. What advice is best supported?
options: Present the conditional ranking and seek local compliance evidence before a firm recommendation
Recommend adoption because the favorable scenario is feasible
Reject because one plausible scenario has losses
Average the two outcomes without assessing how likely each is
q.commonError: Presenting an estimate as a guarantee.
q.feedback: The sign depends on an unresolved local behavior. Reporting that dependence and obtaining relevant evidence is more defensible than selecting or mechanically averaging scenarios.

key: Present the conditional ranking and seek local compliance evidence before a firm recommendation

q.q: A school schedule saves paid staff hours but shifts supervision to families. The measured gain disappears when family time is valued at its next-best use. Which revision follows?
options: Treat the original cash saving as false because the wider net gain disappeared
Report the wider resource comparison and explain why a budget saving need not be a social gain
Keep the original conclusion because only paid hours use scarce resources
Count the family time twice, once as cost and once as a separate loss of the same activity
q.commonError: Treating efficiency as the only criterion of social desirability.
q.feedback: The budget saving can be real while the wider net benefit vanishes. Count the forgone family activity once and distinguish fiscal effects from resource effects.

key: Report the wider resource comparison and explain why a budget saving need not be a social gain

q.q: An adviser reports a narrow forecast interval based on one assumed take-up rate. Credible alternative take-up rates reverse the recommendation. What uncertainty is missing?
options: A value judgment proving which take-up rate is true
Evidence that no economic forecast can ever inform a choice
Uncertainty about the behavioral assumption, beyond precision conditional on that assumption
Only rounding uncertainty in the reported forecast
q.commonError: Presenting an estimate as a guarantee.
q.feedback: A precise estimate conditional on one rate does not capture uncertainty about the rate itself. Report the alternative assumptions and the recommendation reversal.

key: Uncertainty about the behavioral assumption, beyond precision conditional on that assumption

q.q: Two policy models fit the pilot. One attributes improved attendance to transport; the other to reminders sent at the same time. The rollout can fund only one. What evidence most directly helps the adviser choose?
options: A larger pilot that always combines both services
The political popularity of the combined pilot as proof of causality
The pilot's total attendance without a breakdown of interventions
Comparable groups receiving transport alone and reminders alone
q.commonError: Assuming all economist disagreement is partisan or all is empirical.
q.feedback: Separating the interventions tests the competing mechanisms relevant to the actual funding choice. More bundled observations cannot identify which component drove the gain.

key: Comparable groups receiving transport alone and reminders alone

q.q: An economist identifies the schedule with the highest total measured benefit. Citizens prefer another because it guarantees a minimum service level to every district. Which advice respects both roles?
options: Explain the cost of the service guarantee and make the ranking criterion explicit
Treat the citizens' preference as a statistical error in the benefit estimate
Describe the maximizing schedule as morally required by the calculation
Alter the benefit numbers until both schedules receive the same ranking
q.commonError: Giving economists authority to choose society’s values.
q.feedback: Economic analysis can estimate the tradeoff created by the guarantee. Deciding how strongly to value equal minimum access goes beyond identifying the aggregate maximum.

key: Explain the cost of the service guarantee and make the ranking criterion explicit

q.q: A small pilot pays shops to repair items and records strong gains. Nationwide adoption induces shops to relabel routine maintenance as repairs. What should a follow-up evaluation change?
options: Infer zero genuine gains solely because some reporting changed
Measure additional genuine repairs and account for the changed reporting incentive
Use reimbursement counts unchanged because the pilot already validated the measure
Treat all repairs after adoption as caused by the payment
q.commonError: Presenting an estimate as a guarantee.
q.feedback: Scaling changes incentives and can change what the metric measures. Estimate genuine additional repairs against a credible comparison rather than equating paid claims with benefits.

key: Measure additional genuine repairs and account for the changed reporting incentive

q.q: A proposed tax is projected to create $80 million in national efficiency gains but $50 million in losses concentrated in one region. Those regional losses are already included in the national estimate. A domestic transfer could offset them at $8 million of administrative cost, but the regional loss estimate is uncertain. Which advice is sound?
options: Net expected national gain after administration is $72 million; test regional-loss scenarios and compensation feasibility before making a distributional recommendation.
Net expected national gain after compensation is $22 million; subtract the regional losses again because concentration makes them additional costs.
Net expected national gain after compensation is $122 million; add the transfer because recipients experience it as a benefit.
Net expected national gain is $80 million under every scenario; positive national gains guarantee each region can implement compensation itself.
q.commonError: Treating efficiency as the only criterion of social desirability.
q.feedback: The $50 million loss is already in the national ledger and a domestic transfer is redistribution. Administration reduces expected gain to 72. Uncertain regional effects still matter for funding, implementation and social priorities.

key: Net expected national gain after administration is $72 million; test regional-loss scenarios and compensation feasibility before making a distributional recommendation.

q.q: Model A predicts a transit subsidy raises ridership mainly by attracting former drivers. Model B predicts the same total increase mainly by shifting riders from unsubsidized buses. Both fit current totals. The policy goal is fewer car trips. What evidence best discriminates between the models for this decision?
options: Collect more precise total ridership counts after the subsidy; equal predictions imply either model establishes equal car-trip reductions.
Track prior travel modes and changes against a credible untreated comparison; total ridership fit alone cannot identify car-trip displacement.
Choose A because its mechanism matches the goal; a policy-relevant mechanism needs no separate test once totals fit.
Average the predicted ridership increases; averaging identical totals also identifies how many riders switched from cars.
q.commonError: Assuming all economist disagreement is partisan or all is empirical.
q.feedback: Identical ridership predictions can hide different substitution channels. Prior-mode and counterfactual evidence tests whether observed new riders actually displaced car travel.

key: Track prior travel modes and changes against a credible untreated comparison; total ridership fit alone cannot identify car-trip displacement.

q.q: A school policy has estimated net benefits of $12 million and reduces access for rural pupils. An alternative yields $8 million and preserves access. The adopted charter requires preserving rural access unless no feasible alternative exists. What conclusion follows from the estimates and criterion together?
options: The first policy must satisfy the charter because its larger net benefit proves no economically feasible alternative exists.
The alternative’s access benefit proves its unweighted net benefit exceeds $12 million even though the estimate is $8 million.
The first policy leads on unweighted net benefits, but the feasible alternative satisfies the stated access constraint; surplus alone does not justify overriding it.
Neither estimate is positive analysis because the access constraint makes factual policy comparisons inherently normative.
q.commonError: Treating efficiency as the only criterion of social desirability.
q.feedback: The estimates are factual claims about consequences; the charter supplies a normative constraint. A feasible access-preserving alternative exists, so maximizing the listed net benefit is not the only decision rule.

key: The first policy leads on unweighted net benefits, but the feasible alternative satisfies the stated access constraint; surplus alone does not justify overriding it.

q.q: A safety rule would prevent $10 million of harm with full compliance and require $4 million of compliance resources. Current enforcement induces only half the affected firms to comply; assume benefits and compliance costs scale proportionally. An extra $1 million enforcement program would raise compliance to 80%. Which assessment is correct?
options: Net benefit rises from $3 million to $4.8 million; enforcement spending is a transfer and should not reduce the gain.
Net benefit falls from $6 million to $3.8 million; compare actual enforcement with the original full-compliance forecast.
Net benefit stays $6 million; the legal rule fixes compliance benefits regardless of enforcement behavior.
Net benefit rises from $3 million to $3.8 million; the extra enforcement gains $0.8 million despite falling short of full compliance.
q.commonError: Presenting an estimate as a guarantee.
q.feedback: Current net benefit is 0.5(10-4)=3. With stronger enforcement it is 0.8(10-4)-1=3.8. The incremental gain is 0.8, and the correct baseline is current feasible compliance rather than the full-compliance forecast.

key: Net benefit rises from $3 million to $3.8 million; the extra enforcement gains $0.8 million despite falling short of full compliance.
