q.q: Two economists use different demand estimates. What can explain different forecasts?
options: Different scientific judgments about evidence
One economist must have made an arithmetic mistake
Different forecasts can only come from different value judgments
Empirical disagreements cannot be informed by additional evidence.
q.commonError: Assuming all economist disagreement is partisan or all is empirical.
q.feedback: Disagreement can reflect evidence, models, uncertainty, or different values.

key: Different scientific judgments about evidence

q.q: Two advisers share one forecast but rank equity differently. What differs?
options: Their estimates of the policy’s effects
Their normative values
Their definitions of the economic variables
One adviser must have interpreted the data incorrectly.
q.commonError: Assuming all economist disagreement is partisan or all is empirical.
q.feedback: Disagreement can reflect evidence, models, uncertainty, or different values.

key: Their normative values

q.q: A policy raises total surplus but harms one region. What should analysis report?
options: Only the increase in total surplus
Only the regional loss, because any loser makes the policy inefficient
Efficiency and distribution separately
A single efficiency conclusion without reporting who gains and loses.
q.commonError: Treating efficiency as the only criterion of social desirability.
q.feedback: Economic analysis clarifies tradeoffs but does not uniquely rank every social goal.

key: Efficiency and distribution separately

q.q: A rule changes incentives in an unexpected way. What should advisers examine?
options: Only the response the rule was intended to create
Treat unexpected behavior as irrelevant to the policy analysis
Assume the original behavioral prediction remains correct.
Likely behavioral responses and unintended effects
q.commonError: Presenting an estimate as a guarantee.
q.feedback: Responsible advice reports assumptions, uncertainty, and plausible unintended consequences.

key: Likely behavioral responses and unintended effects

q.q: Economists disagree because one trusts a different study. What differs?
options: Their scientific judgment about evidence
Their normative values must differ
One economist must be irrational
Evidence becomes irrelevant once economists disagree.
q.commonError: Assuming all economist disagreement is partisan or all is empirical.
q.feedback: Disagreement can reflect evidence, models, uncertainty, or different values.

key: Their scientific judgment about evidence

q.q: They agree on effects but rank fairness differently. What differs?
options: Their scientific forecasts
Their normative evaluation
One economist must have misread the data
Economic analysis cannot distinguish factual claims from value judgments.
q.commonError: Assuming all economist disagreement is partisan or all is empirical.
q.feedback: Disagreement can reflect evidence, models, uncertainty, or different values.

key: Their normative evaluation

q.q: Why examine enforcement before recommending a rule?
options: Enforcement affects legality but not economic outcomes
Assume full compliance when evaluating a proposed rule
Implementation changes costs and behavior
Implementation costs are irrelevant before adoption.
q.commonError: Presenting an estimate as a guarantee.
q.feedback: Responsible advice reports assumptions, uncertainty, and plausible unintended consequences.

key: Implementation changes costs and behavior

q.q: Can economists scientifically determine society’s values?
options: Yes; economic expertise identifies the morally best outcome
Yes; estimating consequences also determines which values society should hold
No; they can clarify consequences and tradeoffs
Yes; economists receive decision-making authority from their technical expertise.
q.commonError: Giving economists authority to choose society’s values.
q.feedback: Economists can estimate consequences; recommendations also require value judgments.

key: No; they can clarify consequences and tradeoffs

q.q: Does efficiency prove a policy is socially best?
options: Yes; efficiency incorporates every social objective
Yes; distribution does not matter when total surplus rises
Yes; economists can rank competing social values scientifically.
No; other values and distribution may matter
q.commonError: Treating efficiency as the only criterion of social desirability.
q.feedback: Economic analysis clarifies tradeoffs but does not uniquely rank every social goal.

key: No; other values and distribution may matter

q.q: Is a policy forecast a guarantee?
options: No; it depends on evidence and assumptions
Yes, if the forecast comes from a strong model
Yes, if the confidence interval is narrow
Yes, if the economist has no conflict of interest.
q.commonError: Presenting an estimate as a guarantee.
q.feedback: Responsible advice reports assumptions, uncertainty, and plausible unintended consequences.

key: No; it depends on evidence and assumptions

q.q: Must economist disagreement be political?
options: Yes; all disagreement among economists is ideological
No; evidence, models, or values can differ
Yes; economists using the same field must otherwise agree
Yes; empirical evidence cannot produce different interpretations.
q.commonError: Assuming all economist disagreement is partisan or all is empirical.
q.feedback: Disagreement can reflect evidence, models, uncertainty, or different values.

key: No; evidence, models, or values can differ

q.q: A faculty committee asks whether a new attendance rule will improve learning. An economist would first:
options: Identify the behavioral mechanism and evidence needed to test it.
Declare the rule fair or unfair without analysis.
Assume attendance and learning are identical.
Ignore incentives created by the rule.
q.commonError: Failing to transfer policy-analysis logic outside government.
q.feedback: Economic policy reasoning applies to any rule that changes incentives and outcomes.

key: Identify the behavioral mechanism and evidence needed to test it.

q.q: When an economist estimates how a tax will affect employment, the economist is primarily:
options: Making a moral judgment about fairness.
Providing positive analysis about likely consequences.
Guaranteeing the policy will pass.
Setting the tax rate by law.
q.feedback: Economists can estimate consequences without deciding the policy.

key: Providing positive analysis about likely consequences.

q.q: When policymakers ask an economist to compare costs and benefits, the economist should:
options: Hide uncertainty to sound decisive.
Replace evidence with personal preference.
State assumptions and identify relevant tradeoffs.
Ignore who bears the costs.
q.feedback: Good advice makes assumptions, tradeoffs, and uncertainty visible.

key: State assumptions and identify relevant tradeoffs.

q.q: Which activity is most clearly part of an economist’s policy role?
options: Voting on behalf of the legislature.
Enforcing the final regulation.
Declaring one value judgment scientifically correct.
Evaluating evidence about likely behavioral responses.
q.commonError: Giving economists powers they do not possess.
q.feedback: Economists analyze incentives, evidence, and tradeoffs; elected officials make policy choices.

key: Evaluating evidence about likely behavioral responses.

q.q: Two studies estimate opposite effects because one uses a credible natural experiment and the other compares self-selected groups. The strongest appraisal emphasizes:
options: Differences in causal identification.
Which result has the larger number.
Which author supports the preferred policy.
Whether both studies use percentages.
q.commonError: Treating all empirical designs as equally informative.
q.feedback: Policy advice should weigh evidence by its ability to identify causal effects.

key: Differences in causal identification.

q.q: An economist recommends a policy because it maximizes total surplus, while citizens prioritize equal treatment. The disagreement is primarily about:
options: The arithmetic definition of surplus.
The normative criterion used to rank outcomes.
Whether incentives exist.
The distinction between micro and macro topics.
q.commonError: Calling a value disagreement an empirical error.
q.feedback: Economic analysis can measure consequences, but ranking competing values requires a normative criterion.

key: The normative criterion used to rank outcomes.

q.q: A policy model predicts large benefits, but the data come from a different population and period. What is the central concern?
options: Whether the evidence generalizes to the current setting.
Whether the policy has a money price.
Whether economists may use models.
Whether positive analysis is always normative.
q.commonError: Assuming evidence transfers automatically across settings.
q.feedback: Policy advice must consider whether evidence is applicable to the target population and context.

key: Whether the evidence generalizes to the current setting.

q.q: An economist is employed by an agency that benefits from a favorable estimate. What practice best protects credibility?
options: Publish the preferred specification with full calculations, omitting the agency relationship to keep the report technical.
Disclose the agency interest, assumptions, alternatives and uncertainty so others can assess the estimate.
Have an agency colleague check the arithmetic, then report one point estimate to avoid confusing readers.
Report an interval from the chosen model, leaving model selection and alternative specifications to the agency.
q.feedback: Disclosure must address both the institutional interest and methodological discretion. Arithmetic review or an uncertainty interval alone does not reveal how model selection could favor the agency.

key: Disclose the agency interest, assumptions, alternatives and uncertainty so others can assess the estimate.

q.q: A policy has a positive expected net benefit but a small chance of catastrophic loss. Which addition is necessary?
options: A claim that averages eliminate risk.
Removal of all low-probability outcomes.
Risk analysis beyond the expected-value calculation.
A conclusion based only on sunk costs.
q.commonError: Treating expected value as a complete policy criterion.
q.feedback: Low-probability, high-cost outcomes may matter even when expected net benefits are positive.

key: Risk analysis beyond the expected-value calculation.

q.q: A report favors plan A because paid-work savings exceed its cash cost. A requires relatives to provide unpaid care; plan B purchases the same care. What comparison would correct the scope of the advice?
options: Value caregiving time under both plans alongside cash and paid-work effects
Add unpaid care only to B because B records an invoice
Treat unpaid care as free because relatives are not paid
Remove paid-work savings so both plans contain only budget costs
q.feedback: Unpaid time has alternative uses. Comparable benefit-cost scope includes caregiving burdens for A and avoids ignoring a resource merely because B buys it explicitly.

key: Value caregiving time under both plans alongside cash and paid-work effects

q.q: A model favors a recycling program if most households sort correctly. A pilot reports high collection but does not measure contamination; sorting is harder in the rollout area. What should precede the recommendation?
options: Declare the program undesirable solely because compliance is uncertain
Measure correct sorting and test whether the ranking survives realistic rollout compliance
Treat collected tonnage as proof of the required compliance
Use the pilot average unchanged because the same program name is used
q.commonError: Confusing statutory design with actual implementation.
q.feedback: Collection is not the assumed correct sorting. Advice needs the relevant compliance measure and sensitivity to the more difficult rollout setting.

key: Measure correct sorting and test whether the ranking survives realistic rollout compliance

q.q: A consolidation plan has aggregate gains but losses for remote users. A report says compensation makes everyone better off, although no compensation is funded. Which conclusion is warranted?
options: An unfunded transfer can be counted as income already received
Any remote loss proves aggregate gains are mathematically impossible
Potential compensation does not establish actual gains for remote users; report the implemented distribution
Positive total gains mean the remote users must gain indirectly
q.feedback: Aggregate gains can create scope for compensation. Without an implemented transfer, the remote users' losses remain part of the actual policy outcome.

key: Potential compensation does not establish actual gains for remote users; report the implemented distribution

q.q: Two economists use different estimates of demand elasticity and reach different tax projections. What best explains the disagreement?
options: They may share the same framework but use different empirical assumptions.
One of them must reject opportunity cost.
Economic analysis cannot use evidence.
Normative values are the only possible source of disagreement.
q.commonError: Assuming disagreement proves the discipline has no method.
q.feedback: Different estimates and assumptions can produce different forecasts.

key: They may share the same framework but use different empirical assumptions.

q.q: An economist reports that a policy raises total surplus but imposes concentrated losses on one group. What should the report do next?
options: Conclude that everyone benefits.
Separate the efficiency finding from the distributional consequence.
Ignore the losing group because total surplus rose.
Call the distributional judgment a positive fact.
q.commonError: Collapsing efficiency and equity into one claim.
q.feedback: Policy analysis should distinguish aggregate efficiency from distribution.

key: Separate the efficiency finding from the distributional consequence.

q.q: A forecast is highly sensitive to one uncertain parameter. The best policy advice is to:
options: Use only the most favorable value.
Present one estimate as certain.
Report the sensitivity and show results under plausible values.
Remove the parameter from the model.
q.feedback: Decision makers need to know when conclusions depend heavily on uncertain inputs.

key: Report the sensitivity and show results under plausible values.

q.q: A mayor asks whether rent control is “good.” What is the economist’s most useful first response?
options: Answer solely from personal ideology.
Promise there will be no unintended consequences.
Treat the word good as a measurable price.
Clarify the objectives and analyze likely effects and tradeoffs.
q.commonError: Treating vague policy goals as self-defining.
q.feedback: Policy evaluation requires explicit objectives and evidence about consequences.

key: Clarify the objectives and analyze likely effects and tradeoffs.

q.q: Positive policy analysis asks:
options: What consequences are likely to occur.
Which outcome is morally best.
Which party should win.
Which value judgment is scientifically true.
q.feedback: Positive analysis describes or predicts consequences.

key: What consequences are likely to occur.

q.q: When a policy conclusion depends on an assumption, the economist should:
options: Hide it from decision makers.
State the assumption and test how much it matters.
Treat it as a proven fact.
Replace it with a slogan.
q.feedback: Transparent assumptions and sensitivity checks strengthen policy advice.

key: State the assumption and test how much it matters.

q.q: Market equilibrium occurs where:
options: Quantity demanded equals quantity supplied
Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, creating a shortage
Quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded, creating a surplus
The demand curve reaches the price axis
q.feedback: At equilibrium, quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.

key: Quantity demanded equals quantity supplied

q.q: A popular endorsement increases demand for a product while production conditions remain unchanged. How does the market's equilibrium price respond?
options: It increases
It decreases
It remains unchanged
It becomes a shortage at every price
q.feedback: The endorsement shifts demand right. With supply unchanged, buyers compete for the product and the equilibrium price rises.

key: It increases

q.q: If supply increases and demand does not change, what happens to equilibrium price?
options: It decreases
It increases
It remains unchanged because demand did not change.
It increases because more units are available for sale.
q.feedback: An increase in supply lowers equilibrium price when demand is unchanged.

key: It decreases

q.q: A drought reduces supply of wheat while a health trend increases demand for wheat bread. What can be predicted with certainty in the wheat market?
options: Price rises; equilibrium quantity can rise, fall, or stay unchanged.
Quantity rises; equilibrium price can rise, fall, or stay unchanged.
Price and quantity both rise for every possible size of the shifts.
Price and quantity both fall for every possible size of the shifts.
q.feedback: Reduced wheat supply and greater derived demand for wheat both raise its price. They push equilibrium quantity in opposite directions, so quantities require more information.

key: Price rises; equilibrium quantity can rise, fall, or stay unchanged.

q.q: Consumer interest in a product falls while new technology lowers production costs. What can be predicted with certainty?
options: Price falls, but quantity is ambiguous
Quantity rises, but price is ambiguous
Both price and quantity rise
Both price and quantity fall
q.feedback: A demand decrease and supply increase both lower price, but quantity is ambiguous.

key: Price falls, but quantity is ambiguous

q.q: A celebrity endorsement increases demand for a product at the same time input costs rise. What can be predicted with certainty?
options: Equilibrium price rises
Equilibrium quantity rises
Equilibrium quantity falls
Equilibrium price falls
q.feedback: Demand rises and supply falls. Both raise price, but quantity is ambiguous.

key: Equilibrium price rises

q.q: A learner correctly identifies a rightward demand shift with supply fixed. Which paired equilibrium prediction completes the reasoning?
options: Both price and quantity rise
Both price and quantity fall
Price rises while quantity falls
Price falls while quantity rises
q.feedback: A rightward demand shift creates upward pressure on both equilibrium price and equilibrium quantity when supply is fixed.

key: Both price and quantity rise

q.q: Holding demand constant, which equilibrium outcome follows from an increase in supply?
options: Price falls and quantity rises
Price rises and quantity falls
Both rise
Both fall
q.feedback: An increase in supply lowers equilibrium price and raises equilibrium quantity.

key: Price falls and quantity rises

q.q: A new report makes blueberries more attractive to consumers. Production conditions are unchanged. With ordinary downward-sloping demand and upward-sloping supply, what happens to equilibrium price and quantity?
options: Price rises and quantity rises
Price falls and quantity falls
Price rises and quantity falls
Price falls and quantity rises
q.feedback: The report raises willingness to buy blueberries at each price, shifting demand right. With supply unchanged, the new intersection has both a higher price and a higher quantity.

key: Price rises and quantity rises

q.q: Plant disease destroys part of the orange crop. Consumers' willingness to buy oranges is unchanged. With ordinary downward-sloping demand and upward-sloping supply, what happens to equilibrium price and quantity?
options: Price rises and quantity falls
Price falls and quantity rises
Price rises and quantity rises
Price falls and quantity falls
q.feedback: Crop loss reduces the amount growers can supply at each price, shifting supply left. With demand unchanged, oranges become scarcer: equilibrium price rises and quantity falls.

key: Price rises and quantity falls

q.q: Demand increases while supply decreases, and the observed equilibrium quantity is unchanged. Which inference best reconciles the two shifts with that observation?
options: Equilibrium price rises, and the opposing quantity effects happen to offset
Equilibrium price falls, and the two shifts reinforce the quantity effect
Equilibrium quantity is unchanged because neither curve shifts
Equilibrium price is unchanged because the demand and supply shifts are equal
q.feedback: A demand increase and supply decrease both raise equilibrium price. Their quantity effects oppose one another, and the observed unchanged quantity indicates that those effects offset in this case.

key: Equilibrium price rises, and the opposing quantity effects happen to offset

q.q: Demand decreases while supply increases. What can be predicted with certainty?
options: Equilibrium price falls
Equilibrium quantity rises
Equilibrium price rises
Equilibrium quantity falls
q.feedback: Both shifts push price down, but quantity is ambiguous.

key: Equilibrium price falls

q.q: Demand and supply both increase. What can be predicted with certainty?
options: Equilibrium quantity rises
Equilibrium price rises
Equilibrium price falls
Equilibrium quantity falls
q.feedback: Both shifts increase quantity, but price depends on which shift is larger.

key: Equilibrium quantity rises

q.q: Demand and supply both decrease. What can be predicted with certainty?
options: Equilibrium quantity falls
Equilibrium price rises
Equilibrium price falls
Equilibrium quantity rises
q.feedback: Both shifts reduce quantity, but price is ambiguous.

key: Equilibrium quantity falls

q.q: A market initially has Qd = 500 - 10P and Qs = 100 + 10P. Demand then rises to Qd = 600 - 10P. Calculate the new equilibrium price and compare it with the original equilibrium.
options: $25, which is $5 higher
$20, so price is unchanged
$30, which is $10 higher
$15, which is $5 lower
q.feedback: Initially, 500 - 10P = 100 + 10P gives P = $20. After demand rises, 600 - 10P = 100 + 10P gives P = $25, a $5 increase.

key: $25, which is $5 higher

q.q: Demand is Qd = 500 - 10P. Supply shifts from Qs = 100 + 10P to Qs = 40 + 10P. Calculate the new equilibrium quantity and infer the effect of the supply decrease.
options: 270; equilibrium quantity falls from 300
300; equilibrium quantity is unchanged
230; equilibrium quantity falls from 300
350; equilibrium quantity rises from 300
q.feedback: The new equilibrium solves 500 - 10P = 40 + 10P, so P = $23 and Q = 270. Compared with the original Q = 300, the supply decrease lowers equilibrium quantity.

key: 270; equilibrium quantity falls from 300

q.q: A drought reduces wheat supply while a health trend increases demand for wheat bread. Explain which equilibrium effect is certain and which depends on the relative shift sizes.
options: Price rises; quantity is ambiguous because the shifts have opposing quantity effects
Price falls; quantity rises because both shifts increase purchases
Price rises; quantity rises because demand determines both outcomes
Price is ambiguous; quantity falls because supply determines both outcomes
q.feedback: The demand increase and supply decrease both raise price. Demand raises quantity while the supply decrease lowers it, so quantity depends on the relative magnitudes.

key: Price rises; quantity is ambiguous because the shifts have opposing quantity effects

q.q: Production technology lowers costs while consumer interest in the good falls. Explain which equilibrium effect is certain and which depends on the relative shift sizes.
options: Price falls; quantity is ambiguous because the shifts have opposing quantity effects
Price rises; quantity falls because both shifts reduce market availability
Price falls; quantity rises because supply determines both outcomes
Price is ambiguous; quantity falls because demand determines both outcomes
q.feedback: The supply increase and demand decrease both lower price. Supply raises quantity while the demand decrease lowers it, so quantity depends on the relative magnitudes.

key: Price falls; quantity is ambiguous because the shifts have opposing quantity effects

q.q: Refer to the graph. Starting at D1/S1, demand and supply both increase to D2/S2. Which explanation compares the general prediction with the particular equilibrium drawn?
options: Quantity rises for certain; price is generally ambiguous but remains at P2 in this drawing
Price rises for certain; quantity is generally ambiguous but remains at Q1 in this drawing
Both price and quantity are generally fixed because the curves shift together
Quantity falls for certain; price is generally ambiguous but falls to P1 here
q.feedback: Both increases raise equilibrium quantity. Their price effects oppose, so theory alone leaves price ambiguous; the displayed intersections show P2 in both the initial and final equilibria.

key: Quantity rises for certain; price is generally ambiguous but remains at P2 in this drawing

q.q: Refer to the graph. Demand increases from D1 to D2 while supply decreases from S2 to S1. Infer what theory guarantees, then use the plotted equilibria to explain the quantity outcome.
options: Price rises for certain; quantity is generally ambiguous but stays at Q2 in this drawing
Quantity rises for certain; price is generally ambiguous but stays at P2 in this drawing
Price falls for certain; quantity stays at Q2 because both curves shift right
Quantity falls for certain; price stays at P1 because the shifts offset
q.feedback: The demand increase and supply decrease both raise price. Their quantity effects oppose; the graph shows those effects offset at Q2 for this particular pair of shifts.

key: Price rises for certain; quantity is generally ambiguous but stays at Q2 in this drawing

q.q: Refer to the supply and demand shift graph. Starting from D2/S1, demand decreases to D1 while supply increases to S2. What happens?
options: Price falls and quantity stays the same
Price rises and quantity stays the same
Price stays the same and quantity rises
Price falls and quantity falls
q.feedback: D2/S1 gives P3 and Q2. D1/S2 gives P1 and Q2. Price falls while quantity remains Q2.

key: Price falls and quantity stays the same

q.q: Refer to the supply and demand shift graph. If demand and supply both increase, what does this graph show is possible?
options: Quantity rises while price stays the same
Quantity rises while price rises because the demand shift has the larger price effect
Quantity rises while price falls because the supply shift has the larger price effect
Price rises while quantity stays the same because the shifts have equal quantity effects
q.feedback: The graph shows D1/S1 to D2/S2. Both demand and supply increase, quantity rises, and price remains unchanged.

key: Quantity rises while price stays the same

q.q: Refer to the supply and demand shift graph. If demand increases and supply decreases, what does this graph show is possible?
options: Price rises while quantity stays the same
Price falls while quantity rises
Price stays the same while quantity rises
Price falls while quantity stays the same
q.feedback: The graph shows D1/S2 to D2/S1. Demand rises and supply falls, causing price to rise while quantity stays at Q2.

key: Price rises while quantity stays the same

q.q: Refer to the graph. Tastes shift demand from D1 to D2 while supply remains S1. Which explanation uses both intersections to distinguish the demand shift from the market's movement along supply?
options: Demand shifts right, and equilibrium moves along S1 from P2, Q1 to P3, Q2
Supply shifts right, and equilibrium moves along D1 from P2, Q1 to P1, Q2
Demand shifts left, and equilibrium moves along S1 from P3, Q2 to P2, Q1
Supply shifts left, and equilibrium moves along D2 from P2, Q3 to P3, Q2
q.feedback: The taste change shifts the entire demand curve from D1 to D2. Because S1 is fixed, the new intersection is also a movement along S1 to a higher price and quantity.

key: Demand shifts right, and equilibrium moves along S1 from P2, Q1 to P3, Q2

q.q: Refer to the graph. The market moves from D1/S1 to D2/S2. An analyst claims that simultaneous demand and supply increases must leave price unchanged. Then part of the supply increase is reversed: supply lies strictly between S1 and S2 at every shown price, while demand stays D2. Which assessment is correct?
options: The original offset is specific to the graph; afterward price is between P2 and P3 and quantity between Q2 and Q3.
The original offset is a general rule; afterward price stays P2 and quantity stays Q3.
The original offset is specific to the graph; afterward price is between P1 and P2 and quantity exceeds Q3.
The original offset is a general rule; afterward price reaches P3 and quantity falls below Q1.
q.feedback: Both initial increases raise quantity, but their opposing price effects need not cancel in general. They happen to cancel at P2 in this drawing. With D2 fixed, partially reversing S2 toward S1 places the new intersection between (P2,Q3) and (P3,Q2). Price rises above P2, and quantity falls from Q3 but remains above Q2 and the original Q1.

key: The original offset is specific to the graph; afterward price is between P2 and P3 and quantity between Q2 and Q3.

q.q: A disease reduces berry supply while a nutrition trend raises berry demand. The final quantity is above its original level. Which conclusion follows with ordinary downward demand and upward supply?
options: Price is higher; the demand increase more than offsets the supply reduction’s effect on quantity.
Price is lower; greater final quantity proves that supply increased.
Price is unchanged; the higher quantity shows that the two shifts offset completely.
Price is higher; the observed quantity proves that the supply reduction dominated demand.
q.feedback: Both shifts raise price. Supply reduction alone lowers equilibrium quantity, so the observed quantity increase requires the demand effect to outweigh that reduction in the final outcome.

key: Price is higher; the demand increase more than offsets the supply reduction’s effect on quantity.

q.q: Two initially identical device markets face the same increase in demand. Only Market Y also loses a component supplier. Compared with Market X’s final equilibrium, what must be true in Market Y?
options: Y has a higher price and lower quantity, although its quantity relative to the original equilibrium is uncertain.
Y has a lower price and higher quantity, although its quantity relative to the original equilibrium is uncertain.
Y has a higher price and quantity, because both changes increase demand.
Y has the same price and quantity, because both markets face the same demand change.
q.feedback: Starting from X’s final equilibrium, the additional supply reduction in Y raises price and lowers quantity. Compared with the common original equilibrium, Y’s demand increase and supply decrease have opposing quantity effects.

key: Y has a higher price and lower quantity, although its quantity relative to the original equilibrium is uncertain.

q.q: Lunch-delivery demand falls while improved routing lowers delivery costs. Final price is lower and the number of deliveries is unchanged. Which explanation is consistent?
options: Demand fell and supply rose; their quantity effects offset at the final equilibrium.
Demand and supply both fell; their quantity effects offset at the final equilibrium.
Demand and supply both rose; unchanged deliveries reflect offsetting quantity effects.
Only demand fell; a fixed upward-sloping supply curve kept deliveries unchanged.
q.feedback: Lower demand and higher supply both reduce price but have opposite quantity effects. The observed unchanged quantity reflects an offset in this case; it is not a general prediction of those shifts.

key: Demand fell and supply rose; their quantity effects offset at the final equilibrium.

q.q: Bicycles are a normal good. Income and production-input costs rise, yet equilibrium bicycle sales fall. A manager concludes that bicycle demand must have fallen. Evaluate the conclusion.
options: Incorrect: demand rose, but the supply reduction more than offset its effect on quantity; price rose.
Correct: lower equilibrium sales establish a demand decrease even when income rises.
Incorrect: supply rose, but demand fell enough to reduce both price and quantity.
Correct: higher input costs reduce bicycle demand directly while supply stays fixed.
q.feedback: Higher income increases demand for a normal good; higher input costs reduce supply. Both raise price. Lower sales can result when the supply effect dominates quantity, so sales alone do not identify a demand shift.

key: Incorrect: demand rose, but the supply reduction more than offset its effect on quantity; price rose.

q.q: A production improvement increases supply while tastes shift away from the product. An analyst predicts that price and quantity must both fall. What is the precise correction?
options: Price must fall, but quantity falls only if the demand reduction outweighs the supply increase’s quantity effect.
Quantity must fall, but price falls only if the production improvement outweighs the taste change.
Price must rise, but quantity can rise or fall depending on the relative shifts.
Neither direction can be inferred because simultaneous shifts make both variables indeterminate.
q.feedback: Both changes lower equilibrium price. Lower demand reduces quantity while higher supply increases it, so the analyst needs relative effects to assert a quantity decline.

key: Price must fall, but quantity falls only if the demand reduction outweighs the supply increase’s quantity effect.

q.q: A market price is above equilibrium. What pressure does the market create and why?
options: Downward pressure on price because quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded
Upward pressure on price because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied
No pressure because high prices clear every market
Downward pressure on quantity demanded because demand shifts left
q.feedback: A price above equilibrium creates a surplus, so sellers have an incentive to lower price.

key: Downward pressure on price because quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded

q.q: A market price is below equilibrium. What pressure does the market create and why?
options: Upward pressure on price because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied
Downward pressure on price because quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded
No pressure because buyers prefer low prices
A supply increase because the legal price is low
q.feedback: A price below equilibrium creates a shortage, so buyers compete and push price upward.

key: Upward pressure on price because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied

q.q: A coffee shop sees more customers after a celebrity endorsement. At the same time, wages for baristas rise. If the relative sizes of the two shifts are unknown, which equilibrium outcome can be predicted with certainty?
options: Price rises; quantity is ambiguous
Quantity rises; price is ambiguous
Both price and quantity fall
Price falls; quantity rises
q.feedback: Demand increases and supply decreases. Both raise price, but quantity depends on which shift is larger.

key: Price rises; quantity is ambiguous

q.q: A new production method makes shoes cheaper to produce. At the same time, a fashion shift makes shoes less popular. What is certain?
options: Price falls; quantity is ambiguous
Quantity falls; price is ambiguous
Both price and quantity rise
Price rises; quantity falls
q.feedback: Supply increases and demand decreases. Both lower price, but quantity is ambiguous.

key: Price falls; quantity is ambiguous

q.q: A hurricane disrupts production and reduces supply while households expect prices to rise tomorrow and rush to buy today. What is the strongest prediction for today’s market?
options: Price rises; quantity is ambiguous
Quantity rises; price is ambiguous
Both price and quantity fall
Price falls; quantity rises
q.feedback: Expected future price increases raise current demand, while the hurricane lowers supply. Price rises; quantity is ambiguous.

key: Price rises; quantity is ambiguous

q.q: Fewer buyers want a product and several producers exit. Final price is above the starting price. Which interpretation is consistent with both shifts and that observation?
options: Quantity falls; the supply reduction’s upward price effect outweighs the demand reduction’s downward effect.
Quantity rises; the demand reduction’s downward price effect outweighs the supply reduction’s upward effect.
Quantity stays fixed; an increase in price prevents either curve from shifting.
Quantity falls; the higher price proves that demand increased rather than decreased.
q.feedback: Both lower demand and lower supply reduce equilibrium quantity. Their price effects oppose each other; the observed price increase identifies the dominant price effect in this case.

key: Quantity falls; the supply reduction’s upward price effect outweighs the demand reduction’s downward effect.

q.q: A widely reported health study increases consumers’ willingness to buy fresh berries. At the same time, frost destroys part of the berry crop. With ordinary downward-sloping demand and upward-sloping supply, and unknown effect sizes, which equilibrium conclusion is certain?
options: Quantity rises; price may rise or fall because the two changes push price in opposite directions.
Price falls; quantity may rise or fall because lower crop output reduces sellers’ willingness to sell.
Price rises; quantity may rise or fall because the two changes push quantity in opposite directions.
Quantity falls; price may rise or fall because stronger willingness to buy offsets the crop loss.
q.feedback: The health information shifts demand right; crop loss shifts supply left. Both raise price, but demand growth raises quantity while the supply contraction lowers it. Their relative sizes determine the quantity change.

key: Price rises; quantity may rise or fall because the two changes push quantity in opposite directions.

q.q: A market has Qd = 180 - 2P and Qs = 20 + 2P. At every price, demand then falls by 24 units and supply falls by 8 units. Which final change and explanation are correct?
options: Price rises $4 and quantity falls 16 units; demand’s larger reduction raises price.
Price falls $4 and quantity falls 16 units; demand’s larger horizontal reduction dominates the price effect.
Price falls $4 and quantity rises 16 units; both curve reductions expand sales.
Price is unchanged and quantity falls 32 units; the horizontal reductions simply add.
q.feedback: Initially 180 - 2P = 20 + 2P gives P = 40 and Q = 100. After the changes, 156 - 2P = 12 + 2P gives P = 36 and Q = 84. Stating horizontal units makes the comparison of shift sizes well defined.

key: Price falls $4 and quantity falls 16 units; demand’s larger horizontal reduction dominates the price effect.

q.q: Unchanged linear schedules give Qd=900 and Qs=1,150 at $10, and Qd=1,100 and Qs=950 at $8. Sellers currently charge $10. An analyst calls the resulting surplus evidence of a supply shift and predicts it will persist even without a price control. Which correction is complete?
options: The surplus is 250 at $10; price must rise to $11.25 and quantity 1,025, while a $10 ceiling would preserve the gap.
The surplus is 250 at $10; price can fall to $8.75 and quantity 1,025 along unchanged curves, while a $10 floor would preserve the gap.
The shortage is 250 at $10; price can fall to $8.75 and quantity 1,025 only if supply shifts left.
The surplus is 150 at $10; price can fall to $8 and quantity 950, while unchanged curves prevent further adjustment.
q.commonError: Treating a surplus as a shortage or confusing movement along curves with shifts.
q.feedback: The schedules imply Qd=1900-100P and Qs=150+100P. Equating them gives P=8.75 and Q=1025. At 10, excess supply is 250. Price adjustment moves along existing curves; a binding floor at 10 could block the fall and sustain surplus.

key: The surplus is 250 at $10; price can fall to $8.75 and quantity 1,025 along unchanged curves, while a $10 floor would preserve the gap.

q.q: A product goes viral while firms' production conditions remain unchanged. How do the resulting demand shift and movement along supply change equilibrium?
options: Price rises and quantity rises
Price falls and quantity falls
Price rises and quantity falls
Price falls and quantity rises
q.feedback: The viral interest shifts demand right. With supply fixed, the new intersection lies higher and farther right, so equilibrium price and quantity both rise.

key: Price rises and quantity rises

q.q: Supply for a product decreases while demand stays the same. What happens to equilibrium price and quantity?
options: Price rises and quantity falls
Price falls and quantity rises
Price rises and quantity rises
Price falls and quantity falls
q.feedback: A decrease in supply raises equilibrium price and lowers equilibrium quantity.

key: Price rises and quantity falls

q.q: Refer to the supply and demand graph. Which equilibrium is formed by D1 and S2?
options: Price P1 and Quantity Q2
Price P2 and Quantity Q1
Price P3 and Quantity Q2
Price P2 and Quantity Q3
q.feedback: D1 and S2 intersect at the middle vertical guide and the lowest horizontal guide, which is Price P1 and Quantity Q2.

key: Price P1 and Quantity Q2

q.q: Refer to the supply and demand graph. Which equilibrium is formed by D1 and S1?
options: Price P2 and Quantity Q1
Price P1 and Quantity Q2
Price P3 and Quantity Q2
Price P2 and Quantity Q3
q.feedback: D1 and S1 intersect at the left vertical guide and the middle horizontal guide, which is Price P2 and Quantity Q1.

key: Price P2 and Quantity Q1

q.q: Refer to the supply and demand graph. Which equilibrium is formed by D2 and S2?
options: Price P2 and Quantity Q3
Price P1 and Quantity Q2
Price P3 and Quantity Q2
Price P2 and Quantity Q1
q.feedback: D2 and S2 intersect at the right vertical guide and the middle horizontal guide, which is Price P2 and Quantity Q3.

key: Price P2 and Quantity Q3

q.q: Refer to the supply and demand graph. Compared with the equilibrium at D1 and S1, the equilibrium at D2 and S2 shows:
options: The same price but a higher quantity
A lower price and a lower quantity
A higher price and a lower quantity
A lower price and the same quantity
q.feedback: D1 and S1 gives Price P2 and Quantity Q1, while D2 and S2 gives Price P2 and Quantity Q3, so price is the same and quantity is higher.

key: The same price but a higher quantity

q.q: Refer to the supply and demand graph. The market begins at D1 and S1. Supply then increases, followed by an increase in demand. What is the final equilibrium?
options: Price P2 and Quantity Q3
Price P1 and Quantity Q2
Price P2 and Quantity Q1
Price P3 and Quantity Q2
q.feedback: Starting at D1 and S1 gives P2, Q1. A supply increase moves equilibrium to P1, Q2. Then a demand increase moves equilibrium to P2, Q3.

key: Price P2 and Quantity Q3

q.q: Refer to the price-control graph. What is the market equilibrium price and quantity?
options: $30 and 200 units
$20 and 250 units
$40 and 150 units
$50 and 300 units
q.feedback: Equilibrium occurs where supply and demand intersect, which is $30 and 200 units.

key: $30 and 200 units

q.q: At $8, buyers plan to purchase 70 units and sellers plan to sell 110. At $6 both plan 90. No price control prevents adjustment. Which diagnosis and prediction fit the plans?
options: The $8 price creates a 40-unit surplus; price tends toward $6, where planned purchases and sales both equal 90.
The $8 price creates a 40-unit shortage; price tends toward $6, where planned purchases and sales both equal 90.
The $8 price is equilibrium because 70 buyers can be served; unsold units do not create pressure to adjust.
The $6 price creates a 90-unit shortage because buyers’ planned purchases must be added to sellers’ planned sales.
q.feedback: At $8 supply exceeds demand by 110-70=40. Downward pressure moves toward the $6 price where the two planned quantities are equal.

key: The $8 price creates a 40-unit surplus; price tends toward $6, where planned purchases and sales both equal 90.

q.q: Demand increases while supply stays the same. What happens to equilibrium price and quantity?
options: Price rises and quantity rises
Price falls and quantity falls
Price rises and quantity falls
Price falls and quantity rises
q.feedback: The demand increase moves the market to a higher point on the unchanged supply curve, raising both equilibrium price and quantity.

key: Price rises and quantity rises

q.q: Demand shifts right while supply shifts left at the same time. Which equilibrium change can be predicted with certainty?
options: Equilibrium price rises
Equilibrium quantity rises
Equilibrium quantity falls
Equilibrium price falls
q.feedback: Demand rising and supply falling both push price up, but quantity depends on which shift is stronger.

key: Equilibrium price rises

q.q: A market price below equilibrium creates a:
options: Surplus.
Balanced market.
Leftward demand shift.
Shortage.
q.feedback: Below equilibrium, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, creating a shortage.

key: Shortage.

q.q: What pressure does a surplus create in an unregulated market?
options: Sellers lower prices to clear unwanted inventories.
Buyers bid prices higher because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied.
Demand shifts right until buyers absorb every unit offered for sale.
Supply shifts left because firms are holding unwanted inventories.
q.commonError: Reversing the price adjustment associated with a surplus.
q.feedback: When quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded, sellers compete to clear inventory by lowering price.

key: Sellers lower prices to clear unwanted inventories.

q.q: If demand increases while supply is unchanged, equilibrium price and quantity usually:
options: Both decrease.
Both increase.
Price rises and quantity falls.
Price falls and quantity rises.
q.commonError: Using the supply-shift outcome for a demand increase.
q.feedback: A rightward demand shift moves the equilibrium up along the supply curve to a higher price and quantity.

key: Both increase.

q.q: Demand increases while supply decreases. Which equilibrium outcome is certain?
options: The equilibrium quantity rises.
The equilibrium quantity falls.
The equilibrium price rises.
The equilibrium price falls.
q.commonError: Claiming certainty about quantity when the two shifts move quantity in opposite directions.
q.feedback: Both shifts raise price, while demand raises quantity and lower supply reduces quantity.

key: The equilibrium price rises.

q.q: Both demand and supply shift left in the same market. Which equilibrium result can be stated without knowing the shift sizes?
options: The equilibrium price rises.
The equilibrium price falls.
The equilibrium quantity rises.
The equilibrium quantity falls.
q.commonError: Claiming certainty about price when both curves shift left.
q.feedback: Both shifts reduce equilibrium quantity, but their price effects oppose each other.

key: The equilibrium quantity falls.

q.q: At the current price, quantity demanded is 400 and quantity supplied is 520. Which explanation diagnoses the imbalance and traces the adjustment along the existing curves without a price control?
options: A surplus pushes price down, raising quantity demanded and lowering quantity supplied until they converge
A shortage pushes price up, lowering quantity demanded and raising quantity supplied until they converge
A surplus shifts demand right while price remains fixed until inventories clear
A shortage shifts supply left while buyers reduce quantity demanded
q.commonError: Treating a surplus as a shortage or confusing movement along curves with shifts.
q.feedback: Quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded by 120, creating a surplus. Falling price moves the market along both curves: quantity demanded rises and quantity supplied falls toward equilibrium.

key: A surplus pushes price down, raising quantity demanded and lowering quantity supplied until they converge

q.q: At the equilibrium price, quantity demanded is:
options: Greater than quantity supplied.
Equal to quantity supplied.
Less than quantity supplied.
Unrelated to quantity supplied.
q.commonError: Defining equilibrium as a shortage, surplus, or unrelated quantities.
q.feedback: Market equilibrium occurs at the price where buyers’ quantity demanded equals sellers’ quantity supplied.

key: Equal to quantity supplied.

q.q: Demand and supply both increase. The equilibrium quantity rises, but the equilibrium price is unchanged. What does this reveal?
options: Neither curve shifted because an unchanged price proves the market did not move.
Demand increased more than supply, so price should have risen instead of staying fixed.
The price effects offset, while both shifts raise equilibrium quantity.
Supply decreased while demand increased, creating offsetting quantity effects.
q.commonError: Assuming an unchanged price means the market experienced no shifts.
q.feedback: A demand increase raises price and quantity, while a supply increase lowers price and raises quantity. Equal price effects can cancel while quantity rises.

key: The price effects offset, while both shifts raise equilibrium quantity.

q.q: At the current price, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied. What market condition exists?
options: A surplus exists because sellers offer more than buyers want.
A shortage exists because buyers want more than sellers offer.
The market is in equilibrium because both quantities are positive.
Demand must shift left before any price adjustment can occur.
q.commonError: Reversing shortage and surplus or treating disequilibrium as a curve shift.
q.feedback: When quantity demanded is greater than quantity supplied at the current price, the market has a shortage and upward price pressure.

key: A shortage exists because buyers want more than sellers offer.

q.q: What equilibrium price and quantity are shown in the displayed gas market?
options: $3 per gallon and 150 thousand gallons
$2 per gallon and 200 thousand gallons
$4 per gallon and 100 thousand gallons
$3 per gallon and 300 thousand gallons
q.feedback: D0 and S0 intersect at a price of $3 per gallon and a quantity of 150 thousand gallons.

key: $3 per gallon and 150 thousand gallons

q.q: Before either curve shifts, what equilibrium is formed by D0 and S0 in the displayed gas market?
options: $4 and 100 thousand units
$4 and 200 thousand units
$3 and 150 thousand units
$5 and 150 thousand units
q.feedback: The original curves D0 and S0 intersect at price $3 and quantity 150 thousand.

key: $3 and 150 thousand units

q.q: Refer to the graph. The market price starts at $2 and can adjust freely. Which pair of quantity changes would eliminate the initial imbalance with both curves fixed?
options: Quantity demanded falls 50 thousand gallons and quantity supplied rises 50 thousand gallons.
Quantity demanded rises 50 thousand gallons and quantity supplied falls 50 thousand gallons.
Quantity demanded falls 100 thousand gallons and quantity supplied stays fixed.
Demand shifts left 50 thousand gallons and supply shifts right 50 thousand gallons.
q.feedback: At $2, quantity demanded is 200 thousand and quantity supplied is 100 thousand. Price rises to the intersection at $3 and 150 thousand. Each side adjusts by 50 thousand along its existing curve.

key: Quantity demanded falls 50 thousand gallons and quantity supplied rises 50 thousand gallons.

q.q: Refer to the graph. A normal-good market moves from the D1/S1 intersection to the D0/S0 intersection. Which pair of events could explain that change, and what happens to price?
options: Consumer income rises and production becomes cheaper; price falls by $2.
Consumer income falls and production becomes more expensive; price rises by $2.
Consumer income falls and production becomes cheaper; price falls by $2.
Consumer income rises and production becomes more expensive; price rises by $2.
q.feedback: The two intersections have the same quantity, 150 thousand, but prices $5 and $3. D1 to D0 is lower demand, consistent with lower income for a normal good. S1 to S0 is higher supply, consistent with lower cost.

key: Consumer income falls and production becomes cheaper; price falls by $2.

q.q: Refer to the graph. Calculate the disequilibrium at $1 per gallon and explain the price pressure that follows from buyers' and sellers' incentives.
options: A 200-thousand surplus; downward price pressure
A 50-thousand shortage; no price pressure
A 250-thousand surplus; upward price pressure
A 200-thousand shortage; upward price pressure
q.feedback: Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied by 200 thousand gallons. A shortage gives buyers an incentive to bid price upward toward equilibrium.

key: A 200-thousand shortage; upward price pressure

q.q: Starting from D0/S0, suppose demand shifts to D1 while supply remains at S0. What intermediate equilibrium does the graph show?
options: $4 and 100 thousand units
$4 and 200 thousand units
$5 and 150 thousand units
$3 and 150 thousand units
q.feedback: D1 intersects the unchanged S0 curve at price $4 and quantity 200 thousand. A demand increase alone raises both equilibrium price and quantity.

key: $4 and 200 thousand units

q.q: Refer to the graph. Compare the market at $2 with the market at $4, then infer how the two opposite price-adjustment forces both move the market toward the $3 equilibrium.
options: Surplus at $2 pushes price down; shortage at $4 pushes price up.
Shortage at $2 pushes price up; surplus at $4 pushes price down.
Shortage at both prices pushes the market price steadily upward.
Surplus at both prices pushes the market price steadily downward.
q.feedback: A shortage creates upward price pressure and a surplus creates downward pressure. Both adjustment forces point toward the $3 equilibrium.

key: Shortage at $2 pushes price up; surplus at $4 pushes price down.

q.q: Refer to the graph. The market starts at D1/S1 and ends at D0/S0. Demand changes first while supply is initially fixed. Which sequence and explanation fit the graph?
options: First $4 and 200 thousand, then $3 and 150 thousand; demand falls before supply rises.
First $4 and 100 thousand, then $5 and 150 thousand; demand falls before supply falls.
First $3 and 150 thousand, then $4 and 100 thousand; supply rises before demand falls.
First $4 and 100 thousand, then $3 and 150 thousand; demand falls before supply rises.
q.feedback: The initial D1/S1 intersection is $5 and 150 thousand. Holding S1 fixed, lower demand takes the market to D0/S1 at $4 and 100 thousand. Higher supply then takes it to D0/S0 at $3 and 150 thousand.

key: First $4 and 100 thousand, then $3 and 150 thousand; demand falls before supply rises.

q.q: At a price of $2 per gallon in the displayed gas market, what imbalance exists?
options: A surplus of 100 thousand gallons
A shortage of 100 thousand gallons
A shortage of 200 thousand gallons
No shortage or surplus
q.feedback: At $2, quantity demanded is 200 thousand and quantity supplied is 100 thousand, so the shortage is 100 thousand gallons.

key: A shortage of 100 thousand gallons

q.q: Refer to the graph. At $4 per gallon, does the gas market have a shortage, a surplus, or equilibrium, and by how much?
options: A shortage of 100 thousand gallons
A surplus of 200 thousand gallons
A surplus of 100 thousand gallons
No shortage or surplus
q.feedback: At $4, quantity supplied is 200 thousand and quantity demanded is 100 thousand, so the surplus is 100 thousand gallons.

key: A surplus of 100 thousand gallons

q.q: Which pair of market changes is shown when the graph moves from D0/S0 to D1/S1?
options: Demand decreases while supply increases
Both demand and supply increase
Both demand and supply decrease
Demand increases while supply decreases
q.feedback: D1 is to the right of D0, indicating increased demand. S1 is to the left of S0, indicating decreased supply.

key: Demand increases while supply decreases

q.q: After both shifts shown in the graph, what equilibrium is formed by D1 and S1?
options: $5 and 150 thousand units
$3 and 150 thousand units
$4 and 100 thousand units
$4 and 200 thousand units
q.feedback: The new curves D1 and S1 intersect at price $5 and quantity 150 thousand.

key: $5 and 150 thousand units

q.q: With supply fixed at S0, which transition is an increase in demand?
options: D to A
A to B
C to B
D to C
q.imageAlt: The gasoline market has price in dollars vertically and quantity in thousands of gallons per day horizontally. D1 is right of D0 and S1 is left of S0. Intersections are A at D0-S1, quantity 150 and price 5; B at D1-S1, quantity 200 and price 6; C at D1-S0, quantity 250 and price 5; and D at D0-S0, quantity 200 and price 4.
q.feedback: D is D0-S0 and C is D1-S0.
q.graphDescription: The gasoline market has price in dollars vertically and quantity in thousands of gallons per day horizontally. D1 is right of D0 and S1 is left of S0. Intersections are A at D0-S1, quantity 150 and price 5; B at D1-S1, quantity 200 and price 6; C at D1-S0, quantity 250 and price 5; and D at D0-S0, quantity 200 and price 4.

key: D to C

q.q: With supply fixed at S1, which transition isolates increased demand?
options: D to A
D to C
A to B
C to B
q.imageAlt: The taco market has price vertically and quantity horizontally, without numeric tick labels. D1 is right of D0 and S1 is left of S0. A is D0-S1, B is D1-S1, C is D1-S0, and D is D0-S0. A is left of D, C is right of D, and B is vertically above D at the same quantity.
q.feedback: A is D0-S1 and B is D1-S1.
q.graphDescription: The taco market has price vertically and quantity horizontally, without numeric tick labels. D1 is right of D0 and S1 is left of S0. A is D0-S1, B is D1-S1, C is D1-S0, and D is D0-S0. A is left of D, C is right of D, and B is vertically above D at the same quantity.

key: A to B

q.q: Refer to the graph. At the $15 minimum wage, what labor surplus is created?
options: 100 thousand workers
50 thousand workers
150 thousand workers
250 thousand workers
q.imageAlt: The labor market has wage vertically and quantity in thousands of workers horizontally. D0 and S0 intersect at 200 thousand workers and 12 dollars. A wage floor at 15 dollars intersects demand at 150 thousand and supply at 250 thousand.
q.feedback: Labor supplied 250 minus labor demanded 150 equals 100 thousand.
q.graphDescription: The labor market has wage vertically and quantity in thousands of workers horizontally. D0 and S0 intersect at 200 thousand workers and 12 dollars. A wage floor at 15 dollars intersects demand at 150 thousand and supply at 250 thousand.

key: 100 thousand workers

q.q: A city subsidizes apartment construction while also imposing a binding rent ceiling. Which combined result is most likely?
options: More supply can ease—but not necessarily end—rationing under a binding ceiling.
The subsidy makes the ceiling irrelevant in all cases
The ceiling shifts demand left and eliminates scarcity
The policy must create a surplus because supply increases
q.feedback: A supply subsidy can ease shortage pressure, but a binding ceiling can still hold price below equilibrium and cause rationing.

key: More supply can ease—but not necessarily end—rationing under a binding ceiling.

q.q: A binding price ceiling and a tax both reduce market efficiency, but they do so differently. Which statement is correct?
options: A ceiling holds price below equilibrium, while a tax creates a wedge between buyer and seller prices
A ceiling always creates a surplus, while a tax always raises quantity
A tax eliminates scarcity, while a ceiling eliminates opportunity cost
Both policies are the same as a demand increase
q.feedback: A price ceiling directly limits price, while a tax creates a gap between what buyers pay and sellers receive.

key: A ceiling holds price below equilibrium, while a tax creates a wedge between buyer and seller prices

q.q: Which definition best captures an economic incentive?
options: Something that changes the costs or benefits of an action
A rule that removes meaningful choice from an action
The behavior observed after a policy is introduced
A market price recorded before a decision is made
q.feedback: Incentives alter the benefits or costs people consider when choosing.

key: Something that changes the costs or benefits of an action

q.q: A grocery store gives shoppers a reusable-bag credit. Which statement identifies the incentive rather than the response?
options: The credit raises the benefit of bringing a reusable bag
More shoppers bring reusable bags after the credit begins
The store uses fewer disposable bags by month end
Customers approve of the store’s environmental goal
q.commonError: Confusing the changed payoff with the behavior or outcome it may produce.
q.feedback: The credit is the incentive; bag use and waste reduction are possible responses and outcomes.

key: The credit raises the benefit of bringing a reusable bag

q.q: Gas prices rise and more consumers buy fuel-efficient cars. What principle does this show?
options: People respond to incentives
Consumers view fuel economy as unrelated to driving cost
Car buyers respond only after gasoline becomes unavailable
Higher gas prices directly increase the supply of every car
q.feedback: Higher gas prices create an incentive to change behavior.

key: People respond to incentives

q.q: A café doubles loyalty points for visits before 9 a.m. Which response would economic reasoning most directly predict?
options: Some customers become more likely to visit earlier
Every customer must switch to an early visit
The points matter only if converted directly to cash
Earlier visits prove customers approve of the café’s policy
q.commonError: Treating an incentive as a guarantee or requiring it to be cash.
q.feedback: Extra points raise the benefit of early visits, making that behavior more likely for some customers.

key: Some customers become more likely to visit earlier

q.q: A toll is added to a crowded bridge, and some drivers switch routes. What principle does this show?
options: The toll changes the relative cost of routes, prompting some drivers to substitute.
The toll increases bridge capacity, so diverted drivers are evidence of greater supply.
The toll shifts demand for every route equally, leaving relative travel costs unchanged.
The toll changes travel preferences, so monetary costs no longer explain route choice.
q.feedback: The toll raises one route’s cost relative to alternatives. Some drivers substitute; the policy does not itself expand capacity or change every route’s cost equally.

key: The toll changes the relative cost of routes, prompting some drivers to substitute.

q.q: A speed bonus makes workers finish faster, but quality falls. What does this illustrate?
options: The speed reward shifts effort toward measured completion and away from unmeasured quality.
The speed reward raises productivity equally on speed and quality, despite the observed quality decline.
The quality decline shows the reward was too small to influence the workers’ choices.
The faster output shows the reward improved the total value of work despite lower quality.
q.feedback: Workers respond on the rewarded margin, but may substitute away from unmeasured quality. Faster completion alone does not establish higher total value.

key: The speed reward shifts effort toward measured completion and away from unmeasured quality.

q.q: A city gives bus riders a $2 subsidy per ride. Ridership rises, but crowding increases and wait times get longer. What is the best interpretation?
options: The subsidy changed incentives and produced an unintended consequence
The subsidy eliminated scarcity
The subsidy created a price floor
The subsidy proves marginal analysis is irrelevant
q.feedback: The subsidy encouraged more bus use, but the higher ridership created crowding and longer waits.

key: The subsidy changed incentives and produced an unintended consequence

q.q: A policy gives every household $500 to increase spending. Some households spend it, but others save it. What does this show about incentives?
options: People may respond differently to the same incentive
The incentive has no opportunity cost
Markets cannot allocate resources
The policy must create a binding price ceiling
q.feedback: The same incentive can lead to different behavior depending on household needs, expectations, and constraints.

key: People may respond differently to the same incentive

q.q: A university raises parking fines. Students respond by arriving earlier, carpooling more, and contesting tickets more often. What principle ties these reactions together?
options: People respond to incentives, including unintended margins of adjustment
People ignore incentives when rules are created by institutions
Opportunity cost disappears when penalties are legal
Markets allocate resources only when prices are zero
q.feedback: A changed penalty changes behavior, including responses the policy designer may not have wanted.

key: People respond to incentives, including unintended margins of adjustment

q.q: A subscription service makes cancellation require a phone call but lets upgrades occur with one click. Cancellations fall and complaints rise. What is the strongest inference?
options: Exit friction can reduce cancellation despite dissatisfaction; easier upgrades do not remove the cost of leaving.
Stronger service preference best explains retention; complaints mainly show that retained users demand more service quality.
One-click upgrades best explain retention; the phone requirement mainly reallocates existing demand across service tiers.
The phone call screens out low-value cancellations; fewer cancellations therefore indicate higher consumer welfare.
q.commonError: Ignoring inconvenience as a cost or treating retention as complete success.
q.feedback: Retention can rise because leaving now costs more time, even when experience worsens. Neither upgraded service demand nor revealed preference for staying can be inferred without accounting for exit friction.

key: Exit friction can reduce cancellation despite dissatisfaction; easier upgrades do not remove the cost of leaving.

q.q: A repair subsidy pays for every completed repair. Claims rise sharply, but most claimants would have repaired anyway; some shops relabel routine servicing. What evidence best identifies the intended response?
options: Additional genuine repairs relative to comparable users without the subsidy
The total number of paid claims, treating each as a newly induced repair
The size of the subsidy budget, treating expenditure as added repair benefit
The stated repair goal, treating relabeling as evidence of no behavioral response
q.feedback: Separate newly induced repairs from payments for existing behavior and changes in reporting. Claims alone mix these margins and overstate the intended response.

key: Additional genuine repairs relative to comparable users without the subsidy

q.q: A software platform ranks creators by daily posting frequency. Posting rises, but creators split one useful guide into many thin updates. What does the response reveal?
options: The ranking rewards posting frequency, so creators can raise measured output while reducing useful content per post.
The ranking reveals stronger reader demand for short posts, so more posts establish an increase in information value.
The ranking lowers the cost of writing, so thinner posts indicate a productivity gain at unchanged information quality.
The ranking rewards guide quality indirectly, so splitting a guide raises both measured output and the original learning benefit.
q.commonError: Treating improvement in a measured target as improvement in the underlying objective.
q.feedback: Creators can substitute toward the measured posting count and away from unmeasured quality. More posts alone do not identify demand, productivity or learning gains.

key: The ranking rewards posting frequency, so creators can raise measured output while reducing useful content per post.

q.q: A city reduces bus fares to increase ridership. Ridership rises, but crowding makes some riders switch back to cars. What is the strongest lesson?
options: Lower fares attract riders, but congestion raises time costs and feeds back to reduce part of the initial ridership gain.
The initial fare response proves demand shifted right; riders returning to cars show the fare cut later shifted supply left.
Returning riders reveal more elastic money-price demand; their switch implies the initial ridership increase was measured incorrectly.
Crowding raises the service’s money price implicitly; the resulting ridership decline establishes that the fare policy reduced total welfare.
q.feedback: The fare cut lowers one part of the generalized travel cost while crowding raises another. Feedback can offset some ridership gains without contradicting demand theory or determining the net welfare result.

key: Lower fares attract riders, but congestion raises time costs and feeds back to reduce part of the initial ridership gain.

q.q: A town charges for trash bags and collects recycling free. Recycling tonnage rises, but contamination rises too. Which finding would best support successful conservation rather than merely relabeling disposal?
options: Residents report noticing the fee without any measured disposal change
Clean recovered materials rise and total discarded material falls in a comparable audit
Recycling collections rise even if processors reject the extra material
The town collects more bag-fee revenue regardless of waste volumes
q.commonError: Confusing the measured proxy with the underlying goal.
q.feedback: The price difference can induce conservation, sorting or misclassification. Clean recovery and lower total discards distinguish the intended outcomes from shifting trash into recycling bins.

key: Clean recovered materials rise and total discarded material falls in a comparable audit

q.q: A team earns a $20,000 bonus if quarterly sales exceed $1 million. It has $990,000 and can move $20,000 of January sales into December by offering a $2,000 discount. No extra annual units are sold; annual base commissions are unchanged. Which evaluation distinguishes the team’s incentive from the firm’s result?
options: The team gains $20,000 in bonus while the firm loses $22,000 from discount and bonus; higher quarterly sales need not mean higher annual value.
The team gains $18,000 in bonus while the firm gains $18,000; accelerated sales are additional annual revenue.
The team gains nothing because annual units are unchanged; the firm loses only the $2,000 discount.
The team gains $20,000 while the firm gains $18,000; the shifted January revenue is a new annual benefit.
q.commonError: Recognizing only one possible behavioral margin.
q.feedback: Timing crosses the threshold, generating the bonus without additional annual units. Relative to the unchanged annual baseline, the firm pays a $2,000 discount and $20,000 bonus, losing $22,000. The team responds rationally to a metric that need not align with firm value.

key: The team gains $20,000 in bonus while the firm loses $22,000 from discount and bonus; higher quarterly sales need not mean higher annual value.

q.q: An unemployed worker could accept a job paying $500 weekly with $100 of unavoidable weekly commuting cost. Benefits are $400 weekly in month one and $175 later, and stop upon employment. Ignoring other differences, how does the immediate net gain from accepting change, and what can be inferred about search?
options: The gain falls from $100 to $325 weekly; the later benefit cut weakens the incentive because it reduces income.
The gain rises from $0 to $225 weekly; the schedule strengthens the later financial incentive but does not uniquely determine effort.
The gain rises from $0 to $225 weekly; search effort must therefore rise by the same percentage for every worker.
The gain stays $400 weekly; accepting pays the same wage, so changing benefits cannot affect search incentives.
q.commonError: Missing that an incentive changes the next action’s marginal payoff.
q.feedback: The job nets 500-100=400 per week. Relative to benefits, the gain is 400-400=0 initially and 400-175=225 later. Constraints, expectations and preferences also affect search, so effort is not mechanically determined.

key: The gain rises from $0 to $225 weekly; the schedule strengthens the later financial incentive but does not uniquely determine effort.

q.q: A neighborhood app awards a visible badge for weekly recycling. Participation rises among users who value recognition but barely changes for others. What is the best interpretation?
options: A nonmonetary incentive can produce different responses across people
The badge guarantees recycling because everyone can see it
Recognition is not an incentive because no cash changes hands
Different responses prove the badge did not change any payoff
q.commonError: Assuming incentives must be monetary or produce uniform behavior.
q.feedback: Recognition can change expected benefits, while its importance varies across users.

key: A nonmonetary incentive can produce different responses across people

q.q: A new toll reduces traffic on a busy road. What does this show?
options: People respond to the higher cost of using the road
Scarcity has been eliminated
The road is now a public good
Demand for driving must have increased
q.feedback: The toll raises the cost of using the road, which gives drivers an incentive to change behavior.

key: People respond to the higher cost of using the road

q.q: A bonus tied only to sales volume causes excessive discounting. What happened?
options: Workers ignored the bonus and changed discounting for unrelated market reasons
Workers optimized the rewarded metric rather than total profit
The bonus eliminated every tradeoff involved in making sales
Sales volume became a public good shared equally by all firms
q.commonError: Evaluating the rewarded metric without examining its effect on total profit.
q.feedback: The bonus raises the payoff to volume even when discounts make some sales unprofitable.

key: Workers optimized the rewarded metric rather than total profit

q.q: A fee changes behavior for some people but not others. What is the best explanation?
options: The fee is not an incentive.
All people have identical marginal benefits.
People face different constraints, preferences, and alternatives.
Only laws create incentives.
q.commonError: Evaluating incentives without examining margins, metrics, or heterogeneity.
q.feedback: The same fee can change the relative attractiveness of an action by different amounts for different people. Someone with a close substitute may switch, while someone with few alternatives or a high benefit from the action may continue. An unchanged choice does not mean the fee created no incentive.

key: People face different constraints, preferences, and alternatives.

q.q: A policy subsidizes an action many people already planned to take. What limits additional impact?
options: Every payment creates an equal new action.
Subsidies cannot affect behavior.
The action has no opportunity cost.
Much of the spending is inframarginal rather than behavior-changing.
q.commonError: Evaluating incentives without examining margins, metrics, or heterogeneity.
q.feedback: People who would take the action without the subsidy can receive a payment without changing their behavior. Those payments are inframarginal: they support actions already planned rather than inducing additional ones. The policy’s additional impact depends on how many people change their choice because of the subsidy.

key: Much of the spending is inframarginal rather than behavior-changing.

q.q: A professor adds one point for each discussion post. How does the extra point affect the marginal decision to make one more post?
options: The extra point raises the marginal benefit of one more post
The total course grade becomes the cost of every post
Scarcity disappears once points are available
The added point guarantees that every post improves learning
q.commonError: Missing that an incentive changes the next action’s marginal payoff.
q.feedback: The added point changes the marginal benefit of submitting another post; quality is a separate outcome.

key: The extra point raises the marginal benefit of one more post

q.q: A workplace gives public recognition to teams that finish safety training. What does the recognition directly change?
options: The nonmonetary benefit of completing the training
The cash wage paid for every hour of training
The certainty that every employee completes training
The final safety outcome rather than the choice payoff
q.commonError: Treating incentive identification as vocabulary matching or assuming only cash matters.
q.feedback: Recognition can raise the perceived benefit of completing training without guaranteeing it.

key: The nonmonetary benefit of completing the training

q.q: A late fee is intended to:
options: Eliminate opportunity cost.
Reward late payment.
Raise the cost of delaying payment.
Make demand perfectly inelastic.
q.commonError: Reversing the intended direction of a penalty.
q.feedback: A late fee changes the payoff by making delay more costly.

key: Raise the cost of delaying payment.

q.q: A policy rewards hospitals for reducing readmissions. Hospitals improve follow-up care but also become reluctant to admit high-risk patients. What is the strongest evaluation?
options: Lower readmissions establish better care for the original patient population; admission changes are a separate efficiency gain.
High-risk avoidance explains the improvement completely; follow-up changes cannot independently contribute to the measured result.
Better follow-up establishes improved access; compare hospitals using raw readmission rates to retain the selection effect.
Improved follow-up and avoidance of risky patients can both lower readmissions; compare access and risk-adjusted outcomes.
q.commonError: Using one measured outcome as the complete policy verdict.
q.feedback: The bonus changes treatment effort and patient selection. Raw readmissions cannot separate these channels; risk adjustment and access evidence are needed.

key: Improved follow-up and avoidance of risky patients can both lower readmissions; compare access and risk-adjusted outcomes.

q.q: Why can a small probability of a severe penalty sometimes have little deterrent effect?
options: People may discount unlikely enforcement or misperceive the risk.
Only rewards influence behavior.
The expected cost is always equal to the maximum penalty.
Penalties have no opportunity cost.
q.feedback: Behavior depends on the expected and perceived consequence, not just the statutory maximum.

key: People may discount unlikely enforcement or misperceive the risk.

q.q: A tax credit for home improvements is claimed by many households that would have renovated anyway. Why might the credit generate relatively little additional renovation?
options: The credit has no budget cost.
A large share of payments does not change marginal behavior.
Households never respond to prices.
The policy creates a price floor.
q.commonError: Counting subsidized activity as caused by the subsidy.
q.feedback: An incentive is effective at the margin only when it changes decisions that otherwise would differ.

key: A large share of payments does not change marginal behavior.

q.q: The same dollar penalty sharply changes behavior for low-income households but barely affects high-income households. What does this show?
options: All people respond identically to a given dollar amount.
