The penalty is not an incentive.
Responses depend on constraints and the size of the incentive relative to resources.
Income has no role in marginal choices.
q.feedback: A fixed incentive can have different marginal importance for different decision-makers.

key: Responses depend on constraints and the size of the incentive relative to resources.

q.q: A school rewards perfect attendance, and some sick students attend class. This is:
options: Proof that incentives never work.
A positive externality by definition.
An elimination of scarcity.
An unintended response to the incentive.
q.commonError: Evaluating only the intended target behavior.
q.feedback: The reward increased attendance but also encouraged undesirable attendance while ill.

key: An unintended response to the incentive.

q.q: A performance bonus is based only on the number of calls handled, and service quality falls. What design problem occurred?
options: The metric rewarded quantity while omitting quality.
Workers ignored all incentives.
The bonus created a public good.
Higher output necessarily means higher quality.
q.commonError: Assuming the measured target captures the full objective.
q.feedback: People may optimize the rewarded metric at the expense of unmeasured goals.

key: The metric rewarded quantity while omitting quality.

q.q: Which statement best captures an economic incentive?
options: A change in expected benefits or costs that can alter behavior
Only a direct cash payment that rewards the intended behavior
A rule that guarantees every person makes the same choice
The final outcome observed after a policy is introduced
q.commonError: Defining incentives as cash only, guaranteed behavior, or final outcomes.
q.feedback: An incentive changes the payoff to a choice; it need not be monetary or guarantee a result.

key: A change in expected benefits or costs that can alter behavior

q.q: Which statement describes an unintended response to an incentive?
options: A planned result that occurs exactly as policy designers expected
People respond to a rule in a way that produces an unplanned result
Evidence that the original rule created no behavioral pressure at all
A response that every person makes in exactly the same way
q.commonError: Treating an unplanned response as proof that no incentive existed.
q.feedback: People can respond to the changed payoff while producing a side effect the designer did not intend.

key: People respond to a rule in a way that produces an unplanned result

q.q: Scarcity forces a student to choose between work and study. How can a higher wage create an incentive?
options: It raises the opportunity cost of study relative to work
It eliminates the need to choose between uses of time
It guarantees the student stops studying
It changes scarcity into abundance
q.commonError: Missing how a changed alternative payoff alters a scarce-resource choice.
q.feedback: With limited time, the higher wage makes study more costly in forgone earnings.

key: It raises the opportunity cost of study relative to work

q.q: A fee makes one more downtown trip costlier. How does marginal analysis describe the incentive?
options: It raises the marginal cost of the next trip
It raises the total benefit of every past trip
It guarantees no one travels downtown
It removes the opportunity cost of alternatives
q.commonError: Using totals instead of the changed payoff on the next action.
q.feedback: The fee alters the next trip’s marginal cost, which can change the decision.

key: It raises the marginal cost of the next trip

q.q: When a product’s price rises, buyers purchase less while sellers offer more. What common connection explains both responses?
options: The price change creates different incentives for buyers and sellers
Buyers and sellers face identical benefits from the higher price
The higher price guarantees every buyer exits the market
Supply and demand responses require moral approval of the price
q.commonError: Assuming one price creates the same directional incentive on both sides.
q.feedback: A higher price raises buyer cost while raising seller benefit.

key: The price change creates different incentives for buyers and sellers

q.q: A policy aims to reduce congestion but rewards agencies only for bus tickets sold. What problem can this funding rule create?
options: The rewarded measure may redirect behavior away from the stated policy objective
A stated goal automatically determines the behavioral margin
Ticket sales are identical to reduced congestion
An incentive exists only after congestion falls
q.commonError: Confusing a stated purpose, measured target, and final outcome.
q.feedback: Policy design must align the payoff with the behavior and outcome actually sought.

key: The rewarded measure may redirect behavior away from the stated policy objective

q.q: A library begins charging a late fee. What response becomes more likely?
options: More borrowers return books on time
Every borrower returns every book early
Borrowers view late returns as more rewarding
The fee guarantees that no book is ever late
q.commonError: Turning a likely directional response into guaranteed compliance.
q.feedback: The fee raises the cost of delay, so timely return becomes more likely.

key: More borrowers return books on time

q.q: A school offers preferred event seating to students with strong attendance. What kind of payoff changed?
options: A nonmonetary benefit of attending school
The cash wage paid for attending school
The legal penalty for missing school
The final attendance outcome itself
q.commonError: Assuming only direct cash changes can be incentives.
q.feedback: Preferred seating is a noncash benefit that can make attendance more attractive.

key: A nonmonetary benefit of attending school

q.q: A city adds a refundable deposit to beverage bottles. Which choice identifies the incentive?
options: Recovering the deposit by returning the bottle
The number of bottles ultimately recycled
Public support for cleaner streets
A guarantee that every bottle is returned
q.commonError: Confusing the incentive with the eventual recycling outcome.
q.feedback: The refund changes the benefit of returning a bottle; recycling is a possible result.

key: Recovering the deposit by returning the bottle

q.q: A sales representative earns a commission on each completed sale. What does the commission directly do?
options: Raises the benefit of completing another sale
Guarantees that every customer will buy
Makes product quality irrelevant to buyers
Removes the representative’s opportunity costs
q.commonError: Treating a stronger payoff as certain success.
q.feedback: A commission increases the expected benefit of another sale without guaranteeing it.

key: Raises the benefit of completing another sale

q.q: An insurer raises the copay for an optional clinic visit. Holding other factors fixed, patients are most likely to:
options: Become less likely to schedule the visit
Schedule every optional visit immediately
Ignore the copay because costs are not incentives
Treat the copay as a reward for using care
q.commonError: Reversing the response to a higher out-of-pocket cost.
q.feedback: The higher copay raises the cost of the visit, tending to reduce its use.

key: Become less likely to schedule the visit

q.q: A shop offers free shipping only on orders above $50. Which behavior does the threshold encourage?
options: Adding items to bring some orders above $50
Reducing every order below $50
Buying exactly the same basket in every case
Avoiding online shopping regardless of preferences
q.commonError: Ignoring the behavioral pressure created near a threshold.
q.feedback: Customers near $50 gain free shipping by adding items, so basket size may rise.

key: Adding items to bring some orders above $50

q.q: A store offers a one-day discount on umbrellas before a storm. What response is most directly predicted?
options: Some customers become more likely to buy that day
Every shopper buys an umbrella
The discount guarantees the store earns more profit
Customers must morally approve of discounts
q.commonError: Treating a lower price as a guaranteed purchase or profit outcome.
q.feedback: The discount raises the relative benefit of buying now for some customers.

key: Some customers become more likely to buy that day

q.q: A nonprofit grant rewards clients placed in jobs for 30 days. Providers avoid applicants needing intensive support and favor easy placements. Which redesign best preserves effort while limiting selection?
options: Reward sustained outcomes while adjusting targets for client difficulty
Pay only for the raw number of 30-day placements
Remove all performance information from funding decisions
Assume selection disappears when providers share the mission
q.commonError: Using an unadjusted proxy that rewards selection instead of underlying impact.
q.feedback: Longer outcomes and risk adjustment better align the measured target with the mission.

key: Reward sustained outcomes while adjusting targets for client difficulty

q.q: An energy plan combines a peak-hour surcharge, a monthly conservation badge, and a rebate for smart thermostats. Which analysis is strongest?
options: The surcharge targets peak timing, the badge targets status, and the rebate changes equipment cost; responses depend on constraints.
The surcharge and badge both reward lower total use, while the rebate leaves the cost of conservation equipment unchanged.
The rebate targets peak timing, the surcharge targets equipment purchase, and the badge reveals each household’s willingness to pay.
The three measures all lower the same marginal electricity price, so peak-use changes identify their separate contributions.
q.commonError: Collapsing several incentives and response margins into one guaranteed outcome.
q.feedback: These incentives operate on different margins: timing, social recognition and equipment adoption. Neither a uniform response nor lower total consumption follows from a peak-use decline.

key: The surcharge targets peak timing, the badge targets status, and the rebate changes equipment cost; responses depend on constraints.

q.q: A hospital bonus rewards low average treatment cost. Managers discharge patients earlier, but readmissions rise. Which redesign best aligns the incentive with patient outcomes?
options: Include readmissions and health outcomes alongside treatment cost
Increase the reward for low initial cost alone
Judge success only by the number of discharges
Remove monitoring because outcomes vary across patients
q.commonError: Rewarding a narrow cost metric that omits downstream outcomes.
q.feedback: A broader measure reduces the payoff to cost cutting that shifts expense or harm into readmissions.

key: Include readmissions and health outcomes alongside treatment cost

q.q: A fine rises from $100 to $500 while the actual probability of detection falls from 80% to 10%. Drivers are risk neutral and understand those probabilities. Reform C instead keeps the $500 fine and restores detection to 20%. Which comparison of expected penalties is correct?
options: The initial change lowers expected penalty from $80 to $50; C raises it to $100, strengthening deterrence relative to both earlier rules.
The initial change raises expected penalty from $80 to $500; C lowers it to $100 because more detection reduces risk.
The initial change leaves expected penalty at $80; C leaves it unchanged because headline fines determine all deterrence.
The initial change lowers expected penalty from $100 to $50; C restores it only if every violator is detected.
q.feedback: Expected penalty equals probability times fine: 0.8×100=80, 0.1×500=50 and 0.2×500=100. Under the stated behavior assumptions, the headline fine increase can weaken deterrence if detection falls sufficiently.

key: The initial change lowers expected penalty from $80 to $50; C raises it to $100, strengthening deterrence relative to both earlier rules.

q.q: A university funds departments for graduates employed within 30 days. Programs steer students toward quick-placement jobs and away from longer searches for better matches. What is the central design problem?
options: The measured deadline rewards placement speed rather than match quality
Employment funding cannot influence advising behavior
Quick placement guarantees the best long-run outcome
The stated career goal prevents any unintended response
q.commonError: Confusing the measured proxy with the underlying goal.
q.feedback: Departments gain from hitting the short deadline even if longer searches would improve matches.

key: The measured deadline rewards placement speed rather than match quality

q.q: A conservation policy combines a usage fee, public recognition, and exemptions for medical needs. Which assessment is most defensible?
options: Different households face different effective incentives, so response and burden will vary
The usage fee guarantees identical reductions for all households
Recognition is irrelevant because it is not money
Exemptions prove the policy has no behavioral effect
q.commonError: Ignoring multiple incentive types, constraints, and exemptions.
q.feedback: Prices, status, and exemptions change payoffs differently across households.

key: Different households face different effective incentives, so response and burden will vary

q.q: A hospital is paid for each procedure but penalized for readmissions. Which response best reflects both incentives?
options: It may increase profitable procedures while investing in follow-up that lowers readmissions
It must reduce every procedure because penalties dominate rewards
It will ignore follow-up entirely because only direct procedure payments can ever affect hospital behavior
The payment design guarantees the socially optimal treatment mix
q.commonError: Reasoning from only one component of a multi-part payment system.
q.feedback: Procedure payments and readmission penalties act on different behavioral margins.

key: It may increase profitable procedures while investing in follow-up that lowers readmissions

q.q: A school rewards high test pass rates. Administrators shift tutoring toward students just below the cutoff and away from students far behind. What is the strongest interpretation?
options: A threshold metric changes where effort has the highest measured payoff
The reward guarantees equal gains for every student
Tutoring shifts prove the pass-rate reward was not an incentive
The stated goal determines behavior more than the measured target
q.commonError: Ignoring how a cutoff redirects effort across people.
q.feedback: Effort near the pass threshold produces the largest measured return, even if broader learning is the goal.

key: A threshold metric changes where effort has the highest measured payoff

q.q: An environmental fee applies only when emissions exceed a monthly cap. A factory shifts production between months to remain below the cap without lowering annual emissions. What happened?
options: The threshold changed timing rather than the underlying annual outcome
The fee created no incentive because annual emissions stayed constant
Any legal response must satisfy the policy’s broader objective
A fee cannot affect production timing
q.commonError: Equating compliance with the measured threshold to achievement of the ultimate goal.
q.feedback: The incentive altered the monitored margin while leaving annual emissions unchanged.

key: The threshold changed timing rather than the underlying annual outcome

q.q: A procurement office rewards the lowest bid and later faces frequent change orders. Which redesign most directly addresses the incentive problem?
options: Evaluate expected total cost and performance, not the opening bid alone
Raise the reward for submitting any low opening bid regardless of later change orders
Ignore change orders because the initial metric improved
Require every bidder to choose the same production method
q.commonError: Rewarding a proxy that omits costly dimensions of the true objective.
q.feedback: A broader metric reduces the payoff to lowballing the initial bid and recovering revenue later.

key: Evaluate expected total cost and performance, not the opening bid alone

q.q: A deductible rises from $100 to $1,000. Which prediction is best without knowing patient income, health risk, or alternatives?
options: Use of covered services tends to fall, but response size can vary widely
Every patient reduces covered care by exactly the same percentage after the deductible change
No response is possible because insurance already exists
The higher deductible guarantees better health decisions
q.commonError: Inferring an identical or guaranteed response from a common price change.
q.feedback: The higher out-of-pocket cost creates directional pressure, while circumstances shape magnitude.

key: Use of covered services tends to fall, but response size can vary widely

q.q: A police department rewards citation counts. Citations rise, public trust falls, and serious-case work receives less time. Which conclusion is warranted?
options: The metric changed behavior but did not capture the department’s full objective
Falling trust proves the citation reward cannot influence officer behavior or case priorities in any meaningful way
More citations establish that public safety necessarily improved
Economic analysis requires moral approval of the reward
q.commonError: Treating a rewarded count as identical to the underlying public objective.
q.feedback: The reward affects behavior, but the observed metric omits trust and case importance.

key: The metric changed behavior but did not capture the department’s full objective

q.q: A teacher bonus depends on class-average scores. Teachers provide extra review but also discourage low-performing students from testing. What should an evaluator conclude?
options: Higher scores may reflect both extra instruction and changed test participation; compare learning for the original student group.
Higher scores measure extra instruction if bonuses are uniform; excluding weak students then represents improved classroom efficiency.
Changed participation fully explains higher scores; extra review has no independent effect once selection incentives exist.
Average scores remain comparable across years if the test is unchanged; student participation changes affect only the sample size.
q.commonError: Looking only at the intended response or only at the side effect.
q.feedback: The bonus rewards a measured average. Instruction and selection can both change it, so following the original group is needed to distinguish learning from compositional change.

key: Higher scores may reflect both extra instruction and changed test participation; compare learning for the original student group.

q.q: A university receives funding for degrees completed on time. Advising improves, but difficult required courses are weakened. What is the strongest interpretation?
options: Funding rewards completion speed, so advising effort and lower course standards can both improve the metric without equal learning gains.
Funding rewards educational quality, so faster completion and easier courses jointly establish more learning per enrolled student.
Easier courses explain completion gains entirely, so advising improvements cannot contribute to the measured funding outcome.
Faster completion reduces students’ time costs, so course standards have no additional role in evaluating the policy’s net benefit.
q.commonError: Equating the observable target with the complete educational objective.
q.feedback: A completion metric can reward both useful advising and weakened standards. Evaluating educational success requires learning evidence in addition to completion and time savings.

key: Funding rewards completion speed, so advising effort and lower course standards can both improve the metric without equal learning gains.

q.q: A congestion charge is announced, but drivers believe cameras identify only 5% of violators. Which factor most limits deterrence?
options: The low perceived probability of paying the charge
The charge is negative rather than positive
Driving has benefits as well as costs
A legal charge cannot change expected costs
q.commonError: Ignoring perceived enforcement when evaluating an incentive’s strength.
q.feedback: The expected cost depends on both the charge and the chance it is imposed.

key: The low perceived probability of paying the charge

q.q: A health insurer waives copays for preventive visits but raises emergency-room copays. Which response is most defensible?
options: Lower preventive prices and higher emergency prices encourage substitution, but access and urgent needs constrain which patients can switch.
The price changes chiefly reduce total visits; patients with limited preventive access can substitute as readily as other patients.
The preventive subsidy raises income rather than relative prices; changes in emergency use therefore identify only the copay increase.
Emergency use should fall most for unavoidable acute cases; elective preventive care is least responsive to the lower copay.
q.commonError: Predicting certain, uniform substitution from a common payment schedule.
q.feedback: Relative prices favor prevention, but substitution requires access and medical feasibility. Acute emergencies and barriers to preventive care limit the response.

key: Lower preventive prices and higher emergency prices encourage substitution, but access and urgent needs constrain which patients can switch.

q.q: A city pays restaurants for each kilogram of food donated. Donations rise, but some restaurants overproduce near closing time. What does this show?
options: The payment rewards donated kilograms, so it can induce both recovery of surplus food and production that would not otherwise occur.
The payment rewards avoided waste, so additional production confirms that previously wasted food has been redirected efficiently.
Overproduction indicates stronger final-consumer demand; donated kilograms are therefore unrelated to the payment’s production incentive.
Donations transfer food between users, so extra production costs cancel from welfare whenever recipients value the donated meals.
q.commonError: Assuming intended and unintended responses cannot occur together.
q.feedback: A per-kilogram subsidy raises the payoff to donating both existing surplus and newly produced food. The value of donations must be weighed against added production resources and waste.

key: The payment rewards donated kilograms, so it can induce both recovery of surplus food and production that would not otherwise occur.

q.q: A housing program withdraws $1 of aid for each $1 of additional earnings over a threshold. Which behavioral pressure follows?
options: Earning just above the threshold may provide little immediate net gain
Every recipient stops working completely
The rule rewards every additional dollar of earnings with an equal dollar of net income
Aid withdrawal is an outcome rather than an incentive
q.commonError: Ignoring how benefit withdrawal changes the payoff to extra earnings.
q.feedback: The phaseout can sharply reduce the net benefit of crossing the earnings threshold.

key: Earning just above the threshold may provide little immediate net gain

q.q: A credit card offers triple points for travel. One customer travels more; another keeps the same trips and switches cards. What is the lesson?
options: The same reward can change different margins for different consumers
Only the customer who travels more responded to the incentive
A reward is ineffective unless total travel rises for everyone
Card switching cannot be an incentive response
q.commonError: Recognizing only one possible behavioral margin.
q.feedback: The reward can affect travel quantity, payment choice, or neither, depending on alternatives.

key: The same reward can change different margins for different consumers

q.q: A factory posts team safety rankings without cash prizes. Reporting rises, but some teams relabel minor incidents as near misses. Which conclusion is best?
options: Status rewards can change reporting and relabeling; independently measured injuries are needed to identify real safety improvement.
Higher reporting shows actual injuries increased; relabeling minor cases changes only terminology and not the measured ranking.
Relabeling improves risk classification; higher ranking positions therefore identify better safety even without independent injury data.
Noncash status rewards mainly reveal team preferences; higher reported safety establishes that effort rose equally across teams.
q.commonError: Ignoring status incentives or unmeasured changes in classification.
q.feedback: Rankings can motivate reporting and gaming without cash payments. The stem establishes changed records, not improved reporting accuracy or fewer injuries; independent injury evidence is needed.

key: Status rewards can change reporting and relabeling; independently measured injuries are needed to identify real safety improvement.

q.q: A charity matches the first $100 of each donation. A donor planning to give $300 still gives $300. How should the match be evaluated for that donor?
options: It transfers funds but does not change this donor’s marginal giving decision
It necessarily causes an additional $100 donation
The donor did not face an incentive because the entire planned gift amount was chosen before the match
The match reduces the benefit of donating
q.commonError: Counting all subsidized activity as behavior caused by the incentive.
q.feedback: The match applies to the gift, but this donor’s amount is unchanged relative to the alternative.

key: It transfers funds but does not change this donor’s marginal giving decision

q.q: A platform threatens suspension for false listings, but enforcement reviews only complaints from paying users. What response is most plausible?
options: Expected sanctions differ by customer group, so sellers may redirect deception toward users whose complaints do not trigger review.
A uniform suspension penalty creates equal deterrence across users, so different complaint review rules mainly affect paperwork.
Paying users receive more review, so sellers face a stronger incentive to deceive them in order to cover expected sanctions.
The threat discourages entry by dishonest sellers, so surviving sellers’ choices between user groups are unaffected by enforcement.
q.commonError: Ignoring how selective enforcement redirects behavior.
q.feedback: Expected sanctions combine the penalty with the probability of review. Restricting review to paying-user complaints changes the relative payoff to targeting other users.

key: Expected sanctions differ by customer group, so sellers may redirect deception toward users whose complaints do not trigger review.

q.q: A government contract pays builders for finishing early and penalizes visible defects, but not hidden maintenance problems. What risk remains?
options: Rewards cover speed and observable defects, so effort can shift from hidden durability toward the measured dimensions.
The defect penalty prices all quality losses, so earlier completion also establishes greater hidden durability.
The speed reward and defect penalty create opposing incentives, so their combined effect on effort must be zero.
Maintenance is paid later, so hidden durability is a sunk cost and should be excluded from evaluating the contract.
q.commonError: Assuming measured dimensions represent total performance.
q.feedback: When hidden maintenance problems are not penalized, the contract can reward speed and visible quality while encouraging substitution away from durability. Later costs are not thereby sunk.

key: Rewards cover speed and observable defects, so effort can shift from hidden durability toward the measured dimensions.

q.q: A farm subsidy pays per acre planted with one crop. Farmers expand acreage onto less suitable land. Which part is the incentive and which is the response?
options: Per-acre payment is the incentive; expansion onto marginal land is a response
Expanded acreage is the incentive; payment is the outcome
Crop suitability is the incentive; planting is moral approval
The subsidy is neither because planting was already possible
q.commonError: Interchanging a payoff change with the behavior it induces.
q.feedback: The payment changes the benefit of each planted acre; land expansion is a resulting choice.

key: Per-acre payment is the incentive; expansion onto marginal land is a response

q.q: An employer replaces a late-arrival reprimand with a small fee deducted from pay. Some workers become more punctual; others treat lateness as a purchasable option. What does this show?
options: The fee changes both the monetary consequence and its perceived social meaning, allowing deterrence for some and purchased lateness for others.
The fee lowers the monetary cost for every worker, so mixed punctuality must reflect differences in measured arrival times.
The fee strengthens social disapproval for every worker, so treating lateness as purchased shows workers no longer respond to payoffs.
The fee converts lateness into a market transaction, so workers’ prior response to social reprimands is irrelevant to the change.
q.commonError: Assuming monetary and social consequences are interchangeable for everyone.
q.feedback: Replacing a reprimand can alter both financial incentives and social meaning. Responses can differ because workers value money and social sanctions differently.

key: The fee changes both the monetary consequence and its perceived social meaning, allowing deterrence for some and purchased lateness for others.

q.q: A transit agency offers off-peak discounts. Flexible riders shift trips, while shift workers cannot. Which evaluation is strongest?
options: The price incentive changes trip timing mainly for riders with feasible alternatives
The discount is not an incentive because some riders cannot respond
All riders receive identical benefits from changing travel time
The policy guarantees total ridership will rise
q.commonError: Treating inability to respond as evidence that no incentive exists.
q.feedback: The discount changes relative prices, but schedule constraints determine who can act on it.

key: The price incentive changes trip timing mainly for riders with feasible alternatives

q.q: A streaming service removes a cancellation fee but adds a loyalty reward after twelve months. Which margin is most directly affected?
options: The relative payoff to staying through the twelfth month
The quality of every program on the service
The certainty that all subscribers remain
Subscribers’ moral judgment of loyalty programs
q.commonError: Confusing the targeted retention choice with broad outcomes or approval.
q.feedback: The reward changes the benefit of remaining until a specific time threshold.

key: The relative payoff to staying through the twelfth month

q.q: A warranty pays repair shops a flat amount per claim. Shops begin avoiding complex claims and completing simple ones quickly. What caused the pattern?
options: A uniform payment changes the payoff differently for low-cost and high-cost claims
The flat payment guarantees equal service across claims
Avoiding difficult cases proves payments cannot affect selection
Claim complexity is irrelevant whenever prices are fixed
q.commonError: Ignoring how a common payment creates heterogeneous margins across cases.
q.feedback: Simple claims become more profitable relative to complex ones, encouraging selection.

key: A uniform payment changes the payoff differently for low-cost and high-cost claims

q.q: A sports contract pays a large bonus for games played. An injured athlete returns early and performs poorly. Which conclusion is most defensible?
options: The bonus increased pressure to play but did not guarantee a beneficial outcome
The poor performance proves the bonus was not an incentive
Bonuses influence effort but never participation decisions
Playing establishes that the athlete approved of the contract design
q.commonError: Equating a behavioral response with a desirable or certain result.
q.feedback: The bonus changed the payoff to participation, while health and performance remained uncertain.

key: The bonus increased pressure to play but did not guarantee a beneficial outcome

q.q: A nonprofit grant rewards the number of people enrolled, not services completed. Enrollment rises and completion falls. Which measure is being optimized?
options: The funded enrollment count rather than the broader service objective
Completion because it is the organization’s stated mission
Both measures equally because they concern the same clients
Neither measure because nonprofits do not respond to funding
q.commonError: Assuming mission statements dominate the payoff attached to a measured target.
q.feedback: The grant rewards entry into the program, so effort shifts toward enrollment rather than completion.

key: The funded enrollment count rather than the broader service objective

q.q: A delivery platform guarantees a minimum hourly payment only while drivers are actively carrying orders. Which response is plausible?
options: Drivers may favor longer trips or avoid unpaid waiting when choosing orders
Every driver accepts the shortest available trip
The guarantee removes all opportunity costs of time
Payment rules cannot change which orders drivers select
q.commonError: Ignoring how compensation changes the opportunity cost of time and order selection.
q.feedback: The rule changes which activities count as paid time, altering the relative payoff to orders.

key: Drivers may favor longer trips or avoid unpaid waiting when choosing orders

q.q: A city raises water prices after a monthly allowance and also publishes neighborhood conservation rankings. What response should be expected?
options: Price and status pressures may reduce use by different amounts across households
The ranking is irrelevant because only prices are incentives
Every household cuts water use by the same quantity
Lower use is guaranteed wherever both incentives exist
q.commonError: Assuming one incentive type matters or that responses are uniform.
q.feedback: Both monetary cost and social comparison can affect use, with varied strength.

key: Price and status pressures may reduce use by different amounts across households

q.q: A criminal fine is tripled while the probability of detection falls by two-thirds. Without more information, what can be concluded?
options: Expected monetary penalties are unchanged, while perceived detection and risk attitudes can still alter deterrence.
Expected monetary penalties triple, while lower detection only changes the timing of the payment.
Expected monetary penalties fall by two-thirds, while the larger fine affects only the maximum possible loss.
Expected monetary penalties are unchanged, so deterrence must remain unchanged for every risk attitude.
q.commonError: Using only penalty size or only detection probability.
q.feedback: If detection falls to one-third and the fine triples, probability times fine is unchanged. Equal expected money costs do not establish equal perceived or risk-adjusted deterrence.

key: Expected monetary penalties are unchanged, while perceived detection and risk attitudes can still alter deterrence.

q.q: A news site pays writers for clicks, excluding later subscriptions. A sensational headline yields 10,000 more clicks than a sober version and $200 more advertising revenue, but is expected to lose renewals worth $350. Writers expect higher pay from the sensational headline. Which diagnosis and redesign fit?
options: The metric rewards a privately attractive choice that lowers expected site revenue by $150; include retention-adjusted value rather than clicks alone.
The extra clicks raise site revenue by $200 net of renewals; retain the click metric because readers revealed stronger demand.
The lost renewals show writers ignored the incentive; raise the click rate to align their choices with longer-run subscriptions.
The headline lowers site revenue by $550; replace performance pay with a renewal count that ignores advertising value.
q.commonError: Treating a short-run proxy as the complete objective.
q.feedback: Incremental site revenue is 200-350=-150, while click-based pay still rewards the writer. A combined value measure addresses both margins; neither clicks nor renewals alone captures the full comparison.

key: The metric rewards a privately attractive choice that lowers expected site revenue by $150; include retention-adjusted value rather than clicks alone.

q.q: Two households each use 10 peak-hour energy units. A $5 surcharge per unit leads a flexible household to shift 6 units off peak, but a household using continuous medical equipment cannot shift any. A proposed $50 lump-sum credit is independent of peak use. Which evaluation is correct?
options: The surcharge cuts combined peak use by 6 units; the credit relieves bills but preserves the $5 marginal incentive and does not remove the medical constraint.
The surcharge cuts combined peak use by 10 units; the credit removes the $5 marginal incentive for both households.
The surcharge cuts combined peak use by 6 units; a $50 credit necessarily restores the flexible household’s original peak usage.
The surcharge has no incentive effect on the medical household; its unchanged use proves it bears no additional economic cost.
q.commonError: Assuming identical responses or denying an incentive when response is constrained.
q.feedback: Combined peak use falls from 20 to 14. A lump-sum credit does not refund the next peak unit, so the marginal surcharge remains $5. Physical constraints can prevent substitution despite higher cost.

key: The surcharge cuts combined peak use by 6 units; the credit relieves bills but preserves the $5 marginal incentive and does not remove the medical constraint.

q.q: A firm can gain $900 from violating a rule. Detection is currently 10% and the fine is $4,000. Reform A doubles the fine; reform B raises detection to 30% with the original fine. For a risk-neutral firm maximizing expected monetary payoff, which reform deters the violation?
options: Only B: A leaves a $100 expected gain, while B creates a $300 expected loss.
Only A: A creates a $3,100 expected loss, while B leaves a $600 expected gain.
Both: either a larger fine or more inspection necessarily makes expected violation payoff negative.
Neither: the $900 benefit exceeds the detection probability under both reforms.
q.commonError: Focusing on statutory severity rather than expected enforcement.
q.feedback: Current expected penalty is 0.10×4000=400. Under A it is 800, leaving 900-800=100. Under B it is 1200, leaving -300. Compare expected penalties with the benefit rather than headline fines alone.

key: Only B: A leaves a $100 expected gain, while B creates a $300 expected loss.

q.q: A salesperson earns $200 per completed sale but repays it if the product is returned. A risky sale has a 50% return probability and takes effort worth $80. A suitable sale has a 10% return probability and takes effort worth $120. Which choice maximizes expected net commission, and what if chargebacks are removed?
options: With chargebacks choose suitable ($60 versus $20); without them choose risky ($120 versus $80).
With chargebacks choose risky ($120 versus $80); without them choose suitable ($60 versus $20).
Choose risky under both rules because the headline commission is the same and its effort cost is lower.
Choose suitable under both rules because a lower return probability always outweighs any difference in effort.
q.commonError: Considering the reward while ignoring the contingent penalty.
q.feedback: Expected commissions net of effort are 200(0.5)-80=20 and 200(0.9)-120=60. Without repayment they become 200-80=120 and 200-120=80. The return rule changes which sale is privately attractive.

key: With chargebacks choose suitable ($60 versus $20); without them choose risky ($120 versus $80).

q.q: Two jobs have identical duties and working hours. On-site work pays $900 weekly but requires $80 travel spending and 8 travel hours valued at $15 each. Remote work pays $760 with no commute. Which job has the higher net weekly value, and what if travel time falls to 2 hours?
options: Remote leads by $60 initially; after the shorter commute on-site leads by $30.
On-site leads by $140 initially; after the shorter commute it still leads by $140.
Remote leads by $20 initially; after the shorter commute on-site leads by $90.
Remote leads by $60 initially; after the shorter commute it still leads by $60.
q.commonError: Looking only for explicit cash rewards and missing a changed alternative cost.
q.feedback: Initially on-site nets 900-80-8×15=700 versus 760 remotely. With two travel hours it nets 900-80-30=790. A noncash time-cost change can reverse the ranking without a salary change.

key: Remote leads by $60 initially; after the shorter commute on-site leads by $30.

q.q: A clinic receives $20 per reported vaccination. Reports rise from 1,000 to 1,300. An independent audit finds 200 duplicate entries and 1,100 distinct vaccinations; comparable unfunded clinics’ distinct vaccinations rose 5%. If the same trend would have applied, which estimate and incentive diagnosis are strongest?
options: About 50 distinct vaccinations above the 1,050 counterfactual; paying for verified unique patients would reduce rewards for duplicate records.
About 300 distinct vaccinations above baseline; paying for verified unique patients would remove the incentive for useful outreach.
About 100 distinct vaccinations caused by funding; the comparison clinics are irrelevant once an audit verifies the total.
About 250 distinct vaccinations above the counterfactual; duplicate entries are a transfer and should be counted as health benefits.
q.commonError: Equating the rewarded record count with the final health outcome.
q.feedback: The trend-based counterfactual is 1000×1.05=1050. Audited unique vaccinations exceed it by 50, not by the 300 extra reports. Verification reduces the payoff from gaming the record count while retaining a reward for real delivery.

key: About 50 distinct vaccinations above the 1,050 counterfactual; paying for verified unique patients would reduce rewards for duplicate records.

q.q: A warehouse pays a bonus for packages shipped per hour but charges workers for verified damage. What response is most plausible?
options: Workers balance speed against the expected cost of damage
Workers maximize speed because only rewards affect behavior
Damage must fall to zero for the incentives to exist
Every worker chooses the same speed regardless of risk
q.commonError: Considering one incentive while ignoring a simultaneous opposing incentive.
q.feedback: The speed bonus and damage consequence change different parts of the worker’s payoff.

key: Workers balance speed against the expected cost of damage

q.q: A parking fine doubles, but patrols become rare. Why might violations change little?
options: The expected penalty may remain small because enforcement is unlikely
A larger statutory fine can never affect behavior when drivers know it exists
Drivers respond only to rewards, not penalties
Low enforcement guarantees more violations by every driver
q.commonError: Looking only at the posted penalty and ignoring enforcement probability.
q.feedback: Behavior responds to the expected consequence, which depends on both size and enforcement.

key: The expected penalty may remain small because enforcement is unlikely

q.q: Two employees receive the same attendance bonus. One changes her schedule; the other has caregiving duties and cannot. What does this show?
options: The same incentive can produce different responses under different constraints
The bonus was not an incentive for either employee because their outcomes differed
A valid incentive must change everyone’s behavior
Constraints matter only when incentives are nonmonetary
q.commonError: Assuming identical payoffs generate identical responses.
q.feedback: The bonus changes payoffs, but constraints and alternatives shape each response.

key: The same incentive can produce different responses under different constraints

q.q: A delivery app rewards acceptance rate. Some drivers accept poor-fit jobs and cancel later. Which design issue appears?
options: The measured target encourages substitution into a different undesirable action
The reward cannot be an incentive because cancellations rose after accepted jobs
Acceptance rate measures service quality perfectly
The response proves drivers ignored the metric
q.commonError: Evaluating only the rewarded metric and missing substitution.
q.feedback: Drivers improve acceptance statistics while shifting the problem into later cancellations.

key: The measured target encourages substitution into a different undesirable action

q.q: A company offers either a $40 bonus or public recognition for completing training. Some workers value one more than the other. What follows?
options: Monetary and nonmonetary incentives can differ in strength across people
Only the cash option can change expected benefits
Recognition guarantees completion among all workers
Different preferences mean neither option is an incentive
q.commonError: Assuming all people rank monetary and nonmonetary incentives identically.
q.feedback: Both rewards can alter benefits, but their value depends on the decision-maker.

key: Monetary and nonmonetary incentives can differ in strength across people

q.q: A gym charges a missed-appointment fee but waives it when members cancel a day ahead. Which margin does the rule most directly target?
options: Whether members cancel early instead of simply not appearing
Whether every member continues the gym membership
Whether exercise produces health benefits
Whether members morally approve of cancellation rules
q.commonError: Confusing the targeted choice margin with broader outcomes or approval.
q.feedback: The avoidable fee makes advance cancellation more attractive relative to a no-show.

key: Whether members cancel early instead of simply not appearing

q.q: A call center rewards short calls and separately penalizes repeat complaints. How should agents respond?
options: Balance speed against the risk that poor service triggers repeat complaints
Make every call as short as possible because rewards dominate penalties
Ignore both rules unless all agents respond identically
Guarantee perfect service because two incentives are present
q.commonError: Ignoring one side of a multi-part incentive system.
q.feedback: Agents face a reward for speed and an expected cost for unresolved problems.

key: Balance speed against the risk that poor service triggers repeat complaints

q.q: A $500 attendance bonus is offered, but an employee misses work during a medical emergency. Was the bonus still an incentive?
options: Yes; it changed the payoff but did not guarantee attendance
No; an incentive exists only when it changes the observed behavior in every single case
No; bonuses must overcome every constraint
Yes; it guaranteed attendance for all other workers
q.commonError: Defining an incentive by guaranteed compliance.
q.feedback: An incentive changes behavioral pressure; emergencies and other constraints can still dominate.

key: Yes; it changed the payoff but did not guarantee attendance

q.q: An economist says a fine creates an incentive to avoid an action. Does that statement approve of the fine?
options: No; identifying a changed cost is separate from moral approval
Yes; economic analysis always endorses any incentive whose likely response it successfully predicts
Yes; only approved penalties affect behavior
No; fines are outcomes rather than incentives
q.commonError: Confusing descriptive incentive analysis with moral endorsement.
q.feedback: Economists can predict a response without judging the policy desirable.

key: No; identifying a changed cost is separate from moral approval

q.q: Can two people respond differently to the same parking fee?
options: Yes; constraints, preferences, and alternatives can differ
No; the same dollar fee produces the same response
Only if one person misunderstands the fee
No; different responses mean the fee is not an incentive
q.commonError: Assuming the same incentive creates identical behavior.
q.feedback: A common payoff change can matter differently across decision-makers.

key: Yes; constraints, preferences, and alternatives can differ

q.q: A school gives public recognition rather than cash for attendance. Can recognition be an incentive?
options: Yes; nonmonetary benefits can change behavior
No; only money changes benefits or costs
Only if recognition has a fixed cash value
No; recognition is the final policy outcome
q.commonError: Restricting incentives to monetary rewards and penalties.
q.feedback: Status, convenience, rules, and recognition can all change perceived payoffs.

key: Yes; nonmonetary benefits can change behavior

q.q: A large fine is almost never enforced. Why may it have little effect?
options: The expected consequence is weak when detection is very unlikely
Penalties cannot be incentives
The fine guarantees compliance even when detection and enforcement are extremely unlikely
Only the stated policy goal influences behavior
q.feedback: Expected and perceived consequences depend on both severity and the chance of enforcement.

key: The expected consequence is weak when detection is very unlikely

q.q: Refer to the graph. As production moves farther right along bowed PPF0, what happens to the opportunity cost of additional pizzas?
options: It falls as fewer robots are sacrificed per pizza
It rises as more robots are sacrificed per pizza
It stays constant at one robot for each pizza
It becomes zero after production reaches B
q.imageAlt: A bowed PPF0 has pizzas on the horizontal axis and robots on the vertical axis. Point A is at 20 pizzas and 120 robots; point B is at 60 pizzas and 80 robots. The frontier reaches about 125 robots at zero pizzas and 100 pizzas at zero robots.
q.feedback: The frontier becomes steeper as pizza production rises, showing increasing robot cost per pizza.
q.graphDescription: A bowed PPF0 has pizzas on the horizontal axis and robots on the vertical axis. Point A is at 20 pizzas and 120 robots; point B is at 60 pizzas and 80 robots. The frontier reaches about 125 robots at zero pizzas and 100 pizzas at zero robots.

key: It rises as more robots are sacrificed per pizza

q.q: Why is a typical PPF bowed outward from the origin?
options: All resources are equally productive in every use.
Opportunity cost falls as specialization increases.
Specialized resources cause rising opportunity cost.
The economy is producing inside the frontier.
q.commonError: Attributing the bowed shape to equal resource adaptability or inefficiency.
q.feedback: As production shifts, resources increasingly unsuited to the expanding good must be reassigned, raising opportunity cost.

key: Specialized resources cause rising opportunity cost.

q.q: Moving from bundle A to B gains 5 machines and sacrifices 10 tons of food. Moving from B to C gains another 5 machines and sacrifices 20 tons of food. What does the pattern show?
options: The opportunity cost of machines rises from 2 to 4 tons of food per machine.
The opportunity cost of machines falls from 4 to 2 tons per machine.
The opportunity cost remains constant at 3 tons per machine.
Bundle C must lie inside the PPF because its food output is lower.
q.commonError: Comparing total sacrifices without converting each move to cost per additional unit.
q.feedback: The first move costs 10/5 = 2 tons per machine; the second costs 20/5 = 4, showing increasing opportunity cost.

key: The opportunity cost of machines rises from 2 to 4 tons of food per machine.

q.q: A world price below domestic equilibrium creates:
options: Exports
No trade
Imports
A binding quota
q.feedback: When the world price is below the no-trade domestic equilibrium price, domestic quantity demanded exceeds domestic quantity supplied, so the country imports the difference.

key: Imports

q.q: A world price above domestic equilibrium creates:
options: Imports
No trade
A shortage filled by domestic firms only
Exports
q.feedback: When the world price is above the no-trade domestic equilibrium price, domestic quantity supplied exceeds domestic quantity demanded, so the country exports the difference.

key: Exports

q.q: The small-country assumption means:
options: The country cannot influence the world price
The country has no firms
Imports must equal zero
The government cannot use policy
q.feedback: A small country is a price taker in the world market, so its purchases or sales do not change the world price.

key: The country cannot influence the world price

q.q: If Pw equals the no-trade price, the basic model predicts:
options: Maximum imports
No trade
Maximum exports
Tariff revenue
q.feedback: If the world price equals the no-trade equilibrium price, domestic quantity supplied equals domestic quantity demanded at that price, so there is no net import or export incentive.

key: No trade

q.q: Trade raises total surplus but lowers income in one region. This illustrates:
options: Trade has no efficiency gain
Equity is identical to total surplus
Efficiency and equity can point to different concerns
Imports must be banned
q.feedback: Trade can increase total surplus while imposing concentrated losses on particular regions or groups, so efficiency and equity are separate questions.

key: Efficiency and equity can point to different concerns

q.q: Potential compensation means:
options: Losers are automatically paid
No one loses
The government must impose a quota
Winners gain enough in aggregate that compensation could be possible
q.feedback: If total surplus rises, the winners gain enough in aggregate that compensation could be possible, but compensation occurs only if an actual transfer or policy is implemented.

key: Winners gain enough in aggregate that compensation could be possible

q.q: Refer to the graph. Which quantity combination is correct after the tariff?
options: Qs = 50 thousand; Qd = 250 thousand; imports = 200 thousand
Qs = 200 thousand; Qd = 100 thousand; exports = 100 thousand
Qs = Qd = 150 thousand; imports = 0
Qs = 100 thousand; Qd = 200 thousand; imports = 100 thousand
q.feedback: At the tariff-inclusive price of $6, supply is 100 thousand and demand is 200 thousand, leaving 100 thousand imports.

key: Qs = 100 thousand; Qd = 200 thousand; imports = 100 thousand

q.q: In a small importing country, Qd=80-P and Qs=P-20. World price is $30 with unlimited foreign supply. Compare tariffs of $10 and $15 per unit, both with positive imports. What happens to revenue?
options: It rises from $200 to $300: the higher rate applies to the original 20 imports.
It rises from $400 to $525: apply the tariff to all domestic purchases.
It falls from $200 to $150: imports shrink from 20 to 10 despite the higher unit tariff.
It falls from $400 to $150: the initial tariff is collected on both imports and domestic production.
q.feedback: At P=40, Qd=40 and Qs=20, so imports=20 and revenue=10×20=200. At P=45, Qd=35 and Qs=25, so imports=10 and revenue=15×10=150. A higher rate does not guarantee more revenue.

key: It falls from $200 to $150: imports shrink from 20 to 10 despite the higher unit tariff.

q.q: A tariff raises Qs from 10 to 20 and lowers Qd from 50 to 40. Imports fall from:
q.feedback: Before the tariff, imports are 50 − 10 = 40. After the tariff, imports are 40 − 20 = 20, so imports fall from 40 to 20.

q.q: Refer to the tariff graph. What is the production-side deadweight loss?
q.feedback: The production-distortion triangle has area ½ × $10 × 10 = $50.

q.q: Refer to the tariff graph. What is the consumption-side deadweight loss?
q.feedback: The consumption-distortion triangle has area ½ × $10 × 10 = $50.

q.q: Refer to the tariff graph. In this small country, world price stays $30 and the straight domestic curves stay fixed. The displayed tariff is cut from $10 to $5 per unit. Relative to the displayed outcome, how do deadweight loss and government revenue change?
options: Deadweight loss falls by $50; revenue falls by $100.
Deadweight loss falls by $75; revenue rises by $50.
Deadweight loss falls by $75; revenue falls by $50.
Deadweight loss falls by $50; revenue rises by $50.
q.feedback: At a $5 tariff, price is $35, Qs=15 and Qd=45, so imports are 30 and revenue is $150 rather than $200. Each distortion triangle is 0.5 x $5 x 5 = $12.50; total DWL is $25 rather than $100. Thus DWL falls $75 and revenue falls $50. Revenue is a domestic transfer, not part of DWL.

key: Deadweight loss falls by $75; revenue falls by $50.

q.q: A binding quota permits 20 imports and raises domestic price $10 above world price. One-quarter of the licenses are given to foreign exporters; the rest go to domestic residents. Production and consumption distortions total $100, and no resources are spent obtaining licenses. What is the domestic welfare loss?
options: $300: $100 of distortions plus every $200 of quota rents, regardless of ownership.
$100: rent ownership never affects domestic welfare because all rents are transfers worldwide.
$250: $100 of distortions plus $150 of rents retained by domestic residents.
$150: $100 of distortions plus $50 of rents going abroad; $150 of rents stay domestic.
q.feedback: Total rent is 20×10=200. Foreign recipients receive 0.25×200=50, while domestic recipients retain 150. For domestic welfare, add exported rents to the 100 resource distortion loss: 150.

key: $150: $100 of distortions plus $50 of rents going abroad; $150 of rents stay domestic.

q.q: Two binding quota systems create the same $200 of rents and $100 of production/consumption distortions. A costless government auction captures all rents. Free domestic licenses instead induce $30 of real lobbying expenses. Which comparison is correct?
options: Auction loss is $100 and free-license loss $130; the ownership transfer is not a resource loss, but lobbying dissipates resources.
Auction loss is $300 and free-license loss $130; government revenue must be added to deadweight loss.
Auction loss is $100 and free-license loss -$70; private rents are an extra national gain over the auction.
Both losses are $100; lobbying uses money and therefore cannot consume real resources.
q.feedback: Auction receipts and domestic private rents are domestic transfers. With identical market distortions, only the $30 real lobbying difference changes national loss: 100 versus 130.

key: Auction loss is $100 and free-license loss $130; the ownership transfer is not a resource loss, but lobbying dissipates resources.

q.q: A quota generates $200 of rents that currently go to foreign exporters, plus $100 of domestic production/consumption distortions. A reform auctions all rights domestically without changing price or imports, but uses $60 of real administrative resources. What is the change in domestic welfare?
options: A $300 gain: recover foreign rents and eliminate both distortion triangles even though price and imports are unchanged.
A $140 gain: recover $200 in foreign-held rents, then subtract $60 of administration; the $100 distortion remains.
A $60 loss: rent ownership cannot affect domestic welfare, so only administration changes.
A $240 loss: auction payments and administration must both be subtracted from consumers’ unchanged position.
q.feedback: The market distortion is unchanged. National loss falls from 100+200=300 to 100+60=160, an improvement of 140. Capturing previously foreign rents changes domestic income even though the physical allocation stays fixed.

key: A $140 gain: recover $200 in foreign-held rents, then subtract $60 of administration; the $100 distortion remains.

q.q: A small country has Qs=P-20, initial Qd=80-P and world price $30. A $10 tariff initially produces the same imports as a quota of 20. Demand then becomes Qd=100-P. Which comparison follows?
options: With the tariff, P=$50 and imports=20; with the quota, P=$40 and imports=40.
Both policies keep P=$40 and imports=20 because they were initially equivalent.
With the tariff, P=$40 and imports=40; with the quota, P=$50 and imports=20.
Both policies raise P=$50 and imports=40 because demand increases equally under each.
q.feedback: The nonprohibitive tariff keeps P=30+10=40; new imports are (100-40)-(40-20)=40. The quota fixes Qd-Qs=20: 100-P-(P-20)=20, giving P=50. Initial equivalence does not imply equal responses to shocks.

key: With the tariff, P=$40 and imports=40; with the quota, P=$50 and imports=20.

q.q: A small country has Qd=100-P, Qs=P-20 and a binding quota of 20 imports. World price falls from $30 to $20 while domestic schedules and the quota are unchanged. What happens to domestic price and quota rents?
options: Domestic price falls from $50 to $40; rents stay $400 because a quota fixes the price wedge.
Domestic price stays $50; rents fall from $400 to $200 because import cost is lower.
Domestic price falls to $20; unlimited foreign supply removes the binding quota automatically.
Domestic price stays $50; total rents rise from $400 to $600 because the import-right price gap widens.
q.feedback: The quota-clearing equation 100-P-(P-20)=20 gives P=50 at either world price. Rents rise from (50-30)×20=400 to (50-20)×20=600. The quantity cap, not a fixed wedge, is held constant.

key: Domestic price stays $50; total rents rise from $400 to $600 because the import-right price gap widens.

q.q: Demand rises in a small importing country. Under a nonprohibitive fixed tariff, unlimited foreign supply holds domestic price at world price plus tariff. Under a binding quota, the maximum imports cannot rise. Which adjustment difference is most accurate?
options: Tariff imports absorb the extra demand at the unchanged price; quota price rises, inducing more domestic output and restraining consumption.
Tariff price must rise because imports are fixed; quota imports absorb the change because its price wedge is fixed.
Both domestic prices must rise equally; greater demand determines price independently of the trade-policy instrument.
Quota price rises only if domestic supply is vertical; otherwise domestic firms can absorb any demand increase at the same price.
q.feedback: At a fixed tariff-inclusive world price, imports can expand. A binding quota prevents that import response, so price adjusts until more domestic supply and less quantity demanded close the gap. Upward-sloping domestic supply does not keep price fixed.

key: Tariff imports absorb the extra demand at the unchanged price; quota price rises, inducing more domestic output and restraining consumption.

q.q: A tariff lowers domestic consumer surplus by $500, raises producer surplus by $180 and raises government revenue by $200. Administering it uses $20 of additional real resources. Which national accounting is correct?
options: National welfare falls $520; producer gains and revenue do not offset any part of consumer loss.
National welfare falls $140; producer gains and revenue are domestic transfers, while the residual distortion and administration are real losses.
National welfare falls $340; government revenue is a social loss because consumers fund it.
National welfare rises $360; add producer gains and revenue and subtract administration without counting consumer loss.
q.feedback: Before administration, national change is -500+180+200=-120. Additional resource cost gives -140. Revenue and producer gains offset portions of consumer loss rather than being counted again as deadweight loss.

key: National welfare falls $140; producer gains and revenue are domestic transfers, while the residual distortion and administration are real losses.

q.q: Protection would preserve 2,000 jobs for a year at $60 million of real consumer and downstream efficiency cost, with no other benefits in this exercise. A targeted transition program costs $20 million and enables 1,500 workers to obtain equally valued jobs that year. Which comparison informs the employment goal?
options: Protection costs $13,333 per preserved job; transition costs $30,000 per worker and leaves no employment gap.
Protection is necessarily best because it preserves all 2,000 jobs; consumer and downstream costs are irrelevant to an employment goal.
Protection costs $30,000 per preserved job; transition costs about $13,333 per reemployed worker but leaves 500 more workers needing help.
Transition is necessarily best because its total cost is lower; differences in the number of workers helped need not be reported.
q.feedback: Protection costs 60000000/2000=30000 per job-year, versus 20000000/1500≈13333. The targeted program costs less per worker but reaches fewer. Advice should state both the efficiency comparison and the remaining distributional need.

key: Protection costs $30,000 per preserved job; transition costs about $13,333 per reemployed worker but leaves 500 more workers needing help.

q.q: A strategic input faces an outage risk. A broad tariff costs $40 million in expected efficiency losses and would reduce expected outage losses by $15 million. A reserve program costs $12 million and would reduce those losses by $25 million. Both estimates already include operating costs. Which evaluation is best on the stated evidence?
options: The tariff nets $55 million while reserves net $37 million; security benefits should be added to policy costs.
The reserve program nets $25 million while the tariff nets $15 million; resource costs are irrelevant once security is the objective.
The tariff is preferable whenever it reduces imports, even if the reserve program has larger net security benefits.
The reserve program nets $13 million while the tariff nets -$25 million; a real security concern does not establish that broad protection is the best instrument.
q.feedback: Net expected benefits are 25-12=13 million for reserves and 15-40=-25 million for the tariff. The national-security goal is evaluated by the policy’s actual risk reduction and resource cost, not the protection label.

key: The reserve program nets $13 million while the tariff nets -$25 million; a real security concern does not establish that broad protection is the best instrument.

q.q: Temporary protection was justified by a forecast that three years of learning would cut unit resource cost from $12 to $8, below a $9 world price. After five years, audited cost remains $12. Firms request renewal based only on past subsidies and current jobs. Which evidence would most strengthen a renewed learning case?
options: A credible, independently testable mechanism and timetable for additional learning gains exceeding the new consumer and resource costs.
The total subsidy already spent, because recovering sunk public expenditure establishes future learning benefits.
The number of years protection has lasted, because longer duration demonstrates that costs are approaching the target.
Current protected employment alone, because retaining jobs proves unit productivity has improved despite the audited cost.
q.feedback: The promised cost reduction has not occurred, weakening the original rationale. Renewal requires prospective, credible learning evidence and a comparison with additional costs. Sunk subsidies, duration and employment do not establish future productivity gains.

key: A credible, independently testable mechanism and timetable for additional learning gains exceeding the new consumer and resource costs.

q.q: A proposed tariff is estimated to create $40 million of domestic producer gains, $25 million of revenue and $80 million of consumer losses. Retaliation would additionally reduce domestic exporters’ net surplus by $20 million. Assume those export losses are not included in the first ledger. Which national assessment is correct?
options: Net gain is $5 million; retaliation can be ignored because export firms are outside the protected industry.
Net loss is $35 million; retaliation adds a separate export-market loss to the initial $15 million tariff loss.
Net loss is $60 million; government revenue is an extra resource loss rather than a domestic transfer.
Net loss is $15 million; every export loss is automatically included in consumer losses from the original tariff.
q.feedback: The initial national change is 40+25-80=-15 million. Adding the explicitly separate export loss gives -35 million. Revenue is a domestic transfer, while retaliation can impose additional losses in other markets.

key: Net loss is $35 million; retaliation adds a separate export-market loss to the initial $15 million tariff loss.

q.q: Refer to the tariff-regions graph. An analyst counts rectangle B as deadweight loss and excludes the two side triangles. Which correction uses the plotted quantities and prices?
options: B is $400 of revenue; the two $100 side triangles total $200 of deadweight loss.
B is $200 of deadweight loss; the side triangles are domestic producer transfers.
B is $200 of revenue; the two $50 side triangles total $100 of deadweight loss.
B is $100 of revenue; the two side triangles total $200 of deadweight loss.
q.feedback: The wedge is 40-30=10 and post-tariff imports are 40-20=20, so B=200. Each distortion base is 10 units, giving 0.5×10×10=50 on each side. Domestic revenue is a transfer; the distortion triangles sum to 100.

key: B is $200 of revenue; the two $50 side triangles total $100 of deadweight loss.

q.q: Refer to the quota-rent graph. The full import-right rectangle R is first given to foreign firms, then sold at a costless competitive domestic government auction. With the quota and prices unchanged, which result follows?
options: R is $400; the auction raises domestic welfare by $400 and removes the consumption distortion.
R is $200; the auction changes only legal labels, leaving domestic income unchanged.
R is $100; auction revenue is an additional domestic loss because license buyers pay the government.
R is $200; the auction raises domestic welfare by $200 relative to foreign ownership, while the distortion triangles remain.
q.feedback: The price gap is 40-30=10 and imports are 40-20=20, so R=200. Redirecting foreign-held rents to domestic government increases domestic income by 200. Unchanged market quantities leave the distortion triangles unchanged.

key: R is $200; the auction raises domestic welfare by $200 relative to foreign ownership, while the distortion triangles remain.

q.q: Refer to the graph. Which quantity combination is correct under the import quota?
options: Qs = 75 thousand; Qd = 275 thousand; imports = 200 thousand
Qs = 200 thousand; Qd = 150 thousand; exports = 50 thousand
Qs = Qd = 175 thousand; imports = 0
Qs = 150 thousand; Qd = 200 thousand; imports = 50 thousand
q.feedback: At the quota-induced price of $6, domestic supply is 150 thousand and demand is 200 thousand, leaving 50 thousand imports.

key: Qs = 150 thousand; Qd = 200 thousand; imports = 50 thousand

q.q: What surplus concept separates tariff revenue from deadweight loss?
options: All consumer losses are deadweight loss
All producer gains are deadweight loss
Transfers change recipients; deadweight loss removes mutually beneficial trades
Revenue is never part of welfare
q.feedback: Tariff revenue is a transfer to the government, while deadweight loss represents gains from trade that disappear because the tariff distorts production and consumption.

key: Transfers change recipients; deadweight loss removes mutually beneficial trades

q.q: How does comparative advantage support gains from international trade?
options: It requires absolute advantage in every good
It eliminates scarcity
It guarantees equal gains
Specialization follows lower opportunity cost and exchange expands consumption possibilities
q.feedback: Comparative advantage identifies the goods each side can produce at lower opportunity cost. Specialization on that basis can create gains that exchange allows both sides to share.

key: Specialization follows lower opportunity cost and exchange expands consumption possibilities

q.q: Can a country gain from trade if it is less productive in every good?
options: Yes, if opportunity costs differ and it specializes by comparative advantage
No, absolute disadvantage prevents all gains
Only if it bans imports
Only if wages are identical
q.feedback: Yes. Even a country with an absolute disadvantage in every good can gain from trade when opportunity costs differ and it specializes according to comparative advantage.

key: Yes, if opportunity costs differ and it specializes by comparative advantage

q.q: Two small countries open their wheat markets to free trade. Before trade, wheat sells for $40 per sack in Alder and $24 in Birch. The world price is $30 per sack, with no transport costs or trade barriers. Which trade pattern follows?
options: Alder exports; Birch imports.
Alder imports; Birch exports.
Both countries import wheat.
Both countries export wheat.
q.feedback: Compare the $30 world price with each country's no-trade price. In Alder, $30 is below $40, so domestic demand exceeds domestic supply and imports fill the gap. In Birch, $30 is above $24, so domestic supply exceeds domestic demand and the excess is exported. Both face the same world price; their different no-trade prices explain their different trade directions.

key: Alder imports; Birch exports.

q.q: How can supply elasticity affect domestic production response to a tariff?
options: Elasticity eliminates tariff revenue
Elasticity fixes import quantity under every policy
Elasticity makes marginal cost irrelevant
More responsive supply creates a larger production increase and distortion
q.feedback: When domestic supply is more responsive to price, the tariff-induced price increase produces a larger increase in domestic output and therefore a larger production distortion, other things equal.

key: More responsive supply creates a larger production increase and distortion

q.q: How is a tariff connected to a tax wedge?
options: It creates a gap between the domestic buyer price and the world resource price
It creates a gap between domestic quantity supplied and domestic quantity demanded, measured as tax per unit.
It creates a gap between the government’s total tariff receipts and the per-unit price paid for imports.
It creates a gap between the lower domestic buyer price and the unchanged world price after the tariff.
q.feedback: In the small-country importing model, a tariff raises the domestic price above the world price while imports continue. That price difference is the per-unit tax wedge. The import quantity and total tariff revenue are different measures, and the tariff does not lower the domestic buyer price.

key: It creates a gap between the domestic buyer price and the world resource price

q.q: How is tariff deadweight loss connected to lost gains from exchange?
options: It equals tariff revenue
The tariff prevents beneficial imports and induces higher-cost production
It equals all consumer expenditure
It is a payment to foreign firms
q.feedback: The tariff prevents some imports whose value to domestic buyers exceeds their world resource cost and also induces higher-cost domestic production. Those foregone gains create deadweight loss.

key: The tariff prevents beneficial imports and induces higher-cost production

q.q: How can trade move consumption beyond a country’s production possibilities frontier?
options: Trade moves domestic production outside physical constraints
A tariff expands resources automatically
Specialization and exchange separate what is consumed from what is domestically produced
Imports eliminate opportunity cost
q.feedback: Trade does not move domestic production beyond the PPF. Specialization and exchange can instead allow the country to consume a combination of goods that it could not produce by itself.

key: Specialization and exchange separate what is consumed from what is domestically produced

q.q: What does the PPF contribute to trade analysis?
options: It directly calculates tariff revenue
It fixes the world price
It identifies quota rents
It shows opportunity costs and the production tradeoffs behind comparative advantage
q.feedback: The PPF shows the production tradeoffs that determine opportunity costs. Those opportunity costs help identify comparative advantage and the basis for specialization.

key: It shows opportunity costs and the production tradeoffs behind comparative advantage

q.q: What efficiency question should be separated from the equity question in trade?
options: Whether total surplus rises versus how gains and losses are distributed
Whether imports equal exports versus whether prices exist
Whether firms earn revenue versus whether consumers buy
Whether quotas are legal versus whether supply slopes upward
q.feedback: Efficiency asks whether trade raises total surplus. Equity asks how the resulting gains and losses are distributed across people, firms, industries, or regions.

key: Whether total surplus rises versus how gains and losses are distributed

q.q: Why might adjustment assistance be discussed even when trade raises total surplus?
options: Trade eliminates all consumer gains
Some workers and communities can bear concentrated transition costs
Efficiency requires equal outcomes
Imports always reduce total employment
q.feedback: Trade can raise total surplus while imposing concentrated transition costs on particular workers and communities. Adjustment assistance addresses those distributional costs without denying the aggregate gains.

key: Some workers and communities can bear concentrated transition costs

q.q: Arden imposes an $8 tariff and imports 24 units after the tariff. Calculate tariff revenue.
q.feedback: Revenue is $8×24=$192.

q.q: Bellora imposes a $10 tariff and imports 16 units after the tariff. Calculate tariff revenue.
q.feedback: Revenue is $10×16=$160.

q.q: In Arden, an $8 tariff raises domestic production from 10 to 18. Calculate the production-side deadweight loss.
q.feedback: The triangle is ½×$8×8=$32.

q.q: In Bellora, a $10 tariff raises domestic production from 16 to 26. Calculate the production-side deadweight loss.
q.feedback: The triangle is ½×$10×10=$50.

q.q: An $8 tariff reduces domestic consumption from 50 to 42. Calculate the consumption-side deadweight loss.
q.feedback: The triangle is ½×$8×8=$32.

q.q: A binding quota permits 24 imports and creates a $7 price gap. Calculate total quota rent.
q.feedback: Quota rent is $7×24=$168.

q.q: A tariff creates a $45 production-side deadweight loss and a $55 consumption-side deadweight loss. Calculate total tariff deadweight loss.
q.feedback: Total tariff deadweight loss is the sum of the two distortion losses: $45+$55=$100.

q.q: In the small-country trade model, what is the world price?
options: The price available in the world market that the country takes as given
The price selected by the domestic government
The domestic autarky price after trade opens
The tariff-inclusive domestic price
q.feedback: A small country takes the world price as given.

key: The price available in the world market that the country takes as given

q.q: A country becomes an importer of a good when:
options: The world price is above its no-trade domestic equilibrium price
The world price is below its no-trade domestic equilibrium price
Domestic supply is greater than domestic demand at the world price
The government sets a quota equal to zero
q.feedback: A lower world price creates excess domestic demand that is filled by imports.

key: The world price is below its no-trade domestic equilibrium price

q.q: A country becomes an exporter of a good when:
options: The world price is below its no-trade domestic equilibrium price
