Domestic demand is greater than domestic supply at the world price
The world price is above its no-trade domestic equilibrium price
Domestic consumers refuse to buy the good
q.feedback: A higher world price creates excess domestic supply that is sold abroad.

key: The world price is above its no-trade domestic equilibrium price

q.q: A tariff is:
options: A legal maximum on exports
A payment to domestic consumers
A tax on all domestic production
A tax on imported goods
q.feedback: A tariff taxes imported units.

key: A tax on imported goods

q.q: In the basic small-country import model, a tariff normally causes the domestic price to:
options: Rise above the world price
Fall below the world price
Remain at the world price
Become equal to the no-trade quantity
q.feedback: The tariff creates a wedge between the world price and domestic price.

key: Rise above the world price

q.q: A tariff that raises the domestic price generally causes imports to:
options: Increase
Decrease
Remain unchanged
Equal domestic quantity demanded
q.feedback: Domestic production rises and domestic consumption falls, shrinking imports.

key: Decrease

q.q: Tariff revenue equals:
options: Domestic price multiplied by domestic production
Consumer surplus minus producer surplus
Tariff per imported unit multiplied by the number of imported units
The two tariff deadweight-loss triangles
q.feedback: Government revenue is the tariff rate times post-tariff imports.

key: Tariff per imported unit multiplied by the number of imported units

q.q: Why is tariff revenue not deadweight loss?
options: Tariff revenue is retained by domestic firms, so it remains part of producer surplus rather than a social loss
Deadweight loss is the portion of consumer surplus transferred to producers and the government after the tariff
Tariff revenue offsets the production distortion, leaving the consumption distortion as the remaining deadweight loss
Revenue is a transfer to the government, while deadweight loss is surplus that disappears
q.feedback: A transfer changes who receives surplus; deadweight loss is a net loss.

key: Revenue is a transfer to the government, while deadweight loss is surplus that disappears

q.q: An import quota is:
options: A legal limit on the quantity of a good that may be imported
A tax collected on every domestic sale
A subsidy for foreign producers
A minimum price set below the world price
q.feedback: A quota directly limits import quantity.

key: A legal limit on the quantity of a good that may be imported

q.q: A binding import quota normally causes the domestic price to:
options: Fall below the world price
Rise above the world price
Remain permanently at the world price
Equal zero
q.feedback: Restricted imports create scarcity in the domestic market.

key: Rise above the world price

q.q: Quota rents are:
options: The government’s tariff revenue in every quota system
The entire loss of consumer surplus
The price gap created by the quota multiplied by the permitted import quantity
Domestic producers’ total revenue
q.feedback: Quota rents accrue to whoever holds the valuable import rights.

key: The price gap created by the quota multiplied by the permitted import quantity

q.q: When does the government receive quota rents?
options: Whenever any quota is binding
Only when imports fall to zero
Whenever foreign exporters own the licenses
When it auctions the import licenses and keeps the proceeds
q.feedback: Rent distribution depends on who owns or sells the import rights.

key: When it auctions the import licenses and keeps the proceeds

q.q: At an importing country's request, a foreign government caps shipments and gives its exporters the rights free. Which restriction is this?
options: A voluntary export restraint (VER)
An import tariff collected by the importing treasury
An import-license auction held by the importing treasury
A subsidy paid on domestic production
q.feedback: A VER limits exports from the supplying country. With free rights assigned to foreign exporters, those exporters can capture the scarcity rents.

key: A voluntary export restraint (VER)

q.q: Why is “a tariff protects jobs” incomplete economic analysis?
options: The statement is sufficient because preserving employment in the protected sector captures the main national welfare effect
It ignores higher consumer costs, resource shifts, and jobs affected in other industries
Employment effects can be evaluated from the protected industry because tariff costs are unlikely to spill into other sectors
The key missing issue is the effect on foreign workers; domestic consumer and input costs are secondary to that effect
q.feedback: A complete analysis traces costs and effects beyond the protected industry.

key: It ignores higher consumer costs, resource shifts, and jobs affected in other industries

q.q: Which is the strongest way to evaluate a national-security argument for protection?
options: Assume every industry is essential
Reject the argument because trade is always harmless
Compare the security benefit with the policy cost and less costly alternatives
Count only the protected firms’ profits
q.feedback: Security can be legitimate, but the claim still requires evidence and comparison.

key: Compare the security benefit with the policy cost and less costly alternatives

q.q: New domestic pump makers request temporary protection while they learn to match established foreign firms' costs. Which argument are they using?
options: National-security argument
Jobs argument based only on existing employment
Retaliation against a partner's trade barrier
Infant-industry argument
q.feedback: The infant-industry argument claims temporary learning can make a new industry competitive. The label alone does not establish that future benefits exceed current costs.

key: Infant-industry argument

q.q: Why can retaliation make a tariff more costly?
options: Trading partners may restrict the country’s exports, harming additional producers and workers
Trading partners may tax imports from the country, but the proceeds go into the original country’s treasury.
Trading partners may tax imports from the country, making its goods cheaper for foreign customers to buy.
Trading partners may restrict imports from the country, increasing sales opportunities for the country’s exporters.
q.feedback: Retaliation can restrict sales of the country’s exports in foreign markets. Export producers and their workers can therefore lose business in addition to the costs created by the original tariff.

key: Trading partners may restrict the country’s exports, harming additional producers and workers

q.q: Which statement separates efficiency from equity in trade analysis?
options: An efficient outcome must divide gains equally
Trade can raise total surplus while distributing gains and losses unevenly
Equity is measured only by import quantity
If consumers gain, fairness is settled
q.feedback: Efficiency concerns total surplus; equity concerns distribution.

key: Trade can raise total surplus while distributing gains and losses unevenly

q.q: Using the displayed trade graph, is the domestic economy an importer or exporter when the world price is $5?
options: Importer
Exporter
Neither; trade does not occur
The graph does not determine the trade direction
q.feedback: The $5 world price lies below the $7 autarky price, so domestic demand exceeds domestic supply and the country imports.

key: Importer

q.q: At the $10 world price, does this market export or import?
options: Exporter
Importer
Neither; trade does not occur
The graph does not determine the trade direction
q.feedback: The $10 world price lies above the $7 autarky price, so domestic production exceeds domestic consumption and the country exports.

key: Exporter

q.q: In the displayed trade graph, what domestic price results from the $4 world price plus the tariff?
q.feedback: The graph marks the tariff-inclusive domestic price at $6.

q.q: What is the per-unit tariff shown in the displayed trade graph?
q.feedback: The domestic price rises from the $4 world price to $6, so the tariff is $2 per unit.

q.q: In the displayed trade graph, what domestic price results under the import quota?
q.feedback: The graph marks the domestic price under the quota at $6.

q.q: What world price is shown in the displayed trade graph?
q.feedback: The green world-price line is drawn at $3.

q.q: Import access raises consumer surplus by $640 and reduces producer surplus by $390. A proposal uses a $390 lump-sum transfer to restore producers and consumes $35 in real adjustment resources. Which result separates efficiency from distribution?
options: $250 remains because transfers and real adjustment costs are both ignored
$605 remains because the producer transfer creates additional national surplus
$215 of net gain remains, and compensation occurs only because the proposal provides it
$175 is lost because both producer losses and compensation must be subtracted
q.feedback: The trade gain is 640 - 390 = 250. The transfer reallocates that surplus; the real resource cost reduces it to 215. Potential compensation is distinct from this stipulated actual compensation.

key: $215 of net gain remains, and compensation occurs only because the proposal provides it

q.q: A politician says, “Imports destroy domestic production, so imports destroy value.” What is the best response?
options: Imports can lower domestic production, and that loss of domestic output by itself establishes that national welfare falls
Domestic production creates value for the country, whereas imported consumption contributes little to domestic consumer surplus
Imports create net value when the imported quantity is smaller than the domestic production displaced by trade
Imports replace domestic units whose marginal cost exceeds the world price while expanding consumption valued above that price
q.feedback: The welfare gain comes from lower-cost sourcing and additional mutually beneficial consumption.

key: Imports replace domestic units whose marginal cost exceeds the world price while expanding consumption valued above that price

q.q: A politician says, “Exports make the country poorer because goods leave.” What is the best response?
options: Exports move units to buyers willing to pay the higher world price, raising producer and total surplus despite domestic consumer losses
Exports raise the domestic price, so producer gains are offset dollar-for-dollar by losses to domestic consumers
Exports shift goods abroad without changing domestic willingness to pay or opportunity cost, leaving welfare unchanged
Because residents consume fewer units after trade, the country's welfare falls despite the higher world price
q.feedback: Export welfare analysis compares valuations and costs, not just physical flows.

key: Exports move units to buyers willing to pay the higher world price, raising producer and total surplus despite domestic consumer losses

q.q: Which statement correctly treats potential compensation from trade?
options: Losers are automatically compensated through prices
Aggregate gains may make compensation feasible, but actual policy is required for losers to receive it
Potential compensation proves no one loses
Compensation is impossible whenever trade raises total surplus
q.feedback: A Kaldor-Hicks gain does not itself transfer resources.

key: Aggregate gains may make compensation feasible, but actual policy is required for losers to receive it

q.q: A tariff shifts $400 from consumers to domestic producers and $250 to government, while destroying $120 of surplus. What is the consumer loss?
q.feedback: Consumer loss equals producer gain + revenue + deadweight loss: 400+250+120=770.

q.q: Why is the tariff production-side deadweight loss a social loss?
options: Domestic firms receive revenue
Consumers buy imported goods
The government collects tariff revenue
Higher-cost domestic units replace lower-cost imported units
q.feedback: The resource cost rises for units shifted to less efficient domestic production.

key: Higher-cost domestic units replace lower-cost imported units

q.q: Why is the tariff consumption-side deadweight loss a social loss?
options: Consumers stop buying units valued above the world resource cost
Domestic firms sell more units
Government revenue rises
All imported units disappear
q.feedback: The tariff prevents mutually beneficial consumption.

key: Consumers stop buying units valued above the world resource cost

q.q: A small importer has Qd = 100 - P and Qs = P - 20. Pw is $30. A $10 tariff and a quota initially allow 40 imports. Demand then becomes Qd = 120 - P. With all else unchanged, which comparison is correct?
options: Tariff: price $50 and 40 imports; quota: price $40 and 60 imports
Tariff: price $40 and 60 imports; quota: price $50 and 40 imports
Both keep price $40 and imports 40
Both raise price to $50 because a demand increase must raise the world price
q.feedback: The tariff keeps domestic price at 30 + 10 = 40, where imports are 80 - 20 = 60. Under the cap, 120 - P - (P - 20) = 40 implies P = 50.

key: Tariff: price $40 and 60 imports; quota: price $50 and 40 imports

q.q: A quota allows 36 imports at $29 while Pw remains $24. Consumers lose $310 and domestic producers gain $94. Foreign exporters receive the rights free. Relative to free trade, what are the national loss and the global distortion loss, ignoring other effects?
options: $36 national loss; $216 distortion loss
$180 for both because the rents are the only loss
$216 national loss; $36 distortion loss
$310 for both because every dollar lost by consumers disappears
q.feedback: Rents are (29 - 24) × 36 = 180. Domestic surplus falls 310 - 94 = 216. Of this, 180 is transferred abroad; the remaining 36 is destroyed surplus.

key: $216 national loss; $36 distortion loss

q.q: Two quota systems have the same price and import quantity. Rents total $240. System A auctions rights competitively and spends $20 of real resources administering them; system B gives rights free to domestic importers at no resource cost. Ignoring other effects, which comparison is correct?
options: A raises national surplus by $240 because auction receipts are new gains
B loses $240 nationally because private domestic rents leave the country
Both have identical national surplus because administrative costs are transfers
A raises $240 for government, but national surplus is $20 lower than under B
q.feedback: Both keep the $240 rent inside the country; auctioning changes its recipient. The stated real administrative cost makes A $20 worse nationally than B.

key: A raises $240 for government, but national surplus is $20 lower than under B

q.q: A national-security concern applies to one narrowly defined input. Which policy is most economically targeted?
options: A focused resilience policy for that input rather than broad protection across unrelated goods
A tariff on every imported good
A permanent quota on all consumer goods
No comparison of alternatives
q.feedback: Targeting reduces collateral costs while addressing the stated risk.

key: A focused resilience policy for that input rather than broad protection across unrelated goods

q.q: A protected pump industry reports falling average costs. The same decline occurred in unprotected firms using a newly available machine. Which additional evidence is most needed before crediting protection to infant-industry learning?
options: Evidence that protected firms still employ workers, regardless of the source of cost reductions
Evidence that protection generated additional learning whose future benefits exceed its costs
Evidence that import prices exceed zero, proving domestic learning is valuable
Evidence that production increased, proving the tariff caused every cost reduction
q.feedback: A common technology improvement weakens the claim that protection caused the learning. The case needs an additional benefit attributable to the policy and comparison with its costs.

key: Evidence that protection generated additional learning whose future benefits exceed its costs

q.q: A tariff preserves 2,000 jobs in one sector but raises input costs in downstream firms. What analysis is still required?
options: The protected-sector employment effect should be compared with consumer costs, while downstream employment can be treated as secondary
Tariff revenue and protected-sector payroll provide enough information to determine whether the policy raises national welfare
Net employment, consumer costs, fiscal effects, retaliation, and alternative adjustment policies
The job count settles the welfare question once the preserved positions are valued at their current wage payments
q.feedback: Concentrated benefits do not erase dispersed costs.

key: Net employment, consumer costs, fiscal effects, retaliation, and alternative adjustment policies

q.q: Why can a bilateral tariff reduce the protected country’s exports?
options: Foreign retaliation reduces imports into the protected country while higher input prices raise its exporters’ productivity.
The tariff directly taxes domestic export sales while retaliation lowers the world price of every protected input.
Reduced imports mechanically require equal export losses in each industry while input costs remain unchanged.
Foreign retaliation can reduce market access while tariffed inputs raise domestic exporters’ costs.
q.feedback: Exports can fall through retaliatory barriers abroad and higher costs of imported inputs at home. Neither an industry-by-industry identity nor direct taxation of exports is required.

key: Foreign retaliation can reduce market access while tariffed inputs raise domestic exporters’ costs.

q.q: Which statement about a trade deficit is economically valid?
options: It does not by itself measure whether individual trades create gains from exchange
It proves imports have zero consumer value
It proves every domestic industry is shrinking
It equals tariff deadweight loss
q.feedback: The trade balance is not the surplus test for a particular market.

key: It does not by itself measure whether individual trades create gains from exchange

q.q: A small economy has Qd = 78 - P and Qs = P - 18. The world price initially equals its autarky price. Demand then rises by 12 units at every price while Pw stays fixed. What happens?
options: It imports 6 units at $54 because domestic autarky still sets the trading price
It imports 12 units at $48; its new autarky price would be $54
It exports 12 units at $48 because demand has shifted right
It has no trade because Pw equaled the old autarky price
q.feedback: Initially Pw = (78 + 18)/2 = 48. New demand is 90 - P, giving a closed-economy price of 54, but trade holds price at 48: Qd = 42 and Qs = 30.

key: It imports 12 units at $48; its new autarky price would be $54

q.q: A country is large enough that its import tariff could affect the world price. What should an analyst do?
options: Assume the world price must rise by the full tariff
Ignore the assumption because tariffs never affect foreign prices
State that foreign-price effects require a large-country model rather than silently using the small-country result
Treat tariff revenue as foreign surplus
q.feedback: Model conclusions depend on maintained assumptions.

key: State that foreign-price effects require a large-country model rather than silently using the small-country result

q.q: A quota-holder spends resources lobbying to obtain import rights. How does rent seeking affect welfare?
options: It turns all rents into consumer surplus
It can dissipate some quota rents and create additional social cost
It removes the domestic price increase
It guarantees efficient license allocation
q.feedback: Resources spent capturing rents can add to the policy cost.

key: It can dissipate some quota rents and create additional social cost

q.q: A tariff is removed gradually rather than immediately. Which tradeoff is most relevant?
options: A slower phaseout accelerates consumer gains but concentrates all employment adjustment into the first year.
A slower phaseout preserves tariff revenue without delaying efficiency gains because the announced endpoint is unchanged.
A slower phaseout can ease short-run adjustment but prolong higher prices and distortions relative to immediate removal.
A slower phaseout removes distributional losses by spreading them across years, leaving only consumer gains to compare.
q.feedback: Timing affects adjustment capacity as well as how long tariffs distort prices and quantities. Gradual removal can soften disruption while delaying gains; it does not erase distributional losses.

key: A slower phaseout can ease short-run adjustment but prolong higher prices and distortions relative to immediate removal.

q.q: A tariff raises price from $16 to $21. Domestic output rises from 14 to 24 units and domestic purchases fall from 74 to 59. Which revenue calculation and interpretation is correct?
options: $295; every domestic purchase pays the import tariff
$175; the tariff taxes the 35 units still imported
$300; the original import volume remains the tax base
$120; tariff revenue is the value of all domestic production at the tariff rate
q.feedback: The tariff is $5 and the remaining import gap is 59 - 24 = 35. Revenue is $175. Neither total purchases nor pre-tariff imports is the correct tax base.

key: $175; the tariff taxes the 35 units still imported

q.q: At Pw = $18, Qd = 54 and Qs = 20. A quota is set at 34 imports, with no initial price premium. Demand then increases by 10 at every price. If Qd falls by 2 and Qs rises by 3 for each $1 price increase, what does the unchanged quota do?
options: Price remains $18 and imports rise to 44 because the quota was initially harmless
Price rises to $23 because only the demand response matters
Price rises to $20; the initially zero-rent cap now creates $68 in rents
$34 of rents appears because rent always equals the quota quantity
q.feedback: At the old price the new import gap is 44, ten above the cap. Each $1 rise closes the gap by 5, so price rises $2. Rents are $2 × 34 = $68.

key: Price rises to $20; the initially zero-rent cap now creates $68 in rents

q.q: A tariff raises domestic producer surplus but lowers total surplus. Why are these statements consistent?
options: Producer surplus sits outside total surplus, so producer gains and national welfare can move in opposite directions
Consumer losses are fully captured by producer gains, leaving tariff revenue as the source of deadweight loss
Government revenue reduces total surplus dollar-for-dollar even when the revenue is transferred within the country
Producer gains are a transfer from consumers, while additional consumption and production distortions destroy surplus
q.feedback: Transfers and net losses must be separated.

key: Producer gains are a transfer from consumers, while additional consumption and production distortions destroy surplus

q.q: Which comparison best tests whether protection is the least-cost response to worker displacement?
options: Compare it with wage insurance, retraining, mobility aid, and targeted income support
Compare only protected-firm profits
Compare only import quantity before and after
Assume no alternative policies exist
q.feedback: Adjustment goals can be pursued through policies with different efficiency costs.

key: Compare it with wage insurance, retraining, mobility aid, and targeted income support

q.q: An import quota is administered by first-come, first-served licenses. What additional concern arises?
options: The quota cannot bind
License allocation may reward speed or connections rather than lowest distribution cost
Consumers receive all rents automatically
Domestic price must equal zero
q.feedback: Administrative allocation can create inefficiency and rent-seeking.

key: License allocation may reward speed or connections rather than lowest distribution cost

q.q: Demand is P = 68 - Qd and supply is P = 20 + Qs. Pw is $30. A proposed tariff is $18 per imported unit. What is the competitive domestic outcome?
options: Price $48, positive imports and revenue on all purchases
Price $44, but the government collects $18 on every domestic unit
Price $44, no imports and no tariff revenue
Price $30, because a tariff cannot eliminate imports
q.feedback: Autarky price is (68 + 20)/2 = 44. The proposed import cost is 48, above autarky. Domestic trade clears at 44 without imports, so the treasury receives zero tariff revenue.

key: Price $44, no imports and no tariff revenue

q.q: A country imports 24 units when Pw is $20 and exports 16 when Pw is $30. Domestic supply and demand are unchanged and straight. At what world price would net trade be zero?
options: $25, because it must be the midpoint of the quoted prices
$24, equal to the initial imports
$30, because exports determine autarky
$26, between the two observations
q.feedback: Net imports fall from +24 to -16, a 40-unit decline over $10. At 4 units per dollar, eliminating the initial 24-unit import gap requires a $6 rise, to $26.

key: $26, between the two observations

q.q: Using the free-trade and post-tariff markers, calculate the consumer-surplus loss caused by the tariff.
options: $150 thousand
$200 thousand
$450 thousand
$550 thousand
q.feedback: Consumer surplus falls by 1,250 − 800 = 450 thousand dollars.

key: $450 thousand

q.q: Using the free-trade and post-tariff markers, calculate the producer-surplus gain caused by the tariff.
options: $50 thousand
$200 thousand
$450 thousand
$150 thousand
q.feedback: Producer surplus rises by 200 − 50 = 150 thousand dollars.

key: $150 thousand

q.q: Assuming quota rents remain domestic, what total deadweight loss is shown by the displayed trade graph?
options: $112.5 thousand
$150 thousand
$225 thousand
$450 thousand
q.feedback: The two $112.5-thousand distortion triangles sum to $225 thousand.

key: $225 thousand

q.q: Using the world-price and quota-price outcomes, calculate the consumer-surplus loss caused by the quota.
options: $337.5 thousand
$562.5 thousand
$1,400 thousand
$712.5 thousand
q.feedback: Consumer surplus falls by 1,512.5 − 800 = 712.5 thousand dollars.

key: $712.5 thousand

q.q: Refer to the tariff graph. What are post-tariff imports?
options: 10 units
30 units
40 units
20 units
q.feedback: At Pt=$40, Qd=40 and Qs=20, so imports are 20.

key: 20 units

q.q: Refer to the tariff graph. What is tariff revenue?
q.feedback: The tariff is $10 on 20 imports, so revenue is $200.

q.q: Refer to the tariff graph. What is the total deadweight loss?
q.feedback: Each distortion triangle is $50, so total deadweight loss is $100.

q.q: Refer to the tariff-regions graph. Region B represents tariff revenue. Which expression gives its area?
options: $10 × 40 domestic consumption
$30 × 20 imports
$10 × 20 imports
q.feedback: The rectangle has height $10 and width 20 imports.

key: $10 × 20 imports

q.q: Refer to the tariff-regions graph. Which regions represent the two deadweight-loss areas?
options: A and B
B and C
B only
A and C
q.feedback: The side triangles are the production and consumption distortions; the center rectangle is revenue.

key: A and C

q.q: Refer to the quota graph. How many units are imported under the quota?
options: 20 units
10 units
30 units
40 units
q.feedback: The horizontal distance between Qs=20 and Qd=40 is 20.

key: 20 units

q.q: Refer to the quota-rent graph. What is the value of rectangle R?
q.feedback: The domestic-world price gap is $10 across 20 imported units.

q.q: If domestic import licenses are auctioned in the quota-rent graph, how does rectangle R enter domestic welfare?
options: As consumer surplus
As producer surplus
As government revenue rather than deadweight loss
It disappears from all welfare accounting
q.feedback: Auction proceeds are a domestic transfer to the government.

key: As government revenue rather than deadweight loss

q.q: Arden is a small importer of solar panels, with demand P = 80 - Qd and supply P = 20 + Qs. The world price is $30. What is the net national welfare loss from a $8 per-unit tariff?
q.feedback: The tariff reduces total surplus from $1300 to $1236, a loss of $64.

q.q: Bellora is a small importer of coffee beans, with demand P = 94 - Qd and supply P = 26 + Qs. The world price is $42. What is the net national welfare loss from a $10 per-unit tariff?
q.feedback: The tariff reduces total surplus from $1480 to $1380, a loss of $100.

q.q: Caspia is a small importer of bicycles, with demand P = 72 - Qd and supply P = 12 + Qs. The world price is $20. What is the net national welfare loss from a $8 per-unit tariff?
q.feedback: The tariff reduces total surplus from $1384 to $1320, a loss of $64.

q.q: Demer is a small importer of tablets, with demand P = 104 - Qd and supply P = 24 + Qs. The world price is $40. What is the net national welfare loss from a $12 per-unit tariff?
q.feedback: The tariff reduces total surplus from $2176 to $2032, a loss of $144.

q.q: Estara is a small importer of wool blankets, with demand P = 92 - Qd and supply P = 14 + Qs. The world price is $30. What is the net national welfare loss from a $8 per-unit tariff?
q.feedback: The tariff reduces total surplus from $2050 to $1986, a loss of $64.

q.q: Because quantities are measured in thousands, government tariff revenue in the displayed trade graph is:
options: $100 thousand
$300 thousand
$200 thousand
$400 thousand
q.feedback: The tariff is $2 on 100 thousand imports, so revenue is $200 thousand.

key: $200 thousand

q.q: The tariff raises domestic production from 50 thousand to 100 thousand. What is the production-side deadweight loss in the displayed trade graph?
options: $100 thousand
$150 thousand
$200 thousand
$50 thousand
q.feedback: The production triangle is 1/2 × $2 × 50 thousand = $50 thousand.

key: $50 thousand

q.q: The tariff reduces domestic consumption from 250 thousand to 200 thousand. What is the consumption-side deadweight loss in the displayed trade graph?
options: $50 thousand
$25 thousand
$100 thousand
$200 thousand
q.feedback: The consumption triangle is 1/2 × $2 × 50 thousand = $50 thousand.

key: $50 thousand

q.q: What is the total deadweight loss created by the tariff in the displayed trade graph?
options: $50 thousand
$100 thousand
$200 thousand
$300 thousand
q.feedback: The two $50-thousand distortion triangles sum to $100 thousand.

key: $100 thousand

q.q: If domestic license holders receive the quota rents in the displayed trade graph, total quota rents equal:
options: $50 thousand
$225 thousand
$150 thousand
$300 thousand
q.feedback: The $3 price wedge times 50 thousand imports produces $150 thousand in quota rents.

key: $150 thousand

q.q: Compare the free-trade import gap with the quota import gap. By how much do imports fall?
options: 50 thousand
125 thousand
200 thousand
150 thousand
q.feedback: Imports fall from 275 − 75 = 200 thousand to 50 thousand, a decline of 150 thousand.

key: 150 thousand

q.q: The quota raises domestic production from 75 thousand to 150 thousand. What is the production-side deadweight loss in the displayed trade graph?
options: $112.5 thousand
$75 thousand
$150 thousand.
$225 thousand
q.feedback: The production triangle is 1/2 × $3 × 75 thousand = $112.5 thousand.

key: $112.5 thousand

q.q: Use the quota graph to calculate the consumption-side deadweight loss.
options: $50 thousand
$112.5 thousand
$150 thousand.
$225 thousand
q.feedback: The consumption triangle is 1/2 × $3 × 75 thousand = $112.5 thousand.

key: $112.5 thousand

q.q: A Arden report opposes opening the solar panels market because producers would lose. Domestic curves are P = 80 - Qd and P = 20 + Qs; Pw = $30. A proposed lump-sum compensation plan fully covers that loss and uses $10 of real administrative resources. Which assessment follows?

Post-tariff imports: 24 units; government revenue: $240; production distortion: $50; consumption distortion: $50; total deadweight loss: $100.
q.feedback: The tariff raises price to $32 + $10 = $42. At that price, Qd = 86 - 42 = 44 and Qs = 42 - 22 = 20, so imports = 44 - 20 = 24. Revenue = $10 x 24 = $240. Relative to free trade, Qs rises from 10 to 20 and Qd falls from 54 to 44. Production distortion = 0.5 x $10 x (20 - 10) = $50; consumption distortion = 0.5 x $10 x (54 - 44) = $50. Total deadweight loss = $50 + $50 = $100; tariff revenue is a transfer, not deadweight loss.

key: Post-tariff imports: 24 units; government revenue: $240; production distortion: $50; consumption distortion: $50; total deadweight loss: $100.

q.q: Galena's medical gloves market has demand P = 98 - Qd and supply P = 18 + Qs. It imports at Pw = $34, then adds a $8 tariff without affecting the world price. Which complete import, revenue and distortion ledger is correct?
options: Post-tariff imports: 48 units; government revenue: $384; production distortion: $32; consumption distortion: $32; total deadweight loss: $64.
Post-tariff imports: 32 units; government revenue: $256; production distortion: $64; consumption distortion: $32; total deadweight loss: $96.
Post-tariff imports: 32 units; government revenue: $256; production distortion: $32; consumption distortion: $32; total deadweight loss: $64.
Post-tariff imports: 32 units; government revenue: $256; production distortion: $64; consumption distortion: $64; total deadweight loss: $128.
q.feedback: The tariff raises price to $34 + $8 = $42. At that price, Qd = 98 - 42 = 56 and Qs = 42 - 18 = 24, so imports = 56 - 24 = 32. Revenue = $8 x 32 = $256. Relative to free trade, Qs rises from 16 to 24 and Qd falls from 64 to 56. Production distortion = 0.5 x $8 x (24 - 16) = $32; consumption distortion = 0.5 x $8 x (64 - 56) = $32. Total deadweight loss = $32 + $32 = $64; tariff revenue is a transfer, not deadweight loss.

key: Post-tariff imports: 32 units; government revenue: $256; production distortion: $32; consumption distortion: $32; total deadweight loss: $64.

q.q: Haven's garden tools market has demand P = 90 - Qd and supply P = 30 + Qs. It imports at Pw = $44, then adds a $6 tariff without affecting the world price. Which complete import, revenue and distortion ledger is correct?
options: Post-tariff imports: 32 units; government revenue: $192; production distortion: $18; consumption distortion: $18; total deadweight loss: $36.
Post-tariff imports: 20 units; government revenue: $120; production distortion: $18; consumption distortion: $18; total deadweight loss: $36.
Post-tariff imports: 20 units; government revenue: $120; production distortion: $18; consumption distortion: $36; total deadweight loss: $54.
Post-tariff imports: 20 units; government revenue: $120; production distortion: $102; consumption distortion: $18; total deadweight loss: $120.
q.feedback: The tariff raises price to $44 + $6 = $50. At that price, Qd = 90 - 50 = 40 and Qs = 50 - 30 = 20, so imports = 40 - 20 = 20. Revenue = $6 x 20 = $120. Relative to free trade, Qs rises from 14 to 20 and Qd falls from 46 to 40. Production distortion = 0.5 x $6 x (20 - 14) = $18; consumption distortion = 0.5 x $6 x (46 - 40) = $18. Total deadweight loss = $18 + $18 = $36; tariff revenue is a transfer, not deadweight loss.

key: Post-tariff imports: 20 units; government revenue: $120; production distortion: $18; consumption distortion: $18; total deadweight loss: $36.

q.q: Ilyria's paper-roll market has a world price of $26. After a $7 tariff, imports are 28 units. Which welfare ledger is correct?
options: Post-tariff imports: 28 units; government revenue: $196; production distortion: $24.50; consumption distortion: $24.50; total deadweight loss: $49.
Post-tariff imports: 28 units; government revenue: $196; production distortion: $49; consumption distortion: $24.50; total deadweight loss: $73.50.
Post-tariff imports: 28 units; government revenue: $196; production distortion: $49; consumption distortion: $49; total deadweight loss: $98.
Post-tariff imports: 28 units; government revenue: $196; production distortion: $24.50; consumption distortion: $0; total deadweight loss: $24.50.
q.feedback: The tariff raises price to $26 + $7 = $33. At that price, Qd = 78 - 33 = 45 and Qs = 33 - 16 = 17, so imports = 45 - 17 = 28. Revenue = $7 x 28 = $196. Relative to free trade, Qs rises from 10 to 17 and Qd falls from 52 to 45. Production distortion = 0.5 x $7 x (17 - 10) = $24.50; consumption distortion = 0.5 x $7 x (52 - 45) = $24.50. Total deadweight loss = $24.50 + $24.50 = $49; tariff revenue is a transfer, not deadweight loss.

key: Post-tariff imports: 28 units; government revenue: $196; production distortion: $24.50; consumption distortion: $24.50; total deadweight loss: $49.

q.q: Juno imposes a $12 tariff on imported olive oil. Which option correctly separates government revenue from the production and consumption distortion losses?
options: Post-tariff imports: 24 units; government revenue: $288; production distortion: $72; consumption distortion: $144; total deadweight loss: $216.
Post-tariff imports: 24 units; government revenue: $288; production distortion: $192; consumption distortion: $72; total deadweight loss: $264.
Post-tariff imports: 24 units; government revenue: $552; production distortion: $72; consumption distortion: $72; total deadweight loss: $144.
Post-tariff imports: 24 units; government revenue: $288; production distortion: $72; consumption distortion: $72; total deadweight loss: $144.
q.feedback: The tariff raises price to $38 + $12 = $50. At that price, Qd = 96 - 50 = 46 and Qs = 50 - 28 = 22, so imports = 46 - 22 = 24. Revenue = $12 x 24 = $288. Relative to free trade, Qs rises from 10 to 22 and Qd falls from 58 to 46. Production distortion = 0.5 x $12 x (22 - 10) = $72; consumption distortion = 0.5 x $12 x (58 - 46) = $72. Total deadweight loss = $72 + $72 = $144; tariff revenue is a transfer, not deadweight loss.

key: Post-tariff imports: 24 units; government revenue: $288; production distortion: $72; consumption distortion: $72; total deadweight loss: $144.

q.q: Kestrel imposes a $10 tariff to protect domestic backpack producers. Which result correctly tracks the change in imports and national deadweight loss?
options: Post-tariff imports: 24 units; government revenue: $240; production distortion: $100; consumption distortion: $100; total deadweight loss: $200.
Post-tariff imports: 24 units; government revenue: $240; production distortion: $50; consumption distortion: $0; total deadweight loss: $50.
Post-tariff imports: 24 units; government revenue: $240; production distortion: $50; consumption distortion: $50; total deadweight loss: $100.
Post-tariff imports: 24 units; government revenue: $440; production distortion: $50; consumption distortion: $50; total deadweight loss: $100.
q.feedback: The tariff raises price to $34 + $10 = $44. At that price, Qd = 88 - 44 = 44 and Qs = 44 - 24 = 20, so imports = 44 - 20 = 24. Revenue = $10 x 24 = $240. Relative to free trade, Qs rises from 10 to 20 and Qd falls from 54 to 44. Production distortion = 0.5 x $10 x (20 - 10) = $50; consumption distortion = 0.5 x $10 x (54 - 44) = $50. Total deadweight loss = $50 + $50 = $100; tariff revenue is a transfer, not deadweight loss.

key: Post-tariff imports: 24 units; government revenue: $240; production distortion: $50; consumption distortion: $50; total deadweight loss: $100.

q.q: Lydon's steel bolts market has demand P = 102 - Qd and supply P = 20 + Qs. It imports at Pw = $36, then adds a $10 tariff without affecting the world price. Which complete import, revenue and distortion ledger is correct?
options: Post-tariff imports: 50 units; government revenue: $500; production distortion: $50; consumption distortion: $50; total deadweight loss: $100.
Post-tariff imports: 30 units; government revenue: $300; production distortion: $50; consumption distortion: $50; total deadweight loss: $100.
Post-tariff imports: 30 units; government revenue: $560; production distortion: $50; consumption distortion: $50; total deadweight loss: $100.
Post-tariff imports: 30 units; government revenue: $300; production distortion: $100; consumption distortion: $50; total deadweight loss: $150.
q.feedback: The tariff raises price to $36 + $10 = $46. At that price, Qd = 102 - 46 = 56 and Qs = 46 - 20 = 26, so imports = 56 - 26 = 30. Revenue = $10 x 30 = $300. Relative to free trade, Qs rises from 16 to 26 and Qd falls from 66 to 56. Production distortion = 0.5 x $10 x (26 - 16) = $50; consumption distortion = 0.5 x $10 x (66 - 56) = $50. Total deadweight loss = $50 + $50 = $100; tariff revenue is a transfer, not deadweight loss.

key: Post-tariff imports: 30 units; government revenue: $300; production distortion: $50; consumption distortion: $50; total deadweight loss: $100.

q.q: In Arden's market for solar panels, the no-trade equilibrium price is $50 and the world price is $30. What trade position follows?
options: Arden exports the good
No trade occurs because the prices differ
Arden imports the good
The country must impose a tariff before trade occurs
q.feedback: Because $30 is below the domestic equilibrium price $50, the country imports.

key: Arden imports the good

q.q: Assume a small competitive country, unchanged domestic curves, free trade and no transport costs. Bellora’s no-trade coffee price is $60; the world price is $76. Which trade position follows?
options: Bellora imports because world price exceeds its no-trade price.
Bellora has no net trade because world and no-trade prices differ.
Bellora exports because world price exceeds its no-trade price.
Bellora imports because domestic demand exceeds supply at $76.
q.feedback: The world price exceeds the $60 autarky price. At $76, domestic output rises and domestic consumption falls relative to autarky; surplus production is exported.

key: Bellora exports because world price exceeds its no-trade price.

q.q: Assume a small competitive country, unchanged domestic curves, free trade and no transport costs. Caspia’s no-trade bicycle price and world price are both $42. With ordinary upward-sloping supply and downward-sloping demand, what initial net trade is implied?
options: Net exports, because producers can now sell abroad.
Net imports, because buyers can now purchase abroad.
Net exports equal to all domestic production.
No net trade, because domestic supply and demand remain equal.
q.feedback: At the unchanged equilibrium price of $42, domestic quantity supplied equals domestic quantity demanded. Opening trade creates no initial net export or import gap in this model.

key: No net trade, because domestic supply and demand remain equal.

q.q: Assume a small competitive country, unchanged domestic curves, free trade and no transport costs. Demer becomes a net importer of tablets. Relative to its no-trade equilibrium price, where must the world price lie?
options: Below the no-trade price.
Above the no-trade price.
Exactly at the no-trade price.
Its position cannot be inferred from net imports.
q.feedback: Net imports mean domestic demand exceeds domestic supply at the world price. With ordinary demand and supply, that gap occurs below the autarky equilibrium price.

key: Below the no-trade price.

q.q: Assume a small competitive country, unchanged domestic curves, free trade and no transport costs. Estara’s no-trade wool-blanket price is $53, and the world price is $30. Relative to autarky, what happens to domestic production and consumption?
options: Production rises; consumption falls.
Production falls; consumption rises.
Both production and consumption rise.
Both production and consumption fall.
q.feedback: Opening to the lower world price moves domestic producers down supply and consumers down demand: domestic production falls, consumption rises, and imports fill the gap.

key: Production falls; consumption rises.

q.q: Assume a small competitive country, unchanged domestic curves, free trade and no transport costs. At the world price, Faron’s firms produce 90 batches of tiles and its residents consume 60. What is the trade position?
options: Imports of 30 batches.
Exports of 60 batches.
Imports of 150 batches.
Exports of 30 batches.
q.feedback: Domestic production exceeds domestic consumption by 90 - 60 = 30 batches. Those excess batches are exported.

key: Exports of 30 batches.

q.q: Assume a small competitive country, unchanged domestic curves, free trade and no transport costs. Galena exports medical gloves at a world price of $58. What does this imply about its no-trade equilibrium price?
options: It must have been above $58.
It must have equaled $58.
It must have been below $58.
It could have been either above or below $58.
q.feedback: Exports occur when the world price is above autarky: domestic supply exceeds domestic demand. Therefore the no-trade price was below $58.

key: It must have been below $58.

q.q: Assume a small competitive country, unchanged domestic curves, free trade and no transport costs. Haven’s no-trade garden-tool price is $60 and Ilyria’s is $35. Both face a world price of $44. Which prediction follows?
options: Haven imports and Ilyria exports.
Both countries import.
Haven exports and Ilyria imports.
Both countries export.
q.feedback: Compare each domestic no-trade price with the same world price: $44 < $60 makes Haven an importer; $44 > $35 makes Ilyria an exporter. Comparing the two countries’ prices only to one another is insufficient.

key: Haven imports and Ilyria exports.

q.q: Assume a small competitive country, unchanged domestic curves, free trade and no transport costs. At the world price, Ilyria’s residents consume 70 paper rolls while domestic firms supply 45. Which statement reconciles those quantities?
options: Imports provide the remaining 25 rolls.
Exports absorb the remaining 25 rolls.
Imports provide all 70 rolls.
Exports equal all 45 domestically supplied rolls.
q.feedback: Imports equal domestic consumption minus domestic production: 70 - 45 = 25 rolls. Domestic production still supplies part of consumption.

key: Imports provide the remaining 25 rolls.

q.q: Assume a small competitive country, unchanged domestic curves, free trade and no transport costs. Juno’s no-trade olive-oil price is $62. The world price first is $38, then rises to $70. Which change in trade position follows?
options: Exporter at both world prices.
Importer at $38, exporter at $70.
Exporter at $38, importer at $70.
Importer at both world prices.
q.feedback: At $38 below autarky, domestic demand exceeds supply and Juno imports. At $70 above autarky, domestic supply exceeds demand and Juno exports. The position must be reassessed when the world price crosses $62.

key: Importer at $38, exporter at $70.

q.q: A $6 tariff applies to 40 imported units. How much tariff revenue is collected?
q.feedback: Tariff revenue is $6 × 40 = $240.

q.q: After a tariff, domestic production rises from 25 to 35 units while domestic consumption falls from 70 to 60 units. What happens to imports?
options: They rise from 45 to 95 units
They fall from 45 to 25 units
They fall from 70 to 60 units
They stay at 45 units
q.feedback: Imports change from 70−25=45 to 60−35=25.

key: They fall from 45 to 25 units

q.q: A quota permits 30 imports and creates an $8 domestic-world price gap. What is the total quota rent?
q.feedback: Quota rent is $8 × 30 = $240.

q.q: Under a voluntary export restraint, foreign firms receive free rights to supply 45 units. Buyers pay $27 while the unchanged world price is $23. Who receives the $180 scarcity rent?
options: The importing government as tariff revenue
Domestic producers in addition to their producer surplus
Domestic consumers as a price rebate
The foreign firms holding the export rights
q.feedback: The price wedge is $4 and 45 units cross the border: $180. The foreign holders of the free rights receive the rents; the importing treasury collects no tariff.

key: The foreign firms holding the export rights

q.q: A tariff and a quota initially reduce imports to the same amount. Demand then rises. Which policy automatically permits more imports?
options: The tariff, because the import quantity can adjust at the tariff-inclusive price
The quota, because its quantity cap rises automatically
Neither, because demand cannot shift under trade
Both always preserve the same price and imports
q.feedback: A fixed quota holds imports constant; a tariff allows quantity to adjust.

key: The tariff, because the import quantity can adjust at the tariff-inclusive price

q.q: A trade policy creates $300 of producer gains, $180 of government revenue, and $620 of consumer losses. What is the net welfare effect?
options: A $140 gain
A $140 loss
A $500 gain
No net change

key: A $140 loss

q.q: Which evidence would most directly support an infant-industry argument?
options: A promise that protection will never end
Current producer profits alone
A credible path showing temporary learning lowers future costs enough to exceed protection costs
A claim that consumers do not respond to prices
q.feedback: The argument requires a temporary, evidence-based learning mechanism and net benefits.

key: A credible path showing temporary learning lowers future costs enough to exceed protection costs

q.q: Workers in an import-competing industry lose jobs while consumers gain from lower prices. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: Trade has no gains because some workers lose
Every consumer gain should be ignored
Efficiency proves no assistance can be justified
Trade creates aggregate gains but may justify debate over adjustment assistance
q.feedback: Aggregate gains and adjustment costs can coexist.

key: Trade creates aggregate gains but may justify debate over adjustment assistance

q.q: Why does the displayed trade graph show imports when trade opens at Pw = $5?
options: The world price is below the domestic autarky price
The world price is above the domestic autarky price
Domestic supply exceeds domestic demand at $5
The world price equals the autarky price
q.feedback: A small country imports when the world price is below its no-trade equilibrium price.

key: The world price is below the domestic autarky price

q.q: Why does the displayed trade graph show exports when trade opens at Pw = $10?
options: The world price is above the domestic autarky price
The world price is below the domestic autarky price
Domestic demand exceeds domestic supply at $10
The world price is fixed at the autarky price
q.feedback: A world price above the no-trade equilibrium price creates excess domestic supply for export.

key: The world price is above the domestic autarky price

q.q: At the tariff-inclusive price of $6 in the displayed trade graph, domestic production is:
options: 50 thousand
150 thousand
100 thousand
200 thousand
q.feedback: The $6 line intersects domestic supply at Q = 100 thousand.

key: 100 thousand

q.q: Refer to the graph. At the tariff-inclusive price shown, what is domestic quantity demanded?
options: 100 thousand
150 thousand
250 thousand
200 thousand
q.feedback: The $6 line intersects demand at Q = 200 thousand.

key: 200 thousand

q.q: After the tariff in the displayed trade graph, imports equal:
options: 100 thousand
50 thousand
150 thousand
200 thousand
q.feedback: At $6, Qd = 200 thousand and Qs = 100 thousand, so imports are 100 thousand.

key: 100 thousand

q.q: Compared with free trade at Pw = $4, the tariff in the displayed trade graph reduces imports by:
options: 50 thousand
100 thousand
150 thousand
200 thousand
q.feedback: Free-trade imports are 250 − 50 = 200 thousand; after the tariff they are 100 thousand.

key: 100 thousand

q.q: At the quota-induced domestic price of $6 in the displayed trade graph, domestic producers supply:
options: 75 thousand
175 thousand
150 thousand
200 thousand
q.feedback: The $6 line intersects supply at Q = 150 thousand.

key: 150 thousand

q.q: At the quota-induced domestic price of $6 in the displayed trade graph, domestic consumers demand:
options: 150 thousand
175 thousand
275 thousand
200 thousand
q.feedback: The $6 line intersects demand at Q = 200 thousand.

key: 200 thousand

q.q: What import quantity is permitted by the quota shown in the displayed trade graph?
options: 50 thousand
75 thousand
125 thousand
200 thousand
q.feedback: At $6, imports equal Qd − Qs = 200 − 150 = 50 thousand.

key: 50 thousand

q.q: What is the per-unit quota rent implied by the displayed trade graph?
options: $1 per unit
$3 per unit
$6 per unit
$9 per unit
q.feedback: The domestic price is $6 while the world price is $3, creating a $3 price wedge per imported unit.

key: $3 per unit

q.q: A student says a country imports because domestic demand is large. What comparison actually determines importer status?
options: Demand above zero
Domestic supply above zero
World price below the no-trade equilibrium price
Exports in another market
q.feedback: Importer status follows the price comparison, not demand size alone.

key: World price below the no-trade equilibrium price

q.q: A student says abundant domestic supply automatically makes a country an exporter. What is missing?
options: Domestic demand must be zero
A tariff must be imposed
The country must ban imports
The world price must be above the domestic no-trade equilibrium price
q.feedback: Export status depends on the world-price comparison.

key: The world price must be above the domestic no-trade equilibrium price

q.q: Why does possible compensation not prove losers are compensated?
options: Compensation occurs automatically through the world price
Losers have no measurable loss
Total surplus cannot fund transfers
A transfer requires an actual policy or agreement
q.feedback: Feasibility and implementation are different.

key: A transfer requires an actual policy or agreement

q.q: A small importing country faces a world price of $20 per unit and imposes a $4 per-unit tariff. The country cannot affect the world price, and imports continue after the tariff. What domestic price results?
options: $24 per unit
$16 per unit
$20 per unit
$4 per unit
q.feedback: With imports continuing, domestic price equals world price plus the per-unit tariff: $20 + $4 = $24. The tariff adds to the domestic price; it is not subtracted from the world price.

key: $24 per unit

q.q: A tariff raises domestic production and lowers domestic consumption. What happens to imports?
options: They rise
They fall
They are unchanged
They equal domestic production
q.feedback: The gap between demand and supply shrinks.

key: They fall

q.q: A student labels tariff revenue as deadweight loss. What is wrong?
options: Revenue belongs to consumers
Deadweight loss equals producer gain
Revenue is a transfer; deadweight loss is lost surplus
Tariffs never collect revenue
q.feedback: Separate transfers from net losses.

key: Revenue is a transfer; deadweight loss is lost surplus

q.q: Which two effects create tariff deadweight loss?
options: Producer surplus and tariff revenue
Imports and exports
Consumer surplus and quota rent
Production distortion and consumption distortion
q.feedback: The tariff causes too much high-cost domestic production and too little consumption.

key: Production distortion and consumption distortion

q.q: A student says a binding quota leaves price at the world price. What is the correction?
options: The domestic price rises until the import gap equals the quota
The world price rises by law
Domestic supply becomes zero
Demand becomes perfectly elastic
q.feedback: The price adjusts to ration the limited imports.

key: The domestic price rises until the import gap equals the quota

q.q: A student assumes the government always receives quota rents. What determines the recipient?
options: The demand-curve intercept only
Ownership or auction of the import licenses
The no-trade quantity only
The tariff rate
q.feedback: Quota rents follow the license rights.

key: Ownership or auction of the import licenses

q.q: A student says equivalent tariffs and quotas remain identical after demand changes. What is the key difference?
options: A tariff fixes domestic demand
A quota fixes the world price
A tariff fixes the wedge while a quota fixes import quantity
Both fix producer surplus
q.feedback: Different policy instruments adjust differently to shocks.

key: A tariff fixes the wedge while a quota fixes import quantity

q.q: A learner says a voluntary export restraint must earn revenue for the importing treasury. Foreign exporters receive the export rights free. What corrects the claim?
options: Every restriction automatically sends its price wedge to the importing treasury
Domestic producers receive the foreign exporters' rights revenue
Quota rents are destroyed surplus, so no one receives them
The foreign rights holders receive the scarcity rents; a VER is not an import tariff
q.feedback: A VER limits foreign shipments. With the rights held free by foreign firms, the price-wedge receipts accrue abroad. Rent ownership, not the word restriction, determines the recipient.

key: The foreign rights holders receive the scarcity rents; a VER is not an import tariff

q.q: What is missing from the claim “protection saves jobs”?
options: Effects on consumers, downstream industries, exports, and alternative uses of resources
The protected industry’s name
The number of foreign countries only
A promise that prices never change
q.feedback: A complete analysis includes opportunity costs and spillovers.

key: Effects on consumers, downstream industries, exports, and alternative uses of resources

q.q: What is the proper response to a national-security claim?
options: Accept every claim automatically
Evaluate the specific risk, policy cost, and narrower alternatives
Reject every claim automatically
Count only tariff revenue
q.feedback: Security arguments require evidence and proportionality.

key: Evaluate the specific risk, policy cost, and narrower alternatives

q.q: In a small importing country, a tariff usually causes domestic production of the protected good to:
options: Decrease
Remain fixed by definition
Fall to zero
Increase
q.feedback: The tariff raises the domestic price, encouraging domestic producers to supply more.

key: Increase

q.q: In a small importing country, a tariff usually causes domestic consumption of the protected good to:
options: Remain fixed by definition
Become equal to exports
Decrease
Increase
q.feedback: The higher domestic price reduces quantity demanded.

key: Decrease

q.q: Government tariff revenue is generated by:
options: The tariff multiplied by domestic consumption whether imported or not
The tariff per imported unit multiplied by the quantity imported
The world price multiplied by domestic production
Consumer surplus multiplied by producer surplus
q.feedback: Tariff revenue equals the tax rate per imported unit times the number of units still imported.

key: The tariff per imported unit multiplied by the quantity imported

q.q: A binding import quota directly limits:
options: Domestic supply at every price
The quantity that may be imported
The world price in every country
Domestic demand at every price
q.feedback: A quota is a quantitative restriction on imports.

key: The quantity that may be imported

q.q: When a binding quota raises the domestic price above the world price, domestic producers generally:
options: Gain producer surplus
Lose producer surplus
Receive no price effect
Become foreign producers
q.feedback: The higher domestic price benefits domestic sellers.

key: Gain producer surplus

q.q: Quota rent is the value created by:
options: The gap between domestic demand and domestic supply at autarky only
Total consumer surplus before trade
Government tax revenue collected on all domestic production
The gap between the domestic price and world price on the units allowed to be imported
q.feedback: Import licenses can carry value because permitted imports can be bought at the world price and sold at the higher domestic price.

key: The gap between the domestic price and world price on the units allowed to be imported

q.q: A small country has domestic demand P = 54 - Qd and supply P = 18 + Qs. The world price is $28. Which outcome follows when trade opens?
options: It imports 16 units; the price falls and domestic consumers gain
It exports 16 units; the price falls and domestic producers gain
It imports 26 units; every unit consumed must be imported
It imports 16 units; domestic consumers lose from the lower price
q.feedback: Autarky price is $36. At $28, demand is 26 and supply is 10, leaving 16 imports. The lower price benefits domestic consumers.

key: It imports 16 units; the price falls and domestic consumers gain

q.q: At an unchanged world price, domestic mills supply 68 units and residents buy 44. After opening to trade, which combination is consistent with this competitive small-country market?
options: 24 imports, a price below autarky, and a gain to domestic consumers
68 exports, since all domestic output is sold abroad
24 exports, a price below autarky, and a loss to domestic producers
24 exports, a price above autarky, and a gain to domestic producers
q.feedback: The excess of supply over domestic demand is 24 exports. With upward supply and downward demand, this occurs at a world price above autarky, benefiting domestic producers.

key: 24 exports, a price above autarky, and a gain to domestic producers

q.q: Demand is P = 66 - Qd and supply is P = 18 + Qs. A world price of $42 initially produces no trade. If the world price falls to $36 with the curves unchanged, what follows?
options: 12 exports and higher domestic producer surplus
No trade because the original world price equaled autarky
12 imports and higher domestic consumer surplus
30 imports because domestic demand becomes 30
q.feedback: The initial price equals autarky. At $36, Qd = 30 and Qs = 18, so 12 units are imported and consumers gain from the price reduction.

key: 12 imports and higher domestic consumer surplus

q.q: A small country initially imports steel at a world price below its autarky price. Domestic demand then falls sharply while domestic supply is unchanged. What could happen if the shift is large enough?
options: The country cannot change trade status once it opens
The country could import less or even switch to exporting
The country must import more because world price is fixed
The world price must rise to the old autarky price
q.feedback: At the fixed world price, a large demand decrease reduces excess demand and can create excess supply.

key: The country could import less or even switch to exporting

q.q: A small country initially exports wheat because the world price exceeds its autarky price. A productivity improvement shifts domestic supply strongly right. Holding world price fixed, the most likely effect is:
options: Exports increase
Exports decrease because supply rose
The country becomes an importer automatically
World price falls because the small country controls it
q.feedback: At the fixed world price, greater domestic supply increases the excess supply available for export.

key: Exports increase

q.q: A tariff and a voluntary export restraint each allow 45 imports at a domestic price of $27; the world price stays $23. Foreign firms get the VER rights free. How much higher is importing-country surplus under the tariff, holding quantities and other costs equal?
options: $0, because identical prices imply identical national welfare
$1,215, because all spending on imports is government revenue
$180, because the tariff removes both distortion losses
$180, because the price-wedge receipts stay in the importing country
q.feedback: Both restrictions have the same production and consumption distortions. The difference is $4 × 45 = $180: tariff receipts stay domestic while the specified VER rents go abroad.

key: $180, because the price-wedge receipts stay in the importing country

q.q: A quota is set at the current free-trade import quantity and is fully binding only if import demand later rises. Compared with a fixed tariff, what feature makes the quota potentially more restrictive after a demand increase?
options: The tariff fixes import quantity while the quota fixes price
A quota cannot affect price after it is set
The quota fixes import quantity while the domestic price can rise further
The quota automatically lowers the world price to zero
q.feedback: A quantitative ceiling does not expand automatically when import demand rises, so the domestic price can adjust upward.

key: The quota fixes import quantity while the domestic price can rise further

q.q: A proposed tariff would save 2,000 jobs in one industry but raise costs for downstream firms and millions of consumers. What is the best economic evaluation?
options: Compare protected wages with tariff revenue, treating higher input prices as transfers that cannot affect downstream output.
Compare protected jobs with downstream jobs, treating consumer purchasing-power losses as irrelevant when employment rises.
Compare protected-job benefits with consumer, downstream, retaliation and efficiency costs before judging the policy.
Compare imports before and after the tariff, treating fewer imports as the net national benefit of protection.
q.feedback: Saved jobs are one effect. Consumer costs, input-using industries, retaliation and resource distortions can offset benefits; import reductions or selected employment counts do not measure net welfare.

key: Compare protected-job benefits with consumer, downstream, retaliation and efficiency costs before judging the policy.

q.q: An industry requests “temporary” protection but has received it for 25 years and has no measurable productivity improvement. What does this evidence do to the infant-industry argument?
options: It proves consumers receive the tariff revenue
It weakens it because the promised temporary learning benefit has not materialized
It strengthens it because longer protection proves the industry is important
It is irrelevant because infant-industry protection should be permanent
q.feedback: Persistent protection without learning or an exit condition undermines the standard infant-industry rationale.

key: It weakens it because the promised temporary learning benefit has not materialized

q.q: A country imposes a tariff to reduce dependence on a strategic input, but domestic production cannot expand and allied suppliers are available. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: Limited domestic capacity weakens this tariff’s resilience channel; compare allied diversification with the tariff’s added costs.
Higher producer prices establish greater resilience immediately, even if domestic capacity cannot expand.
Lower import dependence is sufficient for resilience, regardless of whether the remaining supply comes from one supplier.
Allied suppliers remove every security risk, making evaluation of diversification costs and reliability unnecessary.
q.feedback: The tariff cannot quickly create the missing domestic capacity. Reliable allied diversification may address the specific risk at lower cost, but its reliability and costs still require comparison.

key: Limited domestic capacity weakens this tariff’s resilience channel; compare allied diversification with the tariff’s added costs.

q.q: A tariff raises domestic producer surplus by $60 million, government revenue by $20 million, and lowers consumer surplus by $105 million. Ignoring other effects, what is the strongest conclusion?
options: National surplus rises by $185 million because all three figures should be added
National surplus rises by $25 million because producer gains exceed revenue
The tariff is efficient because government receives revenue
National surplus falls by $25 million even though protected producers gain
q.feedback: The net change is +60 +20 -105 = -25 million; distributional gains do not erase the aggregate loss.

key: National surplus falls by $25 million even though protected producers gain

q.q: A protection proposal benefits a small organized industry by $50 per person while costing a very large number of consumers $2 each. Why can the policy still attract strong political support?
options: Small individual consumer losses establish a smaller total cost, so support reflects a necessarily positive net benefit.
A large consumer population creates stronger per-person lobbying incentives even when each person loses only a little.
A larger individual stake gives beneficiaries stronger organizing incentives even when small dispersed losses sum to more.
Organized support reveals higher aggregate willingness to pay, so the policy’s national efficiency follows from its passage.
q.feedback: Concentrated stakes can make organizing worthwhile for beneficiaries while small individual losses discourage consumers from organizing. Political support does not establish aggregate net benefits.

key: A larger individual stake gives beneficiaries stronger organizing incentives even when small dispersed losses sum to more.

q.q: A tariff raises the domestic price from $20 to $24. Domestic production rises while domestic consumption falls. What happens to imports?
options: They fall
They rise
They must stay unchanged
They become exports automatically
q.feedback: Imports equal domestic consumption minus domestic production; both changes shrink that gap.

key: They fall

q.q: A $3 tariff is collected on 40 imported units. How much tariff revenue does the government receive?
q.feedback: Revenue is $3 × 40 = $120.

q.q: Why does a small-country tariff reduce total surplus even though it creates government revenue?
options: Producer surplus always falls under a tariff
The world price rises by the full tariff
Some lost consumer surplus becomes deadweight loss rather than a transfer
Government revenue is never part of national surplus
q.feedback: Part of the consumer loss is transferred to producers and government; the production and consumption distortions are net losses.

key: Some lost consumer surplus becomes deadweight loss rather than a transfer

q.q: A quota allows 30 imported units. The domestic price is $18 and the world price is $14. What is total quota rent?
A tariff and quota produce the same domestic price and import quantity. What determines whether their national welfare effects are identical?
options: Whether producers earn any surplus
Who receives the quota rents
Whether domestic consumers exist
Whether the world price is positive
q.feedback: A tariff creates government revenue; a quota can create equivalent rents that may go to domestic or foreign license holders.

key: Who receives the quota rents

q.q: A binding quota is tightened. In the standard import model, which combination is most likely?
options: Domestic price rises and imports fall
Domestic price falls and imports rise
Domestic price and imports both remain fixed
Domestic price falls and exports rise
q.feedback: A tighter quantity limit restricts import supply further and pushes the domestic price upward.

key: Domestic price rises and imports fall

q.q: A domestic industry argues for protection because foreign competition will reduce its employment. What is the main economic weakness in stopping the analysis there?
options: Tariffs never affect prices
It ignores consumer costs and jobs/resources created elsewhere
Employment can never fall in an import-competing industry
Foreign competition always raises domestic producer surplus
q.feedback: A complete welfare analysis includes costs to consumers, resource reallocation, and economy-wide effects.

key: It ignores consumer costs and jobs/resources created elsewhere

q.q: A new domestic battery industry asks for five years of protection while firms learn a production process. Which finding would give the request the strongest economic case?
options: Documented learning-by-doing is expected to lower future costs enough to offset the temporary protection cost
The firms would earn higher profits whenever imports are restricted
Consumers prefer the domestic brand even at a higher price
The industry wants protection with no expiration date
q.feedback: A defensible infant-industry case requires a credible temporary learning benefit large enough to justify the cost of protection.

key: Documented learning-by-doing is expected to lower future costs enough to offset the temporary protection cost

q.q: A national-security case for protecting a product is strongest when:
options: Domestic producers simply want higher profits
Imports come from any foreign country regardless of risk
The protected industry has falling employment
The product is genuinely critical and dependence creates a specific strategic vulnerability
q.feedback: National-security arguments need a concrete strategic externality or vulnerability, not a generic dislike of imports.

key: The product is genuinely critical and dependence creates a specific strategic vulnerability

q.q: How does a tariff connect to the tax-wedge idea from domestic markets?
options: It guarantees the legal and economic burden are identical
It creates a wedge between the world price and the domestic buyer/seller price
It eliminates the role of price
It shifts world demand only
q.feedback: A tariff acts like a tax on imports and raises the domestic price above the world price in the small-country model.

key: It creates a wedge between the world price and the domestic buyer/seller price

q.q: How does tariff deadweight loss connect to surplus analysis?
options: It is the total surplus destroyed by production and consumption distortions
It is the full transfer from consumers to producers
It equals tariff revenue
It is producer surplus after the tariff
q.feedback: The surplus framework identifies the trades and resource uses that no longer maximize gains.

key: It is the total surplus destroyed by production and consumption distortions

q.q: How does a binding quota connect to ordinary supply-and-demand pressure?
options: Import restrictions make domestic supply irrelevant
Restricting imports reduces available supply to the domestic market and raises the domestic price
A quota shifts domestic demand left automatically
A quota fixes the world price and domestic price at zero
q.feedback: The quantity restriction tightens the domestic market and raises price until the permitted import gap is satisfied.

key: Restricting imports reduces available supply to the domestic market and raises the domestic price

q.q: How does quota rent connect to economic rent more generally?
options: A scarce legal right can acquire value because it permits profitable access
Quota rent is a payment for labor only
Economic rent requires a perfectly competitive labor market
Quota rent equals consumer surplus by definition
q.feedback: Import licenses become valuable because the restriction creates a price gap.

key: A scarce legal right can acquire value because it permits profitable access

q.q: Why can auctioning quota licenses make a quota look more like a tariff in national-welfare accounting?
options: Auctioning eliminates the domestic price increase
Auctioning makes imports unlimited
Auctioning turns the quota into an export subsidy
The government captures the quota rent much like tariff revenue
q.feedback: Who receives the rent is a major difference between quotas and tariffs.

key: The government captures the quota rent much like tariff revenue

q.q: A demand increase occurs under a fixed quota. What does the quota teach about quantity controls versus price-based barriers?
options: Both price and imports must stay unchanged
The quota automatically becomes a tariff
The import quantity stays capped while domestic price can rise further
Domestic price stays fixed while imports expand freely
q.feedback: A hard quantity limit adjusts differently from a fixed per-unit tariff when market conditions change.

key: The import quantity stays capped while domestic price can rise further

q.q: A voluntary export restraint gives foreign firms free shipment rights. How does national-welfare accounting connect this arrangement to an equivalent tariff?
options: Count the rents as domestic tax receipts because domestic consumers pay them
Include the same distortions, but subtract rents sent abroad instead of counting domestic tariff revenue
Count only producer gains because no import tax is collected
Treat rents and distortion triangles as the same loss in world welfare
q.feedback: With the same prices and quantities, the distortions match. Foreign rents are a transfer abroad that lowers importing-country welfare relative to domestic tariff receipts; they are not themselves destroyed world surplus.

key: Include the same distortions, but subtract rents sent abroad instead of counting domestic tariff revenue

q.q: How does a quota-versus-tariff comparison connect to policy design?
options: Two policies can create similar price and quantity effects but differ in who receives the transfer
Two policies with matching price and quantity effects must give their revenue or rents to the same recipients.
Two policies with matching import quantities must raise equal government revenue, even when quota licenses are given away.
Two policies can raise the same domestic price, but only the quota distorts domestic production and consumption.
q.feedback: An equivalent tariff and binding quota can produce similar prices and quantities, yet tariff revenue goes to government while quota rents go to the holders of import rights unless those rights are auctioned. Both can distort production and consumption. Policy design must therefore track who receives revenue or rents as well as efficiency effects.

key: Two policies can create similar price and quantity effects but differ in who receives the transfer

q.q: How does evaluating protection connect positive and normative economics?
options: Positive economics decides which distribution is fair
Normative economics calculates tariff revenue mechanically
The two approaches are identical in trade policy
Positive analysis estimates costs and benefits; normative judgment weighs goals and distribution
q.feedback: Trade-policy evaluation separates what a policy does from judgments about whether its goals justify those effects.

key: Positive analysis estimates costs and benefits; normative judgment weighs goals and distribution

q.q: A learner says the world price is the same thing as the country’s no-trade equilibrium price. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: The world price is the external trading price; comparing it with the no-trade price reveals importer or exporter status
The world price should be treated as the domestic equilibrium price after trade, so the two prices coincide by definition
The world price measures domestic producer surplus, while the no-trade price measures domestic consumer surplus
The no-trade price is determined by foreign supply conditions, while the world price comes from domestic supply and demand
q.feedback: Trade status comes from comparing the world price with the domestic autarky equilibrium price.

key: The world price is the external trading price; comparing it with the no-trade price reveals importer or exporter status

q.q: A learner calculates tariff revenue using all domestic consumption rather than imported units. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Multiply the tariff by domestic production plus imports
Use the world price times all consumption
Tariff revenue equals consumer surplus lost
Multiply the tariff per unit by the quantity imported
q.feedback: The tariff is collected on imported units, not on every unit consumed.

key: Multiply the tariff per unit by the quantity imported

q.q: A learner says all consumer surplus lost under a tariff is deadweight loss. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Producer gains are not part of total surplus
Government revenue is always deadweight loss
Some loss is transferred to producers and government; only the unrecovered portion is deadweight loss
All consumer loss disappears from national welfare
