q.feedback: National reach does not make an occupational choice question macro. The extension asks about economy-wide employment, including effects beyond the occupation.

key: Estimate how the rule changes total employment across all occupations

q.q: An equipment rebate shifts purchases toward one technology. A report totals emissions from that technology and labels the study macro because the estimate is national. What is the best correction?
options: A subsidy question is micro even when it studies aggregate output
National sector totals alone do not establish a macro question; examine economy-wide outcomes to make that link
Environmental questions are macro regardless of the unit studied
A national total rules out any microeconomic interpretation
q.commonError: Forcing a question with market and aggregate consequences into only one field.
q.feedback: Geographic reach and environmental relevance do not define macroeconomics. A sector study can be micro; a separate economy-wide output or employment question would establish the macro link.

key: National sector totals alone do not establish a macro question; examine economy-wide outcomes to make that link

q.q: One bank raises loan rates and loses borrowers to rivals. At the same time, national lending declines. What separates a micro finding from an unsupported macro explanation?
options: Rivals gaining customers refutes the reported national decline
The bank's large size makes its pricing decision purely macro
Borrower switching explains the bank's share; economy-wide evidence is needed to explain the total decline
The bank's lost borrowers necessarily equal the national lending decline
q.commonError: Forcing a question with market and aggregate consequences into only one field.
q.feedback: Market-share shifts concern individual institutions. Explaining the aggregate decline requires counting lending across banks and identifying broader mechanisms.

key: Borrower switching explains the bank's share; economy-wide evidence is needed to explain the total decline

q.q: A factory replaces workers with equipment. Its investment rises while other firms postpone purchases. Which statement about the evidence is justified?
options: The factory's higher investment establishes a rise in national investment
Postponement elsewhere makes the factory decision a macro question only
Opposite firm responses make national investment impossible to measure
The factory decision is micro; the direction of national investment requires aggregation
q.commonError: Forcing a question with market and aggregate consequences into only one field.
q.feedback: Individual changes can offset one another. The factory decision and the national total are related but distinct questions.

key: The factory decision is micro; the direction of national investment requires aggregation

q.q: Workers relocate from rural districts to a city. City rents and employment rise. Which claim needs additional economy-wide evidence?
options: National employment rose rather than being redistributed across locations
The city's housing market experienced a local change
The move changed some households' location choices
Employers in the city gained access to more workers
q.commonError: Forcing a question with market and aggregate consequences into only one field.
q.feedback: Local gains can reflect transfers from other locations. National employment must account for origin districts and other responses; city outcomes alone cannot settle it.

key: National employment rose rather than being redistributed across locations

q.q: An industry's average wage rises after its lowest-paid jobs disappear, although every continuing worker's wage stays fixed. What should an analyst conclude before generalizing nationally?
options: Unchanged individual wages prove the reported industry average cannot rise
Composition changed the industry average; neither individual raises nor national wage growth follows
The higher average proves continuing workers received raises
An industry average is automatically the national average when many workers are sampled
q.commonError: Generalizing a narrow sample directly to the national economy.
q.feedback: Removing low-paid jobs changes the mix being averaged. Distinguish composition from individual wage changes, then assess representative national evidence.

key: Composition changed the industry average; neither individual raises nor national wage growth follows

q.q: A national staffing rule raises hospital employment 20% in cities containing three-quarters of the country’s initial hospital jobs and lowers it 10% in the remaining cities. Other employment is not measured. Which analysis correctly connects micro evidence and the aggregate claim?
options: Hospital jobs rise 12.5% overall; the city responses are micro evidence, but total national employment cannot be inferred without other sectors.
Hospital jobs rise 5% overall; averaging the two city growth rates establishes the change in total national employment.
Hospital jobs rise 20% overall; the majority-city response is the macro result and the smaller group can be ignored.
Hospital jobs rise 12.5% overall; that sectoral percentage must also be the percentage change in economy-wide employment.
q.commonError: Forcing a question with market and aggregate consequences into only one field.
q.feedback: Weight by initial hospital jobs: 0.75×20%+0.25×(-10%)=12.5%. Aggregation of one sector does not establish the effect on total employment; other sectors and reallocation matter.

key: Hospital jobs rise 12.5% overall; the city responses are micro evidence, but total national employment cannot be inferred without other sectors.

q.q: A fuel tax raises one fuel price by 10%. Fuel has a 5% fixed weight in a national consumer-price index; all other prices are unchanged for this exercise. A household spends 20% of its budget on that fuel. Which statement correctly links the levels of analysis?
options: The index and household basket both rise 10%; a nationwide tax makes each individual effect identical to the macro effect.
The index rises 0.5%, while that household’s fixed-basket cost rises 2%; the fuel-market, household and aggregate questions are linked but distinct.
The index rises 2%, while the household basket rises 0.5%; national aggregation uses each household’s own expenditure weight.
The index cannot change because the tax affects one product; only a tax on every product can have a macroeconomic effect.
q.commonError: Forcing a question with market and aggregate consequences into only one field.
q.feedback: Under the fixed-basket assumptions, national impact is 0.05×10%=0.5%, and household impact is 0.20×10%=2%. A micro market shock can contribute to an aggregate price measure without having the same effect on each household.

key: The index rises 0.5%, while that household’s fixed-basket cost rises 2%; the fuel-market, household and aggregate questions are linked but distinct.

q.q: A wealthy region accounts for 25% of initial national real consumption. Its consumption rises 12%, while the rest of the country falls 4%. A large survey covers only the wealthy region. Which conclusion is warranted?
options: National real consumption rises 12%; a large sample makes the observed region representative by itself.
National real consumption rises 4%; equally averaging the two regional rates gives the national result.
National real consumption is unchanged; survey size does not fix its unrepresentative coverage.
National real consumption falls 4%; the larger population outside the region makes the wealthy-region change irrelevant.
q.commonError: Generalizing a narrow sample directly to the national economy.
q.feedback: Weight by initial consumption: 0.25×12%+0.75×(-4%)=0%. A precise estimate for one region is not a representative national estimate. Large sample size reduces sampling noise within coverage, not coverage bias.

key: National real consumption is unchanged; survey size does not fix its unrepresentative coverage.

q.q: After a national policy-rate cut, banks serving 60% of initial business lending lower loan rates and lending there rises 10%. Capital-constrained banks serving the rest do not change lending. A commentator predicts every firm invests 10% more. Which correction is strongest?
options: Measured aggregate lending rises 10%; a national rate cut ensures all firms face the same financing change.
Measured aggregate lending rises 5%; equal bank-group averaging identifies both national lending and each firm’s investment.
Measured aggregate lending is unchanged; unchanged lending at constrained banks cancels growth at unconstrained banks.
Measured aggregate lending rises 6%; heterogeneous bank constraints matter, and lending growth alone does not identify every firm’s investment response.
q.commonError: Forcing a question with market and aggregate consequences into only one field.
q.feedback: Weighted lending growth is 0.60×10%+0.40×0%=6%. The macro policy transmits through heterogeneous micro constraints; borrowing changes also need not translate one-for-one into each firm’s investment.

key: Measured aggregate lending rises 6%; heterogeneous bank constraints matter, and lending growth alone does not identify every firm’s investment response.

q.q: A tax credit changes purchases in the electric-bicycle market. Why can the analysis be microeconomic?
options: It focuses on buyers and sellers in one market
It may change tax revenue
It uses a national currency
It was enacted by a government
q.commonError: Classifying by size, institution, or topic word instead of the unit of analysis.
q.feedback: Microeconomics examines households, firms, and particular markets.

key: It focuses on buyers and sellers in one market

q.q: A central bank action is studied through its effect on national spending and inflation. Why is this macroeconomic?
options: Interest rates cannot be studied by microeconomics
The outcomes are economy-wide aggregates
Central banks never affect individual markets
Any government institution defines the field
q.commonError: Calling a large organization macro even when the question concerns one decision-maker.
q.feedback: Macroeconomics examines economy-wide aggregates such as output, inflation, and unemployment.

key: The outcomes are economy-wide aggregates

q.q: A study follows household saving and then asks how total saving affects national investment. What levels appear?
options: Two unrelated micro questions
Only macro because households disappear
Individual choices and an aggregate outcome
Only micro because saving begins at home
q.commonError: Forcing a question with market and aggregate consequences into only one field.
q.feedback: One event can require both market-level and economy-wide analysis.

key: Individual choices and an aggregate outcome

q.q: A retailer has 20,000 stores, but a study asks how that one firm sets delivery fees. What matters for classification?
options: The number of employees alone
Whether fees are quoted in dollars
Whether the retailer operates nationally
The unit of analysis, not the firm’s size
q.commonError: Classifying by size, institution, or topic word instead of the unit of analysis.
q.feedback: Microeconomics examines households, firms, and particular markets.

key: The unit of analysis, not the firm’s size

q.q: Household purchases fall after a national recession begins. What levels interact?
options: Micro choices and macro conditions
Only household-level analysis
Only macroeconomic analysis because the recession is national.
No economic levels
q.commonError: Forcing a question with market and aggregate consequences into only one field.
q.feedback: One event can require both market-level and economy-wide analysis.

key: Micro choices and macro conditions

q.q: A large corporation changes one product’s price. Why is size not decisive?
options: Product prices are macro indicators, even if the evidence covers only one industry
Classification follows the question’s unit of analysis
Corporations cannot be studied microeconomically
Large firms are national aggregates
q.commonError: Classifying by size, institution, or topic word instead of the unit of analysis.
q.feedback: Microeconomics examines households, firms, and particular markets.

key: Classification follows the question’s unit of analysis

q.q: Which question about interest rates is most macroeconomic?
options: How one firm finances equipment
How one borrower chooses a loan
How rates affect total spending and inflation
How one bank prices a mortgage
q.commonError: Calling a large organization macro even when the question concerns one decision-maker.
q.feedback: Macroeconomics examines economy-wide aggregates such as output, inflation, and unemployment.

key: How rates affect total spending and inflation

q.q: Does microeconomics simply mean a topic is physically small?
options: No; micro means only private business
Yes; every small object is a micro topic
No; it refers to individual decision-makers or specific markets
Yes; dataset size determines the field
q.commonError: Classifying by size, institution, or topic word instead of the unit of analysis.
q.feedback: Microeconomics examines households, firms, and particular markets.

key: No; it refers to individual decision-makers or specific markets

q.q: A national corporation sets one product’s price. Is the question automatically macroeconomic?
options: Yes; national firms are economy-wide aggregates
Yes; all corporate decisions are macro
No; prices are outside economics
No; one firm or market can still be microeconomic
q.commonError: Calling a large organization macro even when the question concerns one decision-maker.
q.feedback: Macroeconomics examines economy-wide aggregates such as output, inflation, and unemployment.

key: No; one firm or market can still be microeconomic

q.q: Does government involvement automatically make a question macroeconomic?
options: No; a policy can target one market or decision
Yes; any government policy is automatically macroeconomic.
Yes; taxes cannot be studied microeconomically
No; government choices are noneconomic
q.commonError: Classifying by size, institution, or topic word instead of the unit of analysis.
q.feedback: Microeconomics examines households, firms, and particular markets.

key: No; a policy can target one market or decision

q.q: Can one event legitimately involve both micro and macro analysis?
options: Only when a central bank is involved
Yes; individual responses can affect aggregates and vice versa
Only when no market price changes
No; every event belongs to exactly one field
q.commonError: Forcing a question with market and aggregate consequences into only one field.
q.feedback: One event can require both market-level and economy-wide analysis.

key: Yes; individual responses can affect aggregates and vice versa

q.q: A report tracks the national unemployment rate. What makes the question macroeconomic?
options: It measures an economy-wide labor-market aggregate
It mentions workers employed by individual firms
It uses percentages rather than raw numbers
It concerns an outcome people dislike
q.feedback: Macroeconomics studies economy-wide outcomes such as unemployment, inflation, and total output.

key: It measures an economy-wide labor-market aggregate

q.q: A bakery studies how customers respond to a muffin price increase. What level of analysis is this?
options: Microeconomic because it concerns one product market
Macroeconomic because every price affects inflation
Macroeconomic because a firm employs workers
Neither because bakeries are not economic units
q.commonError: Classifying by size, institution, or topic word instead of the unit of analysis.
q.feedback: Microeconomics examines households, firms, and particular markets.

key: Microeconomic because it concerns one product market

q.q: A report tracks national inflation, unemployment, and total output. What level is being studied?
options: Microeconomic because consumers buy the products
Macroeconomic because the measures are economy-wide
Microeconomic because the report uses prices
Neither because three measures are combined
q.commonError: Calling a large organization macro even when the question concerns one decision-maker.
q.feedback: Macroeconomics examines economy-wide aggregates such as output, inflation, and unemployment.

key: Macroeconomic because the measures are economy-wide

q.q: Which question is most clearly microeconomic?
options: What causes national inflation?
Why did national unemployment rise?
How many workers should a coffee shop hire?
How fast is GDP growing?
q.feedback: A single firm's hiring decision is microeconomic.

key: How many workers should a coffee shop hire?

q.q: A researcher studies how a new tax affects the market for soda. Another researcher studies how inflation affects all consumers. Which pairing is correct?
options: Soda tax is microeconomics; inflation is macroeconomics
Soda tax is macroeconomics; inflation is microeconomics
Both are only microeconomics
Both are only macroeconomics
q.feedback: A specific product market is microeconomics. Economy-wide inflation is macroeconomics.

key: Soda tax is microeconomics; inflation is macroeconomics

q.q: A firm decides how much labor to hire at one restaurant. Which branch of economics is this?
options: Microeconomics
Macroeconomics
Tax incidence
Circular-flow accounting only
q.feedback: A single firm's hiring decision is microeconomics.

key: Microeconomics

q.q: A report studies why inflation rose across the entire economy. Which branch of economics is this?
options: Microeconomics
Macroeconomics
Price ceiling analysis
Opportunity cost only
q.feedback: Inflation across the whole economy is a macroeconomic topic.

key: Macroeconomics

q.q: A university studies one course’s enrollment choices and the institution’s total enrollment trend. This combines:
options: Micro-level choices and an aggregate outcome.
Two unrelated macro questions.
Only a market-failure question.
No economic levels of analysis.
q.commonError: Failing to transfer level-of-analysis reasoning to a nonnational setting.
q.feedback: Individual choices aggregate into broader institutional outcomes, mirroring the micro-macro relationship.

key: Micro-level choices and an aggregate outcome.

q.q: Which question is macroeconomic?
options: Why did one restaurant raise prices?
How does one household choose between rent and food?
Why did a particular firm hire a manager?
Why did the national unemployment rate rise?
q.commonError: Classifying any employment question as microeconomic.
q.feedback: Macroeconomics studies economy-wide aggregates such as national unemployment.

key: Why did the national unemployment rate rise?

q.q: Which research design is most clearly microeconomic despite using a very large dataset?
options: Estimating how individual consumers respond to a change in one product’s price.
Measuring national inflation over time, because all price questions are economy-wide
Explaining long-run growth in real GDP per person.
Forecasting the economy-wide unemployment rate.
q.commonError: Using dataset size rather than unit of analysis.
q.feedback: Microeconomics can use massive data while focusing on individual choices and specific markets.

key: Estimating how individual consumers respond to a change in one product’s price.

q.q: Which statement best characterizes the boundary between micro and macro?
options: Microeconomics studies prices and firms, while macroeconomics studies government policy
The distinction concerns the level and aggregation of the question, not an absolute separation of topics.
Any government policy is automatically macroeconomic
Firm-level outcomes cannot contribute to macroeconomic outcomes.
q.commonError: Treating the fields as disconnected topic lists.
q.feedback: Many issues can be studied at both individual-market and aggregate levels.

key: The distinction concerns the level and aggregation of the question, not an absolute separation of topics.

q.q: A fall in aggregate demand reduces national output, while some firms cut employment more than others. What levels of analysis are present?
options: Only microeconomic analysis because the firms are the ones changing employment.
Macro analysis of the overall contraction and micro analysis of firm responses.
Only macro analysis.
Neither, because both use employment data.
q.commonError: Forcing a mixed question into only one level.
q.feedback: The aggregate shock is macroeconomic; heterogeneous firm choices are microeconomic.

key: Macro analysis of the overall contraction and micro analysis of firm responses.

q.q: A central bank raises interest rates. Which question is most macroeconomic?
options: How will one bank price a particular loan?
How will one household refinance a mortgage?
How will the policy affect inflation and total output?
How will one firm choose a supplier?
q.commonError: Classifying by institution rather than outcome level.
q.feedback: Macroeconomics examines economy-wide inflation and output effects.

key: How will the policy affect inflation and total output?

q.q: A tax changes one product’s price and also affects total consumer spending. Why might both fields be needed?
options: The tax eliminates the distinction between fields.
Only macroeconomics is needed because total consumer spending changes.
Macroeconomics studies only government budgets.
Microeconomics studies the product market; macroeconomics studies aggregate spending.
q.commonError: Assuming a policy belongs exclusively to one field.
q.feedback: One event can have market-level and economy-wide consequences.

key: Microeconomics studies the product market; macroeconomics studies aggregate spending.

q.q: Household purchases fall after an economy-wide income decline. A chain then closes stores, causing further household income losses. Which research plan covers the stated feedback?
options: Link household and firm responses to aggregate income and spending changes
Classify each store closure as macro solely because the chain is nationwide
Study aggregate income alone and infer every household responds equally
Study store choices alone and treat national income as unaffected
q.commonError: Assuming causation runs only from individuals to aggregates or only the reverse.
q.feedback: The mechanism crosses levels: aggregate income affects individual choices, and firm choices feed back into aggregate income. Neither level alone covers the full sequence.

key: Link household and firm responses to aggregate income and spending changes

q.q: A study uses records from every firm to estimate how individual managers choose training. Another totals the resulting output changes across the economy. Which distinction is defensible?
options: The first is macro and the second micro because totals hide choices
The first asks a micro question; the second asks an aggregate macro question
Both are macro because the dataset covers the whole country
Both are micro because firms supply the observations
q.commonError: Failing to identify the shift from unit-level effects to aggregate outcomes.
q.feedback: The question and unit of explanation determine scope. Nationwide firm records can support micro analysis; combining output changes to study the economy is macro analysis.

key: The first asks a micro question; the second asks an aggregate macro question

q.q: Wages rise at every sampled technology firm. The sample excludes shrinking industries and tracks only workers who kept jobs. What is needed before inferring an economy-wide wage change?
options: Confirmation that each sampled firm operates nationally
The largest observed wage increase as an aggregate estimate
Representative coverage and treatment of changes in which workers are observed
A larger sample of the same surviving technology workers
q.commonError: Generalizing a narrow market result to the entire economy.
q.feedback: Both industry selection and changing worker composition can distort aggregation. More observations from the same selected group do not repair those omissions.

key: Representative coverage and treatment of changes in which workers are observed

q.q: A study examines how a minimum wage affects employment in one local industry. This is primarily:
options: Macroeconomic analysis because wages use money.
Neither because policy is involved.
Microeconomic analysis.
Macroeconomic analysis because employment is always aggregate.
q.commonError: Using the topic word rather than the level of analysis.
q.feedback: The focus is a specific market and group of firms and workers.

key: Microeconomic analysis.

q.q: A report studies how household saving decisions collectively affect national investment. Which statement is best?
options: It is purely micro because households are mentioned.
It is purely macro because individual choices do not matter.
It cannot be economic analysis.
It links microeconomic behavior to a macroeconomic outcome.
q.commonError: Treating micro and macro as unrelated silos.
q.feedback: Macroeconomic aggregates emerge from many individual decisions and institutions.

key: It links microeconomic behavior to a macroeconomic outcome.

q.q: Which statement describes the scope of microeconomics?
options: Individual decision-makers and specific markets.
Economy-wide inflation and growth only.
National totals without individual behavior.
Weather patterns.
q.commonError: Confusing micro with small datasets or unimportant topics.
q.feedback: Microeconomics studies choices by households, firms, and specific markets.

key: Individual decision-makers and specific markets.

q.q: Which set of outcomes is primarily macroeconomic?
options: One consumer’s choice between two products.
Economy-wide outcomes such as output, inflation, and unemployment.
One firm’s pricing decision only.
A single transaction between two people.
q.commonError: Confusing macro with any large organization.
q.feedback: Macroeconomics studies aggregates and economy-wide relationships.

key: Economy-wide outcomes such as output, inflation, and unemployment.

q.q: Economists use models mainly to:
options: Simplify reality and isolate important relationships
Include every detail of the economy
Eliminate the need for assumptions
Guarantee policy success
q.feedback: Models deliberately simplify so the important causal relationships can be studied.
q.commonError: Treating a model as either a complete copy of reality or a guaranteed prediction.

key: Simplify reality and isolate important relationships

q.q: A household-choice model omits brand colors and store music. Why can it still help explain how price affects purchases?
options: Those details may not matter for the price relationship
Every omitted detail is assumed not to exist
The model guarantees an exact purchase forecast
Evidence is unnecessary once a model is simple
q.commonError: Treating a focused representation as a literal copy of reality.
q.feedback: Brand colors and store music can be omitted when the model’s purpose is to isolate how purchase quantity responds to price.

key: Those details may not matter for the price relationship

q.q: An economist studying commute time assumes gasoline prices stay unchanged. What is that assumption doing?
options: Claiming gasoline prices never change anywhere in practice
Guaranteeing every commuter makes one choice
Replacing observed travel data with opinion
Holding one influence fixed to isolate another
q.commonError: Treating a conditional assumption as a universal fact.
q.feedback: Holding gasoline prices fixed isolates the relationship between the other modeled factors and commute time.

key: Holding one influence fixed to isolate another

q.q: A delivery study predicts how adding a loading bay affects waiting time, holding staffing fixed. The depot adds a bay and hires loaders. Why can the observed change differ from the prediction?
options: The observation combines two changes; the model isolates one
The fixed-staffing assumption says loaders cannot affect waiting
A useful model must predict the combined change from the bay alone
Any difference shows loading space has no effect
q.feedback: Holding staffing fixed isolates the bay effect. Hiring loaders changes another influence, so the observed combined effect need not equal that conditional prediction.

key: The observation combines two changes; the model isolates one

q.q: A model omitting banks explains routine household-firm payments well. It misses a collapse in purchases when lending stops. Which revision preserves its useful result while addressing the failure?
options: Retain the payment framework and add a credit constraint for the disrupted setting
Use the old fit to treat lending as irrelevant during the disruption
Add banks and treat the expanded model as valid for every question
Discard the payment relationships because an omitted institution mattered once
q.commonError: Using the model without checking its purpose, assumptions, or evidence.
q.feedback: The original abstraction can explain routine flows. When credit becomes a binding constraint, the application needs that mechanism; adding it does not establish universal validity.

key: Retain the payment framework and add a credit constraint for the disrupted setting

q.q: A repair-shop model omits imported parts because local labor usually determines completion time. During a parts embargo it overpredicts repairs, but performs well again after deliveries resume. What does this pattern support?
options: Labor had no explanatory role because the embargo forecast failed
Resumed accuracy proves the embargo observations were measurement errors
Adding parts availability would make all remaining assumptions unnecessary
The omission is useful conditionally; parts availability matters when it constrains repairs
q.commonError: Transferring a result without checking context or omitted factors.
q.feedback: Failure during a parts constraint and recovery afterward support a conditional explanation: labor can govern normal operations while parts govern disrupted operations.

key: The omission is useful conditionally; parts availability matters when it constrains repairs

q.q: A PPF uses only two goods. Why can this simplification still be useful for analyzing scarcity and opportunity cost?
options: The two-good assumption removes scarcity from production
The PPF proves real economies produce only two goods
The graph replaces the need to compare alternatives
The simplification makes the tradeoff easier to see
q.commonError: Rejecting a PPF because its two-good simplification is not literal.
q.feedback: The two-good abstraction exposes scarcity and opportunity cost without describing every output.

key: The simplification makes the tradeoff easier to see

q.q: A model predicts that a training program expands output if trained workers can use available machines. Output stays flat: trainees return to workplaces with no spare machine time. Which conclusion and test fit the evidence?
options: The capacity condition failed; compare similarly trained workplaces with spare machines
Training has no possible effect; repeat the same constrained program
The prediction is normative; ask whether managers approve of training
The model is confirmed; count certificates rather than output
q.feedback: The prediction requires access to machine time. Testing otherwise comparable workplaces with spare capacity checks that condition without treating certificate counts as output gains.

key: The capacity condition failed; compare similarly trained workplaces with spare machines

q.q: A housing model predicts lower purchases when price rises, holding neighborhood quality fixed. In the data, renovated neighborhoods have both higher prices and more purchases. A critic calls this a refutation. Which evaluation and test are most informative?
options: Higher purchases prove demand slopes upward; controlling for quality would remove economically relevant evidence and invalidate the test.
Quality changes may confound the comparison; compare price changes within similar-quality neighborhoods before rejecting the conditional prediction.
The prediction is immune to data because holding quality fixed is an assumption; no observed comparison can challenge it.
Renovation proves quality causes all purchases; the model’s price mechanism is established even without a conditional comparison.
q.commonError: Rejecting a focused assumption merely because the held-constant factor varies in reality.
q.feedback: The model makes a ceteris-paribus prediction. Varying quality may shift demand while price changes, so the raw correlation does not isolate the price effect. Comparable-quality evidence can test the relevant conditional prediction.

key: Quality changes may confound the comparison; compare price changes within similar-quality neighborhoods before rejecting the conditional prediction.

q.q: Two models predict different effects of a tax because one assumes fixed supply and the other allows firms to enter. What should economists do first?
options: Average both tax predictions without examining their assumptions
Choose the model containing the greater number of equations
Match assumptions to the relevant time horizon and evidence
Reject both models simply because their predictions disagree
q.commonError: Choosing between models without matching entry assumptions to the time horizon.
q.feedback: Whether firms can enter depends on the horizon and evidence, so the assumptions determine applicability.

key: Match assumptions to the relevant time horizon and evidence

q.q: A model predicts that a price ceiling causes a shortage, but observed quantity sold does not fall. Which finding would most strongly preserve the model rather than refute it?
options: The ceiling was above the market-clearing price
Consumers preferred other products during the policy
The market included many buyers and sellers
Officials described the ceiling as a fair policy
q.commonError: Applying a binding-ceiling prediction when the legal ceiling may be nonbinding.
q.feedback: A ceiling above equilibrium is nonbinding, so the shortage prediction does not apply.

key: The ceiling was above the market-clearing price

q.q: A simplified model leaves out many real-world details. Why is that useful?
options: It helps isolate the main relationships being studied
It proves the model is false
It makes assumptions unnecessary
It guarantees the model predicts perfectly
q.feedback: Models simplify reality so economists can focus on the most important forces.

key: It helps isolate the main relationships being studied

q.q: A supply-and-demand model holds buyer income fixed. What role does the ceteris paribus assumption play in this analysis?
options: Income is assumed never to change in real markets
The model makes income irrelevant to demand
Ceteris paribus guarantees the prediction is exact
Holding income fixed isolates the price relationship
q.commonError: Using the model without checking its purpose, assumptions, or evidence.
q.feedback: Holding buyer income fixed is the ceteris-paribus condition that lets the model isolate movement caused by price.

key: Holding income fixed isolates the price relationship

q.q: A policy model predicts lower emissions after a fee. What should an analyst check before relying on that prediction in the policy setting?
options: Ignore uncertainty because the model is quantitative
Choose assumptions that produce the preferred result
Test whether behavioral assumptions fit the policy setting
Treat the prediction as proof the policy is desirable
q.commonError: Using the model without checking its purpose, assumptions, or evidence.
q.feedback: The emissions prediction is positive analysis; policy evaluation still requires evidence that the fee changes the modeled behavioral margin.

key: Test whether behavioral assumptions fit the policy setting

q.q: A restaurant model tracks price and customer traffic but omits wall color. When is that simplification useful?
options: When the model must predict every customer exactly
When evidence about traffic is unavailable
When wall color is not important to the question
When wall color is impossible to observe
q.commonError: Using the model without checking its purpose, assumptions, or evidence.
q.feedback: Omitting wall color is useful when it does not materially affect the price-and-traffic relationship the restaurant wants to study.

key: When wall color is not important to the question

q.q: A model is best understood as:
options: A value judgment disguised as a diagram
A focused representation built for a question
A complete copy of every real-world detail
A prediction that cannot be tested with evidence
q.commonError: Using the model without checking its purpose, assumptions, or evidence.
q.feedback: An economic model is a purposeful simplification used to explain or predict selected relationships, not a complete copy of reality.

key: A focused representation built for a question

q.q: A bus-demand study asks what happens when fares rise, with service unchanged. Which condition is an assumption?
options: Bus service remains unchanged during the comparison
Every rider chooses the bus after fares rise
The fare increase has no effect on any rider
The study includes every transportation detail
q.commonError: Using the model without checking its purpose, assumptions, or evidence.
q.feedback: The scenario holds bus service unchanged so any predicted ridership response can be attributed to the fare change.

key: Bus service remains unchanged during the comparison

q.q: Which question is a simple supply-and-demand model designed to address?
options: What every buyer personally values about the product
Which market outcome is morally fairest to society
How every institution in the economy operates
How price and quantity respond when market conditions change
q.commonError: Treating a focused representation as a literal copy of reality.
q.feedback: A basic supply-and-demand model is designed to analyze how market conditions determine equilibrium price and quantity.

key: How price and quantity respond when market conditions change

q.q: Like a map, why can an economic model omit many real-world details and still be useful?
options: Every omitted detail is assumed not to exist
Simplification guarantees perfect predictions
Models replace the need for evidence
Its value depends on serving a focused purpose
q.commonError: Treating a focused representation as a literal copy of reality.
q.feedback: Like a map, a model omits details that do not help answer its chosen question while retaining the relationships that do.

key: Its value depends on serving a focused purpose

q.q: A study holds population constant while examining income and sales. What is population here?
options: A detail declared irrelevant forever
A normative judgment about growth
A condition held fixed for the comparison
A result guaranteed by the model
q.commonError: Using the model without checking its purpose, assumptions, or evidence.
q.feedback: Population is held constant so the study can isolate how income relates to sales rather than combining both influences.

key: A condition held fixed for the comparison

q.q: Which statement best distinguishes a model from reality?
options: A model cannot be compared with evidence
A model represents selected relationships for a purpose
A model reproduces every observed detail exactly
A model becomes true when it contains a graph
q.commonError: Using the model without checking its purpose, assumptions, or evidence.
q.feedback: Reality contains many interacting details; a model selectively represents the mechanisms relevant to a defined purpose.

key: A model represents selected relationships for a purpose

q.q: A complex model predicts purchases accurately, while a simpler model identifies a price mechanism. Which model should be preferred?
options: Always choose the simple model regardless of performance
Average the models because mechanisms cannot be tested
Choose according to whether prediction or explanation is the goal
Always choose the complex model because it has better fit
q.commonError: Choosing by complexity or preference instead of purpose.
q.feedback: Forecast accuracy favors the complex model for prediction, while the simpler model may be better for identifying and communicating the price mechanism.

key: Choose according to whether prediction or explanation is the goal

q.q: A model predicts policy outcomes accurately in several cities, but its proposed mechanism was never measured. What follows?
options: Accurate predictions establish the proposed mechanism locally, though they leave its transfer to other cities uncertain.
Accurate predictions support usefulness in those cities, but competing mechanisms may fit the same outcomes.
Repeated prediction success establishes literal assumptions, though it leaves the mechanism’s policy importance uncertain.
An unmeasured mechanism invalidates the predictions, even if independent outcome data confirm their accuracy.
q.commonError: Treating shared historical fit as proof of one mechanism.
q.feedback: Predictive success is evidence about predictive performance. It does not discriminate between mechanisms that produce the same observable predictions, nor prove every assumption literal.

key: Accurate predictions support usefulness in those cities, but competing mechanisms may fit the same outcomes.

q.q: Two models fit past data, but only one predicts behavior after a new fee. What evidence best separates them?
options: The recommendation preferred by the policymaker
Evidence from the new fee setting where predictions differ
More past outcomes both models already reproduce
The relative length of the two model descriptions
q.commonError: Treating shared historical fit as proof of one mechanism.
q.feedback: The new fee creates an out-of-sample case where the models disagree, so observed post-fee behavior can distinguish them.

key: Evidence from the new fee setting where predictions differ

q.q: A policy conclusion disappears when one plausible assumption changes. What is the strongest evaluation?
options: The conclusion is sensitive and should be qualified
The original conclusion remains fully robust
The alternate assumption should be hidden from users
The model is useless for every other question
q.commonError: Using the model without checking its purpose, assumptions, or evidence.
q.feedback: A conclusion that disappears under one plausible assumption is fragile and should be reported with that sensitivity clearly stated.

key: The conclusion is sensitive and should be qualified

q.q: A larger model fits old data better but predicts new data worse. What does this show?
options: Historical fit proves the larger model is superior
Prediction quality depends only on equation length
The smaller model must omit every relevant mechanism
Added complexity can overfit rather than improve transfer
q.commonError: Assuming additional detail automatically improves a model.
q.feedback: Better historical fit paired with worse new-data prediction is evidence of overfitting rather than a general gain from complexity.

key: Added complexity can overfit rather than improve transfer

q.q: A housing model estimated where construction is flexible is applied where zoning is strict. What is the central concern?
options: Zoning makes housing demand irrelevant
A more detailed model must automatically be correct
The supply assumption may not transfer across cities
Historical estimates are always invalid elsewhere
q.commonError: Transferring a result without checking context or omitted factors.
q.feedback: Strict zoning violates the flexible-construction condition, so transferring the housing estimate may produce poor predictions.

key: The supply assumption may not transfer across cities

q.q: Two labor models fit past employment equally well. One predicts a wage rule raises jobs; the other predicts a decline. What evidence is most useful?
options: The policy outcome preferred by the researcher
Evidence from a setting where their predictions differ
More old observations both models already explain
The number of variables included in each model
q.commonError: Treating shared historical fit as proof of one mechanism.
q.feedback: Evidence from a wage-rule change targets the models’ conflicting employment predictions and is more informative than another shared-fit observation.

key: Evidence from a setting where their predictions differ

q.q: Adding dozens of variables improves historical fit but makes the mechanism impossible to interpret. What tradeoff appears?
options: Fit improved while explanatory clarity declined
Complexity proved the mechanism was causal
Interpretation no longer matters for policy
Every omitted variable has been eliminated
q.commonError: Assuming additional detail automatically improves a model.
q.feedback: The added variables improve fit but reduce interpretability, creating a prediction-versus-mechanism tradeoff.

key: Fit improved while explanatory clarity declined

q.q: A transit model worked before remote work became common but now overpredicts commuting. What should be reconsidered?
options: Whether any historical data can ever be useful
Whether commuting belongs in economics
Whether assumptions matter only in graphs
Whether the old behavioral relationship remains stable
q.commonError: Using the model without checking its purpose, assumptions, or evidence.
q.feedback: Remote work changed the commuting relationship, so the model’s stability and workplace-attendance assumptions need reassessment.

key: Whether the old behavioral relationship remains stable

q.q: A commuting model assumes five workplace days and forecasts trips accurately. Offices then permit two home days; trips fall only among eligible workers. Which explanation best fits both observations?
options: The attendance condition changed; the old relationship may still fit ineligible workers
The old fit proves attendance rules are irrelevant to travel
The failure means trip counts cannot test commuting models
Eligibility differences show the forecast error must be random
q.commonError: Using the model without checking its purpose, assumptions, or evidence.
q.feedback: The concentrated decline links forecast failure to a changed attendance condition. Workers whose conditions did not change provide a useful comparison.

key: The attendance condition changed; the old relationship may still fit ineligible workers

q.q: An ordering model fits stores before app alerts. Later it underpredicts purchases by alert subscribers but fits nonsubscribers. Subscribers also receive discounts. What would best diagnose the missing mechanism?
options: Attribute the full subscriber difference to alerts because the old model omitted them
Treat unchanged nonsubscriber purchases as proof discounts have no effect
Re-estimate one average and assume the subscriber gap disappears
Compare alerts on and off among otherwise comparable buyers facing the same discounts
q.commonError: Using the model without checking its purpose, assumptions, or evidence.
q.feedback: Alerts and discounts change together for subscribers. Holding discounts comparable while varying alerts separates the proposed information mechanism from the price difference.

key: Compare alerts on and off among otherwise comparable buyers facing the same discounts

q.q: A model assumes producers can add capacity within a month. It overpredicts first-month output in districts with permit delays, but predicts annual output well. What scope is best supported?
options: Reject annual predictions because the monthly abstraction failed
Treat permit delays as a change in society's preferences
Use it for the annual question; model permit delays before using its monthly prediction
Use annual accuracy to validate the first-month prediction
q.commonError: Transferring a result without checking context or omitted factors.
q.feedback: The same abstraction can fit one horizon and fail at another. The observed delay matters for the monthly adjustment even when annual capacity catches up.

key: Use it for the annual question; model permit delays before using its monthly prediction

q.q: Two delivery models fit ordinary weeks. Only one includes warehouse capacity. After a warehouse closure, delays rise where spare storage is scarce but not where spare storage is ample. Which further observation would most weaken that mechanism?
options: Both models previously fitted ordinary delivery volumes
Restoring storage leaves the excess delays unchanged under otherwise comparable conditions
The models continue to agree during weeks without closures
Districts with spare storage avoid the initial delay increase
q.commonError: Treating shared historical fit as proof of one mechanism.
q.feedback: If restoring the alleged binding resource leaves delays unchanged, the capacity mechanism needs reassessment. Ordinary-week fit cannot discriminate between the models.

key: Restoring storage leaves the excess delays unchanged under otherwise comparable conditions

q.q: A classroom exchange model predicts quick switching when a better offer appears. Real customers face long contracts. Switching rises only when contracts expire. What follows for applying the model?
options: The choice mechanism may apply at renewal; contract timing limits short-run transfer
Delayed switching refutes the possibility that customers compare offers
The classroom result establishes that contracts carry no switching cost
Observed switching proves the model predicts the timing without modification
q.commonError: Transferring a result without checking context or omitted factors.
q.feedback: Customers may compare offers as modeled but act only when contractual constraints relax. Application must distinguish the renewal margin from immediate switching.

key: The choice mechanism may apply at renewal; contract timing limits short-run transfer

q.q: A model predicts equipment failures using machine age and claims age itself causes failure. It fits old data, but after maintenance is randomized, equally old machines fail at different rates. What can be concluded?
options: The original fit proves maintenance cannot affect failure
The new evidence makes age useless for every forecasting purpose
Randomized maintenance turns a factual prediction into a value judgment
Age can remain predictive while the causal claim needs maintenance evidence
q.commonError: Treating shared historical fit as proof of one mechanism.
q.feedback: Age can proxy for maintenance history. A maintenance effect at a fixed age challenges the proposed causal explanation without automatically erasing age's predictive usefulness.

key: Age can remain predictive while the causal claim needs maintenance evidence

q.q: A model favors plan A over B if participation exceeds 60%. Credible estimates range from 45% to 75%; both plans fit past data. What finding would resolve the model's ranking most directly?
options: A statement that A has the larger possible benefit
Selecting 75% because it yields a definite recommendation
Reliable local evidence placing participation on one side of 60%
More past observations both plans already explain
q.commonError: Using the model without checking its purpose, assumptions, or evidence.
q.feedback: The ranking reverses at the participation threshold. Evidence narrowing participation to one side addresses the decision; preferred endpoints and shared past fit do not.

key: Reliable local evidence placing participation on one side of 60%

q.q: A detailed scheduling model cuts average forecast error but often reverses the recommended shift when uncertain inputs change. A simpler model consistently chooses the shift that performs well in trials. Which evaluation fits this decision?
options: Average the recommended shifts without checking feasibility
Compare decision performance and robustness, rather than forecast error alone
Choose the detailed model because lower average error guarantees better choices
Choose the simpler model solely because fewer variables guarantee validity
q.commonError: Assuming additional detail automatically improves a model.
q.feedback: A forecast metric and a scheduling decision are different objectives. Trial performance and stability under plausible inputs matter when selecting a model for the actual decision.

key: Compare decision performance and robustness, rather than forecast error alone

q.q: A reimbursement model assumes firms keep cost-saving effort unchanged. After payments become more generous, effort falls and actual costs exceed forecasts. Which update addresses both the failure and a future rule change?
options: Model how the payment rule affects effort, then test costs under the new rule
Raise the old cost estimate by a fixed amount for every future rule
Keep effort fixed because that assumption once fitted the data
Call the forecast normative because firms responded strategically
q.commonError: Using the model without checking its purpose, assumptions, or evidence.
q.feedback: Payment rules can change behavior. Modeling and testing that response is more transferable than applying a fixed correction that assumes behavior never changes again.

key: Model how the payment rule affects effort, then test costs under the new rule

q.q: A labor model predicts a payroll subsidy lowers hiring costs and expands employment at flexible wages. In a new region, bargaining agreements guarantee workers the entire subsidy as higher wages while firms’ net hiring costs stay unchanged. Which transfer of the model is defensible?
options: Keep the original employment forecast; a subsidy of the same statutory size must have the same effect under any bargaining rule.
Reject the original model in its own region; failure to transfer proves flexible wages never mattered for employment.
Rework the wage-setting mechanism; the unchanged net hiring cost removes the model’s stated employment-expansion channel.
Predict an equal employment contraction; workers receiving the subsidy necessarily shifts firms’ labor demand left by the same amount.
q.commonError: Transferring a result without checking context or omitted factors.
q.feedback: The original mechanism depends on a reduction in firms’ net labor cost. If wage bargaining absorbs the subsidy completely, that channel is absent. The model may still describe its original institutions, but needs revision for the new setting.

key: Rework the wage-setting mechanism; the unchanged net hiring cost removes the model’s stated employment-expansion channel.

q.q: Two models fit past recessions equally well. One says reduced credit supply cuts investment; the other says weak expected sales reduce both borrowing and investment. A new policy randomly expands credit access for some otherwise comparable firms. Which observation best distinguishes the proposed mechanisms?
options: Borrowing and investment remain correlated in the historical sample after adding more recession years.
Investment rises among newly credit-eligible firms relative to controls without a prior relative improvement in expected sales.
Both models continue to predict the same national investment total during the experiment.
Firms with the strongest expected sales borrow most before the randomized eligibility change.
q.commonError: Treating shared historical fit as proof of one mechanism.
q.feedback: Randomized credit access creates variation separate from firms’ preexisting sales outlook. A relative investment response supports the credit-supply channel; historical co-movement alone is compatible with both mechanisms.

key: Investment rises among newly credit-eligible firms relative to controls without a prior relative improvement in expected sales.

q.q: A simple model forecasts regional employment with 5% out-of-sample error and recommends policy A across plausible parameter values. A complex model lowers error to 4.8%, but small plausible parameter changes reverse its A-versus-B policy ranking. The decision concerns a costly irreversible policy. Which next step is strongest?
options: Report the modest prediction gain and unstable ranking, test sensitive parameters, and assess whether the policy choice is robust enough for this decision.
Choose the complex model because any lower forecast error establishes a more reliable policy ranking.
Choose A solely because the simple model is stable, treating stability as proof that its mechanism and recommendation are correct.
Average the two point recommendations without examining parameters, because averaging eliminates structural uncertainty.
q.commonError: Assuming additional detail automatically improves a model.
q.feedback: Predictive error and decision robustness are different criteria. A small fit improvement may not justify a sensitive irreversible recommendation; testing influential assumptions and reporting ranking uncertainty is more useful than automatic complexity or simplicity.

key: Report the modest prediction gain and unstable ranking, test sensitive parameters, and assess whether the policy choice is robust enough for this decision.

q.q: A wage model assumes workers can change jobs easily, but licenses block movement. What should the analyst do?
options: Reject every wage model regardless of its purpose
Treat licensing as a value judgment rather than evidence
Revise the application because the mobility assumption fails
Keep the prediction because assumptions never affect results
q.commonError: Using the model without checking its purpose, assumptions, or evidence.
q.feedback: Licensing blocks the assumed job mobility, so the analyst should revise the assumption or limit the model’s application.

key: Revise the application because the mobility assumption fails

q.q: A household model predicts spending from income, but families also face new credit limits. Why might the prediction change?
options: Adding any factor guarantees a perfect prediction
An omitted constraint became important in this setting
Income no longer matters in any household decision
The original relationship became a definition
q.commonError: Transferring a result without checking context or omitted factors.
q.feedback: New credit limits add a binding constraint, so income alone no longer predicts the household’s feasible spending response.

key: An omitted constraint became important in this setting

q.q: One inflation model studies demand pressure; another studies supply disruptions. Which should be used after an energy shock?
options: The model containing the relevant supply mechanism
The model with the most equations on the page
Whichever model predicts the preferred policy
Average the two models without checking their assumptions.
q.commonError: Choosing by complexity or preference instead of purpose.
q.feedback: An energy shock operates through supply costs, making the supply-disruption model the more relevant mechanism.

key: The model containing the relevant supply mechanism

q.q: A policy model misses one month of data but explains the broader pattern. What is the best response?
options: Discard the model after any prediction error
Ignore the miss because models cannot be tested
Add variables until the model matches every observation
Investigate the miss without declaring the model useless
q.commonError: Using the model without checking its purpose, assumptions, or evidence.
q.feedback: One missed month need not invalidate a model that explains the broader pattern; the miss should be tested for noise or structural change.

key: Investigate the miss without declaring the model useless

q.q: A restaurant-demand model assumes nearby competitors stay open, but two close. What should happen to the forecast?
options: Reconsider it because a held-constant condition changed
Keep it because assumptions do not affect forecasts
Reject all demand models as permanently useless
Treat competitor closures as a moral judgment
q.commonError: Using the model without checking its purpose, assumptions, or evidence.
q.feedback: Competitor closures violate the forecast’s fixed-competition assumption and may shift demand toward the restaurant.

key: Reconsider it because a held-constant condition changed

q.q: One model explains short-run layoffs; another explains long-run hiring. How should a firm choose?
options: Always select the model with more variables and equations
Average both answers without checking assumptions
Use whichever model supports its preferred plan
Match the model to the time horizon and question
q.commonError: Choosing by complexity or preference instead of purpose.
q.feedback: The firm should match model horizon to its decision: the layoff model for short-run adjustment and the hiring model for long-run planning.

key: Match the model to the time horizon and question

q.q: A model predicts well in rural areas but not dense cities. What is the first question to ask?
options: Would adding any variable guarantee success
Are city outcomes outside economic analysis
Do its assumptions fit both settings equally well
Must every rural observation be discarded
q.commonError: Transferring a result without checking context or omitted factors.
q.feedback: The first review is whether density changes a key mechanism or assumption that held in rural markets.

key: Do its assumptions fit both settings equally well

q.q: Does adding more detail automatically improve a model?
options: Yes; every extra variable improves every model
Yes; realism is the only useful model criterion
No; because simple models never make errors
No; complexity can reduce clarity or prediction quality
q.commonError: Assuming additional detail automatically improves a model.
q.feedback: More detail helps only when it improves relevant explanation or prediction enough to justify added complexity and fragility.

key: No; complexity can reduce clarity or prediction quality

q.q: A prediction assumes income stays fixed. What if income changes?
options: Income must be ignored to protect the model
The assumption proves income never changes
The prediction may need revision because its condition changed
The prediction becomes true by definition
q.commonError: Treating a conditional assumption as a universal fact.
q.feedback: If income changes, the fixed-income prediction no longer isolates price and must be adjusted for an income-driven demand shift.

key: The prediction may need revision because its condition changed

q.q: A model fit past data well. Does that prove its proposed mechanism?
options: No; models cannot provide any useful evidence
No; different mechanisms can fit the same observations
Yes; fit proves every assumed causal step
Yes; past fit guarantees future accuracy
q.commonError: Treating shared historical fit as proof of one mechanism.
q.feedback: Past fit shows descriptive performance, but competing-mechanism evidence is needed to establish the model’s causal explanation.

key: No; different mechanisms can fit the same observations

q.q: When should a model be applied to a new setting?
options: When its important assumptions remain reasonable there
Whenever it worked once in any setting
Only when it contains every possible detail
Whenever it supports the preferred conclusion
q.commonError: Transferring a result without checking context or omitted factors.
q.feedback: A model should transfer only when its important assumptions and mechanisms remain plausible in the new setting.

key: When its important assumptions remain reasonable there

q.q: A demand model predicts fewer purchases after a price increase. How should this positive prediction be evaluated?
options: Compare the conditional prediction with observed evidence
Treat the prediction as a statement of what ought to happen
Accept the mechanism because the prediction sounds plausible
Reject all models whenever one observation differs
q.commonError: Using the model without checking its purpose, assumptions, or evidence.
q.feedback: The demand model makes a testable positive prediction, but its conclusion should be limited to settings where its assumptions describe the relevant buying decision.

key: Compare the conditional prediction with observed evidence

q.q: A manager uses a two-factor model of sales rather than listing every detail of the store. Why?
options: To prove omitted details never affect sales
To avoid comparing predictions with evidence
To focus on relationships relevant to the decision
To guarantee that every forecast is exact
q.commonError: Treating a focused representation as a literal copy of reality.
q.feedback: The manager simplifies to two influential sales drivers so the model remains usable for the decision it is meant to inform.

key: To focus on relationships relevant to the decision

q.q: An economist studies how price affects purchases while holding income constant. Why hold income constant?
options: To turn a positive claim into a value judgment
To isolate the price-purchase relationship
To claim household income never changes
To eliminate uncertainty from all forecasts
q.commonError: Using the model without checking its purpose, assumptions, or evidence.
q.feedback: Holding income constant isolates the effect of price instead of mixing a price response with an income-driven demand shift.

key: To isolate the price-purchase relationship

q.q: A model uses an unrealistic assumption but predicts well in a narrow setting. What is the strongest evaluation?
options: Judge whether the abstraction serves that narrow purpose
Reject the model because every assumption must be literal
Accept the model for all settings without further checks
Treat predictive fit as proof of the assumed mechanism
q.commonError: Using the model without checking its purpose, assumptions, or evidence.
q.feedback: A simplifying assumption need not be literally realistic if the model predicts well for the narrow question and setting in which it is used.

key: Judge whether the abstraction serves that narrow purpose

q.q: Two queue models fit an office before appointments are introduced. One assumes arrivals cluster; the other assumes service is slow. Appointments spread arrivals without changing service time. Which result best distinguishes them?
options: A large wait reduction favors the arrival-clustering explanation
Unchanged service time proves both explanations equally well
The prior fit establishes that slow service caused the queues
Any remaining wait refutes the arrival-clustering explanation
q.commonError: Choosing models by fit alone when mechanisms differ.
q.feedback: Appointments change arrival clustering while service time stays fixed. A large reduction therefore supports clustering as a mechanism, although other sources of waiting may remain.

key: A large wait reduction favors the arrival-clustering explanation

q.q: A model fits historical data but fails after institutions change. Which limitation is most relevant?
options: Relationships estimated under old rules may not remain stable.
Historical data can never be useful.
Institutions are outside economics.
Model assumptions matter only for graphs.
q.commonError: Assuming past empirical relationships are invariant.
q.feedback: Institutional change can alter incentives and the parameters of a model.

key: Relationships estimated under old rules may not remain stable.

q.q: A service model favors shorter forms when training is unchanged, but favors the current forms when a plausible training delay is included. What should the analyst report?
options: A definite preference for shorter forms because simplification is the model's purpose
The ranking depends on the training assumption and needs evidence about that condition
Only the original ranking because the delay is not certain
An average recommendation without identifying why the ranking changed
q.feedback: A plausible change in training conditions reverses the result. Report that sensitivity and seek evidence about the condition instead of presenting either conditional ranking as guaranteed.

key: The ranking depends on the training assumption and needs evidence about that condition

q.q: A highly detailed model predicts poorly because many parameters are estimated imprecisely. What does this illustrate?
options: Simple models always predict perfectly.
Parameters have no role in models.
More complexity can add noise and does not guarantee better prediction.
Prediction quality depends only on graphics.
q.commonError: Assuming complexity automatically improves a model.
q.feedback: Extra detail can create estimation problems and overfitting.

key: More complexity can add noise and does not guarantee better prediction.

q.q: A model predicts that a tax reduces quantity traded, assuming no evasion. Actual evasion is widespread. What should an analyst conclude?
options: The model is useless for every purpose.
The prediction may need revision because a key behavioral assumption fails.
Evasion has no effect on incentives.
The original prediction becomes a normative statement.
q.commonError: Ignoring the role of an assumption when applying a model.
q.feedback: Model conclusions depend on whether important assumptions are reasonable in the setting.

key: The prediction may need revision because a key behavioral assumption fails.

q.q: Two models answer different questions about the same market. How should an economist choose between them?
options: Always choose the more complicated model.
Use whichever gives the preferred answer.
Use the model whose mechanisms and assumptions fit the question.
Assume one model must be universally correct.
q.commonError: Treating model complexity as the sole quality criterion.
q.feedback: Model choice depends on purpose, relevant mechanisms, and evidence.

key: Use the model whose mechanisms and assumptions fit the question.

q.q: A simple model omits a factor that is small in one setting but large in another. What follows?
options: Any omission makes the model worthless.
The factor must be irrelevant everywhere.
The model becomes a definition rather than an explanation.
The model may work in the first setting and fail in the second.
q.commonError: Applying a model without checking context.
q.feedback: The importance of an omitted factor depends on the situation.

key: The model may work in the first setting and fail in the second.

q.q: What role does an assumption play in a model?
options: It replaces the evidence used to test predictions
It makes the model a policy recommendation
It states a condition used to focus the analysis
It guarantees that every result is factually certain
q.commonError: Treating a conditional assumption as a universal fact.
q.feedback: An assumption states a condition held fixed or treated as given so the model can trace a particular relationship.

key: It states a condition used to focus the analysis

q.q: Must a model be rejected because it simplifies reality?
options: No; but only when the model includes a graph
No; judge whether the simplification fits its purpose
Yes; useful models reproduce every real-world detail
Yes; evidence cannot support a simplified explanation
q.commonError: Using the model without checking its purpose, assumptions, or evidence.
q.feedback: Simplification is a design feature; rejection is warranted only when omitted details undermine the model’s purpose or performance.

key: No; judge whether the simplification fits its purpose

q.q: Refer to the graph. Which description correctly separates the demand shift from the movement along supply?
options: Quantity demanded rises only because price falls along D0
Supply shifts right and demand stays fixed
Both curves shift right equally
Demand shifts D0 to D1, and equilibrium moves upward along S0
q.imageAlt: The movie-ticket market has price in dollars on the vertical axis and quantity in thousands on the horizontal axis. S0 is an upward-sloping supply curve. D0 and D1 are downward-sloping demand curves, with D1 lying to the right of D0 at each displayed price. Point A is the D0-S0 intersection at quantity 200 and price $10. Point B is the D1-S0 intersection at quantity 250 and price $12.
q.feedback: Demand changes curves; the higher equilibrium is also a movement along unchanged supply.
q.graphDescription: The movie-ticket market has price in dollars on the vertical axis and quantity in thousands on the horizontal axis. S0 is an upward-sloping supply curve. D0 and D1 are downward-sloping demand curves, with D1 lying to the right of D0 at each displayed price. Point A is the D0-S0 intersection at quantity 200 and price $10. Point B is the D1-S0 intersection at quantity 250 and price $12.

key: Demand shifts D0 to D1, and equilibrium moves upward along S0

q.q: Refer to the graph. Why is the move from A to B a decrease in supply rather than merely a decrease in quantity supplied?
options: Supply itself shifts left from S0 to S1
Quantity supplied rises along the original S0 curve
Demand itself shifts right from D0 to D1
The market stays at A on the original curves
q.imageAlt: The movie-ticket market has price in dollars on the vertical axis and quantity in thousands on the horizontal axis. D0 is a downward-sloping demand curve. S0 and S1 are upward-sloping supply curves, with S1 lying to the left of S0 at each displayed price. Point A is the D0-S0 intersection at quantity 200 and price $10. Point B is the D0-S1 intersection at quantity 150 and price $12.
q.feedback: A quantity-supplied change moves along one curve; here the supply curve itself shifts.
q.graphDescription: The movie-ticket market has price in dollars on the vertical axis and quantity in thousands on the horizontal axis. D0 is a downward-sloping demand curve. S0 and S1 are upward-sloping supply curves, with S1 lying to the left of S0 at each displayed price. Point A is the D0-S0 intersection at quantity 200 and price $10. Point B is the D0-S1 intersection at quantity 150 and price $12.

key: Supply itself shifts left from S0 to S1

q.q: A recreation center assigns its only instructor to swimming lessons instead of the next-best option, a safety workshop. What is the opportunity cost?
options: The value of the safety workshop that is not offered
The instructor’s wage plus every rejected program
Zero because the instructor is already employed
The value of the swimming lessons that were chosen
q.commonError: Using the chosen activity or treating assigned staff as costless.
q.feedback: The safety workshop is the next-best use of the instructor’s time.

key: The value of the safety workshop that is not offered

q.q: If choosing one option means giving up the next-best alternative, the value given up is:
options: Opportunity cost
A sunk cost
A price ceiling
Consumer surplus
q.feedback: Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative forgone.

key: Opportunity cost

q.q: A library can use its only meeting room for a job workshop or a tax-help clinic this evening. It chooses the workshop. What is the opportunity cost?
options: The value of the tax-help clinic that cannot be held
The original cost of constructing and maintaining the meeting room over time
The value of both events added together
Zero because the library already owns the room
q.commonError: Treating an owned resource as costless or adding both options.
q.feedback: The clinic is the next-best use forgone when the room hosts the workshop.

key: The value of the tax-help clinic that cannot be held

q.q: A student spends two hours volunteering instead of preparing for tomorrow’s exam. Which item belongs in the opportunity cost of volunteering?
options: The value of the study time the student gives up
Only the bus fare paid to reach the volunteer site
Every activity the student could have imagined doing
The volunteer work itself because it was the chosen activity
q.feedback: The next-best use of the student’s time can be an opportunity cost without a money price.

key: The value of the study time the student gives up

q.q: A café manager moves one employee from taking orders to preparing deliveries. The next-best use of that employee was serving counter customers. What is forgone?
options: The value of the counter service the employee would have provided
Every task performed anywhere in the café that day
Only the employee’s past training expense
Nothing because the employee remains on the payroll
q.commonError: Ignoring the displaced output of an already-paid worker.
q.feedback: An employee’s time has an opportunity cost equal to its best forgone use.

key: The value of the counter service the employee would have provided

q.q: A student uses a prepaid transit pass to travel to a debate tournament instead of visiting a grandparent. Which item can be part of the tournament’s opportunity cost?
options: The value of the forgone family visit
Only an additional transit fare paid today
The original price of the transit pass in every case
Zero because the pass makes the trip free at the margin
q.commonError: Assuming no new cash payment means no opportunity cost.
q.feedback: The valued family visit is a forgone alternative even without a new fare.

key: The value of the forgone family visit

q.q: An instructor gives three choices: work for $80, study for a test worth $60, or attend a free concert. If the student chooses the concert, what is the opportunity cost?
options: $0 because the concert is free
q.feedback: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative, not every alternative added together. The next best option is the $80 shift.

q.q: A software founder uses a personally owned server for a new service. The server could instead be leased for $18,000, and the founder could earn $70,000 at another firm. Which costs are missing from a cash-expense-only analysis?
options: Forgone lease income and forgone salary
Only the server’s historical purchase price
Every possible technology investment added together
No costs because neither resource requires a new payment
q.commonError: Ignoring opportunity costs of owner-supplied assets and labor.
q.feedback: Owned capital and owner labor have valuable alternative uses that are implicit costs.

key: Forgone lease income and forgone salary

q.q: A museum has already paid a nonrefundable $30,000 deposit for an exhibit. It can proceed for another $12,000 and earn $9,000, or use the gallery for a lecture series worth $7,000. Which item is the opportunity cost of proceeding?
options: The $7,000 lecture series forgone
The $30,000 nonrefundable deposit
The $42,000 total of past and future spending
Zero because the deposit cannot be recovered
q.commonError: Using an irreversible past expenditure instead of the best current alternative.
q.feedback: The deposit is sunk; the lecture series is the best forgone current use.

key: The $7,000 lecture series forgone

q.q: A student can earn $120 working Saturday or attend a free exam review session. If attending the session raises her expected exam score enough to be worth $180 to her, what is the net benefit of attending the review?
q.feedback: The opportunity cost is the $120 in forgone wages. Net benefit is $180 - $120 = $60.

q.q: A researcher initially gives up consulting worth $900 to spend a weekend on a paper. A new consulting request worth $1,400 then becomes available before the weekend begins. If the paper remains the choice, how does its opportunity cost change?
options: It rises from $900 to $1,400 because the next-best alternative changed
It remains $900 because only the original alternatives matter
It becomes $2,300 because both consulting offers must be added
It falls to zero because research produces future benefits
q.commonError: Freezing opportunity cost when the best available alternative changes.
q.feedback: Opportunity cost is forward-looking and updates when the next-best feasible alternative changes.

key: It rises from $900 to $1,400 because the next-best alternative changed
