q.q: A popular clinic charges no appointment fee, but patients must wait four hours. A nearby clinic charges $80 with almost no wait. Which claim correctly compares the options?
options: The free clinic can have a higher full cost for a patient whose time is especially valuable
The free clinic must have zero opportunity cost because its posted price is zero
The paid clinic always has the higher full cost regardless of time values
Waiting time is a sunk cost and cannot affect a current clinic choice
q.commonError: Treating posted price as total economic cost.
q.feedback: The opportunity cost of waiting time can outweigh the difference in money price.

key: The free clinic can have a higher full cost for a patient whose time is especially valuable

q.q: A consultant can attend a workshop or take one of two mutually exclusive Saturday jobs: one pays $480 with $40 travel cost; the other pays $430 remotely. Workshop admission costs $120, including a $50 nonrefundable deposit already paid, and attendance requires $20 travel. From now, what is attendance’s relevant economic cost?
options: $580: the full $120 workshop fee, $20 travel and $440 net job earnings.
$960: $90 of attendance spending plus both jobs’ combined $870 net earnings.
$90: only attendance requires a new payment, so foregone work is not a current cost.
$530: $90 of avoidable workshop/travel spending plus the best forgone job’s $440 net earnings.
q.commonError: Counting only the workshop fee or only the forgone earnings.
q.feedback: The remaining fee is 120-50=70; add 20 travel. The best alternative nets max(480-40,430)=440. Relevant cost is 90+440=530. The nonrefundable deposit is sunk and mutually exclusive jobs are not added.

key: $530: $90 of avoidable workshop/travel spending plus the best forgone job’s $440 net earnings.

q.q: A factory reallocates a shift from valves to pumps. The first 30 pumps displace 40 valves; the next 30 displace 60 more. It needs 45 pumps. A supplier offers those 45 pumps in exchange for 65 valves. Assume constant tradeoffs within each stated block. Which source uses fewer valve-equivalent resources?
options: Make them internally: apply the first-block ratio to all 45 pumps, for a cost of 60 valves.
Make them internally: one pump displaces one valve, for a cost of 45 valves.
Use the supplier: internal production sacrifices 70 valves, compared with 65 through exchange.
Use the supplier: producing any of the second block requires giving up all 100 valves.
q.commonError: Using the first unit’s cost or cumulative cost for the next unit.
q.feedback: The first 30 pumps cost 40 valves. The next 15 cost 15×(60/30)=30 valves, totaling 70. The supplier costs 65, saving 5. Rising opportunity cost requires using the appropriate segment rather than one overall ratio.

key: Use the supplier: internal production sacrifices 70 valves, compared with 65 through exchange.

q.q: A student owns a concert ticket bought for $90. Selling it now would yield $140 less a $10 selling fee. Attending requires $20 parking and rules out a $100 evening job; she can both sell the ticket and work if she skips. What is the relevant economic cost of attending?
options: $160: the $140 posted resale price and parking, excluding the compatible work alternative.
$210: the original $90 purchase, $100 forgone earnings and parking.
$150: the better of resale or work, plus parking, treating those alternatives as mutually exclusive.
$250: $130 net resale value, $100 forgone earnings and $20 parking.
q.commonError: Using personal value or the original ticket price instead of forgone resale value.
q.feedback: If she skips, selling and working are compatible and yield 140-10+100=230. Attendance also costs 20 parking, for a relevant total of 250. The original purchase price is sunk; net resale value remains a current opportunity cost.

key: $250: $130 net resale value, $100 forgone earnings and $20 parking.

q.q: A laboratory assistant works an extra Saturday shift and gives up a study group that would improve preparation for a licensing exam. Which interpretation is best?
options: The value of improved exam preparation is part of the shift’s opportunity cost
The earned wage offsets the study group’s benefit in the opportunity-cost calculation
Transportation and other out-of-pocket expenses make up the shift’s opportunity cost
The opportunity cost combines the values of several unchosen Saturday activities
q.feedback: A valuable nonmonetary alternative can be the next-best option forgone.

key: The value of improved exam preparation is part of the shift’s opportunity cost

q.q: A worker can produce 10 reports or 5 presentations in a day. What is the opportunity cost of one presentation?
options: 2 reports
5 reports
10 reports
50 reports
q.feedback: Giving up 10 reports to gain 5 presentations means each presentation costs 2 reports.

key: 2 reports

q.q: A musician spends an evening rehearsing and gives up both a paid performance worth $220 and family time valued at $160. Which alternative determines the opportunity cost?
options: The $220 performance because it is the more valuable forgone option
The $160 family time because nonmonetary options always rank first
Both alternatives added together for a total of $380
Zero because rehearsal may improve future performance
q.commonError: Adding every rejected option or selecting the lower-valued one.
q.feedback: Only the highest-valued forgone alternative determines opportunity cost.

key: The $220 performance because it is the more valuable forgone option

q.q: A firm uses owned office space that could rent for $24,000. What implicit cost belongs in the decision?
options: The average rent of all comparable office spaces.
$24,000 in forgone rent.
$0 because the space is owned.
The building’s original purchase price.
q.feedback: Forgone rent is the opportunity cost of using the space.

key: $24,000 in forgone rent.

q.q: Tuition is $10,000 and forgone earnings are $30,000. The minimum opportunity cost of attending school is:
q.commonError: Counting only explicit or implicit cost.
q.feedback: Both tuition and forgone earnings are part of the full cost.

q.q: A city assigns its only crew and an $8 million project budget to a rail extension that uses all 12 available crew-weeks. Alternative projects are indivisible and can be sequenced; their resource use and net benefits add. Water repairs need 12 weeks and $8 million, with $24 million net benefit. Drainage needs 5 weeks and $3 million, with $14 million net benefit. Bridge work needs 7 weeks and $5 million, with $15 million net benefit. A hospital upgrade needs 6 weeks and $5 million, with $20 million net benefit. All net benefits already deduct project spending. What is the best feasible alternative forgone by selecting rail?
options: Drainage plus the hospital upgrade, worth $34 million net.
Bridge work plus the hospital upgrade, worth $35 million net.
Drainage plus bridge work, worth $29 million net.
The water-repair project alone, worth $24 million net.
q.commonError: Ignoring joint resource constraints or choosing only the largest single alternative.
q.feedback: Drainage plus the hospital upgrade fits: 11 crew-weeks and $8m, yielding $34m net. Bridge work plus the hospital upgrade would yield $35m but needs 13 weeks and $10m, exceeding both limits. Drainage plus bridge work fits but yields $29m; water repairs yield $24m. The rail choice forgoes the best feasible bundle, worth $34m; do not deduct project spending again.

key: Drainage plus the hospital upgrade, worth $34 million net.

q.q: An owned parcel can support a clinic worth $12 million, housing worth $15 million, or parking worth $5 million. Choosing the clinic has an opportunity cost of:
options: $12 million.
$3 million.
$20 million.
$15 million.
q.commonError: Adding alternatives or using the chosen project’s value.
q.feedback: Housing is the highest-valued forgone use.

key: $15 million.

q.q: Scarcity means a community cannot fund every valued program. If the community funds a clinic, what determines the clinic’s opportunity cost?
options: Funding the clinic requires giving up the best alternative program
Scarcity makes the clinic’s historical spending a sunk cost
Opportunity cost disappears once officials approve a budget
Every unfunded program must be added together as the cost
q.commonError: Seeing scarcity and opportunity cost as unrelated definitions.
q.feedback: Scarcity forces a choice; the best forgone use created by that choice is its opportunity cost.

key: Funding the clinic requires giving up the best alternative program

q.q: Moving along a production possibilities frontier from more food toward more machinery requires giving up food. What does the food forgone measure?
options: The opportunity cost of the additional machinery
The sunk cost of previously produced food
The money price of machinery in the product market
The total value of all unattainable production points
q.commonError: Failing to connect a production tradeoff with opportunity cost.
q.feedback: The output surrendered when production shifts measures the opportunity cost along a PPF.

key: The opportunity cost of the additional machinery

q.q: A student can spend Saturday working for $80 or attending a free concert. If the student attends the concert, the opportunity cost is:
options: The $80 in forgone earnings.
The concert ticket price of $0.
Only the cost of transportation.
Every activity the student could imagine doing.
q.commonError: Looking only for an explicit money payment.
q.feedback: The next-best alternative is working, so the forgone $80 is the opportunity cost.

key: The $80 in forgone earnings.

q.q: A city uses an empty lot for a playground instead of a community garden. The opportunity cost of the playground is:
options: The original purchase price of the lot.
The value of the community garden that is not built.
Zero because the city already owns the land.
The total value of every possible project.
q.feedback: Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best use of the lot.

key: The value of the community garden that is not built.

q.q: A parent attends a free evening class and gives up two hours of family time. Why can the class still have an opportunity cost?
options: The family time is a valued alternative use of those hours
Free classes always charge an unannounced cash fee
Only the building’s operating expense counts as a cost
A zero tuition price eliminates every competing use of the parent’s time
q.commonError: Equating a zero price with zero opportunity cost.
q.feedback: Time has valued alternative uses even when an activity charges no fee.

key: The family time is a valued alternative use of those hours

q.q: A resident can spend Saturday repairing a porch, helping at a food pantry, or hiking. Helping at the pantry is chosen, and porch repair was valued most among the rejected options. What is the relevant forgone alternative?
options: Repairing the porch
Hiking only
Both rejected activities added together
The food-pantry shift that was chosen
q.commonError: Adding all rejected options or selecting the least-valued one.
q.feedback: Opportunity cost uses the single highest-valued rejected alternative.

key: Repairing the porch

q.q: A county can assign an emergency team to wildfire prevention valued at $1.4 million, flood preparation valued at $1.1 million, or routine inspections valued at $0.8 million. Political rules require the flood project. What is its opportunity cost?
options: $1.4 million in forgone wildfire prevention
$2.2 million from both rejected programs
$1.1 million because that is the chosen project’s value
$0.8 million because routine inspections cost the least
q.commonError: Confusing the chosen project, the least-valued option, or the sum of alternatives with opportunity cost.
q.feedback: The wildfire program is the most valuable feasible alternative forgone.

key: $1.4 million in forgone wildfire prevention

q.q: A firm owns a machine that can produce Product X with contribution margin $75,000 or Product Y with contribution margin $92,000. Converting it to Product Z yields $100,000 but costs $15,000. If the firm chooses Z, what is the net benefit relative to the next-best alternative?
q.commonError: Comparing gross returns without subtracting conversion cost and the next-best alternative.
q.feedback: Z nets $85,000, which is $7,000 below the $92,000 next-best use.

q.q: A consultant can accept Project A for a net benefit of $18,000, Project B for $15,000, or Project C for $9,000. If Project A is chosen, its opportunity cost is:
q.commonError: Summing all rejected alternatives or using the chosen benefit.
q.feedback: Project B is the highest-valued forgone alternative.

q.q: A theater has already spent $40,000 designing a production. It can use the booked dates to stage that production, spending $25,000 more for an expected $20,000 return, or use the same dates for a concert expected to net $12,000. If it stages the production, what is the opportunity cost of using those dates, measured by the best forgone use of the dates?
options: $12,000 from the forgone concert
$40,000 already spent on design
$52,000 from adding design and concert values
$5,000 because the remaining production return is below its added cost
q.commonError: Treating a sunk design expense as the current opportunity cost.
q.feedback: Using the dates for the production forgoes the concert's $12,000 net value. The $40,000 design expense is sunk. The production's future spending and return matter for deciding whether to stage it, but they are not the value of the alternative use of the dates.

key: $12,000 from the forgone concert

q.q: A government owns a vacant parcel valued on its books at $20 million and uses it for a courthouse. The land could instead be sold for $14 million or used for housing valued at $18 million. The opportunity cost is:
options: $32 million.
$20 million.
$14 million.
$18 million.
q.commonError: Using the purchase budget or adding rejected uses.
q.feedback: The housing project is the most valuable forgone use.

key: $18 million.

q.q: A worker’s hourly wage rises from $20 to $32. Holding preferences constant, how does this change the opportunity cost of taking an unpaid hour off?
options: Stays at zero because no payment is made.
Equals the combined value of every alternative activity.
Rises by $12 because the forgone hourly wage is higher.
Falls because leisure is now more valuable.
q.commonError: Failing to update opportunity cost when the next-best alternative changes.
q.feedback: The forgone wage from an hour of work is now larger.

key: Rises by $12 because the forgone hourly wage is higher.

q.q: A nonprofit receives a donated building and chooses to use it as offices rather than lease it for $90,000 annually. Which statement is correct?
options: The opportunity cost is the donor’s original purchase price
The opportunity cost is zero because the building was donated
The donation has no purchase price, but office use carries a $90,000 annual opportunity cost.
The opportunity cost is the sum of the values of all possible future uses.
q.commonError: Equating acquisition price with current opportunity cost.
q.feedback: Current opportunity cost is based on the best forgone use, here the lease income.

key: The donation has no purchase price, but office use carries a $90,000 annual opportunity cost.

q.q: A fellowship costs $9,000 in new fees. The student could instead take a job paying $32,000 with $4,000 in work-only expenses, or an assistantship netting $24,000. A $2,000 nonrefundable deposit is already paid under either choice. What current full cost must the fellowship's benefits exceed?
q.commonError: Omitting forgone earnings or nonmoney value.
q.feedback: The best alternative nets $32,000 - $4,000 = $28,000. Add $9,000 in avoidable fellowship fees: $37,000. The deposit is sunk; do not add the rejected assistantship.

q.q: A firm can use a patent internally for expected profit of $3.2 million, license it for $3.8 million, or sell it for $3.5 million. Internal use requires an additional $0.4 million development cost. Relative to the next-best alternative, internal use has a net advantage of:
options: $3.4 million.
-$1.0 million.
-$0.2 million.
$0.6 million.
q.commonError: Ignoring the development cost or comparing with the wrong alternative.
q.feedback: Internal use nets $2.8 million; licensing at $3.8 million is the next-best alternative.

key: -$1.0 million.

q.q: A field team has six weeks. One rejected survey uses all six weeks and is worth 90 points. Two compatible surveys each use three weeks and are worth 52 and 46 points. If the team selects a different six-week project, what value is forgone?
options: 52 points
98 points
90 points
188 points
q.commonError: Using the difference or summing all forgone alternatives.
q.feedback: The feasible pair yields 52 + 46 = 98 points, exceeding the single survey's 90. Compare feasible plans; do not sum mutually exclusive plans.

key: 98 points

q.q: A worker can take a one-day class, work an overtime shift earning $180, or attend a recreational event valued at $120. If the worker takes the class, the opportunity cost is:
options: $300, the sum of both rejected alternatives.
$180, the value of the next-best alternative.
$120, because recreation is not work.
Zero if the class has no tuition.
q.feedback: The overtime shift is the most valuable forgone option, so it determines opportunity cost.

key: $180, the value of the next-best alternative.

q.q: A student pays $12,000 in tuition and gives up $24,000 in earnings to attend school for a year. The opportunity cost is at least:
q.commonError: Counting only tuition or only forgone earnings.
q.feedback: The full opportunity cost includes explicit tuition and forgone earnings.

q.q: A farmer can plant wheat worth $42,000 or soybeans worth $50,000 on the same field. If wheat is planted, the opportunity cost is:
options: $42,000, the value of the wheat that is chosen
$92,000, the combined value of wheat and soybeans
$8,000, the difference between the two crop values.
$50,000 in forgone soybean output.
q.commonError: Using the difference rather than the value of the next-best alternative.
q.feedback: The next-best alternative is the soybean crop worth $50,000.

key: $50,000 in forgone soybean output.

q.q: A firm uses a warehouse it owns for storage instead of renting it out for $30,000 per year. The storage decision has an implicit cost of:
options: The building’s recorded depreciation expense.
$0 because ownership avoids a rental payment.
The difference between neighborhood property values.
$30,000 per year.
q.feedback: Forgone rental income is an implicit opportunity cost.

key: $30,000 per year.

q.q: Opportunity cost is the value of:
options: Every rejected alternative added together.
The next-best alternative given up.
A past cost that cannot be recovered.
Only the money price of the choice.
q.commonError: Using total forgone options or explicit price only.
q.feedback: Opportunity cost is the value of the single next-best forgone alternative.

key: The next-best alternative given up.

q.q: A free event can have an opportunity cost because:
options: Only paid activities have opportunity costs
Attending uses time that could have been used elsewhere.
Past spending determines the opportunity cost of attending
Because the event is free, attending uses no scarce resources.
q.commonError: Equating zero price with zero opportunity cost.
q.feedback: Time and other resources have alternative uses even when admission is free.

key: Attending uses time that could have been used elsewhere.

q.q: An owner uses a building that could rent for $2,000 per month. The implicit cost is:
options: The original purchase price each month.
All possible rents added together.
$2,000 per month.
$0 because the owner owns it.
q.feedback: The best forgone rental income is an implicit opportunity cost.

key: $2,000 per month.

q.q: A student spends a free afternoon practicing piano instead of the next-best option, visiting a friend. What is the opportunity cost?
options: The value of the friend visit that is forgone
Zero because neither activity requires payment
The value of both activities added together
The value of piano practice because it was chosen
q.commonError: Assuming only money payments create opportunity cost.
q.feedback: The valued friend visit is the next-best use of the afternoon forgone.

key: The value of the friend visit that is forgone

q.q: A business uses its owned van for deliveries instead of renting it out for $900 or using it for service calls worth $1,100. What is the delivery decision’s opportunity cost?
options: $1,100 from the service calls
$2,000 from both rejected uses
$900 because rental income is explicit cash
$0 because the business owns the van
q.commonError: Adding uses, privileging cash rent, or treating ownership as costless.
q.feedback: Service calls are the highest-valued alternative use of the van.

key: $1,100 from the service calls

q.q: A worker attends a free six-hour workshop instead of a shift paying $24 per hour and pays $12 for parking. Ignoring benefits, what is the opportunity cost?
options: $156 from forgone wages plus parking
$144 from forgone wages only
$12 because the workshop is free
$132 after subtracting parking
q.commonError: Omitting either forgone wages or an explicit cost.
q.feedback: Six hours at $24 equals $144; adding $12 parking gives $156.

key: $156 from forgone wages plus parking

q.q: A university has already spent $4 million designing a laboratory. It can finish the lab or assign the same construction team to a residence project valued at $11 million. What is the current opportunity cost of finishing the lab?
options: $11 million in forgone residence value
$4 million already spent on design
$15 million from adding both amounts
Zero because laboratory design is complete
q.commonError: Treating sunk design spending as the current alternative forgone.
q.feedback: The design expense is sunk; the residence project is the current best alternative use of the team.

key: $11 million in forgone residence value

q.q: Two producers can make the same goods, but one gives up fewer shirts for each bicycle. How does opportunity cost identify comparative advantage?
options: The producer giving up fewer shirts has comparative advantage in bicycles
The producer making more total goods in both industries must have comparative advantage
The producer with the higher bicycle opportunity cost should specialize
Comparative advantage depends only on money prices of the goods
q.commonError: Assigning comparative advantage to absolute output or higher opportunity cost.
q.feedback: Comparative advantage belongs to the producer with the lower opportunity cost.

key: The producer giving up fewer shirts has comparative advantage in bicycles

q.q: A firm considers producing one additional unit. How does opportunity cost enter a marginal decision?
options: The forgone value of resources used for that unit is compared with its added benefit
Every past expense and every earlier unit’s benefit are added to the next unit’s marginal cost
The total benefit of all earlier units determines the next unit’s cost
Opportunity cost matters only before the first unit is produced
q.commonError: Using sunk or total values instead of additional benefit and cost.
q.feedback: Marginal analysis compares added benefit with the opportunity cost of the next unit.

key: The forgone value of resources used for that unit is compared with its added benefit

q.q: An entrepreneur uses a personally owned building and unpaid owner labor. How do these opportunity costs connect to economic profit?
options: Forgone rent and salary are implicit costs subtracted from accounting profit
Owned inputs disappear from both accounting and economic analysis
Historical purchase prices plus every owner cash withdrawal are charged again each period
Economic profit subtracts every rejected business idea
q.commonError: Treating owner-supplied inputs as free when moving from accounting to economic profit.
q.feedback: Implicit opportunity costs explain why economic profit can be below accounting profit.

key: Forgone rent and salary are implicit costs subtracted from accounting profit

q.q: A workshop gives up progressively more chairs for each additional table. What connection does this create between opportunity cost and the production tradeoff?
options: The opportunity cost of later tables rises as more chairs are forgone
Opportunity cost stays equal to the money price of a table in every production decision
Past chair production becomes a sunk cost of every table
The tradeoff disappears because both goods use the same workshop
q.commonError: Failing to interpret forgone output as the cost of additional production.
q.feedback: The amount of one good forgone measures the opportunity cost of producing more of the other.

key: The opportunity cost of later tables rises as more chairs are forgone

q.q: A nurse can use a lunch break to take a walk or finish a required report. She finishes the report. What is the opportunity cost?
options: The value of the walk she gives up
The value of the completed report
The value of both lunch-break activities added together
Zero because the break is unpaid
q.commonError: Using the chosen activity instead of the forgone alternative.
q.feedback: The walk is the alternative surrendered when the report is chosen.

key: The value of the walk she gives up

q.q: A family spends its last $50 of entertainment money on a museum visit instead of the next-best choice, a movie night. What is the opportunity cost?
options: The value the family placed on movie night
The value of the museum visit itself
Every activity available in the city
Only the family’s earlier spending on unrelated entertainment choices
q.commonError: Confusing the selected benefit with the best option forgone.
q.feedback: Movie night is the next-best alternative given up.

key: The value the family placed on movie night

q.q: A bakery assigns its only decorator to a wedding cake, so a birthday-cake order cannot be completed. Which item is forgone?
options: The value of the birthday-cake order
The decorator’s entire annual salary plus all bakery overhead
Both cake orders added together
Nothing because the decorator remains employed
q.commonError: Ignoring the alternative output of an already-employed worker.
q.feedback: The birthday-cake order is the best displaced use of the decorator’s time.

key: The value of the birthday-cake order

q.q: A nonprofit uses a donated room for tutoring instead of leasing it to a neighborhood group. Which item can be an opportunity cost?
options: The rental value the nonprofit gives up
The donor’s original cost of the room
Zero because the room was donated
Every possible future use combined
q.commonError: Treating a donated or owned resource as costless.
q.feedback: Forgone rental value is an implicit opportunity cost of using the room.

key: The rental value the nonprofit gives up

q.q: A port authority has already installed specialized foundations for a terminal. It can complete the terminal for $40 million and obtain benefits of $55 million, or redirect crews to storm protection worth $22 million. Which comparison is relevant now?
options: Terminal net benefit of $15 million versus $22 million forgone storm protection
All foundation spending plus $40 million versus terminal benefits
Terminal benefits of $55 million versus foundation spending alone
Only the irreversible foundations because they created the current choice
q.commonError: Allowing sunk construction to replace forward-looking incremental costs and alternatives.
q.feedback: Past foundations are sunk; completing nets $15 million and forgoes storm protection worth $22 million.

key: Terminal net benefit of $15 million versus $22 million forgone storm protection

q.q: A retailer uses an owned parcel for parking. The parcel could be leased for $70,000 or used for pickup lockers expected to net $85,000. Parking produces a benefit valued at $90,000. What is the opportunity cost of parking?
options: $85,000 from the locker project
$155,000 from both rejected uses
$5,000 as parking’s net advantage
$70,000 because leasing is a cash transaction
q.commonError: Adding alternatives or using the lower cash-based option.
q.feedback: The locker project is the most valuable feasible use forgone.

key: $85,000 from the locker project

q.q: A one-year program charges $18,000 tuition and $2,000 for required supplies. A student gives up a $44,000 job but gains employer-independent health coverage valued at $4,000 while enrolled. Ignoring future benefits, what is the net opportunity cost?
options: $60,000 after crediting the gained coverage
$64,000 from tuition, supplies, and wages
$44,000 because only forgone earnings count
$20,000 because only explicit payments count
q.commonError: Omitting explicit costs or failing to credit a benefit received.
q.feedback: Costs total $64,000; subtracting the $4,000 gained benefit leaves $60,000.

key: $60,000 after crediting the gained coverage

q.q: A government funds a coastal barrier valued at $30 million. The same engineers could instead complete a water system valued at $34 million or road repairs valued at $21 million. Which statement is correct?
options: The barrier’s opportunity cost is the $34 million water system
$55 million is the cost because both alternatives are rejected
$4 million is the cost because it is the value difference
$30 million is the cost because it is the chosen project’s value
q.commonError: Adding rejected projects or using chosen value or value difference.
q.feedback: The water system is the highest-valued alternative use of the engineers.

key: The barrier’s opportunity cost is the $34 million water system

q.q: A factory bought a machine for $500,000 five years ago. It can now use one shift for parts worth $28,000 or rent the shift to another firm for $31,000. What is the current opportunity cost of producing parts?
options: $31,000 in forgone rental income
$500,000 from the historical purchase
$3,000 as the difference between uses
$28,000 because that is the chosen output
q.commonError: Using historical purchase price or the value difference as opportunity cost.
q.feedback: The purchase price is sunk; current opportunity cost is the best alternative return.

key: $31,000 in forgone rental income

q.q: A researcher devotes ten hours per week for six weeks to an unpaid project instead of consulting at $75 per hour. She also pays a one-time $120 data fee. Ignoring benefits, what is the total opportunity cost?
options: $4,620 from forgone consulting plus the fee
$4,500 from forgone consulting only
$870 from one week of time plus the fee
$120 because the project pays no wage
q.commonError: Ignoring repeated time or the explicit project fee.
q.feedback: Sixty consulting hours cost $4,500; adding the $120 fee gives $4,620.

key: $4,620 from forgone consulting plus the fee

q.q: A student keeps a research placement. A rejected job offers $29,000 but requires $5,000 in extra travel. Another rejected placement pays $20,000 and supplies training valued at $6,000. All other costs and benefits are equal. Which alternative sets the opportunity cost?
options: The other placement, worth $26,000 net
The job, worth its $29,000 salary
Both alternatives together, worth $50,000 net
The job, worth $24,000 net
q.commonError: Adding rejected alternatives or netting chosen benefits against opportunity cost.
q.feedback: The job nets $24,000; the other placement totals $26,000. The best feasible rejected option sets the cost, including noncash training value.

key: The other placement, worth $26,000 net

q.q: A firm has prepaid a nonrefundable software license. It can use it for an internal project, sell the transferable access for $18,000, or use it for a client job earning $25,000 with $9,000 in new expenses. What is the opportunity cost of internal use?
options: $18,000 from resale
$25,000 from the client's gross payment
$16,000 from the client's net payment
Zero because the license fee is sunk
q.commonError: Letting sunk design work displace the best current alternative.
q.feedback: The original payment is sunk, but resale is feasible. Resale yields $18,000, more than the client job's $16,000 net, so $18,000 is forgone.

key: $18,000 from resale

q.q: A volunteer can cover one six-hour shift valued at 15 service points or two compatible three-hour shifts valued at 9 points each. A new placement uses all six hours and requires travel time valued at 2 points, with no other costs. What benefit would make it strictly preferable?
options: More than 20 points
More than 17 points
More than 18 points, ignoring travel
More than 35 points
q.commonError: Assuming opportunity cost must be money or only a value difference.
q.feedback: The best alternative is the pair, worth 18 points. The new placement must also cover 2 points of added travel cost, so strict preference requires benefit above 20.

key: More than 20 points

q.q: A council selects project A. Rejected B is worth 80 points and uses the full budget; C and D are worth 47 and 40 points and fit the budget together, but require the same exclusive specialist slot. What is A's opportunity cost?
options: 80 points
87 points
167 points
47 points
q.commonError: Adding mutually exclusive alternatives or using the difference in values.
q.feedback: C and D cannot be combined because of the specialist constraint. Among feasible alternatives, B's 80 points is highest; budget feasibility alone is insufficient.

key: 80 points

q.q: An owned studio could be leased for $44,000 with $8,000 in landlord expenses, or used for workshops earning $53,000 with $19,000 in new expenses. A chosen community project also needs $7,000 in supplies. What is its full current economic cost?
q.commonError: Adding alternatives or privileging a cash return over a higher noncash value.
q.feedback: Leasing nets $36,000 and workshops net $34,000. Add the community project's $7,000 avoidable supplies to the best forgone use: $43,000.

q.q: A resource stays assigned to project A. Alternative B would yield 76 points before a required setup cost of x; C yields 61 points net. At what setup cost does C begin to set the opportunity cost strictly instead of B?
options: x greater than 15 points
x greater than 61 points
x less than 15 points
x greater than 76 points
q.commonError: Adding alternative uses or reporting the value difference.
q.feedback: Compare B's 76 - x with C's 61. They tie at x = 15; above 15, C is the strictly better forgone use.

key: x greater than 15 points

q.q: Military engineers can repair a base runway, restore a civilian bridge worth $18 million, or reinforce a dam worth $23 million. The runway is selected for strategic reasons. Which economic statement follows?
options: Its opportunity cost is the $23 million dam reinforcement
Its opportunity cost is every civilian project added together
Strategic importance eliminates opportunity cost
Its opportunity cost is the lower-valued bridge project
q.commonError: Assuming a mandated or strategic choice has no opportunity cost.
q.feedback: Even a required choice forgoes the highest-valued feasible alternative use.

key: Its opportunity cost is the $23 million dam reinforcement

q.q: A firm assigns its specialist to defect prevention. The best rejected production project nets $96,000; an energy project nets $82,000. A new tool raises the energy project's net value by $20,000 and leaves other options unchanged. What happens to defect prevention's opportunity cost?
options: It rises by $6,000 to $102,000
It rises by $20,000 to $116,000
It remains $96,000 because the chosen project is unchanged
It becomes $178,000 by adding the original alternatives
q.commonError: Using selected value, summed alternatives, or the difference.
q.feedback: The best alternative changes from production at $96,000 to energy at $102,000. Opportunity cost rises by $6,000, not the tool's full $20,000 gain.

key: It rises by $6,000 to $102,000

q.q: An arena uses a Saturday date for a youth championship valued at $160,000. A concert would net $210,000 and a convention would net $185,000. The championship also requires $15,000 in security spending. What is its full opportunity cost?
options: $225,000 from the concert plus security
$210,000 from the concert alone
$410,000 from both rejected events plus security
$65,000 from the value difference plus security
q.commonError: Omitting explicit cost or adding multiple rejected events.
q.feedback: The best forgone event is $210,000; adding $15,000 security gives $225,000.

key: $225,000 from the concert plus security

q.q: A machine can make 90 filters or 60 pumps per shift at a constant tradeoff. A new contract takes half a shift for pumps and requires calibration that uses another one-sixth of a shift without output. How many filters does accepting the contract forgo?
options: 60 filters
45 filters
30 filters
15 filters
q.commonError: Reversing or ignoring the output tradeoff ratio.
q.feedback: The contract uses two-thirds of a shift: one-half production plus one-sixth calibration. At 90 filters per shift, the forgone output is 60 filters.

key: 60 filters

q.q: A nonprofit has 400 skilled volunteer-hours. A tax clinic would use all hours and create value estimated at $30,000. The best alternative is a housing clinic worth $34,000; a food program worth $20,000 uses different volunteers. What is the tax clinic’s opportunity cost?
options: $34,000 from the housing clinic
$54,000 from both other programs
$4,000 as the difference in clinic values
$30,000 from the tax clinic itself
q.commonError: Including an alternative that does not compete for the constrained resource.
q.feedback: Only feasible competing uses of the same volunteer-hours matter; housing is the best one.

key: $34,000 from the housing clinic

q.q: A farmer plants berries on land that could yield corn worth $48,000 or solar-lease income of $55,000. Berries are expected to net $62,000 after new expenses. Compared with the next-best use of the land, what is the net benefit of planting berries?
q.commonError: Comparing with the wrong land use or adding alternative returns.
q.feedback: The solar lease is the $55,000 opportunity cost; $62,000 minus $55,000 equals $7,000.

q.q: A shift can produce 150 sensors or 100 controllers at a constant tradeoff. A rush order for 40 controllers also prevents a separate setup-free run worth 12 sensors. How many sensors must the order's benefit exceed to justify accepting it?
options: 72 sensors
60 sensors
52 sensors
112 sensors
q.commonError: Using the controller quantity directly or reversing the ratio.
q.feedback: Forty controllers use 40% of the shift and forgo 60 sensors. Add the separate 12-sensor opportunity: total forgone output is 72 sensors.

key: 72 sensors

q.q: A cloud platform uses reserved computing capacity for fraud detection worth $1.8 million. The capacity could instead support search improvements worth $2.1 million or recommendation improvements worth $1.9 million. Reservation fees were prepaid and nonrefundable. What is the current opportunity cost?
options: $2.1 million from search improvements
The nonrefundable reservation fee
$4.0 million from both rejected systems
$0.3 million as the difference from search
q.commonError: Using a prepaid sunk fee or the difference rather than the forgone project.
q.feedback: The prepaid fee is sunk; search is the highest-valued alternative use of capacity.

key: $2.1 million from search improvements

q.q: A researcher keeps a public-interest project. Its best rejected contract netted $41,000. That contract is canceled; a replacement pays $38,000 but requires $9,000 in new expenses, while teaching nets $31,000. How does the opportunity cost change?
options: It falls by $10,000
It falls by $3,000
It falls by $12,000
It rises to $60,000
q.commonError: Treating a no-longer-feasible alternative as the current opportunity cost.
q.feedback: After cancellation, teaching at $31,000 beats the replacement's $29,000 net. The cost falls from $41,000 to $31,000, a $10,000 decrease.

key: It falls by $10,000

q.q: A lab chooses Compound A, which uses its entire allocation of 12 scientist-months and 5 sequencer slots. Instead, Platform B would use all 12 months and 5 slots for $11 million net value. Three smaller projects each need 6 scientist-months: C uses 3 slots and yields $8 million before $2 million in new costs; D uses 2 slots and yields $7 million before $2 million in new costs; E uses 3 slots and yields $10 million before $2 million in new costs. Projects are indivisible, compatible if both resource limits are met, and their net values add. What is the opportunity cost of assigning the resources to Compound A?
options: $13 million: the net value of projects D and E.
$14 million: the net value of projects C and E.
$11 million: the net value of the full Platform B.
$17 million: the gross value of projects D and E.
q.commonError: Selecting the highest-valued infeasible bundle or using gross rather than net alternative value.
q.feedback: Net values are C = $6m, D = $5m and E = $8m. D plus E uses 12 scientist-months and 5 slots and yields $13m. C plus E would yield $14m but needs 6 slots, so it is infeasible. C plus D and Platform B each yield $11m. The best feasible alternative forgone is therefore D plus E, worth $13m net.

key: $13 million: the net value of projects D and E.

q.q: A transportation agency can use its team to start a bus redesign now or use that same team for a safety audit this year and start the redesign next year. The audit has $6 million in benefits, while the one-year delay would add $2 million to redesign costs. These are the only differences between the plans. If the agency starts the redesign now, what is the value of the forgone audit benefits alone, before accounting for the delay-related cost difference?
options: $6 million in forgone safety-audit benefits.
$2 million in avoided redesign-delay costs.
$4 million after netting out delay costs.
$8 million after adding the delay costs.
q.commonError: Confusing a consequence of the chosen timing with the alternative forgone.
q.feedback: The question asks specifically for the audit benefits forgone, which are $6m. The $2m delay cost is a separate consequence avoided by starting now. If comparing the two complete plans instead, doing the audit first would provide $6m in benefits less $2m in added redesign costs, a $4m net advantage.

key: $6 million in forgone safety-audit benefits.

q.q: A free municipal charging station requires a two-hour wait. One driver could earn $35 per hour during that time; another values the same two hours at $20 total. Which statement is best?
options: The first driver faces the larger time opportunity cost
Both drivers face zero cost because charging is free
Both drivers face the same cost because the wait is identical
The second driver faces the larger cost because leisure is nonmonetary
q.commonError: Assuming identical time requirements imply identical opportunity costs.
q.feedback: Opportunity cost depends on the value of each person’s best alternative use of time.

key: The first driver faces the larger time opportunity cost

q.q: A workshop's first table forgoes 3 chairs and its second forgoes 5 more. A buyer offers 4 chairs for each table. Producing both tables just breaks even in chairs, yet producing only the first is better. Why?
options: The second table loses one chair at the margin, offsetting the first table's gain
The second table's opportunity cost equals the average cost of four chairs
Breaking even on the pair proves both tables individually add net benefit
The first table's forgone chairs become a reason to accept the second
q.commonError: Using the first unit’s cost or cumulative cost for the next unit.
q.feedback: The first table gains 4 - 3 = 1 chair; the second gains 4 - 5 = -1. The average hides the unfavorable incremental tradeoff.

key: The second table loses one chair at the margin, offsetting the first table's gain

q.q: A studio chooses an educational stream. A sports broadcast would earn $94,000 before a $21,000 rights fee; a concert nets $77,000. A discount reduces the rights fee by $6,000. What happens to the educational stream's opportunity cost?
options: It rises from $77,000 to $79,000
It rises from $73,000 to $79,000
It stays $77,000 because the concert is unchanged
It rises by $6,000 to $83,000
q.commonError: Comparing gross rather than net alternatives or summing rejected options.
q.feedback: Initially the concert beats sports' $73,000 net. After the discount, sports nets $79,000 and becomes the best alternative. The opportunity cost rises by $2,000.

key: It rises from $77,000 to $79,000

q.q: A foundation has $10 million and one evaluation team. Health uses the full budget and team and yields benefits valued at $14 million. Education yields $13 million using both resources. Two small programs together yield $16 million within the budget, but need two teams. Hiring a second team costs $3 million beyond the available budget. With no borrowing, what is the best feasible alternative forgone if health is chosen?
options: Education at $13 million; the $16 million package is infeasible under the joint budget and staffing limits.
The two-program package at $16 million; a larger benefit makes its extra staffing feasible.
Education plus the small programs at $29 million; all rejected benefits belong in opportunity cost.
$1 million; opportunity cost is health’s gain relative to education rather than the alternative itself.
q.commonError: Selecting the highest-valued infeasible bundle or using gross rather than net alternative value.
q.feedback: Opportunity cost is the value of the best feasible forgone alternative. Education fits both constraints; the two-program package would require unaffordable staffing. The difference in benefits is not the opportunity cost.

key: Education at $13 million; the $16 million package is infeasible under the joint budget and staffing limits.

q.q: A studio selects a film that uses both of its release slots and all 8 available editor-weeks. Its alternatives are indivisible. A documentary uses 1 slot and 3 editor-weeks for $6 million net return. A series uses 1 slot and 5 editor-weeks for $9 million net return. A concert uses 1 slot and 4 editor-weeks, earning $12 million before $2 million of new costs. A festival package uses both slots and 8 editor-weeks for $14 million net return. Projects can be combined when both capacity limits are met, and net returns add. What is the best feasible alternative forgone by selecting the film?
options: The documentary and concert, with $16 million net return.
The series and concert, with $19 million net return.
The documentary and series, with $15 million net return.
The festival package alone, with $14 million net return.
q.commonError: Choosing a capacity-infeasible bundle or failing to compare feasible net-return bundles.
q.feedback: The concert nets $10m. Combining it with the documentary yields $16m and uses 2 slots and 7 editor-weeks. The series plus concert would yield $19m but requires 9 editor-weeks, so it is infeasible. The documentary plus series yields $15m, and the festival package yields $14m. The best feasible use forgone is the $16m documentary-concert bundle.

key: The documentary and concert, with $16 million net return.

q.q: A city has one engineering team for this year. A stadium roof must eventually be repaired, but an approved one-year deferral is feasible at an expected cost of $4 million. Deferring would allow a flood barrier worth $26 million or a transit repair worth $19 million; the same team cannot do both. If the city repairs the roof now, what current alternative value is forgone?
options: $22 million: the flood-barrier benefit net of the feasible deferral cost.
$26 million: the flood-barrier benefit with the cost of making that alternative feasible ignored.
$41 million: both public-project benefits minus the deferral cost.
Zero: an eventual roof requirement removes every feasible current alternative.
q.commonError: Assuming a mandate eliminates opportunity cost or adding rejected projects.
q.feedback: The best current deferral plan yields 26-4=22 million; transit would yield 19-4=15. The future repair obligation does not erase a feasible timing alternative, but its associated cost must be included.

key: $22 million: the flood-barrier benefit net of the feasible deferral cost.

q.q: A machine can make 420 filters or 280 pumps per day at a constant tradeoff. A contract needs 70 pumps; each forgone filter has net value $8. Buying all pumps externally costs $700 plus $80 delivery and leaves the machine free for filters. Which fulfillment method has the lower relevant cost?
options: Buy externally: $780 is below the $840 value of the 105 filters forgone by making pumps.
Make internally: 70 filters are forgone, costing $560 compared with $780 externally.
Make internally: owned machine time has zero current cost, so only the external bill is relevant.
Buy externally: 210 filters are forgone internally, making its relevant cost $1,680.
q.commonError: Reversing the output ratio or using the required pump count directly.
q.feedback: Each pump sacrifices 420/280=1.5 filters; 70 pumps cost 105 filters worth 840. External fulfillment costs 700+80=780 and saves 60 in resource value. Machine ownership does not remove its alternative use.

key: Buy externally: $780 is below the $840 value of the 105 filters forgone by making pumps.

q.q: Maintenance uses a weekend that could otherwise produce a certain $40,000 net value. Before the decision, an urgent order becomes available: a 50% chance of $80,000 net value and a 50% chance of zero; it cannot be combined with the regular order. A guarantee costing $6,000 would make the urgent order’s $80,000 certain. For a risk-neutral manager, what is the opportunity cost of maintenance?
options: $74,000: the guaranteed urgent order is the best feasible alternative after its guarantee cost.
$120,000: add the regular order and the urgent order’s expected value plus its guaranteed gain.
$40,000: the original plan fixes opportunity cost even after a better alternative becomes feasible.
$80,000: use the guaranteed receipt while ignoring the resources needed to obtain the guarantee.
q.commonError: Failing to update opportunity cost when a better feasible alternative appears.
q.feedback: The regular and unguaranteed urgent orders each have expected net value 40,000. The guaranteed order nets 80,000-6,000=74,000 and is feasible before maintenance is chosen. Mutually exclusive alternatives are compared, not added.

key: $74,000: the guaranteed urgent order is the best feasible alternative after its guarantee cost.

q.q: A photographer can accept a portrait job worth $500, an event job worth $650, or spend the day editing a personal project valued at $420. If the portrait job is chosen, what is its opportunity cost?
options: $650 from the event job
$1,070 from both rejected options
$500 from the chosen portrait job
$420 from the least valuable alternative
q.commonError: Adding rejected options or selecting the chosen or least-valued alternative.
q.feedback: The $650 event job is the highest-valued option forgone.

key: $650 from the event job

q.q: A free certification exam takes five hours. A worker would otherwise earn $25 per hour and also pays $15 for transit. Ignoring other effects, what is the opportunity cost?
options: $140 from forgone wages plus transit
$125 from forgone wages only
$15 because only cash payments count
$110 after subtracting transit from wages
q.commonError: Omitting either forgone earnings or an explicit cost.
q.feedback: Five hours of wages equal $125; adding $15 transit gives $140.

key: $140 from forgone wages plus transit

q.q: A printer owned by a design firm can produce client brochures worth $9,000 or internal marketing materials worth $6,500. If it produces internal materials, what is the opportunity cost?
options: $9,000 in forgone client work
$2,500 as the difference in values
$6,500 from the chosen materials
Zero because the firm owns the printer
q.commonError: Using the value difference or treating owned equipment as free.
q.feedback: The best forgone use of the printer is the $9,000 client work.

key: $9,000 in forgone client work

q.q: A student spends three hours at a free festival instead of tutoring for $22 per hour. Ignoring other costs, what is the opportunity cost?
options: $66 in forgone tutoring wages
$22 because only one hourly wage counts
$0 because festival admission is free
$88 from adding the chosen event’s value
q.commonError: Ignoring duration or assuming zero price means zero cost.
q.feedback: Three forgone tutoring hours at $22 each equal $66.

key: $66 in forgone tutoring wages

q.q: A club paid a nonrefundable $2,000 deposit for a banquet. Today it can hold the banquet or use the date for a fundraiser expected to net $3,500. Which amount is the opportunity cost of holding the banquet now?
options: $3,500 from the forgone fundraiser
$2,000 from the nonrefundable deposit
$5,500 from adding both amounts
$1,500 from subtracting the deposit
q.commonError: Substituting a sunk payment for the best current alternative.
q.feedback: The deposit cannot be changed; the fundraiser is the current alternative forgone.

key: $3,500 from the forgone fundraiser

q.q: A mechanic plans to repair personal equipment, giving up a customer job worth $300. Before work begins, a $450 emergency job becomes available. If the personal repair remains the choice, what is its opportunity cost?
options: $450 because the best available alternative changed
$300 because the original plan fixes the cost
$750 because both customer jobs are forgone
$150 because only the increase matters
q.commonError: Failing to update the next-best alternative.
q.feedback: The new $450 job replaces the $300 job as the best option forgone.

key: $450 because the best available alternative changed

q.q: A person rejects options valued at $30, $20, and $5. If another activity is chosen, which rejected value determines its opportunity cost?
options: $30, the highest-valued rejected option
$55, the sum of all rejected options
$5, the least-valued rejected option
$20, the middle rejected option
q.commonError: Adding all rejected alternatives or selecting the least valuable.
q.feedback: Opportunity cost uses one alternative: the highest-valued option forgone.

key: $30, the highest-valued rejected option

q.q: Why can spending an hour in a free park have an opportunity cost?
options: The hour could have been used for another valued activity
Parks always collect a hidden entrance payment
Only travel spending can create opportunity cost
Free time has no alternative uses
q.commonError: Assuming opportunity cost must be monetary.
q.feedback: Time is scarce and can have a valuable next-best use even when no money changes hands.

key: The hour could have been used for another valued activity

q.q: A nonrefundable ticket was bought last month. When deciding whether to attend tonight, what should be treated as sunk?
options: The amount already paid for the ticket
The best activity available tonight
Income that could be earned during the event
A resale price still available tonight
q.commonError: Treating an unrecoverable past payment as a current opportunity cost.
q.feedback: A sunk payment cannot be changed; current alternatives and recoverable values remain relevant.

key: The amount already paid for the ticket

q.q: An owner uses a room that could be rented to someone else. Why is the room not costless?
options: Using it gives up possible rental income
Ownership requires paying its purchase price again
Every imaginable room use must be added together
Only borrowed rooms can have opportunity costs
q.commonError: Assuming owned resources have no opportunity cost.
q.feedback: The best forgone use of an owned resource is an implicit cost.

key: Using it gives up possible rental income

q.q: A worker takes two unpaid hours off instead of working for $18 per hour. What wage value is forgone?
q.commonError: Ignoring duration or assuming unpaid time has no opportunity cost.
q.feedback: Two forgone work hours at $18 each equal $36.

q.q: The economist's role in policy analysis is primarily to:
options: Clarify likely tradeoffs and consequences
Choose everyone's values
Guarantee a policy works
Eliminate scarcity
q.feedback: Economics can analyze consequences and tradeoffs, while value judgments remain separate choices.

key: Clarify likely tradeoffs and consequences

q.q: An economist estimates a policy’s effects, then recommends adoption. What two roles appear?
options: Scientist for the estimate and adviser for the recommendation
Adviser for both because policy is mentioned
Scientist for both because evidence is used
Legislator for the estimate and judge for the advice
q.commonError: Giving economists authority to choose society’s values.
q.feedback: Economists can estimate consequences; recommendations also require value judgments.

key: Scientist for the estimate and adviser for the recommendation

q.q: A policy tradeoff occurs when:
options: Improving one goal makes another goal harder to achieve
A policy has no consequences
Supply equals demand
A tax is legally paid by sellers
q.feedback: Policies often require balancing competing goals rather than delivering only benefits.

key: Improving one goal makes another goal harder to achieve

q.q: An economist predicts job losses and recommends against a rule. What additional judgment turns the prediction into policy advice?
options: The existence of a measurable employment effect
The fact that the rule is a government policy
The recommendation adds a value judgment about the predicted cost
The use of an economic forecast.
q.commonError: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
q.feedback: Separate testable predictions from the value judgment used to recommend a choice.

key: The recommendation adds a value judgment about the predicted cost

q.q: A model predicts a tax effect under stated assumptions. Why is it positive?
options: Because the prediction supports the tax
Because the model is written in technical language
Because the prediction must be true if the assumptions are stated.
Evidence could test the conditional prediction
q.commonError: Assuming objective wording alone makes a claim positive.
q.feedback: Identify what observation could support or contradict the testable component.

key: Evidence could test the conditional prediction

q.q: A library reports that Sunday hours increased visits. What makes this positive?
options: The increase in visits is a desirable outcome
Library officials support Sunday hours
The report is written confidently, so the claim must be true.
Visit records could test the claimed increase
q.commonError: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
q.feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

key: Visit records could test the claimed increase

q.q: “The library should stay open Sundays because access matters.” Why is this normative?
options: It recommends a choice using a value judgment
Sunday visits can be counted
The statement concerns a public institution
Evidence could show whether Sunday hours increase attendance.
q.commonError: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
q.feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

key: It recommends a choice using a value judgment

q.q: A forecast that later proves false can still be positive when:
options: The forecast was made by an expert
Evidence could in principle have tested it
The forecast described an outcome people wanted
The forecast was stated with certainty.
q.commonError: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
q.feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

key: Evidence could in principle have tested it

q.q: Which claim is normative in a school debate?
options: Average class size fell by two students last year
Smaller classes increased per-student spending
The district ought to favor smaller classes despite higher costs
Enrollment is projected to rise next year.
q.commonError: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
q.feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

key: The district ought to favor smaller classes despite higher costs

q.q: Which claim is positive in a transit debate?
options: The city should make transit more affordable
Lower fares are fairer to low-income riders
Expanding transit access is more important than balancing the transit budget.
A lower fare increased weekday ridership
q.commonError: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
q.feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

key: A lower fare increased weekday ridership

q.q: A report defines success only as maximum total surplus. What choice is normative?
options: Calculating total surplus from observed prices and quantities
Selecting total surplus as the sole ranking criterion
Measuring how total surplus changes after the policy
Estimating the policy’s effect on output.
q.commonError: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
q.feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

key: Selecting total surplus as the sole ranking criterion

q.q: Two analysts agree that an archive plan preserves more records but delays public access. One recommends it; the other rejects it. What additional finding would show a factual disagreement as well as a value disagreement?
options: They agree on the delay but differ on whether it is acceptable
They use the same probabilities but prefer different distributions of access
They assign different probabilities to permanent record loss under the alternative
They give different ethical priority to immediate public access
q.commonError: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
q.feedback: Probabilities of record loss are empirical assessments. The other differences concern how agreed consequences should be valued.

key: They assign different probabilities to permanent record loss under the alternative

q.q: A report predicts gains and calls them worth unequal losses. What is normative?
options: The judgment that gains justify the losses
The prediction that the policy creates gains
The estimated size of the gains
The measured distribution of gains and losses.
q.commonError: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
q.feedback: Separate testable predictions from the value judgment used to recommend a choice.

key: The judgment that gains justify the losses

q.q: What best tests “a fee reduces congestion”?
options: A survey asking whether residents support the fee
Traffic counts before and after comparable changes
A council vote to adopt the fee
A statement from officials that congestion will fall.
q.commonError: Assuming objective wording alone makes a claim positive.
q.feedback: Identify what observation could support or contradict the testable component.

key: Traffic counts before and after comparable changes

q.q: Why is “Policy A is responsible” not automatically positive?
options: The statement mentions a policy
The word responsible refers to a measurable outcome
Responsible may hide an unstated value standard
Any sentence about policy performance is positive.
q.commonError: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
q.feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

key: Responsible may hide an unstated value standard

q.q: A subsidy is predicted to raise enrollment and is therefore recommended. Which split is correct?
options: Both parts are positive because enrollment can be measured
Both parts are normative because a subsidy is a policy
The forecast is positive; the recommendation is normative
The forecast is normative; the recommendation is positive.
q.commonError: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
q.feedback: Separate testable predictions from the value judgment used to recommend a choice.

key: The forecast is positive; the recommendation is normative

q.q: “The policy benefits most residents, so it is just.” Where is the normative step?
options: The claim that most residents benefit
The number of residents affected by the policy
The measured size of the benefits.
Calling the distribution just
q.commonError: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
q.feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

key: Calling the distribution just

q.q: What could test the claim that a road fee reduces congestion?
options: Traffic counts around comparable fee changes
A survey asking whether drivers think the fee is fair
A city council vote on the fee
A statement from officials that the fee will work.
q.commonError: Assuming objective wording alone makes a claim positive.
q.feedback: Identify what observation could support or contradict the testable component.

key: Traffic counts around comparable fee changes

q.q: When can “the project has positive net benefits” be positive?
options: Always, because net benefits are measured in dollars
When inputs and the net-benefit rule are empirically checkable
Never, because the word benefits is inherently normative
Only when everyone agrees the project is desirable.
q.commonError: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
q.feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

key: When inputs and the net-benefit rule are empirically checkable

q.q: “The only acceptable policy is universal access.” Why is this normative?
options: Universal access can be measured
The statement refers to a policy outcome
It embeds a value standard despite objective wording
The sentence does not include a numerical prediction.
q.commonError: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
q.feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

key: It embeds a value standard despite objective wording

q.q: A rule lowers costs but is called morally wrong. What can evidence settle?
options: Both the cost effect and whether the rule is morally wrong
Only whether the rule is morally wrong
Neither claim, because the rule is a policy.
The cost effect, but not the moral conclusion by itself
q.commonError: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
q.feedback: Separate testable predictions from the value judgment used to recommend a choice.

key: The cost effect, but not the moral conclusion by itself

q.q: A report finds that a shuttle saves travelers time but increases neighborhood noise. It recommends adoption using travelers' gains alone. Which critique is precise?
options: Time savings become normative when expressed in money
Adding more precise effect estimates removes the need to decide whose welfare counts
The effects are testable; excluding neighbors from the recommendation embeds a value choice
Noise estimates are normative because neighbors dislike the outcome
q.commonError: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
q.feedback: Time and noise effects can be measured. Counting only travelers when recommending a policy assigns standing to one group and excludes another, which is a value choice.

key: The effects are testable; excluding neighbors from the recommendation embeds a value choice

q.q: Two forecasts disagree about whether a new scheduling rule will shorten next year's queues. Both specify measurable waiting times and comparable staffing. What would change their status as positive claims?
options: The forecast with the larger benefit is positive; the other is normative
Both become normative until next year's data exist
Agreement by the forecasters is required before evidence can test them
Neither disagreement nor the future date changes their testable status
q.commonError: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
q.feedback: Positive status depends on empirical testability, not agreement, truth, desirability or whether the outcome has occurred. Later evidence can support one forecast over the other.

key: Neither disagreement nor the future date changes their testable status

q.q: An analyst rejects a delivery plan because predicted delays exceed her stated acceptable limit. Better evidence places delays below that limit, but she still rejects it on privacy grounds. Which interpretation fits?
options: The factual case changed, and the rejection now requires an additional value criterion
The original delay forecast was normative because it supported rejection
The unchanged decision proves the new delay estimate is irrelevant to the original argument
Privacy concerns establish that the revised forecast is false
q.commonError: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
q.feedback: The delay objection no longer follows from the updated evidence and original threshold. A privacy objection can support rejection, but it is a separate normative premise.

key: The factual case changed, and the rejection now requires an additional value criterion

q.q: A planner defines "optimal" as maximizing visits, then claims the chosen schedule is objectively best. Another schedule serves fewer visitors but reaches people with greater need. Which statement is most defensible?
options: A numerical criterion cannot contain a value judgment
Visit maximization identifies an optimum under one criterion, not a uniquely justified social ranking
Calling a result optimal makes its criterion empirically true
The need difference disproves the measured visit counts
q.commonError: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
q.feedback: Optimization can be objective conditional on a criterion. Choosing visits rather than need as the social objective remains a normative judgment.

key: Visit maximization identifies an optimum under one criterion, not a uniquely justified social ranking

q.q: School plan A is predicted to raise scores by 6 points and reduce free time by 4 hours weekly. Plan B raises scores by 4 points and reduces free time by 1 hour. A board declares A preferable because each extra score point is worth at least 2 hours of free time. Which assessment is exact?
options: The outcome predictions are normative; the board’s numerical weighting is positive, and A’s extra 2 points cost 3 hours.
All claims are positive because they contain numbers; A dominates B on both scores and free time.
The weighting is normative, so the score and time predictions cannot be tested against observed outcomes.
The outcome predictions are positive; the board’s weighting is normative, and A’s extra 2 points cost 3 hours relative to B.
q.commonError: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
q.feedback: Comparative predictions imply A adds 2 score points while costing 3 more hours, or 1.5 hours per extra point. Whether that is worthwhile depends on the board’s stated value criterion, not merely on the accuracy of the predictions.

key: The outcome predictions are positive; the board’s weighting is normative, and A’s extra 2 points cost 3 hours relative to B.

q.q: A report says a fee reduced waste and therefore is fair. What is normative?
options: The claim that the fee reduced waste
The measured amount of waste reduction
The judgment that the fee is fair
The fact that a fee was imposed.
q.commonError: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
q.feedback: Separate testable predictions from the value judgment used to recommend a choice.

key: The judgment that the fee is fair

q.q: A weakly supported prediction later fails. What classification remains possible?
options: Normative, because the prediction turned out to be false
Normative, because the evidence supporting it was weak
Neither positive nor normative until the prediction is confirmed.
Positive, because testability does not require truth
q.commonError: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
q.feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

key: Positive, because testability does not require truth

q.q: “Costs rose 8%, so the city should respond.” What is present?
options: A positive measurement plus a normative recommendation
A purely positive statement because it includes a measured percentage
A purely normative statement because it recommends action
Two positive claims because both parts refer to economic conditions.
q.commonError: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
q.feedback: Separate testable predictions from the value judgment used to recommend a choice.

key: A positive measurement plus a normative recommendation

q.q: A program “works,” but no outcome is named. What is missing?
options: A statement that the program is desirable
A measurable claim that evidence could contradict
A recommendation about whether the program should continue
A larger sample of people who support the program.
q.commonError: Assuming objective wording alone makes a claim positive.
q.feedback: Identify what observation could support or contradict the testable component.

key: A measurable claim that evidence could contradict

q.q: “Equal access matters more than maximum output.” What is this?
options: A positive claim because access and output can both be measured
A positive claim because it compares two economic outcomes
A normative ranking of competing values
Neither positive nor normative because no policy is named.
q.commonError: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
q.feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

key: A normative ranking of competing values

q.q: A tax study uses the word efficient for a measurable revenue criterion. Is it necessarily normative?
options: Yes; the word efficient always expresses a value judgment
Yes; any claim about taxes is normative
Yes; a policy criterion cannot be evaluated with evidence.
No; the stated criterion can be tested with evidence
q.commonError: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
q.feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

key: No; the stated criterion can be tested with evidence

q.q: “A bus lane reduced travel time.” What kind of claim is this?
options: Positive and empirically testable
Normative because reduced travel time is desirable
Normative because the statement concerns transportation policy
Neither, because one observed result cannot be tested.
q.commonError: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
q.feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

key: Positive and empirically testable

q.q: “The city ought to accept higher costs for cleaner air.” What kind?
options: Positive because costs and air quality can be measured
Normative because it ranks a tradeoff
Positive because the statement describes a policy tradeoff
Neither, because the statement contains no numerical estimate.
q.commonError: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
q.feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

key: Normative because it ranks a tradeoff

q.q: When does a false forecast remain positive?
options: Only when the forecast describes a desirable outcome
Only when an expert made the forecast
When evidence could have tested the forecast
Never; a false claim cannot be positive.
q.commonError: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
q.feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

key: When evidence could have tested the forecast

q.q: Does positive mean good or favorable?
options: Yes; positive means the outcome is desirable
Yes; positive claims support the policy being discussed
No; it means testable in principle
Yes; positive claims are facts that must be true.
q.commonError: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
q.feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

key: No; it means testable in principle

q.q: Does false automatically mean normative?
options: Yes; normative claims are the claims that turn out to be false
Yes; positive claims must be factually correct
Yes; a claim becomes normative once evidence rejects it.
No; a false claim can still be testable
q.commonError: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
q.feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

key: No; a false claim can still be testable

q.q: Is every policy statement normative?
options: No; policy predictions can be positive
Yes; any statement about government policy is normative
Yes; policy effects cannot be tested with evidence
Yes; mentioning a recommendation makes every related claim normative.
q.commonError: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
q.feedback: Separate testable predictions from the value judgment used to recommend a choice.

key: No; policy predictions can be positive

q.q: Does technical tone guarantee a positive claim?
options: Yes; technical language makes a statement factual
No; technical wording can conceal a value judgment
Yes; numerical language removes value judgments
Yes; professional wording means the claim can be tested.
q.commonError: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
q.feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

key: No; technical wording can conceal a value judgment

q.q: A transit study predicts that a lower fare will increase ridership. Why is this positive?
options: Evidence could test the predicted change
The prediction must be socially desirable
The result is guaranteed to be true
Transit policy contains no value judgment
q.commonError: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
q.feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

key: Evidence could test the predicted change

q.q: A council member says parks should receive more funding because access is fair. Why is this normative?
options: It includes a government budget
It ranks outcomes using a value judgment
It predicts a measurable funding change
It must be supported by all voters
q.commonError: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
q.feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

key: It ranks outcomes using a value judgment

q.q: Which statement is positive?
options: The city should make rent cheaper.
Rent control is unfair.
A binding rent ceiling reduces apartment supply
The best policy is always lower rent.
q.feedback: This is positive because it makes a testable claim about what the policy will do.

key: A binding rent ceiling reduces apartment supply

q.q: What is a positive statement?
options: A testable claim about how the world is
A claim about how the world should be
A statement that is always morally good
A policy recommendation
q.feedback: A positive statement describes or predicts how the world is.

key: A testable claim about how the world is

q.q: An instructor presents this claim: 'A price ceiling below equilibrium creates a shortage.' What kind of statement is this?
options: Normative
Positive
A value judgment
A policy recommendation
