key: At most 50 rentals and excess demand of 200 apartments

q.q: Refer to the graph. Relative to the competitive equilibrium, how do quantity demanded and quantity supplied change at the $1,000 ceiling?
options: Quantity demanded -100; quantity supplied +100.
Quantity demanded +200; quantity supplied unchanged.
Quantity demanded unchanged; quantity supplied -200.
Quantity demanded +100; quantity supplied -100.
q.feedback: At equilibrium both quantities are 150. At $1,000, quantity demanded is 250 and quantity supplied is 50. Demand therefore rises by 100 while supply falls by 100, opening a 200-unit shortage.

key: Quantity demanded +100; quantity supplied -100.

q.q: Refer to the apartment graph. One tenant keeps the same apartment after the displayed ceiling is imposed but now spends time searching and queuing valued at $1,100 per month. With apartment quality unchanged, which evaluation is correct?
options: The tenant gains $1,000 net, and the market has excess demand of 200 apartments
The tenant loses $100 net, and the market has excess demand of 200 apartments
The tenant loses $100 net, and all 200 unmatched applicants must be former tenants
The tenant gains $100 net, and the market has excess supply of 200 apartments
q.feedback: The graph shows rent falling from $2,000 to $1,000, a $1,000 saving. Subtract the stated $1,100 time cost: the continuing tenant loses $100 net. At the ceiling, Qd = 250 and Qs = 50, giving excess demand of 200. The time cost is specified for this tenant, not asserted for every ceiling.

key: The tenant loses $100 net, and the market has excess demand of 200 apartments

q.q: At the $1,000 rent ceiling, what shortage is shown?
options: 50 apartments
200 apartments
150 apartments
300 apartments
q.feedback: Read quantity demanded and quantity supplied at the $1,000 ceiling and subtract: 250 − 50 = 200 apartments.

key: 200 apartments

q.q: Refer to the graph. At the binding $1,000 rent ceiling, what is the maximum number of apartments that can be rented if transactions cannot exceed the number landlords offer?
options: 150 apartments
200 apartments
50 apartments
250 apartments
q.feedback: At $1,000, quantity supplied is only 50 apartments. Even though 250 are demanded, actual transactions cannot exceed the 50 units offered.

key: 50 apartments

q.q: A legal maximum below equilibrium and a legal minimum above equilibrium have what in common?
options: Both are binding price controls
Both create market equilibrium
Both create tax wedges
Both increase quantity traded
q.feedback: A ceiling below equilibrium and a floor above equilibrium both bind because they prevent the market from reaching equilibrium.

key: Both are binding price controls

q.q: Which policy-price pairing is nonbinding?
options: A price ceiling above equilibrium
A price ceiling below equilibrium
A price floor above equilibrium
A rent ceiling below market rent
q.feedback: A price ceiling above equilibrium is nonbinding because the market price can settle below it.

key: A price ceiling above equilibrium

q.q: A price ceiling below equilibrium and a price floor above equilibrium are both:
options: Binding price controls
Examples of market equilibrium
Taxes on sellers
Demand shifters
q.feedback: Both controls are binding because they prevent the market from reaching equilibrium.

key: Binding price controls

q.q: A price floor above equilibrium and a price ceiling below equilibrium both cause problems because:
options: They prevent the market price from adjusting to equilibrium
They eliminate all gains from trade immediately
They make demand and supply irrelevant
They always increase the quantity traded
q.feedback: Binding price controls prevent price from moving to equilibrium, creating shortages or surpluses.

key: They prevent the market price from adjusting to equilibrium

q.q: A minimum legal price is binding only when it is set:
options: Above equilibrium price
Below equilibrium price
Exactly at zero
Below quantity demanded
q.feedback: A price floor binds only when it is above equilibrium price.

key: Above equilibrium price

q.q: A binding price floor usually creates:
options: A surplus
A shortage
A tax wedge
A demand increase
q.feedback: A binding floor keeps price too high, so quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded.

key: A surplus

q.q: A minimum wage is set at $15 when equilibrium wage is $11. What happens?
options: The floor is binding and creates a labor surplus
The floor is nonbinding and has no effect
The floor creates a labor shortage
The floor shifts labor demand right
q.feedback: A floor above equilibrium is binding and creates a surplus.

key: The floor is binding and creates a labor surplus

q.q: A legal minimum price is below equilibrium. Why is it nonbinding?
options: The market price remains above the legal minimum
All floors create surpluses
Buyers must pay the lowest possible price
Supply must fall to zero
q.feedback: A floor below equilibrium does not stop the market from reaching equilibrium.

key: The market price remains above the legal minimum

q.q: A legal minimum price is called:
options: A price floor
A price ceiling
A shortage
A demand shift
q.feedback: A price floor is a legal minimum price.

key: A price floor

q.q: A price floor is binding when it is set:
options: Above equilibrium price
Below equilibrium price
At zero
Only on buyers
q.feedback: A floor must be above equilibrium to prevent price from falling to equilibrium.

key: Above equilibrium price

q.q: A binding price floor creates:
options: A surplus
A shortage
A decrease in supply
A price ceiling
q.feedback: A binding price floor keeps price too high, so quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded.

key: A surplus

q.q: A minimum wage set above equilibrium usually creates:
options: A labor surplus, or unemployment
A labor shortage
A decrease in labor supply
A tax wedge only on buyers
q.feedback: A binding minimum wage is a price floor in the labor market and creates a surplus of labor.

key: A labor surplus, or unemployment

q.q: At a binding price floor, quantity supplied is 90 and quantity demanded is 50. What is the surplus?
options: 40 units
50 units
90 units
140 units
q.feedback: Surplus equals quantity supplied minus quantity demanded: 90 - 50 = 40.

key: 40 units

q.q: Which policy would most likely create a surplus?
options: A binding price floor
A binding price ceiling
A decrease in supply
A nonbinding price floor.
q.feedback: A binding price floor creates a surplus because price is held above equilibrium.

key: A binding price floor

q.q: A minimum wage is set above equilibrium. Some workers earn more, firms demand fewer workers, and more workers want jobs. What is the best synthesis?
options: The wage floor benefits some employed workers but creates a labor surplus for others
The wage floor increases both labor demanded and labor supplied
The wage floor is nonbinding because workers prefer higher wages
The wage floor eliminates the opportunity cost of working
q.feedback: A binding minimum wage raises wages for some workers but creates a surplus of labor because labor supplied exceeds labor demanded.

key: The wage floor benefits some employed workers but creates a labor surplus for others

q.q: A government wants to raise producer income, so it imposes a price floor. Which condition must hold for the policy to actually affect the market?
options: The floor must be above equilibrium price
The floor must be below equilibrium price
The floor must equal zero
The floor must reduce supply
q.feedback: A price floor only binds if it is above the equilibrium price.

key: The floor must be above equilibrium price

q.q: A minimum wage rises from $10 to $15. At $15, firms demand 70,000 workers and 120,000 workers want jobs. What is the labor surplus and what is one likely adjustment?
options: 50,000 workers; firms may automate or reduce hours
50,000 workers; firms must hire all workers
190,000 workers; firms may increase labor demand
70,000 workers; workers stop supplying labor
q.feedback: Labor surplus is 120,000 - 70,000 = 50,000. Firms may respond by reducing hours, automating, or hiring fewer workers.

key: 50,000 workers; firms may automate or reduce hours

q.q: A minimum wage is set at $16 when the equilibrium wage is $12. At $16, firms demand 70,000 workers and 110,000 workers want jobs. What is the best diagnosis?
options: The floor is binding and creates a labor surplus of 40,000 workers
The floor is binding and creates a labor shortage of 40,000 workers
The floor is nonbinding because workers prefer higher wages
The floor increases labor demand by 40,000 workers
q.feedback: A price floor above equilibrium is binding. Labor surplus equals quantity supplied minus quantity demanded, so 110,000 - 70,000 = 40,000 workers.

key: The floor is binding and creates a labor surplus of 40,000 workers

q.q: A minimum wage raises pay for workers who keep their jobs, but firms hire fewer workers and more workers seek jobs. Which statement gives the best economic interpretation?
options: The policy helps some employed workers, but it also creates a labor surplus among workers seeking jobs
The policy helps workers as a group because the higher wage applies to anyone willing to work
The policy helps firms attract more workers, so labor demand rises with the legal wage
The policy leaves employment unchanged because only the legal wage has changed
q.feedback: A binding minimum wage creates winners and losers. Some employed workers earn more, but firms hire fewer workers and a labor surplus appears.

key: The policy helps some employed workers, but it also creates a labor surplus among workers seeking jobs

q.q: A labor market initially has Qd=440-10W and Qs=10W. A minimum wage of $18 is imposed. Later labor demand falls to Qd=280-10W, with supply unchanged. Which account is correct?
options: The floor is initially nonbinding at $22; later it binds at $18, with 100 employed and a labor surplus of 80.
The floor initially binds at $18; later it becomes nonbinding at $14, with 180 employed and no surplus.
The floor is initially nonbinding at $22; later it binds at $18, with 180 employed and a labor shortage of 80.
The floor stays nonbinding because its statutory value is unchanged, so employment remains at the original 220.
q.feedback: Initial equilibrium solves 440-10W=10W, giving W=22. Later equilibrium would be W=14. At the $18 floor, labor demand is 100 and supply 180; employment is demand-limited and excess supply is 80.

key: The floor is initially nonbinding at $22; later it binds at $18, with 100 employed and a labor surplus of 80.

q.q: A binding price floor raises the legal price from $30 to $45. At $45, sellers offer 900 units and buyers want 600 units. Which outcome is most likely?
options: A surplus of 300 units and extra effort by sellers to unload the good
A shortage of 300 units and long lines for buyers
No surplus because sellers prefer the higher price
A demand increase because the higher price signals quality
q.feedback: At the floor, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded by 300 units. Sellers compete to find buyers, often through nonprice margins.

key: A surplus of 300 units and extra effort by sellers to unload the good

q.q: A policy raises the legal price, creates unsold output, and benefits some sellers while making buyers purchase less. Which policy best matches this pattern?
options: A binding price floor
A binding price ceiling
A nonbinding price ceiling
A buyer tax that leaves quantity unchanged
q.feedback: Higher legal price plus unsold output points to a binding price floor.

key: A binding price floor

q.q: The government sets a crop price floor above equilibrium and promises to buy any unsold output. Which result is most likely?
options: Farmers produce more than consumers buy, so the government purchases and stores the surplus
Consumers buy more because the legal price is higher
The policy creates a shortage because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied
The floor is nonbinding because the government participates in the market
q.feedback: A binding price floor creates excess supply. A purchase guarantee shifts the unsold surplus to the government rather than making it disappear.

key: Farmers produce more than consumers buy, so the government purchases and stores the surplus

q.q: At a binding price floor, Qs = 110 and Qd = 80. What is the surplus?
options: 30 units
80 units
110 units
190 units
q.feedback: Surplus equals Qs - Qd: 110 - 80 = 30.

key: 30 units

q.q: At a binding floor, sellers offer 140 units and buyers want 95 units. What happens?
options: A surplus of 45 units
A shortage of 45 units
A surplus of 235 units
No surplus
q.feedback: The surplus is quantity supplied minus quantity demanded: 140 - 95 = 45.

key: A surplus of 45 units

q.q: A grain schedule lists price per sack, sacks buyers want and sacks growers offer: $4: 100, 40; $6: 70, 70; $8: 50, 90. An enforced price floor is $8. What surplus follows?
options: 40 sacks
50 sacks
140 sacks
0 sacks
q.feedback: Use the $8 floor row, not the $6 equilibrium row. Growers offer 90 sacks and buyers want 50, so surplus is 90 - 50 = 40. Adding supply and demand does not measure unsold output.

key: 40 sacks

q.q: At a binding minimum price for milk, farms offer 700 cartons and households want 455. There are no government purchases, and households buy all 455. A clerk calls the 455 sold cartons "the surplus." Which correction is accurate?
options: 245 cartons are unsold; 455 cartons are purchased.
455 cartons are unsold; 245 cartons are purchased.
245 cartons are unmet demand; 455 cartons are purchased.
1,155 cartons are unsold; 455 cartons are purchased.
q.feedback: Purchases are 455 cartons. The surplus is the amount offered but not purchased: 700 - 455 = 245 cartons. Supply exceeds demand, so the gap is unsold output, not unmet demand.

key: 245 cartons are unsold; 455 cartons are purchased.

q.q: A binding price floor is imposed above equilibrium. Quantity supplied is 700 and quantity demanded is 460. What is the surplus?
options: 240 units
460 units
700 units
1,160 units
q.feedback: Surplus is Qs - Qd: 700 - 460 = 240 units.

key: 240 units

q.q: A minimum wage is set at $16 when equilibrium wage is $12. At $16, labor supplied is 95,000 and labor demanded is 72,000. What is the labor surplus?
options: 23,000 workers
72,000 workers
95,000 workers
167,000 workers
q.feedback: The labor surplus is labor supplied minus labor demanded: 95,000 - 72,000 = 23,000.

key: 23,000 workers

q.q: A price floor is set below equilibrium. Why does it usually have no effect?
options: The market price remains above the legal minimum
Because all price floors create surpluses
Because buyers must pay the legal minimum even if equilibrium is higher
Because quantity demanded must equal zero
q.feedback: A nonbinding floor is below equilibrium, so the market can still reach equilibrium above the legal minimum.

key: The market price remains above the legal minimum

q.q: A binding agricultural price floor causes farmers to produce more than buyers want to purchase. What problem follows?
options: Unsold surplus output
A shortage of the crop
A lower legal price
A rightward demand shift
q.feedback: A binding price floor creates a surplus because quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded.

key: Unsold surplus output

q.q: Refer to the price-control graph. If a price floor is set at $20, what happens?
options: It is nonbinding because it is below equilibrium
It creates a shortage of 100 units
It creates a surplus of 100 units
It forces price up to $40
q.feedback: Equilibrium is $30. A floor at $20 is below equilibrium, so it does not prevent the market from reaching $30.

key: It is nonbinding because it is below equilibrium

q.q: Refer to the price-control graph. If a price floor is set at $50, what surplus results?
options: 200 units
100 units
300 units
400 units
q.feedback: At $50, quantity supplied is 300 and quantity demanded is 100. The surplus is 300 - 100 = 200 units.

key: 200 units

q.q: Refer to the price-control graph. A policy holds the price at $40. What is the full market result if the policy is a legal minimum?
options: A binding price floor with a surplus of 100 units
A nonbinding price floor with no effect
A binding price ceiling with a shortage of 100 units
A nonbinding price ceiling with no effect
q.feedback: $40 is above the $30 equilibrium, so a legal minimum at $40 is a binding floor. Qs is 250 and Qd is 150, so the surplus is 100.

key: A binding price floor with a surplus of 100 units

q.q: Refer to the price-control graph. At $50, what are quantity demanded and quantity supplied?
options: Quantity demanded is 100 and quantity supplied is 300
Quantity demanded is 300 and quantity supplied is 100
Quantity demanded is 150 and quantity supplied is 250
Quantity demanded is 250 and quantity supplied is 150
q.feedback: At a high price of $50, buyers demand 100 units while sellers supply 300 units.

key: Quantity demanded is 100 and quantity supplied is 300

q.q: Refer to the graph. A $40 floor is enforced. Private buyers purchase their quantity demanded, and government buys 50 additional units at the floor. If sellers produce the quantity on supply, what remains unsold and what does government spend?
options: 50 units remain unsold; government spends $2,000
100 units remain unsold; government spends $2,000
50 units remain unsold; government spends $4,000
No units remain unsold; government spends $2,000
q.feedback: At $40, Qs = 250 and private Qd = 150. Government absorbs 50 of the 100-unit gap, leaving 50 unsold. Its spending is 50 × $40 = $2,000. Desired supply does not become private demand.

key: 50 units remain unsold; government spends $2,000

q.q: Refer to the price-control graph. A price floor of $10 is imposed. Which answer is best?
options: The floor is nonbinding because it is below the $30 equilibrium price
The floor is binding because it is below the $30 equilibrium price
The floor creates a shortage because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied
The floor creates a surplus because quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded
q.feedback: A floor below equilibrium does not restrict the market price, so it is nonbinding.

key: The floor is nonbinding because it is below the $30 equilibrium price

q.q: A minimum wage is set above the equilibrium wage. Some workers receive higher pay, firms hire fewer workers, and more workers seek jobs. What is the cleanest interpretation?
options: The floor helps some employed workers but creates a labor surplus
The floor helps all workers because everyone now earns the legal wage
The floor raises labor demand because the wage is higher
The floor is nonbinding because firms still hire some workers
q.feedback: A binding wage floor creates winners among some employed workers and losers among workers unable to find jobs.

key: The floor helps some employed workers but creates a labor surplus

q.q: After a higher hourly minimum wage, a firm raises hourly pay but reduces scheduled hours and employer-paid training. A report calls the higher hourly rate proof that every worker gained. Which review addresses the missing incentive responses?
options: Compare hours, total earnings and training changes for affected workers
Use the hourly rate alone because other employment terms are not wages
Infer that lower hours prove every worker lost despite higher hourly pay
Treat the firm's adjustment as proof it did not respond to the wage rule
q.feedback: The hourly rate is only one margin. Hours and training can change in response, so worker outcomes require the combined compensation and work changes; no additional price-floor mechanics are needed.

key: Compare hours, total earnings and training changes for affected workers

q.q: A legal minimum price is set below equilibrium. A student predicts a surplus. What is wrong?
options: A floor below equilibrium is nonbinding and does not create a surplus
Any price floor always creates a surplus
A floor below equilibrium creates a shortage
A floor below equilibrium is actually a price ceiling
q.feedback: A price floor binds only when it is above equilibrium.

key: A floor below equilibrium is nonbinding and does not create a surplus

q.q: At a price floor of $18, quantity supplied is 900 units and quantity demanded is 550 units. Which answer best states the result?
options: A surplus of 350 units
A shortage of 350 units
A surplus of 550 units
A shortage of 900 units
q.feedback: Surplus equals quantity supplied minus quantity demanded: 900 - 550 = 350.

key: A surplus of 350 units

q.q: A binding price floor on milk leaves producers with unsold inventory. Which hidden cost is most likely?
options: Waste, storage costs, or government purchases to support the price
Long lines among buyers because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied
Black-market premiums from buyers competing for scarce milk
No cost because producers receive a higher legal price
q.feedback: A binding floor creates a surplus, which can lead to waste, storage costs, or policy costs.

key: Waste, storage costs, or government purchases to support the price

q.q: A wage floor raises pay for workers who keep jobs but reduces entry-level openings. Which economic idea best frames the policy debate?
options: An efficiency-equity tradeoff
A movement along the PPF with no opportunity cost
A nonbinding ceiling
A fixed CPI basket
q.feedback: The policy can improve outcomes for some workers while reducing efficiency or job access for others.

key: An efficiency-equity tradeoff

q.q: A minimum wage is set above equilibrium, but employment does not fall much. Which explanation best fits supply and demand logic?
options: Labor demand may be relatively inelastic over that range
The law of demand has been disproven
The wage floor must be below equilibrium
Higher wages always increase quantity demanded for labor
q.feedback: If labor demand is relatively inelastic, employment may fall only modestly when wages rise.

key: Labor demand may be relatively inelastic over that range

q.q: A wage floor of $16 is initially below an $18 equilibrium wage. Demand then falls; without the floor the new wage would be $14. At $16, firms now demand 90 workers and 130 want jobs. With all demanded jobs filled, what is the correct diagnosis?
options: The floor remains nonbinding, with 130 employed and no surplus
The floor changes from nonbinding to binding, with 130 employed and a 40-worker shortage
The floor changes from nonbinding to binding, with 90 employed and a 40-worker surplus
The floor was binding in both periods, with employment fixed at 90
q.feedback: Initially the legal minimum of $16 permits the $18 equilibrium. After demand falls, it prevents adjustment to $14. Labor demand limits employment to 90, while 130 − 90 = 40 willing workers are unmatched. Binding status depends on the current equilibrium.

key: The floor changes from nonbinding to binding, with 90 employed and a 40-worker surplus

q.q: At a binding price floor, sellers offer 1,900 units and buyers demand 1,250. The government purchases 300 units. How much unsold surplus remains?
q.feedback: Initial surplus is 650 units. Government purchases of 300 leave 350 unsold.

q.q: A binding agricultural price floor is removed. Holding other conditions constant, which adjustment is expected?
options: Price rises, quantity demanded falls, and quantity supplied rises
Price falls, quantity demanded rises, and quantity supplied falls
Price and quantity supplied both rise
A shortage necessarily replaces the surplus
q.feedback: Removing the floor allows price to fall toward equilibrium, raising demand and reducing supply.

key: Price falls, quantity demanded rises, and quantity supplied falls

q.q: A minimum wage is set below the equilibrium wage. What is the likely result?
options: The minimum wage is not binding
It creates unemployment
It creates a labor shortage
It shifts labor demand right
q.feedback: A price floor below equilibrium does not prevent the market wage from reaching equilibrium.

key: The minimum wage is not binding

q.q: A minimum wage is set above equilibrium. Labor supplied is 120,000 and labor demanded is 80,000. What is the labor surplus?
options: 40,000 workers
80,000 workers
120,000 workers
200,000 workers
q.feedback: The surplus is quantity supplied minus quantity demanded: 120,000 - 80,000 = 40,000.

key: 40,000 workers

q.q: A binding price floor in an agricultural market may lead to:
options: Unsold surplus output
A shortage of the crop
A lower legal price
A movement down the demand curve caused by lower price
q.feedback: A binding price floor keeps price above equilibrium, so quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded.

key: Unsold surplus output

q.q: Refer to the graph. If the government sets a price floor at $40, is the price floor binding?
options: Yes, because it is above the equilibrium price
No, because it is above the equilibrium price
Yes, because it is below the equilibrium price
No, because all price floors are nonbinding
q.feedback: A price floor is binding when it is above equilibrium. Here, $40 is above the $30 equilibrium price.

key: Yes, because it is above the equilibrium price

q.q: Refer to the graph. At a price floor of $40, what is quantity demanded?
options: 150 units
250 units
200 units
300 units
q.feedback: At $40, the demand curve shows quantity demanded of 150 units.

key: 150 units

q.q: Refer to the graph. At a price floor of $40, what is quantity supplied?
options: 250 units
150 units
200 units
100 units
q.feedback: At $40, the supply curve shows quantity supplied of 250 units.

key: 250 units

q.q: Refer to the graph. If the government sets a price floor at $40, what surplus results?
options: 100 units
50 units
150 units
400 units
q.feedback: At $40, quantity supplied is 250 and quantity demanded is 150. The surplus is 250 - 150 = 100 units.

key: 100 units

q.q: A legal minimum wage of $10 is shown on the labor-market graph. How should this policy be classified?
options: Nonbinding floor: $10 is above equilibrium.
Binding ceiling: $10 is above equilibrium.
Binding floor: $10 is above equilibrium.
Nonbinding ceiling: $10 is below equilibrium.
q.feedback: A price floor is binding when it is set above equilibrium. The $10 wage floor sits above the $7 market-clearing wage.

key: Binding floor: $10 is above equilibrium.

q.q: A student says the $10 minimum wage raises employment to 250 thousand because 250 thousand workers are willing to work. What is the strongest correction using the graph?
options: Employment is 250k; every willing worker is hired.
Employment stays 175k; the wage floor does not affect hiring.
Employment is 100k; 150k workers remain without jobs.
Employment is 100k; the 150k gap is a labor shortage.
q.feedback: A binding minimum wage creates excess labor supply, not automatic jobs. At $10, firms demand 100 thousand workers while 250 thousand seek work.

key: Employment is 100k; 150k workers remain without jobs.

q.q: Refer to the graph. Compared with competitive equilibrium, how do the quantities of labor supplied and demanded change at the $10 minimum wage?
options: Quantity of labor supplied decreases by 75 thousand; quantity demanded increases by 75 thousand.
Quantity of labor supplied increases by 75 thousand; quantity demanded decreases by 75 thousand.
Quantity of labor supplied increases by 150 thousand; quantity demanded is unchanged.
Quantity of labor supplied is unchanged; quantity demanded decreases by 150 thousand.
q.feedback: At equilibrium, both labor supplied and demanded equal 175 thousand. At $10, labor supplied is 250 thousand and labor demanded is 100 thousand, so the two 75-thousand movements create the 150-thousand surplus.

key: Quantity of labor supplied increases by 75 thousand; quantity demanded decreases by 75 thousand.

q.q: Refer to the labor graph. The displayed minimum wage is repealed and the market returns to A. Assume all jobs demanded are filled for one hour each. Which comparison accounts for the lower wage and changed employment?
options: Employment rises by 150,000, excess labor supply disappears, and hourly payroll rises by $750,000
Employment falls by 75,000 and hourly payroll falls by $225,000
Employment rises by 75,000, but hourly payroll falls by $300,000
Employment rises by 75,000, excess labor supply disappears, and hourly payroll rises by $225,000
q.feedback: With the $10 floor, employment is 100,000, willing workers number 250,000, and payroll is $1,000,000. At A, 175,000 workers earn $7, so payroll is $1,225,000 and excess supply is zero. Employment rises 75,000; payroll rises $225,000 even though the wage falls.

key: Employment rises by 75,000, excess labor supply disappears, and hourly payroll rises by $225,000

q.q: Refer to the graph. At the $10 minimum wage, what labor surplus results?
options: 75 thousand workers
100 thousand workers
350 thousand workers
150 thousand workers
q.feedback: At $10, labor supplied is 250 thousand workers and labor demanded is 100 thousand, so the labor surplus is 150 thousand workers.

key: 150 thousand workers

q.q: Refer to the graph. At the binding $10 minimum wage, how many workers are employed?
options: 100 thousand workers
150 thousand workers
175 thousand workers
250 thousand workers
q.feedback: At $10, firms demand 100 thousand workers. The larger 250-thousand labor supply does not force firms to hire beyond their quantity demanded.

key: 100 thousand workers

q.q: With full resource use and constant tradeoffs, an economy can make 100 food units or 50 medical units. Medical-only technology doubles maximum medical output, leaving maximum food unchanged. At 60 food, compare feasible medical output before and after; then assess an observed rise from an interior point to the old frontier.
options: Medical capacity rises from 20 to 50; every output increase from an interior point proves the whole frontier shifted equally.
Medical capacity stays 20 because food technology is unchanged; only a move to a new point on the old line is possible.
Medical capacity rises from 40 to 80; an interior-to-frontier move reduces efficiency because fewer resources remain idle.
Medical capacity at 60 food rises from 20 to 40; the separate interior-to-old-frontier move is improved utilization, not evidence of that technology shift.
q.commonError: Confusing movement toward the frontier with a shift of productive capacity.
q.feedback: The old linear frontier is M=50(1-F/100), giving 20 at F=60. The new one is M=100(1-F/100), giving 40. An interior-to-frontier move under old technology improves utilization without identifying a capacity change.

key: Medical capacity at 60 food rises from 20 to 40; the separate interior-to-old-frontier move is improved utilization, not evidence of that technology shift.

q.q: An economy initially produces 60 units of each good inside a frontier that permits 80 of each together. Reemploying idle labor reaches 80 of each. New machinery then permits 100 of each together. A planner attributes the entire increase to growth in productive capacity. Which counterfactual best exposes the error?
options: Without new machinery, reemployment could still reach 80 of each; only the later extension beyond the old feasible set demonstrates added capacity.
Without reemployment, machinery could not affect the frontier, because a frontier is defined by actual rather than possible output.
Without new machinery, output must remain at 60 of each, because any increase in both goods requires an outward frontier shift.
Without reemployment, the old frontier would automatically move inward to the observed 60-unit bundle.
q.commonError: Confusing movement toward the frontier with a shift of productive capacity.
q.feedback: Initial unused resources explain movement from 60 to 80 under the old feasible set. Machinery changes what can be produced, permitting 100 of each. Observed output growth combines utilization and capacity changes; it cannot all be labeled a frontier shift.

key: Without new machinery, reemployment could still reach 80 of each; only the later extension beyond the old feasible set demonstrates added capacity.

q.q: Is a point inside the PPF unattainable?
options: Yes; any point not on the frontier is unattainable
Yes; only points on the PPF are feasible
Yes; producing inside the frontier requires more resources than the economy has.
No; it is attainable but inefficient
q.feedback: A point inside the PPF is attainable with current resources but productively inefficient because some capacity is unused.

key: No; it is attainable but inefficient

q.q: Does moving along a PPF represent economic growth?
options: No; it reallocates production on the same frontier
Yes; any movement to a different production mix is economic growth
Yes; producing more of one good means productive capacity has increased
Yes; moving along the frontier shifts it outward.
q.commonError: Confusing movement toward the frontier with a shift of productive capacity.
q.feedback: Movement along one PPF reallocates production between goods; economic growth requires an outward shift of the frontier.

key: No; it reallocates production on the same frontier

q.q: What shifts a PPF outward?
options: Moving from one point to another on the existing frontier
More resources, better technology, or improved productive capacity
Reallocating idle resources without changing productive capacity
Producing more of one good by giving up some of the other.
q.commonError: Confusing movement toward the frontier with a shift of productive capacity.
q.feedback: More resources, improved technology, or better institutions can expand productive capacity and shift the PPF outward.

key: More resources, better technology, or improved productive capacity

q.q: Why can opportunity cost rise along a bowed-out PPF?
options: Because the money price of the expanding good rises
Because the economy becomes less efficient as it moves along the frontier
Resources differ in suitability across uses
Because scarcity disappears for the good produced in larger quantities.
q.feedback: Specialized resources are less adaptable as production shifts toward one good, so each additional unit can require a larger sacrifice.

key: Resources differ in suitability across uses

q.q: Refer to the movie-ticket graph. Streaming subscriptions are substitutes for theater visits. With production conditions unchanged, which event could take equilibrium from A to B?
options: Streaming subscriptions become more expensive, increasing demand for movie tickets.
Streaming subscriptions become cheaper, increasing demand for movie tickets.
The movie-ticket price rises by itself, shifting demand for movie tickets right.
Theaters face lower operating costs, shifting supply of movie tickets right.
q.imageAlt: The movie-ticket market has price in dollars on the vertical axis and quantity in thousands on the horizontal axis. S0 is an upward-sloping supply curve. D0 and D1 are downward-sloping demand curves, with D1 lying to the right of D0 at each displayed price. Point A is the D0-S0 intersection at quantity 200 and price $10. Point B is the D1-S0 intersection at quantity 250 and price $12.
q.feedback: A lies on D0 and S0; B lies on D1 and S0. Demand has increased while supply stays fixed. A higher substitute price can cause that shift; the higher ticket price is a result, not a demand shifter.
q.graphDescription: The movie-ticket market has price in dollars on the vertical axis and quantity in thousands on the horizontal axis. S0 is an upward-sloping supply curve. D0 and D1 are downward-sloping demand curves, with D1 lying to the right of D0 at each displayed price. Point A is the D0-S0 intersection at quantity 200 and price $10. Point B is the D1-S0 intersection at quantity 250 and price $12.

key: Streaming subscriptions become more expensive, increasing demand for movie tickets.

q.q: Scarcity exists because:
options: Resources are limited while wants are unlimited
Market prices sometimes rise
Some goods are provided publicly
Production adjusts slowly to demand
q.feedback: Scarcity is the fundamental condition of limited resources relative to unlimited wants.

key: Resources are limited while wants are unlimited

q.q: A community has one available parcel and can build either an elementary school or a recreation complex this year, but not both. What is illustrated most directly?
options: Scarcity, because one limited parcel has competing valued uses
A shortage, because the community temporarily ran out of buildings
Equality, because both projects would serve the same residents
Abundance, because the parcel can support at least one project
q.commonError: Confusing scarcity with a temporary shortage or simple absence.
q.feedback: The parcel is limited relative to competing valued uses, so the community must choose.

key: Scarcity, because one limited parcel has competing valued uses

q.q: A school has more requests for tutoring than its staff can serve this week. Which fact makes tutoring time scarce?
options: Limited tutor-hours have several valued uses and cannot meet every request
The school has permanently run out of every kind of educational service
Families differ in income even if every tutoring request could be served
The school charges a price below the market-clearing price for tutoring
q.commonError: Confusing scarcity with poverty, high prices, or a temporary stockout.
q.feedback: Tutor-hours are limited relative to the competing requests for them.

key: Limited tutor-hours have several valued uses and cannot meet every request

q.q: A community center has one gym available tonight. Scheduling a youth league means canceling an adult exercise class. What does that choice show?
options: Using the fixed gym for one valued activity leaves less access for another
The community has permanently exhausted every recreation resource
The gym stops being scarce once managers publish the schedule
Both groups receive equal access because the choice is publicly announced
q.commonError: Ignoring the displaced use of a fixed resource.
q.feedback: Assigning the fixed gym to one activity displaces another valued use.

key: Using the fixed gym for one valued activity leaves less access for another

q.q: Efficiency is primarily about:
options: Giving everyone identical outcomes
Eliminating all tradeoffs
Getting the greatest total value from available resources.
Ensuring that no one ever loses from a change.
q.feedback: Efficiency concerns how much total value is produced from scarce resources.

key: Getting the greatest total value from available resources.

q.q: A town spends its entire emergency fund on flood barriers instead of fire equipment. The central issue is:
options: An elimination of scarcity through public spending.
A shortage created by a price floor.
A tradeoff among competing uses of limited funds.
A gain from comparative advantage.
q.feedback: The same limited fund cannot fully finance both priorities.

key: A tradeoff among competing uses of limited funds.

q.q: A policy raises total output but widens the income gap. Which pair best describes the possible outcome?
options: Lower efficiency and higher equality.
No change in either criterion.
Scarcity and shortage become identical.
Higher efficiency and lower equality.
q.commonError: Treating efficiency and equality as one measure.
q.feedback: Total output and distribution can move in opposite directions.

key: Higher efficiency and lower equality.

q.q: Why does a zero-price service still face scarcity?
options: It still uses limited labor, space, equipment, and user time
A zero price guarantees enough capacity for every possible user
Only services sold for money can require scarce productive inputs
Free access removes every competing use of the service resources
q.commonError: Equating free access with unlimited resources.
q.feedback: Money price and resource scarcity are different issues.

key: It still uses limited labor, space, equipment, and user time

q.q: A city allocates scarce shelter beds by medical vulnerability instead of willingness to pay. What changes?
options: The allocation rule changes, while the limited number of beds does not
The vulnerability rule immediately creates enough beds for every applicant
The beds stop being scarce because recipients do not bid a money price
The rule makes efficiency and equality identical measures of the outcome
q.commonError: Assuming rationing rules remove the constraint.
q.feedback: The rule determines recipients but does not create more beds.

key: The allocation rule changes, while the limited number of beds does not

q.q: A technology raises output and reduces input use, yet firms still choose among projects. Why?
options: Remaining capital, skilled labor, time, and wants still create choices
Higher productivity guarantees that every available project can be funded
Only government agencies continue to face tradeoffs after technology improves
Productivity growth changes scarcity into a temporary market shortage
q.feedback: Productivity relaxes constraints but does not remove all competing uses.

key: Remaining capital, skilled labor, time, and wants still create choices

q.q: Which evaluation is most complete for a policy that increases output but harms a vulnerable group?
options: Reject the policy solely because one group loses
Assume there is no tradeoff because output rises
Evaluate only the change in total output.
Assess both the total gains and the distribution of gains and losses.
q.commonError: Using only one criterion in a multi-dimensional judgment.
q.feedback: Economic evaluation should separate efficiency from distributional effects.

key: Assess both the total gains and the distribution of gains and losses.

q.q: A library extends weekend hours but must reduce weekday staffing. What does this demonstrate?
options: A market surplus
The end of scarcity
A tradeoff in the use of limited staff time.
A guarantee that everyone benefits equally.
q.commonError: Failing to transfer the tradeoff idea to a service setting.
q.feedback: More staffing in one period leaves less staffing available in another.

key: A tradeoff in the use of limited staff time.

q.q: A food bank receives more donations but still cannot meet every request. Which conclusion is best?
options: The food bank now faces only a temporary shortage
The additional resources reduce the constraint but do not eliminate scarcity.
No allocation rule is needed once donations increase
Scarcity disappears whenever supply increases.
q.commonError: Assuming more resources remove all unmet wants.
q.feedback: More resources can ease scarcity while competing needs remain.

key: The additional resources reduce the constraint but do not eliminate scarcity.

q.q: A wealthy city can afford more services than before, yet this year it must choose between expanding transit and replacing aging water lines. Why does scarcity remain?
options: Its budget, crews, and construction time are still limited relative to valued projects
Wealth makes every desired project physically impossible to complete
Higher income automatically creates a temporary market shortage
The city faces scarcity only if both projects charge a money price
q.commonError: Treating scarcity as a problem only for poor societies.
q.feedback: Greater wealth relaxes constraints, but limited resources still have competing uses.

key: Its budget, crews, and construction time are still limited relative to valued projects

q.q: A free campus workshop still involves scarcity because:
options: It still uses limited seats, instructor time, and student time
A zero price makes every required resource unlimited in supply
Only the workshop topic, rather than its inputs, can be scarce
Free admission creates a legal ceiling on every campus price
q.commonError: Assuming a zero money price means no scarce resources are used.
q.feedback: A zero admission price does not make space, labor, or time unlimited.

key: It still uses limited seats, instructor time, and student time

q.q: A coastal city can use a limited parcel for flood protection, affordable housing, or commercial development. Which analysis best respects scarcity?
options: Compare feasible parcel uses, incremental benefits and displaced uses, making the distribution of gains and losses explicit.
Rank uses by expected cash revenue, counting public benefits only when the city can charge users for them.
Rank uses by the number of beneficiaries, treating benefit size and displaced alternatives as secondary tie-breakers.
Divide the parcel equally among uses, treating equal area shares as sufficient evidence of equal benefit and efficiency.
q.commonError: Listing benefits without confronting mutually exclusive uses.
q.feedback: A scarce parcel requires a feasible comparison of valued uses, including nonmarket benefits and distribution. Cash revenue, beneficiary counts or equal acreage alone can miss opportunity costs and competing criteria.

key: Compare feasible parcel uses, incremental benefits and displaced uses, making the distribution of gains and losses explicit.

q.q: A policy expands total production, reduces pollution, and requires a small tax increase. Which statement is most defensible?
options: Several goals may improve, while taxes and inputs still have alternative uses
Several benefits mean the policy uses no scarce resources or public funds
Scarcity matters only when total production falls after the policy change
Any tax increase proves the policy reduces both efficiency and equality
q.commonError: Using a single outcome to judge a multi-dimensional policy.
q.feedback: A complete tradeoff analysis includes gains, resource use, financing, and distribution.

key: Several goals may improve, while taxes and inputs still have alternative uses

q.q: Which claim commits the clearest scarcity error?
options: Cheap copying means digital production and distribution use no scarce inputs
Higher productivity can relax a binding resource constraint without ending scarcity
A zero money price can still require scarce server capacity and user time
Allocation rules can change who receives access to a capacity-limited service
q.commonError: Equating low marginal copying cost with zero resource use.
q.feedback: Creation, servers, bandwidth, attention, and time remain scarce even when copying is inexpensive.

key: Cheap copying means digital production and distribution use no scarce inputs

q.q: During a drought, a city allocates water first to hospitals, then households, and lastly decorative landscaping. The policy most clearly reflects:
options: A market surplus caused by excess supply.
A guarantee that the allocation is both perfectly efficient and perfectly equal.
A scarcity-driven tradeoff among uses with different social priorities.
A claim that water has no opportunity cost.
q.commonError: Focusing on one beneficiary while ignoring displaced uses.
q.feedback: Drought limits the available water, so the city must rank competing uses.

key: A scarcity-driven tradeoff among uses with different social priorities.

q.q: A hospital has one intensive-care bed and two equally ill patients. Which conclusion follows from scarcity?
options: Any allocation rule leaves at least one valued use of the bed unmet
An equal lottery creates enough capacity to treat both patients fully
No money price means the intensive-care bed is not economically scarce
A medically fair rule removes the physical limit on available treatment
q.commonError: Assuming fairness can remove the underlying constraint.
q.feedback: Scarcity means not every valued use can be satisfied, regardless of the allocation rule.

key: Any allocation rule leaves at least one valued use of the bed unmet

q.q: A policy increases total output but leaves the lowest-income group worse off. Which judgment is most accurate?
options: It may improve total output while worsening the distribution of gains
It must improve both efficiency and equality because output increased
It eliminates scarcity because the economy can now produce more output
It cannot improve efficiency because at least one affected group loses
q.commonError: Assuming efficiency and equality are the same criterion.
q.feedback: Efficiency and distribution are separate dimensions, so they can move in opposite directions.

key: It may improve total output while worsening the distribution of gains

q.q: A government reserves scarce vaccine doses for people at highest medical risk rather than for those willing to pay most. The rule primarily changes:
options: How the scarce doses are allocated, not whether the doses are scarce.
The definition of scarcity itself
The number of vaccine doses physically available
Whether people still compete for the limited doses.
q.commonError: Believing an allocation rule removes scarcity.
q.feedback: Allocation rules determine who receives scarce goods; they do not erase the resource limit.

key: How the scarce doses are allocated, not whether the doses are scarce.

q.q: An economy can produce more clean energy only by using engineers and materials currently employed elsewhere. Which statement is strongest?
options: The project still trades off against other uses of engineers and materials
Government financing makes the engineers and materials no longer scarce
Large environmental benefits remove every resource cost from the project
Only privately financed energy projects compete for productive resources
q.commonError: Assuming socially valuable projects are costless in resource terms.
q.feedback: Benefits do not eliminate the need to redirect scarce labor and materials from other uses.

key: The project still trades off against other uses of engineers and materials

q.q: A reform raises average income and narrows the income gap but requires more administrative resources. Which statement is warranted?
options: Efficiency and equality cannot improve at the same time
Publicly funded administrative resources are not scarce
The reform may improve both efficiency and equality while still using scarce resources.
There is no tradeoff because average income and equality both improve.
q.commonError: Treating tradeoffs as proof that every objective must worsen.
q.feedback: Some policies can improve multiple outcomes, but resource use and implementation constraints still matter.

key: The reform may improve both efficiency and equality while still using scarce resources.

q.q: A region faces limited electricity during a heat wave. It can prioritize hospitals, households, or energy-intensive factories. Which response is the most complete economic analysis?
options: Compare marginal benefits and forgone uses across feasible allocations, then show the health, output and distribution tradeoffs.
Prioritize immediate health effects, treating displaced production and later income losses as outside the economic comparison.
Prioritize measured dollar output losses, treating unpriced household and hospital benefits as equal across allocations.
Give each group the same percentage reduction, treating proportional rationing as sufficient evidence of the best allocation.
q.commonError: Reducing a scarcity problem to a single efficiency or fairness rule.
q.feedback: Electricity has competing health, household and productive uses. Economic evaluation compares marginal gains and displaced benefits while stating distributional priorities; health-only, cash-only and proportional rules each impose a particular criterion.

key: Compare marginal benefits and forgone uses across feasible allocations, then show the health, output and distribution tradeoffs.

q.q: A government can increase disaster preparedness by diverting engineers from current infrastructure repairs. The preparedness program is highly valuable. What still follows?
options: Public projects do not compete for scarce inputs
Its value does not remove the tradeoff created by limited engineering capacity.
Only money, not skilled labor, can be scarce
A highly valuable program has no resource cost.
q.commonError: Treating high value as proof of no sacrifice.
q.feedback: Even high-value projects require scarce labor, time, and materials that could serve other purposes.

key: Its value does not remove the tradeoff created by limited engineering capacity.

q.q: An allocation rule maximizes total output but concentrates nearly all gains among a small group. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: The rule may be efficient by one criterion while raising serious equality concerns.
Scarcity prevents economists from discussing how gains are distributed
High total output automatically makes the allocation equal
Any unequal allocation must reduce total output.
q.commonError: Using efficiency as a complete moral judgment.
q.feedback: Efficiency and equality are distinct criteria and should be evaluated separately.

key: The rule may be efficient by one criterion while raising serious equality concerns.

q.q: A breakthrough makes desalination much cheaper, but coastal land, energy, pipelines, and environmental capacity remain limited. Which statement is best?
options: Cheaper desalination reduces water opportunity cost to zero, leaving land and energy limits relevant only for other industries.
Cheaper desalination relaxes one constraint, but land, energy and delivery limits can become the binding sources of tradeoffs.
Cheaper desalination makes physical water abundant, so any remaining scarcity must be explained entirely by monopoly pricing.
Cheaper desalination expands output proportionally at every stage, so pipelines and environmental limits become less binding automatically.
q.commonError: Assuming one technological improvement removes all constraints.
q.feedback: A productivity improvement changes which resource limits output. Complementary land, energy, networks and environmental capacity remain scarce and need not expand with desalination technology.

key: Cheaper desalination relaxes one constraint, but land, energy and delivery limits can become the binding sources of tradeoffs.

q.q: A city can fund either a new fire station or several neighborhood parks with the same budget. This illustrates:
options: A tradeoff created by competing uses of a limited city budget
An end to scarcity created by collecting and spending local taxes
A temporary shortage produced by fixing a public-service price
A specialization gain created by assigning each project to a district
q.commonError: Missing the tradeoff because both projects are socially valuable.
q.feedback: Limited funds force the city to choose among competing uses.

key: A tradeoff created by competing uses of a limited city budget

q.q: A student has three free hours and wants to study, work, exercise, and sleep more. The central economic problem is:
options: The student must choose the option with the highest money return.
The student faces no scarcity because time has no price.
The student cannot fully satisfy all competing uses of time.
Only the work option has a cost.
q.commonError: Ignoring time as a scarce resource.
q.feedback: Time is scarce, so not every desired activity can be expanded at once.

key: The student cannot fully satisfy all competing uses of time.

q.q: Which statement best distinguishes efficiency from equality?
options: Efficiency concerns total value; equality concerns its distribution
Efficiency requires equal shares; equality requires maximum output
Efficiency and equality describe the same resource-allocation goal
Efficiency concerns prices; equality concerns physical production
q.commonError: Treating efficiency and equality as synonyms.
q.feedback: Efficiency focuses on the size of the economic pie; equality focuses on its distribution.

key: Efficiency concerns total value; equality concerns its distribution

q.q: A new technology doubles crop yields. What happens to scarcity?
options: Scarcity disappears because higher crop output satisfies every want
Scarcity becomes a shortage because technology changes only prices
The crop constraint eases, but land, time, and other wants remain
The technology removes the need to choose among all production uses
q.feedback: Greater productivity relaxes constraints but does not remove limited resources or competing wants.

key: The crop constraint eases, but land, time, and other wants remain

q.q: After a storm, a store cannot meet customers' bottled-water purchases at its posted price. A delivery then provides enough water to meet those purchases. Producing and delivering the water still uses materials and truck time that could serve other purposes. What changed, and what remains?
options: The stockout ended; using materials and truck time still involves scarcity.
Both stockout and scarcity ended because buyers can obtain water again.
Scarcity ended; the stockout remains because producing water still uses resources.
Neither condition ended because the store still has a finite water inventory.
q.commonError: Confusing a market shortage with the universal condition of scarcity.
q.feedback: The delivery resolves this store's stockout at the posted price. Scarcity remains because materials and truck time have alternative uses and cannot satisfy every want. Duration is not the defining difference, and finite inventory alone does not imply unmet purchases at the prevailing price.

key: The stockout ended; using materials and truck time still involves scarcity.

q.q: Scarcity exists when:
options: A seller earns a profit
Limited resources cannot satisfy every competing want.
A store temporarily runs out of one item
A price is legally fixed.
q.commonError: Confusing scarcity with shortage or regulation.
q.feedback: Scarcity is the general condition of limited resources relative to wants.

key: Limited resources cannot satisfy every competing want.

q.q: Which statement describes efficiency rather than equality?
options: Resources are arranged to generate the greatest total value
Resources are divided into identical shares for every person
Income differences are removed regardless of total production
Every affected group receives the same gain from the policy
q.commonError: Confusing production efficiency with distributional equality.
q.feedback: Efficiency focuses on total value from resources.

key: Resources are arranged to generate the greatest total value

q.q: A tradeoff occurs because:
options: Using a limited resource one way restricts another valued use
Every choice requires an explicit payment made with money
Only public agencies must choose among competing resource uses
A high-benefit choice stops using scarce inputs and worker time
q.commonError: Ignoring nonmoney resources and alternative uses.
q.feedback: Tradeoffs arise whenever scarce resources have competing uses.

key: Using a limited resource one way restricts another valued use

q.q: A classroom has 24 seats and 31 students who want to attend. Which statement identifies the scarce resource?
options: The 24 available classroom seats
The seven students without seats
The tuition paid by every student
The number of courses in the catalog
q.commonError: Naming unmet wants rather than the resource that constrains them.
q.feedback: Seats are the limited resource relative to enrollment demand.

key: The 24 available classroom seats

q.q: A county gives more reservoir water to farms during planting season, leaving less for lawn irrigation and some industrial uses. What is the best interpretation?
options: A limited resource is being shifted among competing users
The county has eliminated scarcity by choosing agriculture
Only users paying the highest price face a water tradeoff
The reduced uses prove the reservoir has a temporary leak
q.commonError: Treating a priority decision as elimination of the resource constraint.
q.feedback: Prioritizing farms reallocates water and reduces what remains for other users.

key: A limited resource is being shifted among competing users

q.q: A space agency has one launch window for a weather satellite or a communications satellite. Both have large benefits. Which claim is least defensible?
options: Large benefits allow both satellites to use the same launch window
Choosing either mission forgoes the other mission’s near-term benefits
The launch window remains scarce even if the agency receives more money
A complete choice compares benefits, timing, and affected users
q.commonError: Assuming positive benefits make mutually exclusive projects jointly feasible.
q.feedback: Value does not allow two missions to occupy one fixed launch window.

key: Large benefits allow both satellites to use the same launch window

q.q: A campus uses its only open parcel for a laboratory instead of student housing. Scarcity creates a tradeoff; which concept names the next-best alternative forgone?
options: Opportunity cost
Market equilibrium
Price elasticity
Monetary neutrality
q.commonError: Recognizing a tradeoff without connecting it to the next-best forgone alternative.
q.feedback: Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative given up when scarcity forces a choice.

key: Opportunity cost

q.q: A factory divides fixed labor and machine time between medical devices and water filters. Which model displays the feasible production combinations created by this scarcity?
options: A production possibilities frontier
A consumer price index
A money-demand curve
A Phillips curve
q.commonError: Recognizing limited resources without connecting them to feasible production combinations.
q.feedback: A PPF represents the combinations possible when scarce productive resources have competing uses.

key: A production possibilities frontier

q.q: A hospital has eight nurse-hours available for either a vaccination clinic or follow-up calls. What is the scarce resource?
options: The eight available nurse-hours
The number of patients who value care
The absence of a money price for calls
The hospital building in every future period
q.commonError: Naming a want or a price instead of the binding resource constraint.
q.feedback: The limited nurse-hours cannot be used fully for both services.

key: The eight available nurse-hours

q.q: A family uses its monthly budget to replace a broken refrigerator, leaving less for a planned vacation. What is the tradeoff?
options: Refrigerator spending leaves less budget for the vacation
The refrigerator creates unlimited future income
The vacation becomes a temporary market shortage
The family no longer faces scarcity after buying an appliance
q.commonError: Recognizing the purchase but not the displaced use of the budget.
q.feedback: Using the fixed budget for one purpose reduces what remains for another.

key: Refrigerator spending leaves less budget for the vacation

q.q: A bakery can use its oven this hour for bread or pastries, but there is not enough oven time for both batches. What choice is forced by scarcity?
options: How to allocate the limited oven time
How to eliminate every customer want
How to create a legal price ceiling
How to make flour an unlimited resource
q.commonError: Overlooking production time as the constrained resource.
q.feedback: Limited oven time with competing uses requires an allocation choice.

key: How to allocate the limited oven time

q.q: A reservoir currently contains enough water for all essential uses, but not for every lawn, pool, factory, and farm request. Which conclusion is correct?
options: Water is scarce because not every valued use can be satisfied
Water is abundant because essential uses can be satisfied
A shortage exists only because the reservoir charges too much
Scarcity ends whenever some users receive the resource
q.commonError: Treating partial adequacy as proof that a resource is nonscarce.
q.feedback: Scarcity remains when the available amount cannot satisfy every competing use.

key: Water is scarce because not every valued use can be satisfied

q.q: After a flood, a county can use its emergency fund for temporary housing or immediate levee repairs. Housing aids displaced families now; repairs reduce future risk. What must an economic analysis include?
options: Current beneficiaries, future risk reduction, and the use forgone under either choice
Only the number of residents receiving immediate housing assistance
Only the engineering estimate for the levee repair project
A claim that emergency spending makes the county budget unlimited
q.commonError: Evaluating one time horizon while ignoring the competing use and affected groups.
q.feedback: Scarcity requires comparing both uses, their timing, and who gains or loses.

key: Current beneficiaries, future risk reduction, and the use forgone under either choice

q.q: Automation reduces the labor needed in a warehouse, but expansion still requires scarce electricity, loading space, and computing capacity. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: Automation changes the constraint mix rather than abolishing scarcity
Automation abolishes scarcity because fewer workers are required
The remaining limits are shortages caused only by incorrect prices
Every expansion becomes feasible once one input requirement falls
q.commonError: Treating a productivity gain as the elimination of all production choices.
q.feedback: Reducing one input requirement can leave other resources as binding constraints.

key: Automation changes the constraint mix rather than abolishing scarcity

q.q: A low-income household and a wealthy household both have 24 hours in a day, but very different financial options. Which statement correctly distinguishes poverty from scarcity?
options: Poverty concerns limited material means; both households still face scarce time
Only the low-income household faces scarcity because wealth removes all constraints
Both households are poor because neither can create more hours in a day
Scarcity describes temporary stockouts, while poverty describes every tradeoff
q.commonError: Equating scarcity with poverty and overlooking universal nonmoney constraints.
q.feedback: Poverty and scarcity are different: scarcity persists across income levels.

key: Poverty concerns limited material means; both households still face scarce time

q.q: A delivery disruption leaves a hospital temporarily short of oxygen cylinders, while its limited budget also restricts how many backup systems it can maintain. Which statement is accurate?
options: The disruption is a shortage; the budget tradeoff reflects ongoing scarcity
Both conditions are temporary shortages because money is involved
Both conditions are scarcity only if oxygen receives a market price
The backup budget eliminates scarcity once deliveries resume
q.commonError: Collapsing a temporary supply disruption and a persistent resource constraint.
q.feedback: The disruption leaves fewer cylinders available than the hospital needs under current conditions. The budget constraint requires choices among backup systems and other uses of funds, illustrating scarcity. This particular disruption is temporary; shortages need not be temporary, and scarcity is not limited to the long run.

key: The disruption is a shortage; the budget tradeoff reflects ongoing scarcity

q.q: Following an earthquake, a hospital has one surgical team for trauma cases, routine emergencies, and patients already scheduled. Which policy best acknowledges scarcity without pretending one criterion settles the decision?
options: Compare expected health gains, urgency and displaced treatment under feasible schedules, stating how the priority rule weights them.
Treat trauma first in every case, using the emergency label as sufficient evidence that postponed care has lower marginal value.
Preserve scheduled order in every case, using earlier commitments as sufficient evidence that urgent arrivals have lower priority.
Allocate equal team time to each group, using equal shares as sufficient evidence of both fair treatment and greatest health gain.
q.commonError: Using one allocation criterion while ignoring displaced care and distribution.
q.feedback: The surgical team has competing uses with differences in urgency, benefits and forgone care. No label or equal-time rule settles every dimension without evaluating the feasible alternatives.

key: Compare expected health gains, urgency and displaced treatment under feasible schedules, stating how the priority rule weights them.

q.q: A city can zone a waterfront parcel for housing, a flood barrier, or a public park. A developer claims housing demand makes the other uses economically irrelevant. What is the strongest response?
options: High housing value does not erase the flood and recreation benefits forgone
Market demand makes the parcel physically available for all three uses
Public benefits matter only when users pay an admission price
Choosing housing proves the other uses were not valued by anyone
q.commonError: Treating the chosen use as proof that forgone uses have no value.
q.feedback: Scarcity makes the benefits of mutually exclusive uses economically relevant.

key: High housing value does not erase the flood and recreation benefits forgone

q.q: A laboratory has idle testing machines but fully occupied specialist staff. It buys more machines, then shifts specialists from quality checks to testing. Tests rise and errors rise. What best explains the result?
options: The equipment purchase left the staff constraint; reallocation increased tests at a quality cost
More tests prove the original equipment constraint was the only limit
Idle machines mean the extra tests had no opportunity cost
The rise in errors shows there was no expansion in testing
q.commonError: Assuming expansion of one input removes complementary-input constraints.
q.feedback: Specialist time remained scarce. Reassigning it raised testing by sacrificing quality checks, so the extra machines alone did not remove the tradeoff.

key: The equipment purchase left the staff constraint; reallocation increased tests at a quality cost

q.q: A factory that builds both emergency generators and defense equipment receives a fixed allocation of skilled machinist-hours. Why does a larger government budget not automatically remove the production tradeoff this quarter?
options: Money cannot instantly create the specialized labor and machine time required
Government purchases never use resources that have alternative civilian uses
A larger budget converts every physical constraint into an accounting entry
Defense production eliminates scarcity whenever national security is valuable
q.commonError: Treating additional financing as immediate creation of specialized capacity.
q.feedback: Nominal funding cannot instantly expand every real resource needed for production.

key: Money cannot instantly create the specialized labor and machine time required

q.q: During a drought, a river authority must allocate water among cities, farms, and minimum ecosystem flows. Which statement avoids both an efficiency-only and a fairness-only mistake?
options: Compare total and ecological benefits while showing how each feasible rule distributes losses among users.
Maximize measured market output while counting ecosystem flows only when the authority can collect a fee.
Equalize percentage cuts across users while treating equal reductions as proof of equal welfare losses.
Preserve historical allocations while treating prior entitlements as evidence of the highest current marginal benefits.
q.commonError: Using efficiency or equality as a complete allocation rule without examining the other.
q.feedback: Benefits, ecosystem effects and distribution must be distinguished. Prices, proportional reductions and historical shares can each omit relevant marginal values or impose a distributional rule.

key: Compare total and ecological benefits while showing how each feasible rule distributes losses among users.

q.q: A university can admit more students by enlarging lectures, but laboratory space and advising time remain fixed. What does the enrollment expansion demonstrate?
options: Relaxing one capacity limit can intensify other educational tradeoffs
Larger lectures eliminate scarcity throughout the university
Advising time becomes abundant when tuition revenue increases
Laboratory capacity matters only for programs charging separate fees
q.commonError: Ignoring constraints that become more important after another constraint relaxes.
q.feedback: The binding limit can move from lecture seats to labs or advising.

key: Relaxing one capacity limit can intensify other educational tradeoffs

q.q: A region has surplus generation but a fully used transmission line. A subsidy expands generation again. Delivered power stays flat. Which proposal addresses the observed limit without claiming scarcity disappears?
options: Expand transmission, then reassess other constrained resources and forgone uses
Expand generation further because surplus generation measures delivered capacity
Declare electricity costless because some generated power goes unused
Treat unchanged deliveries as proof that users place no value on power
q.commonError: Treating abundant output at one stage as abundance throughout a system.
q.feedback: Transmission is the observed bottleneck. Relaxing it may expand deliveries, but construction resources and other constraints still have alternative uses.

key: Expand transmission, then reassess other constrained resources and forgone uses

q.q: A public agency reassigns cybersecurity analysts to clear a benefits-processing backlog. Which consequence must be included even if the backlog is urgent?
options: The forgone security monitoring performed by the same scarce analysts
The analysts become nonscarce because both assignments serve the public
The backlog creates more analyst-hours by increasing social need
Only the agency payroll, not analyst time, has an alternative use
q.commonError: Letting urgency obscure the alternative output of a fixed workforce.
q.feedback: Urgency can affect priorities but does not remove the forgone use of analyst time.

key: The forgone security monitoring performed by the same scarce analysts

q.q: A government funds both climate adaptation and transit by postponing courthouse maintenance. Officials call the package “tradeoff-free” because two programs expand. What is wrong?
options: The postponed maintenance is a displaced use of scarce public resources
Two expanding programs guarantee that no group bears a cost
Deferred maintenance is not a cost until a courthouse closes
Public borrowing makes labor and materials immediately unlimited
q.commonError: Ignoring a less visible displaced use when multiple visible goals improve.
q.feedback: A package can advance several goals while shifting costs to another use or time.

key: The postponed maintenance is a displaced use of scarce public resources

q.q: Automation frees assembly hours. Managers assign them to inspection, reducing defects, but product development gets no extra staff. Which counterfactual is needed to evaluate the allocation?
options: What those same hours would have achieved in development relative to the inspection gain
What the robot cost before the hours were freed, counted as the entire current tradeoff
The sum of benefits from inspection and development as if both received the hours
Whether inspection has a cash price rather than a nonmonetary benefit
q.commonError: Assuming labor-saving technology eliminates choice over the released resources.
q.feedback: The technology relaxes one constraint; it does not determine the best use of freed labor. Compare inspection with the feasible development alternative.

key: What those same hours would have achieved in development relative to the inspection gain

q.q: A wealthy country can afford either a high-speed rail network or a major hospital modernization program sooner, but construction crews and materials cannot complete both on the same schedule. What does this show?
options: Wealth expands options without eliminating real resource constraints
Wealth eliminates scarcity whenever both projects have positive benefits
Only lower-income countries face tradeoffs involving public infrastructure
The conflict is a temporary shortage caused entirely by incorrect prices
q.commonError: Treating national wealth as freedom from physical and time constraints.
q.feedback: Wealth increases capacity, but real inputs and time remain limited.

key: Wealth expands options without eliminating real resource constraints

q.q: A transit authority postpones track maintenance to accelerate a network extension. The extension raises capacity next year but increases breakdown risk now. Which analysis best captures the dynamic tradeoff?
options: Compare current reliability losses with future capacity gains and their distribution
Count only future riders because maintenance creates no new visible service
Treat postponed work as costless until a breakdown actually occurs
Assume future capacity removes the present scarcity of repair crews
q.commonError: Ignoring intertemporal costs because their effects are delayed or uncertain.
q.feedback: Scarcity links present resource use to future benefits and risks.

key: Compare current reliability losses with future capacity gains and their distribution

q.q: Route A delivers more meals but skips isolated households. Route B reaches every district but delivers fewer meals. An official calls A superior because total deliveries are higher. What evidence and judgment are still needed?
options: Who loses access, and how that loss is weighed against additional deliveries
Only more precise meal totals, because totals establish distributional fairness
Only whether either route has positive benefits, because that settles the ranking
Proof that isolated households are costly, which makes their access irrelevant
q.commonError: Using the total output result as a complete judgment about distribution.
q.feedback: A higher total establishes a production advantage under that metric. Ranking the routes also requires the distribution of access and an explicit weight on it.

key: Who loses access, and how that loss is weighed against additional deliveries

q.q: A mineral discovery expands deposits, but refining staff are fully occupied. Exporting unrefined ore can fund training; keeping it for later refining forgoes that revenue. Which statement follows?
options: More deposits expand options, while refining and the timing of resource use still involve tradeoffs
The discovery removes scarcity because the mineral stock increased
Keeping the ore has no cost because it remains physically available
Export revenue proves immediate export is best under every future-use objective
q.commonError: Assuming discovery of one resource makes the complete production system unconstrained.
q.feedback: The deposit gain does not eliminate the refining constraint. Holding ore preserves a future option but forgoes a feasible current use, including financing training.

key: More deposits expand options, while refining and the timing of resource use still involve tradeoffs

q.q: A state has one construction workforce for unsafe bridges, aging schools, and storm-water upgrades. Which proposal most clearly hides the tradeoff?
options: Complete all projects immediately because each has benefits greater than zero
Rank projects by expected benefits, urgency, and displaced work
Phase projects as crews and materials become available
State which communities wait under each feasible schedule
q.commonError: Treating positive benefits as proof that mutually competing projects are jointly feasible.
q.feedback: Positive benefits do not create the crews and materials required to do everything at once.

key: Complete all projects immediately because each has benefits greater than zero

q.q: A fishery can allow a larger catch this season or preserve more breeding stock for future seasons. Which feature makes this a scarcity problem rather than only a biological fact?
