Wf remains $34 and Ww $26, with employment 52; each side still bears $4 relative to the untaxed $30 wage.
Wf rises to $38 and Ww stays $30, with employment 44; firms bear all tax whenever labor demand slopes down.
q.feedback: The wedge is Wf-Ww=8 regardless of remitter. Solve 120-2(Ww+8)=2Ww: Ww=26, Wf=34 and L=52. Without tax W=30. Employer and worker burdens are 4 each, unchanged by the statutory relabeling.

key: Wf remains $34 and Ww $26, with employment 52; each side still bears $4 relative to the untaxed $30 wage.

q.q: Tax incidence means:
options: How the burden of a tax is divided between buyers and sellers
The legal maximum price
The number of firms in a market
The quantity demanded at every price
q.feedback: Tax incidence is about who bears the burden of the tax, not just who sends the payment.

key: How the burden of a tax is divided between buyers and sellers

q.q: The side of the market that is less elastic usually bears:
options: More of the tax burden
None of the tax burden
Less of the tax burden because it changes behavior less.
All of the producer surplus
q.feedback: The less elastic side bears more of the tax burden because it responds less to price changes.

key: More of the tax burden

q.q: If demand is less elastic than supply, who bears more of a tax?
options: Buyers
Sellers
Neither side
Only the government
q.feedback: Buyers bear more because demand is less elastic than supply.

key: Buyers

q.q: If supply is less elastic than demand, who bears more of a tax?
options: Sellers
Buyers
Neither side
Whichever side is legally required to remit the tax.
q.feedback: Sellers bear more because supply is less elastic than demand.

key: Sellers

q.q: A policy analyst says a tax legally placed on sellers will be paid entirely by sellers. What is wrong with this claim?
options: Legal assignment does not determine economic incidence
Sellers always pass the entire tax to buyers
Buyers always avoid taxes completely
A seller tax is the same as a price floor
q.feedback: Economic tax burden depends on market responses and elasticities, not only on who legally sends payment.

key: Legal assignment does not determine economic incidence

q.q: A $12 tax causes buyers to pay $7 more and sellers to receive $5 less. Demand is likely less elastic than supply because:
options: Buyers bear more of the tax burden
Sellers bear more of the tax burden
The legal tax must have been placed on buyers
The tax increased quantity sold
q.feedback: The less elastic side bears more of the tax burden. Buyers bear $7, so demand is likely less elastic.

key: Buyers bear more of the tax burden

q.q: A tax is imposed on a good with highly inelastic demand and elastic supply. Which policy outcome is most likely?
options: Buyers bear most of the burden and quantity falls relatively little
Sellers bear most of the burden and quantity falls dramatically
Buyers bear no burden because sellers legally pay
The tax creates a surplus equal to the tax
q.feedback: Inelastic demand means buyers bear more and reduce quantity less in response to the tax.

key: Buyers bear most of the burden and quantity falls relatively little

q.q: A tax is imposed on a good with elastic demand and highly inelastic supply. Which result is most likely?
options: Sellers bear most of the burden
Buyers bear most of the burden
Demand increases because the tax is high
The legal assignment alone determines burden
q.feedback: The less elastic side bears more. If supply is highly inelastic, sellers bear most of the tax.

key: Sellers bear most of the burden

q.q: Before a tax, price is $40 and 500 units trade. Afterward buyers pay $46, sellers keep $34, and 420 units trade. What is the buyers’ tax burden on the units still traded, as distinct from the entire change in consumer surplus?
q.feedback: The per-unit buyer burden is $46 − $40 = $6. On 420 continuing units, its rectangle is $2,520. The full CS change also includes lost gains from the 80 missing trades; the rectangle alone does not measure that entire loss.

q.q: A market moves from $40 and 500 units before a tax to a buyer price of $46, seller receipt of $34, and 420 units afterward. What is the seller-burden rectangle on units still traded, excluding the surplus lost on missing trades?
q.feedback: The seller loses $40 − $34 = $6 per continuing unit, so the rectangle is $6 × 420 = $2,520. Using 500 applies the burden to trades that no longer occur. The $12 wedge times 420 is total revenue, not the seller share alone.

q.q: A tax is imposed on sellers. Before the tax, price is $20 and quantity is 300. After the tax, buyers pay $24, sellers receive $18, and quantity is 240. Which statement is correct?
options: Tax wedge: $6; buyer burden: $4 per unit; seller burden: $2 per unit; quantity falls by 60 units.
Tax wedge: $6; buyer burden: $2 per unit; seller burden: $4 per unit; quantity falls by 60 units.
Tax wedge: $6; buyer burden: $0 per unit; seller burden: $6 per unit; quantity falls by 60 units.
Tax wedge: $6; buyer burden: $4 per unit; seller burden: $2 per unit; quantity falls by 240 units.
q.feedback: The tax wedge is $24 - $18 = $6 per unit. Relative to the original $20 price, buyers bear $24 - $20 = $4 per unit and sellers bear $20 - $18 = $2 per unit; these burdens sum to $6. Quantity falls by 300 - 240 = 60 units. The 240 units are the new quantity, not the decrease. Requiring sellers to remit the tax does not make them bear its entire economic burden.

key: Tax wedge: $6; buyer burden: $4 per unit; seller burden: $2 per unit; quantity falls by 60 units.

q.q: A student says, 'The price rose after the tax, so buyers paid the entire tax.' What is the flaw?
options: Buyers bear only the increase above the old equilibrium price.
Any price increase means buyers pay everything
Sellers cannot bear taxes if buyers pay more
Tax incidence is unrelated to prices
q.feedback: Buyers bear the part of the tax reflected in the higher price they pay; sellers bear the part reflected in the lower price they receive.

key: Buyers bear only the increase above the old equilibrium price.

q.q: A tax on cigarettes causes only a small drop in smoking even though buyers face a noticeably higher price. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Demand is relatively inelastic
Demand is perfectly elastic
Supply increased after the tax
The tax created a price floor
q.feedback: If quantity falls only a little after a tax, demand is likely relatively inelastic.

key: Demand is relatively inelastic

q.q: A $6 tax is imposed. Before the tax, buyers paid $20. After the tax, buyers pay $24 and sellers receive $18. How much of the tax burden falls on buyers and sellers?
options: Buyers bear $4 and sellers bear $2
Buyers bear $2 and sellers bear $4
Buyers bear all $6 and sellers bear $0
Buyers bear $24 and sellers bear $18
q.feedback: Buyers now pay $4 more than before. Sellers receive $2 less than before. The $6 tax burden is split $4 on buyers and $2 on sellers.

key: Buyers bear $4 and sellers bear $2

q.q: Demand is much less elastic than supply. A tax is imposed on the good. Who bears more of the tax burden, and why?
options: Buyers bear more because they are less able to reduce quantity demanded
Sellers bear more because supply is more elastic
Buyers and sellers must split the burden equally
Sellers bear more because buyers pay the tax through the market price
q.feedback: The less elastic side bears more of the tax because it is less able to change behavior in response to the tax.

key: Buyers bear more because they are less able to reduce quantity demanded

q.q: Supply is much less elastic than demand. A tax is imposed. What is the likely result?
options: Sellers bear more of the burden because quantity supplied is less responsive
Buyers bear more of the burden because demand is more elastic
The burden must be equal because the tax wedge is fixed
The side required to remit the tax bears more because statutory payment determines the economic burden
q.feedback: The less elastic side bears more of the tax. If supply is less elastic than demand, sellers bear more of the burden.

key: Sellers bear more of the burden because quantity supplied is less responsive

q.q: A $5 tax causes buyers to pay $3 more than before and sellers to receive $2 less than before. How is the burden split?
options: Buyers bear $3 and sellers bear $2
Buyers bear $2 and sellers bear $3
Sellers bear all $5
Buyers bear all $5
q.feedback: The buyer burden is the price increase paid by buyers. The seller burden is the price decrease received by sellers.

key: Buyers bear $3 and sellers bear $2

q.q: Before a tax, buyers pay $30 and sellers receive $30. After a tax, buyers pay $34 and sellers receive $27. Who bears more of the burden?
options: Buyers
Sellers
They split it equally
No one bears any burden
q.feedback: Buyers pay $4 more, while sellers receive $3 less. Buyers bear more of the burden.

key: Buyers

q.q: A tax is legally imposed on sellers, but buyers end up paying most of the burden. What does this show?
options: Economic incidence does not depend only on legal assignment
Sellers never pay taxes
Buyers must have become the statutory taxpayers when the market price changed.
The tax must be a price ceiling
q.feedback: Who legally pays the tax does not determine who bears the economic burden.

key: Economic incidence does not depend only on legal assignment

q.q: If demand is less elastic than supply, why do buyers bear more of a tax?
options: Buyers are less able to reduce quantity demanded when price rises
Buyers legally pay all taxes
Sellers are less able to adjust quantity supplied
Demand shifts right after the tax
q.feedback: The less elastic side adjusts less, so it bears more of the tax burden.

key: Buyers are less able to reduce quantity demanded when price rises

q.q: If supply is perfectly inelastic and demand is elastic, who bears the tax burden?
options: Sellers bear all of it.
Buyers bear all of it
No one bears it
The government bears it because supply is vertical
q.feedback: With perfectly inelastic supply, quantity supplied cannot respond to the tax. Sellers therefore bear the entire tax burden through a lower net price received.

key: Sellers bear all of it.

q.q: Refer to the tax incidence graph. What is the buyers’ tax burden on the units still traded, excluding surplus lost on missing trades?
q.feedback: The per-unit buyer burden is $3 relative to the original $15 price. Multiplying by 80 continuing units gives $240. The full welfare loss for that side also includes surplus lost on trades that no longer occur.

q.q: Refer to the tax incidence graph. What is the seller-burden rectangle on the units still traded, excluding surplus lost on missing trades?
q.feedback: The per-unit seller burden is $3 relative to the original $15 price. Multiplying by 80 continuing units gives $240. The full welfare loss for that side also includes surplus lost on trades that no longer occur.

q.q: Refer to the tax incidence graph. What is the combined buyer- and seller-burden rectangle on units still traded, which becomes government revenue?
q.feedback: The $6 wedge applies to 80 continuing trades, so the rectangle is $480. This is the combined per-unit incidence times taxed quantity. Lost gains from the missing trades are additional welfare loss and are not government revenue.

q.q: Refer to the tax incidence graph. For the units still purchased after the tax, what is the total extra payment by buyers relative to paying the original price for those same units? This question excludes the welfare effect of purchases forgone.
options: $300: $3 extra on the original 100 units.
$480: the full $6 tax on the remaining 80 units.
$240: $3 extra on the remaining 80 units.
$540: the change in sellers’ total receipts.
q.feedback: The buyer price rises from $15 to $18 and 80 units are purchased after tax. For these continuing purchases, the extra payment is ($18 - $15) x 80 = $240. Using all 100 original units includes purchases no longer made; using $6 assigns the seller burden to buyers.

key: $240: $3 extra on the remaining 80 units.

q.q: Refer to the tax incidence graph. A seller group divides the fall in total net-of-tax sales receipts by the 80 units still sold and calls the result its tax burden per continuing unit. Why is that calculation misleading?
options: The $540 receipt decline includes fewer units sold; the price burden on each continuing unit is $3.
The $540 receipt decline is entirely a price effect; the burden on each continuing unit is $6.75.
The $240 receipt decline includes fewer units sold; the price burden on each continuing unit is $6.
The $300 receipt decline is entirely a quantity effect; the price burden on each continuing unit is $0.
q.feedback: Receipts fall from $15 x 100 = $1,500 to $12 x 80 = $960, a $540 decline. This combines $300 from 20 fewer units valued at the old price and $240 from receiving $3 less on each of 80 continuing sales. The per-unit seller tax burden is $15 - $12 = $3; gross receipts are not a measure of producer surplus.

key: The $540 receipt decline includes fewer units sold; the price burden on each continuing unit is $3.

q.q: Refer to the tax graph. Using the original equilibrium as the benchmark, how is the per-unit tax burden divided?
options: Buyers bear $3 and sellers $3, so each bears half
Buyers bear $6 and sellers $0, because the buyer price is highest
Buyers bear $0 and sellers $6, because the shifted curve is supply
Buyers bear $18 and sellers $12, equal to the two after-tax prices
q.feedback: The original price is $15. Buyers now pay $18, an increase of $3, while sellers keep $12, a decrease of $3. These burdens sum to the $6 wedge. Neither legal remittance nor the full price level measures incidence.

key: Buyers bear $3 and sellers $3, so each bears half

q.q: Refer to the tax graph. If the same per-unit tax is collected from buyers instead of sellers, with demand and supply unchanged, which outcome follows?
options: Buyers still pay $18 in total, sellers keep $12, and 80 units trade
Buyers pay $21 in total, sellers keep $15, and 80 units trade
Buyers pay $18 in total, sellers keep $18, and 100 units trade
Buyers pay $15 in total, sellers keep $9, and 100 units trade
q.feedback: The graph establishes a $6 wedge at quantity 80, with total buyer payment $18 and net seller receipt $12. Changing the remitter preserves this wedge and equilibrium. Under buyer remittance, buyers pay sellers $12 and government $6; that does not make the economic buyer burden $6.

key: Buyers still pay $18 in total, sellers keep $12, and 80 units trade

q.q: Refer to the tax graph. A seller argues that its legal duty to remit the tax means it bears the entire revenue rectangle. What do the price changes and continuing quantity show?
options: Each side bears $3 per unit and $240 of the $480 rectangle
Sellers bear $6 per unit and all $480 of the rectangle
Each side bears $3 per unit and $300 of the $600 rectangle
Buyers bear $6 per unit and all $480 of the rectangle
q.feedback: Relative to $15, buyers pay $3 more and sellers receive $3 less. At 80 units, each incidence rectangle is $240, together equaling $480 of revenue. Remitting the money is different from bearing the price burden; these rectangles exclude gains lost on missing trades.

key: Each side bears $3 per unit and $240 of the $480 rectangle

q.q: A $4 tax is placed on concert tickets. Buyers pay $2.50 more than before, sellers receive $1.50 less than before, and fewer tickets are sold. Which statement is strongest?
options: The burden is shared, quantity falls, and the side less able to adjust bears more
The burden falls only on sellers because the legal tax is charged to sellers
The burden falls only on buyers because the buyer price increased
The burden disappears because tax revenue offsets the lower quantity sold
q.feedback: Legal responsibility for the tax does not determine economic burden. The wedge is shared and quantity falls.

key: The burden is shared, quantity falls, and the side less able to adjust bears more

q.q: A market has an $8 tax, a total buyer price of $26 and a net seller receipt of $18. Buyers bear 75% of the per-unit burden. What was the untaxed price, and which side is less price responsive over this change?
options: $20; buyers
$24; sellers
$20; sellers
$24; buyers
q.feedback: Buyer burden is 0.75 × $8 = $6, so the old price was $26 − $6 = $20. Sellers bear the remaining $2, since $20 − $18 = $2. Under the standard tax-incidence comparison, the side bearing more of the wedge is less price responsive.

key: $20; buyers

q.q: A seller-side tax shifts the supply curve upward. Which statement best explains why buyers still pay part of the tax?
options: Elasticities determine how the tax is split.
Buyers voluntarily pay taxes for sellers
The demand curve shifts right by the tax amount
The tax creates a price ceiling
q.feedback: Legal remittance does not determine economic burden. Prices adjust based on supply and demand elasticities.

key: Elasticities determine how the tax is split.

q.q: A tax is placed on buyers instead of sellers. In a standard supply-demand model, why is the final outcome similar to an equal seller tax?
options: Both taxes create the same buyer–seller price wedge.
Only buyer taxes reduce quantity
Only seller taxes raise prices
The tax disappears if buyers legally pay it
q.feedback: A buyer tax or seller tax of the same size creates the same wedge and reduces quantity similarly.

key: Both taxes create the same buyer–seller price wedge.

q.q: In a competitive cigarette market, demand is less price-elastic than supply. A small per-unit tax is collected from sellers. With other market conditions unchanged, which conclusion about the economic burden follows?
options: Buyers bear more because demand is less price-responsive than supply.
Sellers bear more because the government collects the tax from sellers.
Each side bears half because both participate in the taxed transactions.
Buyers bear the entire tax because demand is less elastic than supply.
q.commonError: Assigning economic tax burden by statutory collection rather than relative elasticity.
q.feedback: Buyers bear the larger share because demand is less elastic than supply: buyers adjust quantity less readily when prices change. Collecting the tax from sellers does not determine economic incidence. The stated comparison does not imply that buyers bear the entire tax.

key: Buyers bear more because demand is less price-responsive than supply.

q.q: In a competitive luxury-boat rental market, demand is more price-elastic than supply. A small per-unit tax is collected from renters. With other market conditions unchanged, which conclusion is best supported?
options: Sellers are more likely to bear more of the tax burden.
Buyers are more likely to bear more of the tax burden.
Buyers and sellers are likely to share the tax burden equally.
Sellers are likely to bear the entire tax because they receive payment.
q.commonError: Assigning economic tax burden by statutory collection rather than relative elasticity.
q.feedback: Supply is less elastic than demand, so sellers are less able to adjust quantity and bear the larger share through lower net receipts. Collecting the tax from renters does not make renters bear the larger share. Relative inelasticity does not imply that sellers bear the entire tax.

key: Sellers are more likely to bear more of the tax burden.

q.q: Before tax, price is $20. After tax, buyers pay $24 and sellers receive $18. Which statement correctly splits the burden?
options: Buyers bear $4 and sellers bear $2
Buyers bear $2 and sellers bear $4
Buyers bear $6 and sellers bear $0
Buyers bear $24 and sellers bear $18
q.feedback: Buyers pay $4 more than before, while sellers receive $2 less than before.

key: Buyers bear $4 and sellers bear $2

q.q: A $6 tax is legally remitted by buyers. Before it, 120 repairs sold for $25 each; afterward, 100 repairs sell, buyers pay $29 in total and firms keep $23. A firm says buyer remittance leaves its sales receipts unaffected. What refutes the claim?
options: Net sales receipts fall by $700, although the seller burden is only $2 per remaining repair
Net sales receipts fall by $600, equal to the full government receipt
Net sales receipts rise by $400, because buyers pay $4 more per repair
Net sales receipts remain $3,000, because firms do not remit the tax
q.feedback: Firms initially receive 120 × $25 = $3,000, then 100 × $23 = $2,300: a $700 decline. Only $200 is the $2 price burden on continuing repairs; $500 reflects lost sales at the old price. Sales receipts are not profit or producer surplus. Legal remittance does not shield firms from price and quantity changes.

key: Net sales receipts fall by $700, although the seller burden is only $2 per remaining repair

q.q: Supply is perfectly inelastic at 200 units and demand slopes downward. A $6 tax is imposed in a competitive market with no externalities or collection costs. Which combination follows?
options: Sellers bear $6 per unit, revenue is $1,200, and deadweight loss is zero
Buyers bear $6 per unit, revenue is $1,200, and deadweight loss is zero
Sellers bear $6 per unit, revenue is $1,200, and deadweight loss is $1,200
Buyers and sellers each bear $3, revenue is $600, and quantity falls
q.feedback: The vertical supply curve holds quantity at 200. Buyers pay the same demand price at that quantity, so sellers absorb the full $6 wedge through lower net receipts. Revenue is $1,200. With no trades lost and no other distortions in the stated model, tax revenue is a transfer and there is no deadweight loss.

key: Sellers bear $6 per unit, revenue is $1,200, and deadweight loss is zero

q.q: A tax is imposed on a market where demand is perfectly inelastic. Who bears the tax burden?
options: Buyers bear the burden because quantity demanded does not respond
Sellers bear the burden because they collect the money
The government bears the burden
No one bears the burden because quantity does not change
q.feedback: If buyers do not change quantity demanded at all, buyers bear the tax burden.

key: Buyers bear the burden because quantity demanded does not respond

q.q: A tax causes buyers to pay more, sellers to receive less, and quantity to fall. Which statement is false?
options: The side legally assigned the tax must bear the entire burden
The tax creates a wedge between buyer and seller prices
The market quantity falls after the tax
Buyers and sellers can both be worse off per unit traded
q.feedback: The legal assignment does not determine the entire burden. Market elasticities matter.

key: The side legally assigned the tax must bear the entire burden

q.q: In a competitive market, demand elasticity is Ed=-0.25 and supply elasticity Es=1.20 near equilibrium. A small unit tax is introduced. Later, buyers gain substitutes and Ed becomes -1.50 while Es stays 1.20. Which comparison is best, holding the initial price, quantity and tax size comparable?
options: Buyers initially bear more; afterward sellers bear more, and the stronger demand response makes the tax-induced quantity reduction larger.
Sellers initially bear more; afterward buyers bear more, and stronger demand response makes the quantity reduction smaller.
Buyers bear more in both cases because the negative sign makes demand less elastic than every positive supply elasticity.
Burden shares reverse only if the law changes the tax remitter; elasticity changes affect quantity but not economic incidence.
q.feedback: Compare absolute elasticities. Initially 0.25<1.20, so buyers are less responsive and bear more. Later 1.50>1.20, so sellers are relatively less responsive. Greater demand responsiveness also increases the quantity response to a comparable small tax.

key: Buyers initially bear more; afterward sellers bear more, and the stronger demand response makes the tax-induced quantity reduction larger.

q.q: Demand elasticity is -1.80 and supply elasticity is 0.20 in a market. A small tax is imposed on sellers. Over time, sellers gain alternative uses for their resources and supply elasticity rises to 2.40, with demand elasticity unchanged. Compare equal small taxes from the same initial price and quantity. Which evaluation is correct?
options: Buyers initially bear more, but sellers bear more later; the legal seller tax becomes binding only in the long run.
Sellers initially bear more, but buyers bear more later; greater supply responsiveness also increases the quantity response to the tax.
Sellers bear more in both periods because the statute requires them to remit the tax, regardless of alternatives.
Burden becomes exactly equal later because both elasticity magnitudes exceed one, making relative sizes irrelevant.
q.feedback: Initially supply magnitude 0.20 is below demand magnitude 1.80, so sellers bear more. Later supply magnitude 2.40 exceeds demand, so buyers bear more. More responsive supply permits a greater quantity adjustment under a comparable small tax.

key: Sellers initially bear more, but buyers bear more later; greater supply responsiveness also increases the quantity response to the tax.

q.q: Before a tax, market price is $40. After a $12 unit tax, buyers pay $43 and sellers receive $31. A reform puts legal remittance on buyers without changing behavior or the tax size. Which combined inference is supported?
options: Buyers bear 75% and sellers 25%; demand is relatively less elastic, and remittance alone reverses the $43/$31 price pair.
Buyers bear 25% and sellers 75%; supply is relatively less elastic, and remittance alone leaves the $43/$31 price pair unchanged.
Buyers bear 25% and sellers 75%; demand is relatively less elastic, so buyer remittance makes buyers bear the entire $12.
Buyers bear 50% and sellers 50%; the $12 wedge must be split evenly once both sides participate in the market.
q.feedback: Buyer burden is 43-40=3 and seller burden 40-31=9, totaling 12. Shares are 3/12=25% and 9/12=75%. In the standard model the less elastic side bears more, indicating relatively less elastic supply. Legal remittance alone does not alter the wedge equilibrium.

key: Buyers bear 25% and sellers 75%; supply is relatively less elastic, and remittance alone leaves the $43/$31 price pair unchanged.

q.q: A $6 tax causes buyers to pay $4 more than before and sellers to receive $2 less than before. Who bears more of the tax burden?
options: Buyers
Sellers
Both sides bear zero burden
Only the government
q.feedback: Buyers bear $4 of the $6 tax, while sellers bear $2, so buyers bear more.

key: Buyers

q.q: A tax is legally imposed on sellers, but buyers pay most of the burden. What explains this?
options: Legal assignment does not determine economic burden
Sellers always avoid all taxes
Buyers became legally responsible for the tax after prices adjusted.
The market must have a price ceiling
q.feedback: Tax burden depends on market responses, not just who is legally assigned to pay.

key: Legal assignment does not determine economic burden

q.q: If demand is very inelastic and supply is elastic, who likely bears more of a tax?
options: Buyers
Sellers
Both sides bear exactly zero
The side with more firms always bears it
q.feedback: The less elastic side bears more of the tax burden. Here, that is buyers.

key: Buyers

q.q: If supply is very inelastic and demand is elastic, who likely bears more of a tax?
options: Sellers
Buyers
Only the government
No one because demand is elastic
q.feedback: The less elastic side bears more of the burden. Here, that is sellers.

key: Sellers

q.q: Why does the more elastic side of a market tend to bear less of a tax?
options: It can adjust its behavior more easily in response to the tax.
A binding price floor absorbs part of the tax.
Elasticity affects only the legal assignment of the tax.
The more elastic side cannot change quantity when price changes.
q.feedback: The more elastic side can respond more easily, so it bears less of the tax burden.

key: It can adjust its behavior more easily in response to the tax.

q.q: Refer to the tax incidence graph. How much of the tax burden is paid by buyers?
q.feedback: Buyers paid $15 before the tax and pay $18 after the tax, so their burden is $3.

q.q: Refer to the tax incidence graph. How much of the tax burden is paid by sellers?
q.feedback: Sellers received $15 before the tax and receive $12 after the tax, so their burden is $3.

q.q: Refer to the tax incidence graph. Who bears more of the tax burden?
options: Buyers and sellers share the burden equally
Buyers bear all of the burden
Sellers bear all of the burden
No one bears the burden
q.feedback: Buyers pay $3 more and sellers receive $3 less, so the burden is split equally.

key: Buyers and sellers share the burden equally

q.q: A student says, 'If sellers legally pay the tax, buyers avoid the burden.' What is wrong?
options: Elasticities, not legal labels, determine burden
The statement is always correct
Sellers cannot change prices
Taxes do not affect buyers
q.feedback: Legal assignment does not determine who bears the economic burden.

key: Elasticities, not legal labels, determine burden

q.q: The less elastic side of the market usually bears:
options: More of the tax burden
Less of the tax burden
None of the tax burden
Only the portion of the tax named in the statute.
q.feedback: The less elastic side adjusts less, so it bears more of the tax burden.

key: More of the tax burden

q.q: When demand is less elastic than supply, which side is less able to avoid the tax?
options: Buyers
Sellers
Neither side
Only the government
q.feedback: If demand is less elastic, buyers bear more of the tax burden.

key: Buyers

q.q: A tax causes buyers to pay $5 more and sellers to receive $2 less. Which side likely has less elastic behavior?
options: Buyers
Sellers
Neither side
The government
q.feedback: The side bearing more of the tax is usually less elastic. Buyers bear $5, so demand is likely less elastic.

key: Buyers

q.q: Supply is less elastic than demand. Who is expected to bear more of a tax?
options: Sellers
Buyers
Both sides bear zero
Only the legal taxpayer
q.feedback: The less elastic side bears more of the tax. If supply is less elastic, sellers bear more.

key: Sellers

q.q: Refer to the graph. At the post-tax quantity of 60 thousand movies, what price do sellers receive?
options: $10.50 per movie
$13.50 per movie
$7.50 per movie
$6.00 per movie
q.feedback: At quantity 60 thousand, the shifted demand curve intersects supply at $7.50. That is the amount sellers receive before the buyer remits the tax.

key: $7.50 per movie

q.q: Refer to the graph. Under the buyer-remitted $6 tax, buyers pay the seller $7.50 and remit $6 separately. The tax is now collected from sellers, with unchanged curves and compliance. A cinema proposes charging $13.50 plus another $6 to preserve its receipt. Which corrected invoice and burden calculation fits the same competitive equilibrium?
options: Invoice $13.50 plus $6; buyers bear $9 and sellers bear $3 relative to $10.50.
Invoice $7.50 including tax; buyers gain $3 and sellers bear $9 relative to $10.50.
Invoice $10.50 including tax; buyers bear $0 and sellers bear $6 relative to $10.50.
Invoice $13.50 including tax; buyers bear $3 and sellers bear $3 relative to $10.50.
q.feedback: The $6 wedge remains: buyers pay $13.50 in total and sellers retain $7.50 after remittance, at 60 thousand tickets. Seller remittance means the $13.50 invoice includes the tax. Against the untaxed $10.50 price, each side bears $3. Adding another $6 would double-count the tax and would not be the same equilibrium.

key: Invoice $13.50 including tax; buyers bear $3 and sellers bear $3 relative to $10.50.

q.q: Refer to the tax graph. If sellers instead remitted the same tax, with both curves fixed, which bundle would give the total buyer payment, net seller receipt and quantity?
options: $7.50 paid, $13.50 received, and 60,000 units traded
$13.50 paid, $7.50 received, and 60,000 units traded
$13.50 paid, $7.50 received, and 100,000 units traded
$10.50 paid, $4.50 received, and 100,000 units traded
q.feedback: Supply intersects Demand with tax at 60,000 units and $7.50 received by sellers. At that quantity, original demand gives the $13.50 total buyer payment. The $6 difference goes to government. Switching remittance to sellers preserves these total and net prices and quantity.

key: $13.50 paid, $7.50 received, and 60,000 units traded

q.q: Refer to the tax graph. A proposal shifts remittance to sellers while keeping the tax unchanged. Which forecast correctly combines revenue and economic incidence?
options: Revenue stays $600,000; buyers and sellers each bear $3 per unit
Revenue stays $360,000; sellers now bear the entire $6 per unit
Revenue falls to $180,000; only the new legal remitter has a burden
Revenue stays $360,000; buyers and sellers each bear $3 per unit
q.feedback: The wedge is $13.50 − $7.50 = $6 and 60,000 units trade, giving $360,000 in revenue. Relative to the original $10.50 price, buyer and seller burdens are each $3. The same fixed curves and wedge yield the same equilibrium under seller remittance.

key: Revenue stays $360,000; buyers and sellers each bear $3 per unit

q.q: Refer to the graph. What per-unit tax wedge is created by the buyer-side tax?
options: $3 per movie
$7.50 per movie
$21 per movie
$6 per movie
q.feedback: At the post-tax quantity, read the buyer price and seller receipt from the graph and take the difference: $13.50 − $7.50 = $6.

key: $6 per movie

q.q: Refer to the graph. Which side bears more of the buyer-side tax?
options: Neither; the burden is split equally.
Buyers bear more of the tax than sellers.
Sellers bear more of the tax than buyers.
Neither side bears any economic tax burden.
q.feedback: Buyers pay $3 more than the original $10.50 price, while sellers receive $3 less. The legal placement on buyers does not make buyers bear the entire tax.

key: Neither; the burden is split equally.

q.q: Which elasticity inference fits the graph?
options: Supply is less elastic; buyers bear more
Demand is more elastic; buyers bear more
Demand is less elastic; buyers bear more
Elasticity is irrelevant to the burden split
q.imageAlt: The concert-ticket market has price vertically and quantity in thousands horizontally. D0 and S0 intersect at A, quantity 200 and price 10 dollars. Supply with tax intersects demand at quantity 150 and buyer price 16; original supply there gives seller price 8.
q.feedback: Demand is less elastic than supply in the graph, and buyers bear the larger share of the tax burden. Those two observations are consistent with the rule that the less elastic side bears more of a tax.
q.graphDescription: The concert-ticket market has price vertically and quantity in thousands horizontally. D0 and S0 intersect at A, quantity 200 and price 10 dollars. Supply with tax intersects demand at quantity 150 and buyer price 16; original supply there gives seller price 8.

key: Demand is less elastic; buyers bear more

q.q: Refer to the graph. Which side bears more of the $8 tax, and what does that imply about relative elasticity?
options: Buyers bear 6 dollars; demand is less elastic
Sellers bear 2 dollars; supply is more elastic
Buyers bear all 8 dollars; demand is perfectly inelastic
Sellers bear $6; supply is less elastic.
q.imageAlt: The rideshare market has price per trip vertically and quantity in thousands per day horizontally. D0 and steep S0 intersect at A, quantity 200 and price 10 dollars. Supply with tax intersects demand at quantity 150 and buyer price 12; original supply there gives seller price 4.
q.feedback: The seller price falls by $6 while the buyer price rises by $2. Sellers therefore bear more of the tax, consistent with supply being less elastic than demand.
q.graphDescription: The rideshare market has price per trip vertically and quantity in thousands per day horizontally. D0 and steep S0 intersect at A, quantity 200 and price 10 dollars. Supply with tax intersects demand at quantity 150 and buyer price 12; original supply there gives seller price 4.

key: Sellers bear $6; supply is less elastic.

q.q: Refer to the graph. The tax is legally imposed on buyers. Which statement correctly describes who remits the tax, who bears the economic burden, and what the burden split implies about elasticity?
options: Buyers remit the tax, bear all $8, and are more elastic.
Sellers remit the tax, bear $6, and are less elastic.
Sellers bear $2, implying perfectly elastic supply.
Buyers remit the tax, bear $6, and are less elastic.
q.imageAlt: The concert-ticket market has price vertically and quantity in thousands horizontally. D0 and S0 intersect at A, quantity 200 and price 10 dollars. Demand with tax intersects supply at quantity 150 and seller price 8; original demand there gives buyer price 16.
q.feedback: The buyer-side tax is legally assigned to buyers, but prices split burden 6 to buyers and 2 to sellers.
q.graphDescription: The concert-ticket market has price vertically and quantity in thousands horizontally. D0 and S0 intersect at A, quantity 200 and price 10 dollars. Demand with tax intersects supply at quantity 150 and seller price 8; original demand there gives buyer price 16.

key: Buyers remit the tax, bear $6, and are less elastic.

q.q: A tax levied on sellers and an equal tax levied on buyers are generally:
options: Equivalent in their market effects
Completely unrelated
Opposite in their effect on quantity
Always paid only by sellers
q.feedback: A tax on buyers or sellers creates the same wedge and similar market effects.

key: Equivalent in their market effects

q.q: A seller tax and a buyer tax of the same size create the same wedge in the same market. What does this imply about the market outcome?
options: The market outcome is equivalent even if the legal payer differs
The seller tax always hurts sellers more
The buyer tax always hurts buyers more
Only the tax on sellers reduces quantity
q.feedback: Equivalent taxes on buyers or sellers create the same wedge and market outcome.

key: The market outcome is equivalent even if the legal payer differs

q.q: A $4 tax on buyers and a $4 tax on sellers create the same wedge in the same market. What should happen to the market outcome?
options: The outcome should be equivalent
The buyer tax must hurt only buyers
The seller tax must hurt only sellers
Only the seller tax reduces quantity
q.feedback: Equivalent taxes on buyers or sellers create the same wedge and market outcome.

key: The outcome should be equivalent

q.q: Voluntary trade can benefit both sides when:
options: Each expects to gain from the exchange
One side is forced to trade
Prices are zero
All goods are identical
q.feedback: People voluntarily trade because each expects the exchange to make them better off.
q.commonError: Assuming higher combined output makes every possible exchange mutually beneficial.

key: Each expects to gain from the exchange

q.q: Two neighbors specialize in the chores for which each gives up less valuable alternative work, then exchange help. Why can both benefit?
options: Specialization can raise combined output available to share
Exchange makes both neighbors completely self-sufficient.
Scarcity disappears once the chores are divided
The faster neighbor must perform every chore
q.commonError: Treating trade as zero-sum or assigning every task to the fastest producer.
q.feedback: Different opportunity costs can make specialization and voluntary exchange beneficial.

key: Specialization can raise combined output available to share

q.q: A policy improves efficiency but reduces equality. What does this illustrate?
options: A tradeoff
A shortage
A movement along demand
Perfect competition
q.feedback: A tradeoff requires weighing competing goals; improvement in one dimension can come at a cost in another.

key: A tradeoff

q.q: A clinic assigns its limited nurse-hours to the cases expected to produce the greatest total health benefit. Which goal is the clinic emphasizing?
options: Efficiency in the use of its limited clinical resources
Equality through identical treatment time for every patient
Abundance because the clinic can schedule some patients
A shortage caused by setting the price of care too low
q.commonError: Confusing efficient resource use with equal distribution.
q.feedback: Efficiency asks whether scarce resources generate the greatest total value.

key: Efficiency in the use of its limited clinical resources

q.q: A scholarship office divides a fixed fund so every eligible student receives the same award. Which goal is it emphasizing?
options: Equality in how the available scholarship funds are distributed
Efficiency measured only by the total number of degrees completed
Abundance created by dividing the existing fund into equal shares
A shortage created by charging students a below-market tuition
q.commonError: Confusing equal distribution with maximum total value.
q.feedback: Equality concerns how benefits or prosperity are distributed across people.

key: Equality in how the available scholarship funds are distributed

q.q: A student can either study for an exam or work a shift, but not both. What does this illustrate?
options: A tradeoff
A tax wedge
A price ceiling
A surplus
q.feedback: A tradeoff exists because choosing one option means giving up another.

key: A tradeoff

q.q: A policy improves equity but reduces total surplus. Which answer best frames the issue?
options: It presents an efficiency-equity tradeoff requiring both criteria
It proves the policy is desirable because equity necessarily dominates
It proves the policy is undesirable because total surplus necessarily dominates
It removes scarcity because one distributional goal improves
q.feedback: Policies often involve tradeoffs. A reduction in efficiency may or may not be justified by equity goals.

key: It presents an efficiency-equity tradeoff requiring both criteria

q.q: A safety process uses the same technicians as production. Managers fund more materials and predict that both safety checks and output can rise without any other change. Which missing condition matters most?
options: Whether technician time can expand or become more productive
Whether the materials budget is recorded as a public or private expense
Whether both activities produce positive benefits in isolation
Whether managers prefer safety checks to output
q.feedback: More materials do not relax a binding technician constraint. Expanding both activities requires spare technician capacity, added time or a productivity improvement.

key: Whether technician time can expand or become more productive

q.q: One crew can inspect 18 bridges or repair 6 mains per month at a constant tradeoff. A plan requires at least 6 inspections and proposes 5 main repairs. Extra funding cannot add crew time this month. Which revision is feasible, and what does the limit show?
options: Keep 6 inspections and reduce repairs to 4; money alone does not supply the missing crew capacity.
Keep 6 inspections and 5 repairs; separate maximum outputs can be combined without sacrificing either.
Keep 6 inspections and reduce repairs to 2; one repair displaces six bridge inspections.
Cancel every main repair; any minimum inspection requirement uses the crew’s entire monthly capacity.
q.commonError: Ignoring the displaced use of a fixed resource.
q.feedback: Each main repair costs 18/6=3 inspections. Six inspections use one-third of capacity, leaving two-thirds for 4 repairs. The proposed 6/18+5/6=7/6 of a crew-month is infeasible even with enough funding.

key: Keep 6 inspections and reduce repairs to 4; money alone does not supply the missing crew capacity.

q.q: A stricter safety standard is expected to avoid $12 million of accident losses, require $7 million of real compliance resources and reduce variety valued at $3 million as small firms exit. A targeted alternative avoids $10 million, costs $4 million and loses $1 million of variety. Which evaluation follows from these estimates?
options: The alternative has $5 million net benefit versus $2 million for the stricter rule; neither safety benefits nor entry losses alone settle the comparison.
The stricter rule has $12 million net benefit because a safety benefit should not be offset by lost variety or compliance inputs.
The alternative has $9 million net benefit because only the lost variety is a real opportunity cost.
The stricter rule must be rejected regardless of benefits because any reduction in small-firm entry proves inefficiency.
q.commonError: Using a single outcome to judge a multi-dimensional policy.
q.feedback: The stricter standard nets 12-7-3=2 million; the alternative nets 10-4-1=5 million. Entry-related variety and real compliance inputs are relevant costs, but their existence alone is not enough to reject all safety policies.

key: The alternative has $5 million net benefit versus $2 million for the stricter rule; neither safety benefits nor entry losses alone settle the comparison.

q.q: A disaster agency compares feasible stockpiles A: 24,000 meals and 4,000 kits, and B: 12,000 meals and 6,000 kits. Each added kit between these plans has expected relief value equal to 8 meals. A separate proposal C has 24,000 meals and 6,000 kits but exceeds storage capacity. Which decision follows under that valuation?
options: Choose B over A: 2,000 extra kits cost 12,000 meals but are valued at 16,000 meals; C remains infeasible despite its larger gross benefits.
Choose A over B: 2,000 extra kits cost only 2 meals each, making the higher kit allocation wasteful.
Choose C: its larger benefit makes the storage constraint economically irrelevant.
Choose B over A: the extra kits are free because both plans have positive relief benefits.
q.commonError: Ignoring the displaced use of a fixed resource.
q.feedback: The move A→B sacrifices 12000/2000=6 meals per kit. At a value of 8, its net gain is 2000×8-12000=4000 meal-equivalents. Benefits do not make the capacity-violating proposal C feasible.

key: Choose B over A: 2,000 extra kits cost 12,000 meals but are valued at 16,000 meals; C remains infeasible despite its larger gross benefits.

q.q: A policy improves equality but reduces total output. What tradeoff is being shown?
options: Efficiency versus equality
Supply versus quantity supplied
Positive versus normative
Ceiling versus floor
q.feedback: The policy improves distribution but reduces total output, so the tradeoff is efficiency versus equality.

key: Efficiency versus equality
